entries.title: The Baigong "pipes" of Qinghai
entries.mainstream: Pipe-like structures in and around White Mountain (Baigongshan), about 40 km south-west of Delingha in Qinghai, China, found in and near a cave and along the shore of Lake Toson. They became famous through Chinese newspaper reports in June 2002, which described "rusty" iron pipes; a local smeltery analysis reported about 30% iron oxide with much silica and calcium oxide. A 2003 report said Chinese scientists had found organic plant material and tree rings in them, so they were judged to be fossilised trees or roots; the local government promotes them as a tourist attraction.

alternatives.label: Artificial pipes (popular claim)
alternatives.text: Media and alternative writers presented them as ancient or non-human iron plumbing, sometimes linked to an extraterrestrial base; this view relies on the pipe-like shape and iron content.

alternatives.label: Natural formations
alternatives.text: Mainstream explanation: iron-rich concretions formed around fossil tree roots; the oxide analysis is consistent with natural minerals such as calcite and iron oxides.

entries.title: The Library of Alexandria: burned once, or faded away?
entries.dateNote: Founded early 3rd century BCE; gradual decline to the 3rd–4th centuries CE
entries.mainstream: Part of the Mouseion research institution in Alexandria, Egypt, probably built under Ptolemy II Philadelphus after plans attributed to Demetrius of Phalerum and Ptolemy I. The Ptolemies aggressively acquired papyrus scrolls (estimates range from 40,000 to 700,000), and scholars there included Callimachus (whose Pinakes is sometimes called the first library catalogue), Eratosthenes (who estimated Earth's circumference) and Hero (who described a steam engine). Its decline was gradual: a purge of intellectuals in 145 BCE under Ptolemy VIII, a fire during Julius Caesar's siege in 48 BCE (extent unclear; Strabo still visited the Mouseion c. 20 BCE), dwindling Roman support, and Aurelian's destruction of its quarter around 272 CE. The daughter library in the Serapeum was demolished in 391 CE under Bishop Theophilus.

alternatives.label: Single catastrophic burning (popular view)
alternatives.text: Popular culture often imagines one great fire destroying all ancient knowledge, blamed on Caesar, Christians or the Arab conquest.

alternatives.label: Arab-conquest story (disputed)
alternatives.text: Later Arabic sources, the earliest being al-Qifti centuries afterwards, say Caliph Omar ordered the books burned after the conquest of 642 CE; since Eusèbe Renaudot (1713) most scholars have been sceptical because of the time gap and the authors' political motives.

alternatives.label: Lost-knowledge speculation
alternatives.text: Some alternative writers suggest the library held records of lost civilisations or advanced science; there is no inventory to test this, and much classical literature survived through copies elsewhere.

media.title: What really happened to the Library of Alexandria? - Elizabeth Cox

entries.title: Wagadu and the serpent Bida
entries.dateNote: Wagadu rose c. 3rd century CE; fell c. 1203
entries.mainstream: The Ghana Empire (Wagadu in Soninke), in what is now south-eastern Mauritania and western Mali, was described by Arab writers from the 9th century onward and fell to the Sosso around 1203. Soninke oral traditions say the ancestor Dinga came "from the east" and had to kill a serpent deity, Bida, or make a pact with it: one maiden sacrificed each year in return for rainfall (and in some versions a constant supply of gold). Wagadu fell when a noble killed Bida to save a maiden (against her wish), unleashing a curse of seven years of drought and famine; some versions add that the gold moved to Bure. Archaeology at Dhar Tichitt shows complex ancestral Soninke settlements by about 1600 BCE.

alternatives.label: Memory of real change (interpretation)
alternatives.text: Pythons are associated with water and the seasonal rains, and snake deities are prominent in West African religions; one reading is that the drought and the moving gold echo real Sahelian drying and the shift of gold production from Bambuk to Bure.

alternatives.label: Foreign-origin theories (rejected)
alternatives.text: Some 16th–17th-century chronicles claimed Ghana's rulers were "white" Berbers; modern scholars generally reject this, and earlier Arab accounts describe Ghana's rulers as Black.

alternatives.label: Myth as charter
alternatives.text: The serpent pact can be read as a charter legitimising the ruling clans and the sacred bond between king, rain and land, a pattern found in other sacred-kingship traditions.

entries.title: Gedi: the abandoned Swahili town in the forest
entries.mainstream: A walled medieval Swahili stone town in the Arabuko-Sokoke Forest near the coast of Kenya, occupied from as early as the 11th century and abandoned by the mid-17th century (UNESCO World Heritage: the Historic Town and Archaeological Site of Gedi). It has mosques, a palace, stone houses, grid streets, storm-water sumps and lavatories; finds include Chinese porcelain and coins, Islamic glazed wares, Venetian beads and cowries. Its prosperity peaked in the 15th–16th centuries. Excavated by James Kirkman from 1948. Local Giriama (Mijikenda) people regard it as sacred and say it is guarded by the spirits of its priests, the "Old Ones", who curse anyone who harms it.

alternatives.label: Why abandoned?
alternatives.text: Explanations include Portuguese attempts to monopolise trade and armed intervention, a falling water table (the well by the Great Mosque was deepened), a Wazimba raid along the coast in 1589, and Oromo migrations and raids.

alternatives.label: Spirit-guarded ruin (local tradition)
alternatives.text: For many Giriama the site is still inhabited by ancestral and evil spirits; respecting it is a religious obligation rather than a mystery to be solved.

sources.title: UNESCO: The Historic Town and Archaeological Site of Gedi

media.title: Kenya’s ancient Gedi city holds secrets of lost civilisations and efforts to save it from decay

entries.title: Inkanyamba, the storm serpent of Howick Falls
entries.mainstream: In Zulu and Xhosa lore of South Africa, the inkanyamba (Xhosa: "snake cloud" or "snake in the sky", i.e. tornado) is a huge serpent whose coils reach from heaven to earth, the cause of tornadoes and a storm, water and hail power. It is said to live in rivers and pools of KwaZulu-Natal, above all the pool below Howick Falls on the Umgeni River ("Howie"), and around Hogsback in the Eastern Cape. Its anger brings summer storms; appeasing it brings rain and fertility. Shiny corrugated-iron roofs are said to attract it, mistaking them for water. A game ranger reported a horse-headed serpent on the Umgeni in 1962, with further local sightings in 1974, 1981 and 1995.

alternatives.label: Living creature (cryptozoology)
alternatives.text: Some treat the sightings as an unknown large eel or serpent.

alternatives.label: Misidentification or hoax
alternatives.text: Commentators suggest Nile crocodiles, large eels or hoaxes to promote tourism.

alternatives.label: Weather spirit
alternatives.text: In traditional belief it is better understood as the spirit of the storm itself, comparable to other African and Australian rain serpents.

entries.title: Lake Nyos: the lake that exploded
entries.mainstream: On the night of 21 August 1986 Lake Nyos, a crater lake in north-western Cameroon, released some 100,000–300,000 tons of carbon dioxide in a limnic eruption. The heavier-than-air cloud flowed down the valleys and suffocated 1,746 people and 3,500 livestock up to about 25 km away. Two years earlier a similar event had occurred at Lake Monoun; these are the only two recorded limnic eruptions in modern history. Degassing pipes were installed from 2001, and by 2019 the lake had reached a near steady state.

alternatives.label: Legends of "bad lakes"
alternatives.text: Anthropologist Eugenia Shanklin documented that stories of misbehaving or exploding lakes had circulated in the Cameroon Grassfields for decades before 1986, collected over 80 years by ethnographers, administrators and missionaries; some read them as memories of earlier gas releases.

alternatives.label: What triggered it?
alternatives.text: Most geologists suspect a landslide; others propose a small volcanic eruption on the lake bed or cold rainwater; some argue no trigger was needed because the CO2 layering is inherently unstable.

alternatives.label: Biblical analogy (speculative)
alternatives.text: The 2006 documentary The Exodus Decoded used Lake Nyos to suggest a natural explanation for some biblical plagues.

sources.title: Exploding lakes in myth and reality: an African case study

media.title: Lake Nyos disaster survivors to return home after 30 years

entries.title: The Black Death
entries.mainstream: A plague pandemic that struck Europe, the Middle East and North Africa in 1346–1353, killing up to 50 million people: around 30–60% of Europe's population and about a third of the Middle East's. It was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, confirmed by ancient-DNA studies of victims (Bos et al. 2011), and in 2022 genomes from 1338–39 graves near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan, whose tombstones name "pestilence", pointed to its source in central Eurasia. It reached Europe via Genoese ships from Kaffa in Crimea in 1347. Europe's population did not recover its 14th-century level until the 16th century.

alternatives.label: Contemporary explanations
alternatives.text: The Paris Medical Faculty blamed a conjunction of planets causing "a great pestilence in the air"; many saw divine punishment, prompting flagellant movements; others blamed Jews, foreigners, lepers and beggars. In the Strasbourg massacre of February 1349 about 2,000 Jews were murdered.

alternatives.label: How it spread (debated)
alternatives.text: The classic model is rat-flea-human; a 2018 model argued spread by human fleas and body lice fits death records better, and archaeologist Barney Sloane argued there is too little evidence of rat die-offs in medieval London.

sources.title: A draft genome of Yersinia pestis from victims of the Black Death
The source of the Black Death in fourteenth-century central Eurasia

entries.title: The Green Children of Woolpit
entries.mainstream: Two children with greenish skin reportedly appeared one summer in the 12th century (possibly under King Stephen, 1135–54) at Woolpit, Suffolk. They spoke an unknown language and would eat only raw broad beans; in time they ate other food and lost their colour, but the boy died. The girl, after learning English, said they came from a land where the sun never shone and the light was like twilight, called St Martin's Land (one version adds that everything there was green). The only near-contemporary accounts are by William of Newburgh (c. 1189) and Ralph of Coggeshall (1220s), who drew on Sir Richard de Calne.

alternatives.label: Lost Flemish children (Harris, 1998)
alternatives.text: Paul Harris proposed they were orphans of persecuted Flemish immigrants from Fornham St Martin, perhaps after the Battle of Fornham (1173), green from malnutrition (chlorosis); John Clark questioned his use of the evidence.

alternatives.label: Otherworld or extraterrestrials
alternatives.text: Others see a folktale of visitors from another world, underground or extraterrestrial; Robert Burton (1621) said they "fell from Heaven", an idea used in Francis Godwin's early science fiction The Man in the Moone (1638).

alternatives.label: Ritual or literature
alternatives.text: Folklorist Martin Walsh reads it as a garbled harvest (Martinmas) ritual; some literary scholars see it as a chronicler's reflection on outsiders and identity; William Camden (1586) thought it a hoax.

entries.title: The dancing plague of 1518
entries.mainstream: From July to September 1518 between about 50 and 400 people in Strasbourg danced uncontrollably for days or weeks. It began on 14 July when a woman, Frau Troffea, started dancing in the street; within days more than thirty joined her. Physician notes, cathedral sermons, chronicles and city-council records agree that people danced; they do not say why. Dancers collapsed from exhaustion and some may have died, though the number of deaths is disputed and some claims (up to 15 a day) come from later accounts. The outbreak subsided in early September.

alternatives.label: Stress-induced mass psychogenic illness (Waller)
alternatives.text: Historian John Waller argues that famine, disease and fear of supernatural punishment (such as St Vitus's curse) put people into an altered state in which dancing spread; it is the most popular explanation.

alternatives.label: Ergot poisoning
alternatives.text: Some propose ergotism from fungus-infected rye; Waller replies that ergot victims could hardly dance for days and would not all react the same way.

alternatives.label: Divine punishment (contemporary view)
alternatives.text: Many in Strasbourg feared a punishment from Saint Vitus, believed to compel sinners to dance. Physicians prescribed dancing it out, with guild halls and musicians reportedly provided; when that backfired the council banned public dancing and music and sent dancers to the shrine of St Vitus with red shoes, crosses and holy water. Earlier dancing manias (St Vitus's and St John's dances) occurred in medieval central Europe.

sources.title: A forgotten plague: making sense of dancing mania

media.title: A Dancing Disease KILLED People: The Dancing Plague Of 1518 | Earth Science

entries.title: The Salem witch trials
entries.mainstream: Between February 1692 and May 1693 more than 200 people in colonial Massachusetts were accused of witchcraft, starting in Salem Village (now Danvers) when girls including Betty Parris and Abigail Williams showed fits. Thirty were found guilty and nineteen hanged; Giles Corey died under torture for refusing to plead, and at least five died in jail. Much evidence was "spectral evidence" – testimony that the accused's apparition tormented the afflicted. The trials ended when leading clergy doubted that evidence. Several accusers later admitted fabricating charges; the convictions were annulled in 1711, more victims were exonerated in 1957 and 2001, and the last, Elizabeth Johnson Jr., in 2022.

alternatives.label: Mass hysteria and social conflict
alternatives.text: Historians link the panic to stress from frontier wars with Native Americans, village factional feuds (e.g. the Putnam family), and jealousy, spite and need for attention.

alternatives.label: Ergot poisoning
alternatives.text: Linnda Caporael (1976) proposed convulsive ergotism from infected rye bread; critics argue the symptoms and pattern do not fit well.

alternatives.label: Other medical theories
alternatives.text: Researchers have also suggested bird-borne encephalitis lethargica and sleep paralysis for the night-time "attacks".

alternatives.label: Real witchcraft (contemporary view)
alternatives.text: Most people at the time, including the judges, believed the Devil was really at work; some ministers such as Increase Mather urged caution about spectral evidence.

sources.title: Ergotism: The Satan Loosed in Salem?

media.title: What really happened during the Salem Witch Trials - Brian A. Pavlac

entries.title: Oisín in Tír na nÓg: three years that were three hundred
entries.dateNote: Fenian Cycle setting c. 3rd century CE; surviving texts medieval
entries.mainstream: In Irish myth (the Fenian Cycle), Oisín, poet son of Fionn mac Cumhaill, is taken by the fairy woman Niamh of the Golden Hair to Tír na nÓg, "the land of the young". After what seems three years he wants to see his comrades, the Fianna. Niamh lends him her white horse and warns him not to touch the ground. In Ireland he finds that 300 years have passed; leaning to help men move a stone, he falls from the horse and instantly becomes a withered old man. In some versions he tells the stories of the Fianna to Saint Patrick before he dies.

alternatives.label: Christian frame
alternatives.text: The meeting with Saint Patrick (as in the Acallam na Senórach) sets the old heroes against the new faith; versions differ on whether Oisín defends druidism or converts.

alternatives.label: Cross-cultural motif
alternatives.text: It closely parallels Urashima Tarō (Japan) and King Kakudmi (India): time runs differently in the otherworld and the return home is catastrophic; folklorists class such tales together (ATU 681 and related).

alternatives.label: Modern readings (speculative)
alternatives.text: Some modern writers liken such stories to time dilation or to "missing time" in UFO narratives.

entries.title: The Mary Celeste: the ship found empty
entries.mainstream: On 4 December 1872 the Canadian brigantine Dei Gratia found the American-registered Mary Celeste adrift and deserted between the Azores and Portugal, seaworthy, under partial sail, with her lifeboat missing. She had left New York for Genoa on 7 November with Captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife and infant daughter and seven crew, and a cargo of 1,701 barrels of alcohol. The last log entry (25 November) put her off Santa Maria in the Azores. Cargo, provisions and personal belongings were intact; no one aboard was ever seen again. The Gibraltar salvage hearings considered mutiny, piracy and insurance fraud but found no convincing evidence.

alternatives.label: Abandoned in fear
alternatives.text: A widely discussed explanation is that the crew took to the lifeboat as a temporary precaution (e.g. fearing the alcohol cargo or a leak) and lost the ship; Briggs's cousin Oliver Cobb suggested such a temporary transfer.

alternatives.label: Other natural hypotheses
alternatives.text: Alcohol fumes from the cargo, a seaquake, waterspouts, or attack by a giant squid.

alternatives.label: Paranormal and fiction
alternatives.text: Arthur Conan Doyle's 1884 story "J. Habakuk Jephson's Statement" added false details (and the "Marie Celeste" spelling); paranormal explanations followed. In 1885 a later captain deliberately wrecked her off Haiti in an insurance fraud.

media.author: Unconfirmed, possibly Honore Pellegrin (1800–c.1870). This speculative attribution is suggested in Paul Begg: Mary Celes
media.title: Mary_Celeste_as_Amazon_in_1861_(cropped).jpg
The True Story of the Mary Celeste

entries.title: Hawaiki, the Polynesian homeland and land of the dead
entries.dateNote: Undated ancestral tradition; Māori arrival in Aotearoa c. late 13th century
entries.mainstream: In Polynesian tradition Hawaiki (ʻAvaiki in the Cook Islands, Savaiʻi in Samoa, Havaiʻi in Tahiti, Hawaiʻi in Hawaiʻi) is the original homeland from which ancestors sailed across the Pacific in open canoes; Māori trace their ancestry to groups arriving in Aotearoa in about 40 named waka. It is also the underworld to which spirits return after death – in New Zealand via Cape Reinga (Te Rerenga Wairua) at the northern tip. Linguists reconstruct the word as Proto-Nuclear Polynesian *sawaiki. Anne Salmond states that Havaiʻi is the old name of Raiatea; when Cook reached New Zealand in 1769, the Raiatean navigator Tupaia discussed Hawaiki and Rangiatea with Māori priests.

alternatives.label: A real island (Raiatea and the Society Islands)
alternatives.text: Many scholars identify the Māori Hawaiki with Raiatea (Havaiʻi) in the Society Islands; DNA, linguistic, botanical and archaeological evidence trace Polynesians ultimately to island East Asia, possibly Taiwan.

alternatives.label: Ancestors rather than a place
alternatives.text: Because cognates mean "spirits" (Samoan saualiʻi) and "chiefs" (Tongan houʻeiki), some scholars think Hawaiki originally meant chiefly ancestors and the social order rather than one location.

alternatives.label: Accidental drift vs deliberate voyaging
alternatives.text: Until the early 21st century many anthropologists thought settlement happened by accidental drift; revived double-hulled canoes sailing with traditional navigation (Polynesian Voyaging Society) have shown deliberate voyages were feasible. Thor Heyerdahl's 1947 Kon-Tiki raft argued for settlement from South America, which genetic evidence does not support, although sweet potatoes show some contact with the Americas.

media.title: How did Polynesian wayfinders navigate the Pacific Ocean? - Alan Tamayose and Shantell De Silva

entries.title: The Min Min lights of outback Australia
entries.dateNote: Aboriginal traditions predate colonisation; Min Min Hotel sighting 1918
entries.mainstream: Fuzzy, disc-shaped lights reported hovering just above the horizon in outback Australia, mostly in the Channel Country of western Queensland (Boulia), but also from Brewarrina in New South Wales to the Pilbara (reported by the Ngarluma people). Stories about them exist in several Aboriginal cultures from before colonisation; a stockman's sighting at the Min Min Hotel in 1918 is often cited, and a possible 1838 account may describe something else. In folklore the lights follow or approach people, vanish when shot at, keep pace with moving cars, and anyone who chases and catches them never returns.

alternatives.label: Fata Morgana mirage (Pettigrew)
alternatives.text: Scientist Jack Pettigrew proposed that a temperature inversion refracts distant lights from beyond the horizon – campfires in early accounts (stationary lights), car headlights later (moving lights).

alternatives.label: Bioluminescence or geophysics
alternatives.text: Pettigrew also floated glowing insects or owls, and piezoelectric or marsh-gas effects; no such animal has been found, and the lights are seen where the geology does not suit those effects.

alternatives.label: Spirits or unknown phenomenon
alternatives.text: In Aboriginal traditions the lights are bound up with spirits and country; in settler folklore they are an eerie, unknowable presence. Similar "ghost lights" are reported worldwide (Hessdalen, Marfa, the Naga fireballs).

entries.title: The Yowie, Australia's "hairy man"
entries.mainstream: An ape-like, hairy, bipedal creature of Australian folklore, 2.1–3.6 m tall, with origins in Aboriginal oral history, particularly in the eastern states, where it has many names (Quinkin in parts of Queensland; Ghindaring, Jurrawarra, Doolaga and others in New South Wales). Rev. William Ridley recorded "Yō-wī" among the Gamilaraay in 1875 as a spirit that roams at night. Nineteenth-century settlers wrote of the "Yahoo" or "hairy man of the wood"; newspaper reports of "indigenous apes" followed. A AU$200,000 reward offered in the mid-1970s for a captured Yowie was never claimed.

alternatives.label: Relict ape or early human (cryptozoology)
alternatives.text: Self-described cryptozoologist Rex Gilroy, who claims over 3,000 reports since the mid-1970s, argues for a surviving population of extinct apes or early Homo.

alternatives.label: Folklore and misreading
alternatives.text: Historian Graham Joyner (1977) documented 19th-century "yahoo" reports and argues the modern Yowie barely existed before the mid-1970s and grew from conflating those accounts; footprint reports are inconsistent in shape and toe number.

alternatives.label: Aboriginal tradition
alternatives.text: Some Aboriginal accounts describe the hairy beings as an ancient people or as spirits, a meaning distinct from the zoological "ape" framing.

entries.title: The Wendigo: the spirit of hunger
entries.mainstream: In the beliefs of Algonquian-speaking peoples (Ojibwe, Saulteaux, Cree, Naskapi, Innu) the wendigo is a malevolent cannibal spirit linked with the north, winter, cold and famine: gaunt to emaciation, ash-grey, sometimes a giant that grows as it eats, with a heart of ice. It can possess people, giving them insatiable hunger for human flesh; people who broke the cannibalism taboo could become wendigos. The Jesuit Relations described such cases in 1661. In the winter of 1878 Plains Cree trapper Swift Runner killed and ate his family although emergency food supplies were within reach, and was later executed; in 1907 Oji-Cree leader Jack Fiddler, famed for defeating wendigos, was arrested for killing people believed to be turning wendigo.

alternatives.label: Wendigo psychosis (culture-bound syndrome)
alternatives.text: Psychiatrists described "wendigo psychosis", an intense craving for human flesh and fear of becoming a cannibal; in the 1980s researchers debated whether it was a real syndrome or a fabrication of credulous anthropologists, with others citing credible eyewitness accounts.

alternatives.label: Moral and social meaning
alternatives.text: Many First Nations writers treat the wendigo as the embodiment of greed and selfishness; some communities see insatiable greed and environmental destruction as wendigo symptoms. A satirical famine dance (wiindigookaanzhimowin) reinforced the taboo.

alternatives.label: Literary monster
alternatives.text: Algernon Blackwood's 1910 novella The Wendigo popularised the word in English horror fiction.

entries.title: Foo fighters: the lights that chased WWII pilots
entries.mainstream: Allied aircrews in the Second World War reported glowing balls and lights that seemed to follow their aircraft over Europe and the Pacific. RAF crews reported lights following them from as early as March 1942; the name came from the US 415th Night Fighter Squadron in November 1944, after radar operator Donald J. Meiers borrowed "foo" from the Smokey Stover comic strip ("where there's foo, there's fire"). On 13 December 1944 Allied headquarters in Paris described the phenomenon in a press release as a "new German weapon". In the Pacific, crews described a large burning sphere that "just hung in the sky".

alternatives.label: Enemy secret weapon (wartime view)
alternatives.text: Witnesses presumed they were German or Japanese devices; one wartime intelligence assessment suggested some were Me 262 jets or flak rockets while admitting the evidence was "sketchy".

alternatives.label: Natural or optical phenomena
alternatives.text: The 1953 Robertson Panel suggested electrostatic effects like St Elmo's fire, electromagnetic phenomena, or light reflecting from ice crystals; ball lightning has also been proposed.

alternatives.label: Early UAP (ufology)
alternatives.text: Many ufologists see foo fighters as among the first military UAP encounters, a precursor of the 1947 "flying saucer" wave.

entries.title: The Dyatlov Pass incident
entries.mainstream: On the night of 1–2 February 1959 nine experienced ski hikers from the Ural Polytechnical Institute, led by Igor Dyatlov, cut their way out of their tent on the slopes of Kholat Syakhl in the northern Urals and fled, poorly dressed, into temperatures as low as −40 °C. Six died of hypothermia; three had severe trauma (skull and chest injuries without matching external wounds), and some bodies found in a creek in May lacked eyes or a tongue. The Soviet inquest concluded a "compelling natural force" had killed them and sealed the files. Russian prosecutors reopened the case in 2019 and in 2020 concluded that an avalanche most likely forced them out of the tent.

alternatives.label: Slab avalanche
alternatives.text: Gaume and Puzrin (2021) modelled how a small slab avalanche, triggered by cutting the slope for the tent and by wind-blown snow, could cause the injuries; critics note that the site showed no obvious signs of an avalanche, that more than 100 later expeditions reported no avalanche conditions, and that terrain analyses judge the spot unlikely for one.

alternatives.label: Other natural causes
alternatives.text: Katabatic winds, infrasound-induced panic, or ball lightning.

alternatives.label: Human or military causes
alternatives.text: Speculation has included an attack by Mansi reindeer herders (rejected by the original investigation), fugitives, a botched spy meeting, or military rocket or nuclear tests (some radiation was found on one victim's clothing).

alternatives.label: UFO and paranormal theories
alternatives.text: Another hiking group about 50 km south reported strange orange spheres in the sky that night, and similar spheres were reported in the area in February–March 1959 (witnesses came forward years later); these feed UFO theories, though nothing directly links them to the deaths.

sources.title: Mechanisms of slab avalanche release and impact in the Dyatlov Pass incident in 1959

entries.title: The Chelyabinsk meteor
entries.mainstream: On the morning of 15 February 2013 an undetected near-Earth asteroid about 18 m across and about 9,100 tonnes entered the atmosphere over the southern Urals at about 19 km/s and exploded at around 30 km altitude above Chelyabinsk Oblast. The flash was briefly brighter than the Sun and some witnesses felt its heat. The airburst released energy equivalent to 400–500 kilotonnes of TNT, about 30 times the Hiroshima bomb, measured by infrasound stations built to detect nuclear tests. The shock wave damaged about 7,200 buildings and injured 1,491 people, mostly from flying glass; no one died. A fragment punched a hole in frozen Lake Chebarkul. It was the largest object to enter the atmosphere since Tunguska in 1908.

alternatives.label: Coincidence with 2012 DA14
alternatives.text: It arrived on the same day as the predicted close pass of asteroid 2012 DA14 but on a different orbit; scientists regard the timing as coincidence.

alternatives.label: Planetary defence
alternatives.text: It showed that objects approaching from the Sun's direction can arrive unseen, spurring calls for better surveys and an international warning network.

alternatives.label: Ancient parallels (interpretation)
alternatives.text: Its video record of a fireball, blast and falling stones is sometimes compared with ancient accounts of fire from the sky and with the disputed Younger Dryas impact hypothesis.

entries.title: Harbin "Dragon Man": a skull hidden in a well, and a face for the Denisovans
entries.dateNote: At least c. 146,000 years old; surfaced 2018, described 2021
entries.mainstream: A nearly complete archaic human skull said to have been found in 1933 by a labourer building a railway bridge over the Songhua River in Harbin, north-east China, during the Japanese occupation. According to the account given to scientists, he hid it in an abandoned well; his family revealed it only in 2018, and it went to the Hebei GEO University. Described in 2021, it is at least about 146,000 years old (late Middle Pleistocene), has a huge braincase (about 1,420 cc), very heavy brow ridges, a broad flat face and large teeth, and was named the type of a new species, Homo longi ("dragon man", after Heilongjiang, "Black Dragon River"). In 2025 two studies led by Fu Qiaomei recovered proteins from the skull and mitochondrial DNA from dental calculus on its teeth, both pointing to the Denisovans – a group previously known almost only from a finger bone, teeth and genomes.

alternatives.label: Denisovan identity
alternatives.text: The 2025 molecular results led many researchers to treat the Harbin skull as the first fairly complete Denisovan cranium, giving a face to a population known from DNA traces in living people, especially in Oceania and East Asia.

alternatives.label: Naming dispute
alternatives.text: Whether the right name is Homo longi, a Denisovan population within another species, or something else is debated; species names for Middle Pleistocene Asian fossils (Dali, Jinniushan, Xiahe) are contested.

alternatives.label: Find story
alternatives.text: The 1933 discovery and well-hiding story comes from family testimony and cannot be independently checked, so the exact find spot is uncertain; geochemical comparison of the skull with Songhua River sediments was used to support it.

entries.changed: 2010: Denisovans identified from a finger bone genome. 2018: Harbin skull handed to scientists. 2021: named Homo longi. 2025: protein and mitochondrial DNA evidence link it to the Denisovans.

sources.title: Late Middle Pleistocene Harbin cranium represents a new Homo species

entries.title: Homo luzonensis: a small human species on an island in the Philippines
entries.dateNote: Fossils c. 134,000 (earlier estimate ≥50,000) years ago; hominins on Luzon by c. 709,000 years ago
entries.mainstream: Teeth, finger and toe bones and part of a thigh bone from Callao Cave on Luzon, the Philippines, were assigned in 2019 to a new species, Homo luzonensis. A first toe bone was reported in 2010 as possibly modern human; further finds showed an odd mix of small, fairly modern-looking molars with curved finger and toe bones resembling Australopithecus. The remains were first dated to at least 50,000–67,000 years ago; a 2023 study gave about 134,000 years. Separately, butchered rhinoceros bones and stone tools from Kalinga, Luzon, show hominins were on the island by about 709,000 years ago – which means some early humans crossed open sea to get there. Locally the species is nicknamed "Ubag", after a mythical caveman.

alternatives.label: Island dwarfing
alternatives.text: Like Homo floresiensis on Flores, H. luzonensis may be a lineage that became small after long isolation on an island; how its ancestors (perhaps Homo erectus or an earlier hominin) crossed the sea is unknown – rafting after storms or tsunamis has been suggested.

alternatives.label: Not a separate species?
alternatives.text: Some researchers argue the few bones are too limited to define a species and could belong to a variable known population; no DNA has been recovered.

alternatives.label: Folklore echoes (speculative)
alternatives.text: Philippine and Indonesian stories of small wild forest people are sometimes linked in popular writing to these island hominins; no evidence connects such stories to populations that died out tens of thousands of years ago.

sources.title: A new species of Homo from the Late Pleistocene of the Philippines

entries.title: Chavín de Huántar: the oracle temple of underground galleries
entries.mainstream: A ceremonial centre at 3,180 m in the Andes of north-central Peru, built and rebuilt from about 1200 BCE and used until about 500–400 BCE by the Chavín culture, whose art style spread widely across Peru. Its stone temples are honeycombed with narrow, dark, stone-lined galleries and ventilation and drainage ducts. At a gallery crossing stands the Lanzón, a 4.5 m carved granite blade showing a fanged deity, probably the centre of an oracle. Carved heads on the outer walls show humans turning into fanged, snot-nosed beings, and a relief of a figure holding a San Pedro cactus (a mescaline source) has been read as evidence of ritual drug use. In 2001 excavations led by John Rick found 20 decorated Strombus-shell trumpets (pututus) inside the galleries. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.

alternatives.label: Engineered experience
alternatives.text: Rick and others argue the temple was designed to disorient and awe visitors – darkness, rushing water in ducts, conch-trumpet sounds and psychoactive substances – helping a priestly elite build authority; acoustic studies (e.g. at Stanford) have tested how sound travelled in the galleries.

alternatives.label: Pilgrimage centre vs capital
alternatives.text: Chavín is now usually seen as a pilgrimage and oracle centre, not the capital of an empire; how its art style spread so far is still debated.

alternatives.label: Fringe readings
alternatives.text: Popular alternative writers have presented the transforming-head sculptures as non-human beings or the galleries as advanced technology; these readings are speculative and contradicted by the archaeological context.

sources.title: The Evolution of Authority and Power at Chavin de Huantar, Peru

entries.title: Kuélap and the Chachapoyas "cloud warriors"
entries.dateNote: Occupied c. 5th century–c. 1570; main building phase c. 900–1100
entries.mainstream: A walled settlement on a ridge about 3,000 m up above the Utcubamba valley in Amazonas, northern Peru, built by the Chachapoyas culture. Occupation began around the 5th–6th century CE, most of its structures date from about 900–1100, and it was abandoned around 1570 after the Spanish conquest. Limestone walls 10–20 m high enclose about six hectares and over 400 mostly round buildings, decorated with zigzag and rhomboid friezes, entered through funnel-like passages only one person wide. The Inca conquered the Chachapoyas in the late 15th century. A judge from Chachapoyas, Juan Crisóstomo Nieto, rediscovered the site in 1843; part of the wall collapsed in April 2022.

alternatives.label: Fortress or town
alternatives.text: Its walls and narrow gates suggest defence, but it was also a densely lived-in town and burial place; the balance is debated.

alternatives.label: "White" Chachapoyas (unsupported)
alternatives.text: Spanish chroniclers described some Chachapoya people as fair-skinned, and some 20th-century writers (e.g. Jacques de Mahieu) proposed Viking or other Old World origins; there is no archaeological or genetic support, and the Chachapoyas are regarded as an indigenous Andean–Amazonian culture.

entries.title: The elongated skulls of Paracas
entries.mainstream: The Paracas culture of Peru's south coast (about 800–100 BCE) is famous for its necropolis textiles and for the skulls Julio Tello excavated from shaft tombs (the Paracas Cavernas) in the late 1920s. Most of these skulls were deliberately reshaped in infancy by binding the head with boards or cloth – artificial cranial deformation, practised in many Andean societies and around the world – producing tall or long heads. Paracas skulls also show some of the earliest trepanation (surgical skull opening) in the Americas, with many patients surviving. Mainstream bioarchaeology treats the long skulls as a cultural practice marking identity, status or group membership.

alternatives.label: Non-human or hybrid origin (speculative)
alternatives.text: From about 2014, promoters including Brien Foerster publicised preliminary DNA tests said to show unusual or unknown lineages and claimed the skulls had larger volume than human skulls; these results were not published in a peer-reviewed journal and are rejected by specialists, who note contamination risks and that binding changes shape, not brain size.

alternatives.label: Cultural explanation
alternatives.text: Physical anthropologists point to the wear patterns of binding, ceramics depicting shaped heads, and identical practices documented ethnographically, all consistent with ordinary humans.

entries.title: Sacsayhuamán: walls that fit "without a knife blade"
entries.mainstream: A massive complex on a hill above Cusco, the Inca capital, whose three tiers of zigzag terrace walls are built of huge polygonal limestone and andesite blocks fitted so tightly that, it is often said, a knife blade cannot be slid between them; the largest blocks are estimated at well over 100 tonnes. Spanish chroniclers recorded Inca oral history that it was begun under Pachacuti in the 15th century and continued under Topa Inca and Huayna Capac, with thousands of labourers. It was the scene of fierce fighting in Manco Inca's siege of Cusco in 1536, after which the Spanish quarried much of it for buildings in the city. In the 1980s architect Jean-Pierre Protzen showed experimentally that such blocks could be shaped and fitted with hammerstones and repeated trial fitting.

alternatives.label: Older builders (speculative)
alternatives.text: Some alternative writers argue the largest walls predate the Inca and were built by a lost civilisation or with lost technology; no dated evidence supports a pre-Inca origin for the megalithic walls, and Inca quarries, ramps and tool marks are documented.

alternatives.label: Stone-softening legends
alternatives.text: Stories of a plant juice that makes rock soft like clay (repeated by Percy Fawcett among others) are folklore; there is no physical or chemical evidence of softened stone at Inca sites.

entries.title: Khipu: Inca knotted cords – accounts, or a lost writing?
entries.dateNote: Wari precursors 1st millennium CE; Inca use c. 1400–1532, continued into colonial period
entries.mainstream: Khipu (quipu) are bundles of cotton or camelid-fibre cords whose knots, colours, positions and plying stored information; precursors go back to the Wari state in the 1st millennium CE, and the Inca empire used them for censuses, tribute and calendars, read by specialists called khipukamayuq. In 1912 Leland Locke showed that many khipu record numbers in a base-10 positional system. Just under 1,400 survive, many destroyed by the Spanish as idolatrous. In 2005 Gary Urton and Carrie Brezine showed hierarchical accounting relationships between khipu from Puruchuco; in 2018 Manny Medrano and Urton matched six colonial-era khipu from the Santa Valley to a Spanish census, linking cord colours and ply to social categories.

alternatives.label: Narrative writing
alternatives.text: Spanish chroniclers said some khipu recorded histories, laws and stories. Sabine Hyland (2017) reported an 18th-century narrative khipu from Collata whose community described it as a letter, with an estimated 95 distinct cord-signs – enough for a logosyllabic system – but this is not yet deciphered.

alternatives.label: Mostly numerical
alternatives.text: Other scholars think most khipu were accounting devices plus memory aids for trained readers, not full writing; no general decipherment of non-numerical khipu exists.

entries.title: Paititi: the last refuge of the Inca
entries.mainstream: Paititi is a legendary lost Inca city or rich land said to lie east of the Andes in the rainforests of south-east Peru, northern Bolivia or north-west Brazil. In Peruvian versions it is the refuge of the culture hero Inkarri, who withdrew to the jungle and will one day return; others tie it to Incas fleeing the Spanish after the fall of Vilcabamba in 1572. Colonial documents from 1570 onward describe expeditions in search of it, and in 2001 a Jesuit report of about 1600 by missionary Andrés López, describing a jungle city rich in gold, was found in Rome (it is third-hand). Modern expeditions – some fatal, like the 1971 Nichols expedition – have found Inca remains, petroglyphs at Pusharo and natural "pyramids" at Paratoari, but no lost city.

alternatives.label: Historical kernel
alternatives.text: Historians including Martti Pärssinen and Ari Siiriäinen link the legend to real Inca expansion into the Amazon lowlands; a Finnish–Bolivian dig at Las Piedras (2001–2003) found some imperial Inca pottery, but its Inca origin is disputed.

alternatives.label: Utopian myth
alternatives.text: Others treat Paititi like El Dorado – a myth of a hidden kingdom that grew with colonial treasure-seeking and with hopes of Inca return.

entries.title: The children of Llullaillaco: Inca sacrifice at 6,700 metres
entries.mainstream: On 16 March 1999 Johan Reinhard, Constanza Ceruti and their team found three Inca children buried near the 6,739 m summit of Llullaillaco volcano on the Argentina–Chile border – one of the highest archaeological sites on Earth. A girl of about 13 (the "Maiden"), and a younger boy and girl died around 1500 in a capacocha ceremony, in which chosen children were taken to sacred mountains and sacrificed. Freezing, dry conditions preserved organs, hair and clothing. Analysis of the Maiden's hair (Wilson et al., PNAS 2013) showed her diet and coca and alcohol consumption rose sharply over her last year, especially in the final weeks, consistent with ritual preparation and sedation. The younger girl's body was later struck by lightning. They are displayed at the Museum of High Altitude Archaeology in Salta.

alternatives.label: Interpretation
alternatives.text: Researchers read the changes as a staged transformation of the children into sacred offerings, linking empire, mountains and state religion; how willing the children or families were is unknowable.

alternatives.label: Ethics
alternatives.text: Indigenous groups and others have criticised displaying the bodies; the museum shows them one at a time under controlled conditions.

entries.title: The Fuente Magna bowl: Sumerian writing at Lake Titicaca?
entries.mainstream: A large stone vessel reportedly found around 1950 by a farmer near Chua on Lake Titicaca, Bolivia, and now in the Museo de Metales Preciosos in La Paz. Its cultural affiliation, date and find context are uncertain. Its inner surface carries a face and engraved marks that some promoters, especially since the 2000s, have claimed are proto-Sumerian or cuneiform writing, implying ancient Mesopotamian contact with South America. Archaeologist Alexander Joffe has suggested the marks are geometric filler or deliberate gibberish, and that the face looks more like Tiwanaku-era work (c. 200–1000 CE).

alternatives.label: Old World contact (speculative)
alternatives.text: Proponents read the marks as a Sumerian text and link the bowl to similar claims about the Pokotia monolith; no specialist in cuneiform has published a confirmed reading, and no other Mesopotamian material is known in the Andes.

alternatives.label: Mainstream view
alternatives.text: Without a secure find context or dating, most archaeologists treat the bowl as an undated local object of uncertain authenticity and the "inscription" as non-linguistic.

entries.title: The Oxus Civilisation (BMAC): a forgotten Bronze Age heartland
entries.mainstream: The Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, or Oxus Civilisation, flourished from about 2300 to 1700 BCE (some say from 2500) in what is now Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, northern Afghanistan and north-eastern Iran. Excavated mostly from the 1970s by Viktor Sarianidi, sites such as Gonur Depe in the Murghab delta had monumental walled compounds, palaces, temples, irrigation, fine metalwork, stamp seals and elaborate burials, and traded with Mesopotamia, Elam and the Indus civilisation. It was largely unknown to the wider world until the late 20th century. Ancient DNA (Narasimhan et al., Science 2019) shows BMAC people descended mainly from Iranian-plateau and Anatolian-related farmers, with little steppe ancestry, while a few individuals show contacts with the Indus world and the steppe.

alternatives.label: Soma/haoma rituals
alternatives.text: Sarianidi argued that vessels at Gonur temples held residues of ephedra, poppy or cannabis used to prepare the sacred drink known as soma in the Rigveda and haoma in the Avesta; other researchers dispute the identifications.

alternatives.label: Indo-Iranian link
alternatives.text: Whether BMAC influenced early Indo-Iranian speakers passing through Central Asia (as words and religious ideas suggest to some linguists) is debated; the 2019 genetic data indicate steppe groups mixed in after its height.

alternatives.label: Wider name
alternatives.text: Recent surveys in north-eastern Iran have led some scholars to propose the broader term "Greater Khorasan Civilisation".

sources.title: The formation of human populations in South and Central Asia

entries.title: Arkaim: a Bronze Age ring-town, and a magnet for Aryan and esoteric myths
entries.mainstream: A fortified circular settlement of the Sintashta culture in the steppe of the southern Urals (Chelyabinsk region, Russia), dated to about 2150–1650 BCE (most activity c. 2100–1800). It was found in 1987 by archaeologists surveying an area due to be flooded for a reservoir; the discovery led to the flooding being cancelled and a nature-and-history reserve created. Concentric rings of walls with houses built against them surround a central square; Sintashta sites also produced some of the earliest known spoked-wheel chariots, and are linked by many scholars to early Indo-Iranian speakers.

alternatives.label: Aryan homeland and "Russian Stonehenge" (speculative)
alternatives.text: Since the early 1990s Arkaim has been promoted by Russian nationalists, neo-pagans and esoteric groups as the homeland of the "Aryans", the birthplace of Zoroaster, an astronomical observatory or a place of special energies; archaeologists including Victor Shnirelman have documented and criticised these claims, which go well beyond the evidence.

alternatives.label: Cosmological town plan
alternatives.text: Some scholars compare the ring plan with ideal cities in the Rigveda and Avesta; this is an interpretation, not proof of a direct link.

sources.title: Passions about Arkaim: Russian Nationalism, the Aryans, and the Politics of Archaeology

entries.title: The Golden Man of Issyk
entries.mainstream: In 1969 Kemal Akishev's team excavated a side chamber of the Issyk kurgan, about 50 km east of Almaty in south-eastern Kazakhstan, part of a cemetery of 45 royal mounds. It held the skeleton of a young Saka (eastern Scythian) individual aged 16–18 with about 4,000 gold ornaments: a tall pointed headdress with gold plaques of horses, snow leopards and birds, gold-covered clothing, an iron sword and dagger and a gold-tipped arrow, plus a silver cup with a short inscription in a still undeciphered script. The burial is dated to about the 4th–3rd century BCE (some say earlier). Reconstructed as the "Golden Man" on a winged snow leopard, the figure became a national symbol of independent Kazakhstan and crowns the Independence Monument in Almaty.

alternatives.label: Prince or princess?
alternatives.text: The skeleton's sex has never been firmly established; some researchers have argued the grave goods, including earrings, suit a woman, which would make the national symbol a "Golden Woman" – a question bound up with steppe traditions of armed women.

alternatives.label: The Issyk inscription
alternatives.text: The 26 or so signs on the silver cup have been variously read as an Iranian (Saka) language in a variant of Kharosthi or as an old Turkic script; no reading is accepted.

entries.title: Amazons: Greek myth and the armed women of the steppe
entries.dateNote: Myths attested from c. 8th–7th century BCE; steppe burials c. 7th century BCE–4th century CE
entries.mainstream: In Greek myth the Amazons were a nation of mounted women warriors and archers who fought Heracles, Achilles and Theseus and lived at the edge of the known world, often placed at Themiscyra on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia. Herodotus (5th century BCE) claimed the Sauromatae of the steppes descended from Amazons and Scythians, and that their women rode, hunted and fought. Archaeology has since found many Scythian and Sarmatian graves of women buried with bows, arrows, spears and horse gear, some with battle wounds: by some counts about 20% of warrior graves on the lower Don and Volga, and up to a quarter of Sarmatian military burials, are female. In 2019 Russian archaeologists reported a Scythian burial near Voronezh with armed women of several generations, one wearing a golden headdress.

alternatives.label: Myth rooted in reality
alternatives.text: Historians such as Adrienne Mayor argue Greek contact with steppe peoples whose women fought on horseback inspired the Amazon stories.

alternatives.label: Literary creation
alternatives.text: Others stress that the Greek Amazons are largely an inverted mirror of Greek gender norms; armed women in graves do not prove all-female societies, which have no archaeological support.

entries.title: Ulugh Beg's observatory: a 40-metre sextant in Samarkand
entries.mainstream: Ulugh Beg (1394–1449), grandson of Timur and ruler of Samarkand, built a three-storey observatory in the 1420s around a giant meridian arc (the Fakhri sextant) about 40 m in radius, cut partly into a trench in the hill. With astronomers including Jamshid al-Kashi and Ali Qushji he produced the Zij-i Sultani (completed c. 1437), with a catalogue of 1,018 stars – the first major independent star catalogue since Ptolemy – and a value for the sidereal year accurate to within about a minute. After Ulugh Beg was killed in 1449 on the orders of his son, the observatory was destroyed and its location forgotten; archaeologist Vasily Vyatkin rediscovered the sextant trench in 1908.

alternatives.label: Accuracy
alternatives.text: Analysis by Verbunt and van Gent (2012) showed most of his star positions were newly measured rather than copied from Ptolemy, and generally more accurate.

alternatives.label: Science and power
alternatives.text: His fate is often told as a clash between science and religious conservatism; historians note dynastic politics and succession struggles were at least as important.

sources.title: The star catalogues of Ptolemaios and Ulugh Beg

entries.title: Tamgaly petroglyphs and the "sun-headed" figures
entries.mainstream: About 5,000 petroglyphs pecked into rock outcrops in a gorge about 170 km north-west of Almaty, Kazakhstan, made from the Bronze Age (mid-2nd millennium BCE) up to the 19th–20th centuries. The most famous Bronze Age carvings show human figures with large round heads ringed by rays and dots, usually read as solar deities, alongside dancers, archers in animal masks, bulls, horses, chariots and birthing women. The site, with nearby altars and burials, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.

alternatives.label: Solar deities
alternatives.text: Archaeologists interpret the sun-heads as gods or shamans connected with sun worship in Bronze Age steppe religion; similar figures appear at other sites in Kazakhstan and Siberia.

alternatives.label: Ancient astronauts (speculative)
alternatives.text: Popular ancient-astronaut writing presents the rayed heads as helmeted visitors from space; there is no evidence for this, and rayed or haloed heads are a widespread way of depicting divine or solar beings.

entries.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
entries.mainstream: From 1946–47, when Bedouin shepherds found jars of scrolls in a cave near Qumran on the north-west shore of the Dead Sea, until 1956, about 15,000 fragments from some 900–1,000 manuscripts were recovered from eleven caves. Written mostly in Hebrew, also Aramaic and Greek, between the 3rd century BCE and the 1st century CE, they include the oldest surviving copies of almost every book of the Hebrew Bible – the Great Isaiah Scroll is about 1,000 years older than the previously oldest known Hebrew manuscripts – plus community rules, hymns, calendars, commentaries and apocalyptic works such as the War Scroll. New science keeps extracting information: DNA from the animal skins (Cell, 2020) helped group fragments, and AI handwriting analysis (PLOS ONE, 2021) suggested the Isaiah Scroll was written by two scribes.

alternatives.label: Who wrote them
alternatives.text: The classic view links them to an Essene-like sect living at Qumran; others (e.g. Norman Golb) argue they were libraries brought from Jerusalem and hidden before the Roman destruction of 70 CE; the debate continues.

alternatives.label: Forgeries
alternatives.text: Since 2002 dozens of "new" fragments sold on the antiquities market appeared; in 2020 investigators concluded that all 16 fragments held by the Museum of the Bible in Washington were modern forgeries.

alternatives.label: Conspiracy claims
alternatives.text: Delays in publication into the 1990s fed claims that the scrolls held secrets damaging to Christianity; once fully published they revealed no such content, though they transformed understanding of Second Temple Judaism.

entries.title: The Copper Scroll: a treasure map from Qumran
entries.mainstream: Found in 1952 in Qumran Cave 3, the Copper Scroll (3Q15) differs from all the other Dead Sea Scrolls: it is engraved on a sheet of copper (about 1% tin) roughly 2.4 m long, and it is not literature but a list of 64 hiding places of gold, silver, vessels and scrolls – "in the ruin that is in the valley of Achor, under the steps...". Too corroded to unroll, it was cut into strips at the Manchester College of Technology in 1955–56. Its Hebrew is closer to that of the Mishnah, and it is dated to around 50–100 CE. The quantities, if read literally, would total many tonnes of precious metal. John Allegro led a search in 1960 and found nothing; no listed cache has ever been identified. It is displayed at the Jordan Museum in Amman.

alternatives.label: Temple treasure
alternatives.text: Many scholars think it records real treasures of the Jerusalem Temple hidden before the Roman destruction of 70 CE.

alternatives.label: Folklore or fiction
alternatives.text: Others see it as legend, an exaggerated inventory or a ritual text; the sheer amounts make a literal reading hard to accept.

alternatives.label: Treasure hunting
alternatives.text: Amateur searchers continue to claim to have decoded its locations; none has produced verified finds.

entries.title: Derinkuyu: an underground city for 20,000 people
entries.dateNote: Possible origins 8th–7th century BCE; main expansion Byzantine era; rediscovered 1963
entries.mainstream: One of over 200 underground settlements carved into the soft volcanic tuff of Cappadocia, central Turkey, Derinkuyu reaches about 85 m deep across many levels, with ventilation shafts, wells, stables, wine and oil presses, chapels and storerooms, and rolling stone doors that could be closed from inside. It is connected to the underground city of Kaymaklı by a tunnel several kilometres long. The first chambers may have been dug by Phrygians around the 8th–7th centuries BCE; Xenophon (c. 400 BCE) described people in Anatolia living in underground houses. It was greatly enlarged in the Byzantine era, especially during Arab–Byzantine wars (c. 780–1180), and used by local Christians as a refuge into the 20th century. Forgotten by outsiders, it was rediscovered in 1963 when a resident knocked through a basement wall during renovations.

alternatives.label: Dating
alternatives.text: Because carved rock is hard to date, the earliest phase is uncertain; Phrygian, Hittite and later origins have all been proposed.

alternatives.label: Ancient catastrophe refuge (speculative)
alternatives.text: Some alternative writers suggest the cities were dug much earlier to shelter people from a catastrophe or ice-age conditions; there is no dated evidence for a prehistoric origin.

sources.title: UNESCO: Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia

media.title: Exploring Turkey’s ancient underground city - BBC News

entries.title: The Ark of the Covenant: lost, hidden or in Aksum?
entries.dateNote: Biblical tradition; absent from records after 587/586 BCE
entries.mainstream: In the Hebrew Bible the Ark of the Covenant was a gold-covered acacia chest made at Mount Sinai to hold the tablets of the law, carried before the Israelites, and later placed in the inner sanctuary of Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem. It disappears from the biblical record; it is not listed among the treasures taken when the Babylonians destroyed the Temple in 587/586 BCE. Jewish traditions say it was taken to Babylon, hidden by King Josiah beneath the Temple, or concealed by Jeremiah in a cave on Mount Nebo. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church holds that it was brought to Ethiopia by Menelik I, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba (as told in the Kebra Nagast), and is kept in a chapel at Aksum guarded by a single monk; every Ethiopian church holds a replica tablet (tabot). The Lemba of southern Africa tell of a sacred drum, the ngoma lungundu, as their ark.

alternatives.label: Historical question
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether the Ark existed and what it was; no archaeological trace has been found, and the Aksum object has never been shown to outsiders.

alternatives.label: Lemba ngoma
alternatives.text: In 2007 historian Tudor Parfitt identified a wooden drum-like object in a Harare museum as the Lemba ngoma lungundu, radiocarbon dated to about 1350 CE; it is a revered object in its own right, not the biblical Ark.

alternatives.label: Fringe theories (speculative)
alternatives.text: Claims that the Ark was an electrical device or was found by amateur explorers (e.g. Ron Wyatt) are unsupported.

media.title: Looking for the Ark of the Covenant - World's Most Dangerous Roads - BBC

entries.title: The Durupınar formation: "Noah's Ark" in the hills of Ararat
entries.mainstream: A boat-shaped limonite formation about 164 m long on Mount Tendürek in eastern Turkey, about 29 km south of the summit of Mount Ararat. It drew attention after Turkish army captain İlhan Durupınar noticed it on aerial survey photographs in 1959; Life magazine published it in 1960. American adventurer Ron Wyatt promoted it as the petrified remains of Noah's Ark from 1977, and salvage expert David Fasold, who first supported the idea, later rejected it. Geologist Lorence Collins and Fasold published a study in 1996 concluding it is a natural structure, a view shared by the young-earth creationist geologist Andrew Snelling and by Turkish geologists. Turkey nonetheless created a visitor centre at the site.

alternatives.label: Ark claim
alternatives.text: Supporters point to its shape, length close to the biblical 300 cubits, claimed regular iron readings and "anchor stones" nearby; these were not confirmed by independent study.

alternatives.label: Natural formation
alternatives.text: Geologists explain the shape as a doubly plunging syncline or mudflow around a rock outcrop; similar shapes occur nearby.

sources.title: Bogus “Noah's Ark” from Turkey Exposed as a Common Geologic Structure

entries.title: Etemenanki: the real Tower of Babel?
entries.mainstream: Etemenanki ("Temple of the foundation of heaven and earth") was the great ziggurat of the god Marduk in Babylon. Its earliest phases are uncertain; it was rebuilt by Nabopolassar and completed by Nebuchadnezzar II in the 6th century BCE, when the Jews were in exile in Babylon. Cuneiform texts give its base as about 91 m square and imply a height of about the same, in seven stages topped by a temple. Herodotus described a tower of eight levels. It was damaged after Persian conquest, and Alexander the Great ordered it cleared for rebuilding, which never happened; little more than the foundation outline survives. A black stone stele in the Schøyen Collection, published by Andrew George in 2011, shows Nebuchadnezzar beside the stepped tower.

alternatives.label: Origin of the Babel story
alternatives.text: Many scholars think Genesis 11 – a tower reaching heaven, halted by God confusing human languages – was inspired by Babylon's ziggurats, probably Etemenanki, encountered during or before the exile.

alternatives.label: Older parallel
alternatives.text: A Sumerian epic, Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta, contains a passage in which the god Enki changes or confuses the speech of humanity, which some see as a precursor of the confusion-of-tongues motif; its interpretation is debated.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta

entries.title: Ban Chiang: the "world's oldest bronze" that wasn't
entries.dateNote: Occupation from c. 1500 BCE (or earlier) to c. 200 CE; first bronze c. 2000 or c. 1000 BCE depending on chronology
entries.mainstream: A prehistoric village and cemetery in Udon Thani province, north-east Thailand. In August 1966 Harvard student Steve Young tripped over a tree root and fell onto the rims of buried painted pots; the distinctive red-on-buff pottery set off widespread looting. Early thermoluminescence dates on unprovenanced sherds (about 4420–3400 BCE) and the 1974–75 University of Pennsylvania–Thai Fine Arts Department excavations led by Chester Gorman and Pisit Charoenwongsa suggested Ban Chiang had the world's earliest bronze casting, overturning the idea that metallurgy spread to Southeast Asia from China. Later radiocarbon work cut those dates sharply. The famous painted pots turned out to be late (about 300 BCE–200 CE). UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992.

alternatives.label: Long chronology
alternatives.text: Joyce White and colleagues place the first bronze at about 2000 BCE, possibly reaching Thailand from the Seima–Turbino metalworking tradition of the steppe by a route bypassing central China.

alternatives.label: Short chronology
alternatives.text: Charles Higham and colleagues, using AMS dates on human and pig bone (2011, 2015), put Neolithic occupation from about the 16th century BCE and the first bronze around 1000 BCE, after bronze working in China; this is now widely accepted, but debate continues.

entries.changed: 1966: discovered. Early 1970s: thermoluminescence suggests 4th millennium BCE bronze. 1974–75: excavations; claims of world's earliest bronze. 2011–2015: AMS bone dates support a bronze start around 1000 BCE; long-chronology advocates contest this.

sources.title: A New Chronology for the Bronze Age of Northeastern Thailand and Its Implications for Southeast Asian Prehistory
The Transmission of Early Bronze Technology to Thailand: New Perspectives

entries.title: Srivijaya: the forgotten empire of the straits
entries.dateNote: Late 7th–11th century; rediscovered by scholarship in 1918
entries.mainstream: A Buddhist kingdom centred on Palembang in south-east Sumatra that dominated the Strait of Malacca and much of western maritime Southeast Asia from the late 7th to the 11th century. The Chinese monk Yijing stayed there in 671 to study Sanskrit and described over a thousand monks; the Kedukan Bukit inscription of 682–683 in Old Malay records the founding expedition of Dapunta Hyang Sri Jayanasa. Srivijaya grew rich on trade between China, India and the Islamic world and was raided by the Chola empire of south India around 1025, after which it declined. It was then almost completely forgotten – even in Palembang – until the French scholar George Cœdès showed in 1918 that Chinese records of "Sanfoqi" and Old Malay inscriptions referred to the same empire.

alternatives.label: Thalassocracy or land power
alternatives.text: It is traditionally called a maritime empire; recent research argues its power rested more on land and alliances, with fleets mainly in support.

alternatives.label: Where was the capital?
alternatives.text: Palembang is the leading candidate, but Jambi and other sites have been proposed; few urban remains survive, perhaps because much of the population lived in houses on rafts and stilts along the Musi river, as a 13th-century Chinese account describes.

entries.changed: Before 1918: unknown as a single empire. 1918: Cœdès identifies Srivijaya. 1920s: news reaches Indonesians, and Srivijaya becomes a symbol of national history.

entries.title: Orang pendek: the "short person" of Sumatra's forests
entries.dateNote: Reports since at least the early 20th century
entries.mainstream: In Indonesian folklore the orang pendek ("short person") is a creature said to live in the remote mountain forests of Sumatra, especially around Mount Kerinci. Witnesses – local villagers, Dutch colonists from the early 20th century and later Western researchers – describe a ground-dwelling, upright-walking ape-like being about 80–150 cm tall, covered in short fur. British writer Debbie Martyr and others have searched for it since the 1990s, collecting footprint casts and hair samples; analyses have been inconclusive. Interest grew after the 2004 discovery of the small human species Homo floresiensis on nearby Flores.

alternatives.label: Unknown primate (speculative)
alternatives.text: Supporters suggest an undiscovered ape, perhaps related to orangutans or gibbons, or even a surviving small hominin; no specimen, clear photograph or verified DNA has been produced.

alternatives.label: Misidentification and folklore
alternatives.text: Sceptics suggest sightings of sun bears, orangutans or gibbons, combined with traditions about forest people.

entries.title: The manananggal and Southeast Asia's flying severed spirits
entries.dateNote: Recorded from Spanish colonial period; older oral origins
entries.mainstream: In Philippine (especially Visayan) folklore, the manananggal ("remover") is a woman who at night separates her upper body from her legs, sprouts bat-like wings and flies off to prey on pregnant women, using a long proboscis-like tongue to drink blood or take the unborn child. It was said to explain sudden miscarriages. It can be killed by sprinkling salt, garlic or ash on the abandoned lower half, so it cannot rejoin it before dawn. Spanish colonial writers recorded similar beings in the late 16th century. Strikingly similar creatures appear across Southeast Asia: the penanggalan of Malaysia, the krasue of Thailand and the ap of Cambodia are flying female heads trailing their entrails, also feared by pregnant women and new mothers.

alternatives.label: Explaining tragedy
alternatives.text: Folklorists read these beings as ways of explaining miscarriage, infant death and illness, and of policing women who were outsiders, widows or healers.

alternatives.label: Shared origin
alternatives.text: The near-identical flying-head beings across the region suggest a shared old Austronesian–mainland Southeast Asian belief, spread by contact; the routes are not established.

entries.title: Huakaʻi pō: the Night Marchers of Hawaiʻi
entries.dateNote: Pre-contact tradition; written accounts from the 19th century onward
entries.mainstream: In Hawaiian tradition the huakaʻi pō ("night procession") or ʻoiʻo are processions of ghostly ancient warriors, chiefs and gods who march at night to and from old battlefields, heiau (temples) and sacred places, often on nights sacred to Kāne, Kū, Lono or Kanaloa. They are announced by drums, chanting, conch-shell trumpets, flickering torches and a musty smell, and they walk without touching the ground. Anyone who looks at them may be killed unless they lie face down in respect or a marcher recognises them as a descendant. Accounts continue to be reported today, and some building sites have been rerouted out of respect for marching paths.

alternatives.label: Religious and social meaning
alternatives.text: Scholars see the stories as expressing chiefly sacredness (kapu) – commoners once had to prostrate before high chiefs – and continuing ties between the living, ancestors and land.

alternatives.label: Natural explanations
alternatives.text: Sceptics suggest sounds of wind and surf, fog lights or lava glow, and suggestion; believers regard the experiences as real encounters.

media.title: Night Marchers (with Lopaka Kapanui) | WHAT SCHOOL YOU WENT?

entries.title: Latte stones: the megalithic pillars of the Mariana Islands
entries.mainstream: Latte are two-part stone pillars – a tapering shaft (haligi) topped by a hemispherical capstone (tasa), flat side up – arranged in two parallel rows to raise houses of the ancient Chamorro people of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands. They appear around 900 CE, became widespread, and were abandoned within about two centuries after Magellan arrived in 1521 and Spanish colonisation began. The tallest still standing, at the House of Taga on Tinian, is about 5 m; at the As Nieves quarry on Rota, unfinished shafts would have stood about 8 m, with a shaft of 34 tonnes and a cap of 22 tonnes. Burials were often placed between the pillars. In Chamorro belief the taotaomoʻna (ancestral spirits) dwell at latte sites, and people traditionally ask permission before entering the jungle.

alternatives.label: Why the caps?
alternatives.text: Archaeologists debate whether the capstones kept rats out of raised storehouses, simply supported floors, or primarily signalled rank and lineage.

alternatives.label: Giant builders (folklore)
alternatives.text: Chamorro legend tells of the strongman chief Taga raising the pillars on Tinian; mainstream archaeology attributes them to organised community labour with stone tools and levers.

media.title: The Lost Latte: Bringing a CHamoru Treasure Home

entries.title: Rai stones of Yap: money that never moves
entries.dateNote: Begun c. 15th–16th century by tradition; stopped early 20th century
entries.mainstream: Rai are large disc-shaped stones with central holes, carved from crystalline limestone quarried on Palau about 400 km away and brought by canoe and raft to the Yap islands in Micronesia, where around 6,000 survive; the largest, on Rumung, is 3.6 m across and about 4 tonnes. Oral tradition says the practice began some 500–600 years ago when the navigator Anagumang was guided by a god to Palau's shining stone. Rai were exchanged in marriages, alliances and compensations; big stones were rarely moved, and ownership changed by public agreement, recorded in oral history. A stone lost at sea in transit could still be owned and exchanged. From the 1870s the Irish-American trader David O'Keefe used his ship and iron tools to bring larger stones in return for copra, which flooded the system; these newer stones were valued less than older ones whose histories (including lives lost in transport) were known.

alternatives.label: Money as shared belief
alternatives.text: Economists from Milton Friedman onward use rai to show that money's value can rest entirely on shared records and trust; some note parallels with ledgers and cryptocurrencies.

alternatives.label: Not just money
alternatives.text: Anthropologists caution that rai were prestige valuables embedded in social relations, not everyday currency.

entries.title: John Frum: the cargo cult of Tanna
entries.dateNote: Late 1930s onward; John Frum Day 15 February
entries.mainstream: John Frum is a figure in a religious and political movement on Tanna island in Vanuatu (then the New Hebrides) which arose in the late 1930s and spread in the early 1940s. Followers rejected missionaries, money and colonial rule and returned to kastom (custom), expecting John Frum – often pictured as an American serviceman – to bring "cargo", wealth and freedom. The arrival of tens of thousands of US troops with vast supplies during the Second World War gave the movement the features of a "cargo cult": drill with bamboo rifles, red crosses and the American flag. It survives as a church and political party; 15 February is celebrated as John Frum Day, though followers have declined to a few hundred. In 1959 David Attenborough interviewed a leader who described John Frum as a tall white man who would "bring plenty cargo".

alternatives.label: Who was John Frum?
alternatives.text: Accounts variously make him a local man called Manehivi using the alias, a spirit seen in kava visions, a manifestation of the god Keraperamun, or the name of a returning saviour ("John from America" is a popular but uncertain etymology).

alternatives.label: Beyond "cargo cult"
alternatives.text: Anthropologists such as Lamont Lindstrom stress that the movement is a sophisticated anti-colonial and custom-revival movement; the "cargo cult" label is often seen as reductive and colonial.

alternatives.label: Ancient-astronaut analogy
alternatives.text: The movement is often cited in ancient-astronaut literature as a model for how ancient people might have worshipped technologically advanced visitors; this is an analogy, not evidence that such visits occurred.

sources.title: Chapter Six. Knowledge of Cargo, Knowledge of Cult: Truth and Power on Tanna, Vanuatu

entries.title: The Somerton Man and the "Tamám Shud" mystery
entries.mainstream: On 1 December 1948 a well-dressed man was found dead on Somerton Park beach, Adelaide, South Australia, with no identification and all labels removed from his clothes. The cause of death was never determined; poison was suspected but not found. Months later a tiny rolled scrap printed "Tamám Shud" ("it is finished", from the last page of Omar Khayyám's Rubáiyát) was found in a hidden trouser pocket; the torn copy of the book turned up with a nurse's phone number and five lines of capital letters resembling a code, never deciphered. Cold War spy theories flourished. His body was exhumed in 2021, and in July 2022 University of Adelaide professor Derek Abbott and genealogist Colleen Fitzpatrick announced, from genetic genealogy on his hair, that he was Carl "Charles" Webb, a Melbourne electrical engineer born in 1905.

alternatives.label: Identification
alternatives.text: The Webb identification is widely reported and supported by family-tree evidence; South Australia Police and Forensic Science SA had not formally confirmed it at the time of the announcement.

alternatives.label: Spy or private tragedy
alternatives.text: Speculation about espionage, a secret code and an undetectable poison persists; the identification suggests a private life story, but how and why he died remains unknown.

alternatives.label: The code
alternatives.text: The letters may be an acrostic or initialism of a prayer or poem rather than a cipher; none of the proposed solutions is generally accepted.

sources.title: Finding Somerton Man: How DNA, AI Facial Reconstruction, and Sheer Grit Cracked a 75-Year-Old Cold Case
