entries.title: The Tower of Jericho: the world's first tower, aligned to the solstice?
entries.mainstream: A solid stone tower about 8.5 m high and 9 m across at its base, with an internal staircase of 22 steps, built at Jericho (Tell es-Sultan) in the Jordan Valley around 8300–8000 BCE by Pre-Pottery Neolithic A villagers – over 5,000 years before the Egyptian pyramids. Kathleen Kenyon excavated it in the 1950s along with a wall and ditch, and called Jericho the oldest walled town in the world. Ancient Jericho/Tell es-Sultan was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

alternatives.label: Defence, flood barrier or ritual
alternatives.text: Kenyon saw the tower and wall as defences; Ofer Bar-Yosef argued the wall protected against floods and debris, and that the tower had a communal or ritual role.

alternatives.label: Solstice shadow
alternatives.text: Ran Barkai and Roy Liran (2008) noted that on the summer solstice the setting sun drops behind Mount Quruntul so that the mountain's shadow falls first on the tower and then over the settlement; they suggest the tower was built to mark this and to create social cohesion – an interpretation others regard as possible but unproven.

alternatives.label: The biblical walls
alternatives.text: Kenyon also found that Jericho had no standing walls when the Israelites would have arrived in the Late Bronze Age, contradicting a literal reading of the fall of Jericho in the Book of Joshua; some excavators (e.g. Bryant Wood) dispute her dating.

media.title: Jericho - The First City on Earth? // Ancient History Documentary

entries.title: The Cave of Swimmers: swimming in the Sahara
entries.mainstream: A rock shelter in Wadi Sura on the Gilf Kebir plateau of south-western Egypt, in one of the driest places on Earth, whose Neolithic paintings show small human figures with bent limbs apparently swimming, as well as giraffes and other animals. The Hungarian explorer László Almásy found it in October 1933 and argued in 1934 that the painters had lived when the Sahara was wet – an idea so new that his editor added footnotes disagreeing. It is now known that during the African Humid Period (about 9000–3500 BCE) the Sahara had lakes, grasslands and hippos, and that people moved in and out of it as rainfall changed. In 2002 a much larger painted shelter nearby, the "Cave of Beasts" (Wadi Sura II), was found, with thousands of figures and strange headless beasts. The site featured in the novel and film The English Patient and has since been damaged by visitors.

alternatives.label: Real swimmers
alternatives.text: The traditional reading sees the paintings as scenes of swimming in nearby lakes, proof of a green Sahara.

alternatives.label: Symbolic swimmers
alternatives.text: Researchers such as András Zboray argue the figures are symbolic, perhaps spirits or the dead floating in a mythical watery realm; Egyptian anthropologist Yasser Al-Laithy compared them to the swimming souls in the Book of Gates in the tomb of Ramesses VI – a speculative link to later Egyptian religion.

entries.changed: 1934: Almásy's wet-Sahara idea treated as eccentric. Late 20th century: palaeoclimate research confirms a Green Sahara. 2006: Kuper and Kröpelin map how human occupation followed Holocene rainfall.

sources.title: Climate-Controlled Holocene Occupation in the Sahara: Motor of Africa's Evolution

entries.title: Bigo bya Mugenyi and the vanished Chwezi demigods
entries.mainstream: Bigo bya Mugenyi in south-western Uganda is a system of ditches and banks more than 10 km long on the south bank of the Katonga River, enclosing a central group of four enclosures and mounds; it has been dated to roughly 1300–1500 CE and called Uganda's largest ancient monument. Banyoro, Batooro and Banyankole oral traditions link it with the Chwezi (Bachwezi), the semi-legendary second dynasty of the Kitara empire – rulers with supernatural powers who, according to some traditions, left or vanished mysteriously after evil omens, some say into lakes. The Chwezi are still venerated as spirits through spirit mediums (the kubandwa cult) across the Great Lakes region, and the Bito dynasty of Bunyoro claims to have succeeded them.

alternatives.label: Historical dynasty
alternatives.text: Some historians treat the Chwezi as a real ruling group of the 14th–15th centuries whose capital may have been Bigo or Ntusi; others see them as a pantheon of spirits later turned into kings in tradition. Peter Schmidt links Chwezi spirit cults to early iron-working communities.

alternatives.label: Defence or cattle and elephants
alternatives.text: Colonial-era writers saw the earthworks as forts; later archaeologists suggest the outer ditches kept elephants from crops or cattle in, and the inner works marked elite power.

alternatives.label: Hamitic myth (discredited)
alternatives.text: Colonial writers claimed the Chwezi were light-skinned foreign invaders who brought civilisation – the racist "Hamitic hypothesis"; historians conclude they were a local Bantu-speaking aristocracy, and local tradition distinguishes them from the Bahima herders.

entries.title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin: 130 children who left in 1284
entries.dateNote: Event dated 26 June 1284; earliest records c. 1300 (window) and c. 1440 (manuscript)
entries.mainstream: The legend tells of a piper in coloured clothes who rid Hamelin, in Lower Saxony, of rats; when the town refused to pay, he returned and led away its children, who vanished into a hill. The rats were a later addition (16th century). The core is older and stranger: a church window installed around 1300 (destroyed 1660) showed the piper and children in white, and the Lüneburg manuscript (c. 1440–50) states that on the feast of Saints John and Paul (26 June) 1284 a well-dressed young man playing a silver pipe led 130 children out of the town to the place of execution, where they vanished. Hamelin dated events from the children's departure, and to this day music and dancing are not allowed in the street the children are said to have taken, the Bungelosenstrasse.

alternatives.label: Emigration
alternatives.text: The favoured historical theory is that young townspeople were recruited by a "locator" to settle lands in eastern Europe; linguist Jürgen Udolph found Hamelin-area family names concentrated in Prignitz, Uckermark and Pomerania.

alternatives.label: Death in disguise
alternatives.text: Others propose disease, a landslide or sinkhole, drowning in the Weser, a dancing mania, a Children's Crusade, or a battle such as Sedemünder (1260), with the piper as a figure of Death.

alternatives.label: Folklore motif
alternatives.text: Stories of a magical musician or otherworldly being leading people into a hill echo widespread European fairy lore; any supernatural reading is unsupported.

entries.title: The Carrington Event: the day the sky caught fire
entries.mainstream: On 1 September 1859 British astronomers Richard Carrington and Richard Hodgson independently saw a brilliant white-light flare on the Sun – the first solar flare ever recorded. About 17.6 hours later a coronal mass ejection struck Earth, causing the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history (1–2 September). Auroras were seen close to the tropics, including in the Caribbean, and were bright enough in places to read by; some people thought dawn had come or cities were burning. Telegraph systems across Europe and North America failed, operators received shocks, paper caught fire from sparks, and some lines carried messages on auroral currents alone with batteries disconnected. A storm of similar size today could badly damage power grids and satellites; a large CME narrowly missed Earth in July 2012.

alternatives.label: Even bigger storms
alternatives.text: Radiocarbon spikes in tree rings found by Fusa Miyake and colleagues (2012, 2013) show sudden cosmic-ray events around 774–775 and 993–994 CE, now usually attributed to extreme solar storms far larger than Carrington; links to a "red crucifix" in the sky recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 774 are suggestive but speculative.

alternatives.label: Size estimates
alternatives.text: Estimates of the 1859 storm's magnitude vary by method; some later storms (e.g. 1921) may have been comparable.

sources.title: The extreme magnetic storm of 1–2 September 1859
A signature of cosmic-ray increase in ad 774–775 from tree rings in Japan

media.title: ScienceCasts: Carrington Class Coronal Mass Ejection Narrowly Misses Earth

entries.title: The Hum: a low drone that only some people hear
entries.mainstream: Since at least the 1970s, residents of places including Bristol (UK), Taos (New Mexico), Largs (Scotland), Auckland and Windsor (Ontario) have reported a persistent, low-frequency hum or drone, often worse at night and indoors, that others nearby cannot hear. A study of the Taos Hum in the early 1990s found about 2% of residents heard it, each at a different frequency between about 32 and 80 Hz. Some hums have been traced to machines: the West Seattle Hum to a vacuum pump offloading ships, the Wellington Hum probably to a ship's diesel generator, and the Windsor Hum to steelworks on Zug Island near Detroit – reports stopped when the U.S. Steel blast furnaces shut in April 2020. Many cases remain unexplained.

alternatives.label: Not one phenomenon
alternatives.text: Audiologists such as David Baguley suggest roughly a third of cases have a physical environmental source and the rest involve heightened attention to background sounds, tinnitus or spontaneous otoacoustic emissions produced by the ear itself.

alternatives.label: Exotic causes (speculative)
alternatives.text: Suggested causes such as secret military VLF/ELF transmitters, gas pipelines or Earth's natural vibrations (microseisms) circulate widely; none has been shown to explain the reports.

media.title: Can You Hear A Hum? | Earth Science

entries.title: The Baltic Sea anomaly: a sunken UFO on the seabed?
entries.mainstream: In June 2011 the Swedish treasure-hunting team Ocean X, led by Peter Lindberg and Dennis Åsberg, released a blurry side-scan sonar image from the floor of the northern Baltic (Gulf of Bothnia), about 90 m down, showing a roughly circular object some 60 m across with a long "runway" trail behind it. Tabloid coverage from 2012 compared it to the Millennium Falcon from Star Wars and speculated about a crashed UFO or Nazi anti-submarine device. Stone samples given to Stockholm University geologist Volker Brüchert were mostly granite, gneiss and sandstone, with a loose basalt piece – consistent with rocks carried by ice-age glaciers. Geologists consider the feature a natural glacial formation, and the "runway" part of a field of similar drumlin-like mounds.

alternatives.label: Unexplained object (speculative)
alternatives.text: The team and supporters said the shapes looked artificial, with right angles and stair-like features, and suggested something unusual; no independent survey has supported this.

alternatives.label: Sonar artefacts
alternatives.text: Side-scan sonar images are easily misread, and the original image was low resolution; experts also stressed they had only seen media images, not raw data.

entries.title: The Late Heavy Bombardment: a storm of impacts 3.9 billion years ago, or an illusion?
entries.mainstream: When rocks brought back by the Apollo missions were dated in the 1970s, many impact-melt samples gave ages clustered around 3.9 billion years. Researchers proposed a "lunar cataclysm": a spike in asteroid and comet impacts on the Moon – and by implication on the early Earth – hundreds of millions of years after the planets formed, often dated about 4.1–3.8 billion years ago. The Nice model of giant-planet migration (2005) offered a mechanism, with Jupiter and Saturn shifting orbits and scattering small bodies inward. The idea matters for the origin of life, because the earliest evidence for life on Earth falls in or close to this window.

alternatives.label: Sampling bias
alternatives.text: Critics argue the Apollo landing sites all sit near the Imbrium basin, so many samples may record a single giant impact and its ejecta rather than a solar-system-wide storm; lunar meteorites, which sample the Moon more randomly, show ages spread out rather than clustered.

alternatives.label: Illusory spike
alternatives.text: A 2016 analysis by Boehnke and Harrison argued that the apparent 3.9-billion-year spike could be produced by how argon-dating results reset and are interpreted, and that impacts may instead have declined gradually.

alternatives.label: Cataclysm survives
alternatives.text: Supporters point to dynamical models and to impact signatures in old crust as evidence that some late surge did occur, though perhaps earlier or smaller than first proposed; the question is open.

entries.changed: 1970s: Apollo sample ages lead to the "lunar cataclysm" idea. 2005: the Nice model offers a cause. 2010s: lunar meteorites and re-analyses of dating cast doubt on a sharp spike.

entries.title: The Ediacaran biota: Earth's first large living things, and the girl nobody believed
entries.mainstream: Soft-bodied organisms – fronds, discs, quilted mats and tube-like forms – left impressions in sea-floor sediments from about 575 to 539 million years ago, before the Cambrian explosion. Reg Sprigg noticed "jellyfishes" in the Ediacara Hills of South Australia in 1946, but they were assumed to be Cambrian. In England's Charnwood Forest a 15-year-old girl, Tina Negus, found a frond fossil in 1956 and was not believed; schoolboy Roger Mason found it again in 1957 and it was named Charnia, proving complex life existed in the Precambrian. In 2018 cholesterol-derived molecules preserved with Dickinsonia fossils from Russia were used to argue that Dickinsonia was an animal.

alternatives.label: Early animals
alternatives.text: Many palaeontologists see at least some Ediacarans (Kimberella, Dickinsonia, Spriggina) as early animals or relatives of later animal groups.

alternatives.label: A failed experiment
alternatives.text: Adolf Seilacher proposed that many quilted forms belonged to a separate, extinct kingdom (Vendobionta) unrelated to later animals – an "evolutionary experiment" that died out; others have suggested lichens, giant protists or fungi for some forms.

alternatives.label: A lost first world
alternatives.text: Because most Ediacaran forms vanish by the Cambrian, they are sometimes described as an earlier biosphere that was largely replaced; whether this was a mass extinction or gradual turnover is debated.

entries.changed: 1946: Ediacara fossils found but thought Cambrian. 1956–57: Charnia proves Precambrian complex life. 2018: biomarkers suggest Dickinsonia was an animal.

sources.title: Ancient steroids establish the Ediacaran fossilDickinsoniaas one of the earliest animals

media.title: How We Identified One of Earth’s Earliest Animals

entries.title: Lascaux: the cave found by a dog, and the "star map" debate
entries.mainstream: On 12 September 1940, 18-year-old Marcel Ravidat found the entrance to a cave near Montignac in the Dordogne, France, at a hole left by an uprooted tree that his dog was investigating. He returned with three friends, Jacques Marsal, Georges Agnel and Simon Coencas, and found more than 600 wall paintings – nearly 6,000 figures in all, including horses, aurochs, stags and bison, plus human figures and abstract signs – and a famous scene in a shaft of a bird-headed man beside a wounded bison. The paintings are usually dated about 17,000–22,000 years ago (early Magdalenian). Breath and lighting from visitors caused lichens and crystals to grow, and the cave was closed to the public in 1963; visitors now see replicas.

alternatives.label: Hunting magic and ritual
alternatives.text: Early interpretations (Abbé Breuil) saw the images as hunting magic; later researchers proposed shamanic trance imagery (David Lewis-Williams and Jean Clottes) or structured mythological symbolism (André Leroi-Gourhan).

alternatives.label: Sky maps (speculative)
alternatives.text: Researchers such as Michael Rappenglück have proposed that dots near the aurochs represent the Pleiades and that other figures map star groups such as the "summer triangle"; most archaeologists consider these readings unproven.

alternatives.label: Signs as proto-writing (debated)
alternatives.text: The repeated abstract signs in Lascaux and other caves have been studied as a possible shared symbol system; no meaning has been agreed.

sources.title: UNESCO: Prehistoric Sites and Decorated Caves of the Vézère Valley

entries.title: The Varna necropolis: the oldest gold treasure in the world
entries.mainstream: In October 1972 excavator operator Raycho Marinov, digging a trench in an industrial zone of Varna on Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, uncovered a Copper Age cemetery. Some 294 graves dated about 4560–4340 BCE contained copper tools, flint blades, pottery and more than 3,000 gold objects. Grave 43 held a man buried with more gold than has been found in the whole rest of the world for that period, together with a sceptre; it was first called a prince's grave and is now also interpreted as a high-status metalworker. Some of the richest graves are cenotaphs with no skeleton, a few with clay masks decorated with gold.

alternatives.label: First elites
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists see Varna as the earliest clear evidence of a social elite marked by gold and symbols of authority, more than a thousand years before the pharaohs.

alternatives.label: A lost first civilisation of Europe
alternatives.text: Bulgarian and international exhibitions (e.g. "The Oldest Gold in the World – The First European Civilization", Japan 1982) presented Varna and related Balkan Copper Age cultures as an early European civilisation that collapsed around 4000 BCE; others think "civilisation" overstates a chiefdom-level society.

alternatives.label: Why it ended
alternatives.text: The end of the Balkan Copper Age cultures has been linked to climate change, social breakdown or the arrival of steppe groups; the causes are debated.

entries.title: Carnac: thousands of standing stones, and soldiers turned to stone
entries.mainstream: Around the village of Carnac in Brittany, France, more than 3,000 prehistoric standing stones (menhirs) are arranged in long parallel rows, together with dolmens, tumuli and single menhirs. They were raised by Neolithic communities, mostly between about 4500 and 3300 BCE. Their purpose is unknown: they may have marked processional routes, territories or ancestral or calendar rituals. A local Christian legend says the stones are pagan soldiers who were pursuing Pope Cornelius when he turned them to stone; another tradition calls one tumulus "Caesar's mound", an observatory used by Julius Caesar in his war with the Veneti in 56 BCE.

alternatives.label: Astronomical alignment (debated)
alternatives.text: Alexander Thom and others proposed in the 1970s that the rows formed a lunar observatory; later researchers found the alignments only loosely astronomical.

alternatives.label: Ancestral and territorial markers
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists favour interpretations as ritual or social monuments linking communities to land and ancestors.

alternatives.label: Earth energies (speculative)
alternatives.text: Popular alternative writers link the rows to telluric currents, ley lines or lost Atlantean knowledge; there is no evidence for these ideas.

entries.title: Newgrange: the winter-solstice tomb and the home of the Irish gods
entries.dateNote: Built c. 3200 BCE; solstice light observed 1967
entries.mainstream: A great passage tomb in the Boyne Valley, Ireland, built about 3200–3100 BCE – older than Stonehenge's stone phase and the Giza pyramids. A "roof-box" above the entrance lets the rising sun shine down the 19 m passage into the central chamber for about 17 minutes around the winter solstice; archaeologist Michael O'Kelly was the first in modern times to observe this, on 21 December 1967. Medieval Irish literature calls the site Brú na Bóinne, the dwelling of the Dagda and his son Aengus, one of the Tuatha Dé Danann, the old gods believed to live inside the mounds (síde). A 2020 genome study found that a man buried in the chamber was the child of a first-degree incestuous union, which the authors interpreted as a sign of a ruling elite like those of some god-kings.

alternatives.label: Solar myth encoded
alternatives.text: Some scholars suggest that the tale in which the Dagda makes "the sun stand still" while Aengus is conceived echoes the solstice light entering the chamber; others see this as a modern reading of medieval texts.

alternatives.label: Reconstruction disputes
alternatives.text: O'Kelly's 1960s–70s rebuilding of the white quartz façade is controversial, and in 2016 one archaeologist claimed the roof-box itself was partly fabricated; most specialists defend the excavation evidence.

alternatives.label: Dynasty of priest-kings
alternatives.text: The incest finding has been read as evidence of a hereditary elite claiming divine status; critics caution that one burial cannot define a whole society.

sources.title: A dynastic elite in monumental Neolithic society
UNESCO: Brú na Bóinne – Archaeological Ensemble of the Bend of the Boyne

entries.title: Skara Brae: the Stone Age village uncovered by a storm
entries.mainstream: In the winter of 1850 a severe storm stripped sand and turf from a mound on the Bay of Skaill in Orkney, Scotland, exposing the walls of stone houses. Excavations later revealed Europe's most complete Neolithic village, occupied from about 3180 to 2500 BCE: eight linked houses with stone beds, hearths, shelved "dressers" and covered drains, joined by roofed passages. A storm in 1924 damaged part of the site again, prompting full excavation. It is part of the Heart of Neolithic Orkney World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Sudden abandonment
alternatives.text: A popular story says the village was abandoned in haste during a great sandstorm, with necklaces and pins left behind; some writers compared it to Pompeii.

alternatives.label: Gradual decline
alternatives.text: Archaeologists such as Anna Ritchie argue the burial in sand was gradual and the village had already been abandoned, perhaps as the climate became colder and wetter; the reason is unknown.

alternatives.label: Threat today
alternatives.text: Rising seas and storms now threaten the site, which could be partly destroyed by one exceptional storm.

media.title: Skara Brae: The 'Dark Secret' Hidden Inside 5,000-Year-Old House | BBC Timestamp

entries.title: Knossos, the Labyrinth and the Minotaur
entries.dateNote: Palace c. 1900–1350 BCE; myth recorded in Greek sources from c. 7th–5th c. BCE
entries.mainstream: Greek myth says King Minos of Crete had the craftsman Daedalus build the Labyrinth to hold the Minotaur, a bull-headed man born to Queen Pasiphae; Athens sent young men and women to be devoured until Theseus killed it with the help of Ariadne's thread. From 1900 Arthur Evans excavated the Bronze Age palace complex of Knossos, a sprawling many-roomed building of the Minoan civilisation (named by Evans after Minos), with frescoes of bull-leaping and many images of double axes (labrys). Evans and others linked the maze-like palace to the Labyrinth. Linear B tablets contain the word da-pu₂-ri-to, apparently a Mycenaean Greek rendering of "labyrinth".

alternatives.label: Memory of a real palace
alternatives.text: Many scholars think the myth preserves Greek memories of Minoan Crete: a confusing palace, bull rituals and a sea power that once dominated the Aegean.

alternatives.label: Word origin
alternatives.text: The derivation of "labyrinth" from labrys ("house of the double axe"), proposed in 1892, is popular but lost ground after Linear B was deciphered; some linguists see it as speculative and suggest other roots.

alternatives.label: Evans's reconstruction
alternatives.text: Evans's concrete reconstructions and his picture of peaceful priest-kings shaped the modern image of the Minoans; later archaeologists argue he projected his own ideas onto the ruins.

media.title: The scientific origins of the Minotaur - Matt Kaplan

entries.title: The Oracle of Delphi: did the Pythia breathe intoxicating gas?
entries.dateNote: Oracle active c. 8th c. BCE – late 4th c. CE
entries.mainstream: For more than a thousand years the Pythia, priestess of Apollo at Delphi, gave prophecies that shaped Greek decisions on wars and colonies. Ancient writers including Plutarch – himself a priest at Delphi around 100 CE – described a pneuma (vapour) rising in the temple and a sweet smell when the god was present. Early 20th-century excavators found no chasm and many scholars dismissed the vapours as myth. In 2001 geologist Jelle Zeilinga de Boer, archaeologist John Hale and colleagues reported two faults crossing beneath the temple and traces of light hydrocarbon gases, including ethylene, in a nearby spring, proposing that gas seeping through the fractured limestone induced a trance.

alternatives.label: Ethylene trance
alternatives.text: Supporters note that ethylene was once used as an anaesthetic and in low doses can produce euphoria and altered speech, resembling ancient descriptions of the Pythia.

alternatives.label: Gas too weak
alternatives.text: Other researchers argued the measured concentrations were far too low, that ethylene is unlikely from this geology, and proposed other gases such as methane or carbon dioxide, or none at all; historian Daryn Lehoux called the ethylene hypothesis "impossible".

alternatives.label: Ritual performance
alternatives.text: Many classicists see the Pythia's state as a ritual or cultural performance, with priests interpreting her words, and do not require any gas.

entries.changed: Ancient: vapours described. Early 1900s: French excavations find no chasm; vapours dismissed. 2001: faults and gas traces revive a geological explanation, which remains contested.

sources.title: New evidence for the geological origins of the ancient Delphic oracle (Greece)

media.title: A day in the life of the oracle of Delphi - Mark Robinson

entries.title: Tollund Man and the bog bodies of northern Europe
entries.mainstream: On 8 May 1950 peat cutters Viggo and Emil Højgaard found a body so well preserved in a bog near Silkeborg, Denmark, that they thought it was a recent murder victim. Tollund Man had died by hanging between about 405 and 380 BCE, in the Pre-Roman Iron Age; a plaited hide noose was still around his neck, and he wore a pointed sheepskin cap and a belt. His last meal was a porridge of barley, flax and wild seeds. Hundreds of bog bodies are known from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Britain and Ireland, many showing violent deaths, preserved by acidic, oxygen-poor peat.

alternatives.label: Sacrifice to gods
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists interpret Tollund Man and similar bodies as human sacrifices or ritual killings, placed deliberately in bogs seen as gateways to the otherworld.

alternatives.label: Executions
alternatives.text: The Roman writer Tacitus (Germania, c. 98 CE) described Germanic peoples drowning traitors and the shameful in marshes; some bog bodies may be punished criminals or outcasts.

alternatives.label: Kings and failed rulers
alternatives.text: Studies of Irish bog bodies such as Old Croghan Man suggest some were kings or candidates killed when crops failed, linked to sacral kingship; this interpretation is debated.

media.title: The mystery of Europe's most famous bog bodies | BBC Global

entries.title: The steppe migration: ancient DNA and the spread of Indo-European languages
entries.mainstream: Linguists have long known that languages from Ireland to India – the Indo-European family – descend from a common ancestor. In 1956 Marija Gimbutas proposed the "Kurgan hypothesis": horse-riding pastoralists from the Pontic–Caspian steppe spread these languages. In 2015 two large ancient-DNA studies (Haak et al.; Allentoft et al.) found that around 3000–2500 BCE people related to the steppe Yamnaya culture contributed a large share of ancestry to Europeans of the Corded Ware culture, a population turnover that the authors linked to the spread of at least some Indo-European languages. Later work traced steppe ancestry into South Asia in the 2nd millennium BCE.

alternatives.label: Steppe homeland
alternatives.text: Many linguists and geneticists now consider the steppe hypothesis best supported, at least for Europe.

alternatives.label: Anatolian farming hypothesis
alternatives.text: Colin Renfrew (1987) proposed Indo-European spread with farming from Anatolia around 7000 BCE; some researchers argue for an ultimate homeland south of the Caucasus, with the steppe as a secondary stage.

alternatives.label: Out of India and other views
alternatives.text: A minority view, influential in some Indian debates, holds that Indo-European languages spread out of India; most geneticists and linguists reject this, but the 2019 Rakhigarhi genome (no steppe ancestry in a Harappan individual) is cited by both sides.

alternatives.label: Genes are not languages
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists caution that DNA tracks people, not languages or cultures, and that "migration" narratives can echo 19th–20th-century nationalist misuse of the Indo-European idea.

entries.changed: 1956: Kurgan hypothesis. 1987: Anatolian hypothesis. 2015: ancient DNA reveals massive steppe-related migration into Europe.

sources.title: Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe

entries.title: The Tuniit: the "giants" who were in the Arctic before the Inuit
entries.dateNote: Dorset culture c. 500 BCE – c. 1300 CE (perhaps later in places)
entries.mainstream: Inuit oral histories across Arctic Canada and Greenland tell of the Tuniit (singular Tuniq), people who lived in the land before the Inuit arrived: in some accounts giants, taller and stronger than the Inuit yet shy and "easily put to flight", who built stone houses and spoke a simple language; some elders describe peaceful contact, others conflict. Archaeologists identify the Tuniit with the Dorset culture, a Palaeo-Inuit people present from about 500 BCE who hunted seals and walrus and made distinctive carvings in ivory and wood. The Thule people, ancestors of today's Inuit, spread east from Alaska from around 1000–1200 CE, and the Dorset disappeared by about 1300–1500 CE. A 2014 ancient-DNA study found the Dorset were genetically distinct from the Thule, with almost no interbreeding.

alternatives.label: Oral memory of real people
alternatives.text: Many researchers and Inuit historians see the Tuniit stories as memories of the Dorset, preserved for centuries, though how much the legends record real contact is debated.

alternatives.label: Why they vanished
alternatives.text: Proposed causes include climate change, competition with or violence from the better-equipped Thule, and introduced diseases; none is proven.

alternatives.label: Giants or not
alternatives.text: The "giant" image may reflect the Dorset's strength or the stature of strangers in stories; there is no skeletal evidence that Dorset people were unusually tall.

sources.title: The genetic prehistory of the New World Arctic

entries.title: Sedna, mother of the sea beasts
entries.dateNote: Inuit oral tradition (Thule ancestors in the eastern Arctic from c. 1000–1200 CE); recorded by Franz Boas in 1888
entries.mainstream: In Inuit religion the sea goddess known as Sedna, Nuliajuk, Takannaaluk or Arnaqquassaaq lives in a house at the bottom of the sea and controls the seals, walruses and whales. Versions differ, but at the centre a young woman is thrown overboard from a boat by her father; as she clings to the side he cuts off her fingers, joint by joint, and each piece becomes a sea mammal. When people break taboos, the dirt of their misdeeds tangles her hair and she withholds the animals; an angakkuq (shaman) must travel to her under the sea and comb and braid her hair, which she cannot do without fingers, before hunting can succeed. Traditional women's tattoos (kakiniit) on fingers allude to the story. Franz Boas published Central Inuit versions in 1888.

alternatives.label: Moral ecology
alternatives.text: Anthropologists read the story as linking human conduct to the supply of animals: taboo-breaking pollutes the sea and causes famine.

alternatives.label: Shamanic journey
alternatives.text: The shaman's underwater journey to appease her is a classic example of spirit travel to another world, a theme found across Arctic and Siberian traditions.

alternatives.label: Cross-cultural echoes
alternatives.text: Comparisons are made with other "mistress of animals" figures and with mermaid and water-spirit traditions such as Mami Wata; whether these share any common origin is speculative.

entries.title: Franklin's lost expedition: Inuit testimony ignored for 160 years
entries.dateNote: Sailed 1845; ships abandoned 1848; wrecks found 2014 and 2016
entries.mainstream: In 1845 Sir John Franklin sailed from England with 129 men in HMS Erebus and HMS Terror to complete the Northwest Passage. The ships were trapped in ice off King William Island in September 1846; a note found in 1859 recorded that Franklin had died in June 1847 and the survivors abandoned the ships in April 1848 to walk south, and all died. In 1854 John Rae reported Inuit accounts of starving men and of cannibalism, which caused outrage in Britain and were dismissed by figures including Charles Dickens. Inuit testimony collected by Charles Francis Hall and others, and later studied by David Woodman and Inuk historian Louie Kamookak, helped guide searches: Parks Canada found Erebus in 2014, and the Arctic Research Foundation found Terror in Terror Bay in 2016 after an Inuk crew member, Sammy Kogvik, reported seeing a mast sticking through the ice years earlier.

alternatives.label: Stories proven true
alternatives.text: Bone studies (cut marks and "pot polishing") published in 2015 support the Inuit accounts of cannibalism, and the wreck locations agree broadly with Inuit testimony about a ship sinking far to the south.

alternatives.label: Lead poisoning, scurvy or zinc?
alternatives.text: Lead from tinned food and water systems was long blamed; later studies emphasise scurvy, malnutrition, tuberculosis and possibly zinc deficiency, and the relative roles are debated.

alternatives.label: Legends and the uncanny
alternatives.text: The mystery inspired ghost stories and fiction, including Dan Simmons's novel The Terror (2007) and its 2018 TV adaptation, which add a supernatural creature drawn loosely from Inuit lore.

entries.changed: 1854: Inuit reports of cannibalism rejected in Britain. 1859: Victory Point note found. 1990s: Inuit testimony re-examined. 2014/2016: both wrecks found, consistent with Inuit accounts.

media.title: What happened to this doomed Arctic expedition? #shorts ￼

entries.title: Mesa Verde: the cliff dwellings that were abandoned in a generation
entries.dateNote: Cliff dwellings c. 1190–1280 CE; region left by c. 1300
entries.mainstream: Ancestral Puebloans farmed the Mesa Verde region of south-western Colorado from about 600 CE. Late in the 12th century they began to build villages inside cliff alcoves, including Cliff Palace with about 150 rooms; tree-ring dates show most construction between about 1190 and 1260. By about 1285–1300 the whole region was emptied, as people migrated south to the Rio Grande and Arizona, where their descendants live in today's Pueblos (such as Hopi, Zuni and the Rio Grande Pueblos). Ranchers Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason publicised Cliff Palace in 1888; Mesa Verde became a US national park in 1906.

alternatives.label: Drought and conflict
alternatives.text: Archaeologists link the departure to the "Great Drought" of 1276–1299 seen in tree rings, overdependence on maize, deforestation and rising violence, shown by defensive towers and some evidence of massacres.

alternatives.label: Pull, not just push
alternatives.text: Some scholars stress the attraction of new religious movements (such as the katsina tradition) and communities in the south, rather than collapse alone.

alternatives.label: Migration, not disappearance
alternatives.text: Pueblo people reject the popular idea that the Anasazi "mysteriously vanished": their oral histories describe a planned migration, and they regard Mesa Verde as an ancestral home.

media.title: Mesa Verde's Cliffside Dwellings Show a Glimpse of History | National Geographic

entries.title: Yaya's gourd: the Taíno story of how the ocean was born
entries.mainstream: The earliest written record of an Indigenous American religion is the account of the Taíno of Hispaniola compiled in the 1490s by the friar Ramón Pané on Columbus's orders (the original is lost; it survives in an Italian translation). In one myth the supreme spirit Yaya killed his rebellious son Yayael and hung his bones in a gourd from the roof. When the gourd was opened, the bones had turned into fish. Four brothers born of one mother later crept in to eat the fish, dropped the gourd as Yaya returned, and it broke: so much water poured out that it covered the earth and became the sea, full of fish. The Taíno kept the bones of ancestors in hanging gourds or baskets and venerated zemís, spirit beings embodied in carved objects.

alternatives.label: Flood and origin myth
alternatives.text: The broken gourd is read both as an origin story for the sea and as one of the many flood stories of the Americas.

alternatives.label: Ancestors give life
alternatives.text: Scholars note that the myth makes ancestral bones a source of life and food, matching Taíno burial practice.

alternatives.label: A filtered record
alternatives.text: Pané spoke a different language, worked through interpreters and wrote as a missionary, so the account is fragmentary and its accuracy is debated.

media.title: The Taino myth of the cursed creator - Bill Keegan

entries.title: The "extinct" Taíno: a people written off in 1550, found in living DNA
entries.dateNote: Declared extinct c. 1550; ancient genome published 2018
entries.mainstream: The Taíno were the main people of the Greater Antilles and the Bahamas when Columbus landed in 1492. War, enslavement and epidemics caused a catastrophic decline, and Spanish documents declared them extinct as early as about 1550; history books long repeated this. In 2018 a team sequenced the genome of a woman buried in the Bahamas (Preacher's Cave) around the 8th–10th century and found that present-day Puerto Ricans were more closely related to her than to any other Indigenous American group. Many people in Puerto Rico, Cuba and the Dominican Republic carry Indigenous mitochondrial DNA (passed down the female line), and Taíno words, crops and practices survive.

alternatives.label: Survival through mixing
alternatives.text: Researchers and Taíno descendant groups argue that the Taíno were absorbed through intermarriage and creolisation rather than wiped out, and that their identity persisted.

alternatives.label: Ancestry is not identity
alternatives.text: Some historians caution that small percentages of Indigenous ancestry do not by themselves show cultural continuity, and the modern Taíno revival is debated.

alternatives.label: Myth of extinction
alternatives.text: Scholars note that the "extinction" narrative suited colonial claims to land and labour.

entries.changed: 16th century: declared extinct. 20th century: textbooks repeat it. 2000s–2018: mitochondrial and ancient-DNA studies show substantial Taíno ancestry in living Caribbean people.

sources.title: Origins and genetic legacies of the Caribbean Taino

entries.title: Port Royal: the "wickedest city on Earth" that sank in an afternoon
entries.mainstream: Port Royal, on a sand spit at the mouth of Kingston Harbour, Jamaica, was the busiest English port in the Americas in the 1660s–80s and a base for buccaneers such as Henry Morgan; it was nicknamed the "Sodom of the New World" and "the wickedest city on Earth". On 7 June 1692 an earthquake liquefied the sandy ground and about two-thirds of the town slid or sank into the sea; a pocket watch recovered from the seabed in the 1960s stopped at 11:43. Between 1,000 and 3,000 people died in the earthquake and tsunami, and about 2,000 more of disease afterwards. Underwater excavations, including a 10-year Texas A&M project from 1981, have mapped streets and buildings preserved beneath the harbour.

alternatives.label: Divine judgement
alternatives.text: Many preachers at the time, in Jamaica and England, presented the disaster as God's punishment of a sinful city, comparing it to Sodom and Gomorrah.

alternatives.label: Natural hazard
alternatives.text: Geologists explain the destruction by liquefaction of the saturated sand spit; another earthquake in 1907 liquefied it again.

alternatives.label: A real "sunken city"
alternatives.text: Port Royal is often cited alongside legendary drowned cities (Atlantis, Ys, Dwarka) as an example of a city genuinely swallowed by the sea within memory.

entries.title: Clairvius Narcisse and the "zombie powder" debate
entries.mainstream: In Haitian Vodou belief a bokor (sorcerer) can raise a dead person as a zombi, a soulless labourer under his control. Clairvius Narcisse was admitted to the Albert Schweitzer Hospital in Deschapelles, Haiti, in April 1962, was declared dead and buried on 2 May 1962. In 1980 a man identifying himself as Narcisse approached his sister in L'Estère, saying he had been dug up, drugged and forced to work on a plantation. Ethnobotanist Wade Davis, then a Harvard graduate student, investigated and in The Serpent and the Rainbow (1985) proposed that a powder containing tetrodotoxin from pufferfish could induce a death-like coma, followed by Datura to keep victims confused.

alternatives.label: Pharmacological zombies
alternatives.text: Davis argued that zombification was a real social sanction, using toxins to produce apparent death and resurrection.

alternatives.label: Toxin not found
alternatives.text: Toxicologists Kao and Yasumoto (1986) and others found little or no tetrodotoxin in powder samples; critics called the work bad science, and Davis replied that preparations vary.

alternatives.label: Psychiatric and social explanations
alternatives.text: Some researchers suggest that people identified as zombies were often mentally ill or brain-damaged wanderers taken in by families; others stress that the zombi belief reflects the memory of slavery in Haiti.

entries.title: The Bimini Road: a road to Atlantis on the Bahamas seabed?
entries.mainstream: On 2 September 1968 diver-zoologist Joseph Manson Valentine and companions found a straight line of rounded limestone blocks nearly 0.8 km long in about 5.5 m of water off North Bimini in the Bahamas. Followers of the psychic Edgar Cayce, who had predicted in 1940 that part of Atlantis would rise near Bimini in 1968 or 1969, hailed it as an Atlantean road or wall. Geologists, including Eugene Shinn of the US Geological Survey, found the blocks are beachrock – sand and shells naturally cemented on a beach – that cracked into rectangular slabs; cores show the bedding runs continuously across blocks, and radiocarbon dates suggest the beachrock formed about 3,000 years ago.

alternatives.label: Atlantean or human-made (speculative)
alternatives.text: Valentine, Graham Hancock and others argue that the alignment, apparent "prop" stones and right angles show deliberate construction, perhaps a harbour or breakwater from a time of lower sea level.

alternatives.label: Natural beachrock
alternatives.text: Most geologists regard it as natural, noting identical beachrock pavements elsewhere, such as at Loggerhead Key in the Dry Tortugas, and that radiocarbon dates are far too young for an Ice Age civilisation.

alternatives.label: Self-fulfilling prophecy
alternatives.text: Sceptics note that the find in the very year of Cayce's prediction drove interest; supporters see the timing as significant.

entries.title: The Bermuda Triangle
entries.mainstream: The idea that ships and aircraft vanish unusually often in a triangle of the western Atlantic between Miami, Bermuda and San Juan, Puerto Rico, grew from a 1950 Associated Press article and was named by Vincent Gaddis in the February 1964 Argosy article "The Deadly Bermuda Triangle". Books by Charles Berlitz (1974) and others made it a global legend. Cases cited include the collier USS Cyclops (lost with 306 aboard in 1918), Flight 19 (five US Navy Avenger torpedo bombers lost on 5 December 1945, along with a rescue flying boat), and the airliners Star Tiger (1948) and Star Ariel (1949). Librarian Larry Kusche's The Bermuda Triangle Mystery: Solved (1975) found that many stories were exaggerated, misdated, happened elsewhere or had ordinary explanations such as storms.

alternatives.label: Exotic causes (speculative)
alternatives.text: Proposed explanations include Atlantean energy crystals, magnetic anomalies, time warps, UFOs and sudden methane eruptions from the seabed; none has been demonstrated.

alternatives.label: No more losses than elsewhere
alternatives.text: Kusche, the US Coast Guard and NOAA say the number of disappearances is not unusually high for one of the world's busiest shipping and flying areas; the insurer Lloyd's of London does not charge higher rates there.

alternatives.label: Real hazards
alternatives.text: The area has the Gulf Stream, sudden storms, hurricanes and some of the deepest Atlantic waters, which make wreckage hard to find.

sources.title: NOAA Ocean Service: What is the Bermuda Triangle?

entries.title: The chupacabra: a vampire beast born in 1995
entries.mainstream: In March 1995 farmers in Puerto Rico began reporting livestock – goats, sheep, chickens – killed with puncture wounds and said to be drained of blood; more than 200 reports followed that year. Comedian Silverio Pérez is credited with coining the name chupacabras ("goat-sucker") on his radio show. In August 1995 Madelyne Tolentino of Canóvanas described a bipedal creature with large dark eyes and spines down its back. Reports spread to Mexico, the southern United States, Chile and Argentina. Later US "chupacabras", including Texas carcasses examined from 2004 onward, were identified by DNA and veterinarians as coyotes, dogs or hybrids with severe sarcoptic mange.

alternatives.label: Unknown predator or alien pet (speculative)
alternatives.text: Some believers proposed an unknown animal, a creature escaped from secret US genetic experiments, or an extraterrestrial animal; there is no physical evidence for any of these.

alternatives.label: Film-inspired eyewitness
alternatives.text: After a five-year investigation, Benjamin Radford (Tracking the Chupacabra, 2011) concluded that Tolentino's description closely matched the alien Sil from the 1995 film Species, which she had seen.

alternatives.label: Ordinary predators
alternatives.text: Necropsies of supposed victims found ordinary bite wounds from dogs and other animals; the blood draining was not confirmed.

entries.title: Bhimbetka: India's painted rock shelters and the oldest-art debate
entries.dateNote: Paintings from the Mesolithic (perhaps Upper Palaeolithic) to medieval times; rediscovered 1957
entries.mainstream: In 1957 archaeologist V. S. Wakankar, travelling through Madhya Pradesh, noticed sandstone outcrops resembling painted-cave country he had seen in Spain and France; his team found what became the Bhimbetka rock shelters, a World Heritage Site since 2003. More than 700 shelters have been identified, around 400 with paintings of hunting, dancing, animals, riders and later war scenes, spanning from the Mesolithic (and perhaps the Upper Palaeolithic) to the medieval period. The site's name is popularly linked to Bhima, the strong Pandava hero of the Mahabharata, said to have rested there.

alternatives.label: Very old art
alternatives.text: Wakankar dated the earliest paintings to the Upper Palaeolithic, perhaps up to 40,000 years ago; others place most paintings much later, from about 10,000 BCE onward, as direct dating is limited.

alternatives.label: Lower Palaeolithic cupules (debated)
alternatives.text: Rock-art researcher Robert Bednarik argued that cup-shaped marks (cupules) in the Auditorium Cave lie in Acheulian (Lower Palaeolithic) layers and could be among the oldest known human markings anywhere; this is contested because cupules are hard to date.

alternatives.label: Living tradition
alternatives.text: Scholars note that local Adivasi communities still make paintings with similar motifs, suggesting a very long continuity of practice.

entries.title: Mehrgarh: early farmers of South Asia and the first dentists
entries.dateNote: First settlement c. 7000 BCE (excavators) or c. 5250 BCE (revised)
entries.mainstream: Mehrgarh, near the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, Pakistan, was discovered in 1974 by the French Archaeological Mission led by Jean-François and Catherine Jarrige. It is one of the earliest farming and herding villages in South Asia, with mud-brick houses, barley and wheat, cattle, sheep and goats, and later pottery and copper working; occupation continued for thousands of years, foreshadowing the Indus Civilisation. In 2006 researchers reported in Nature eleven molar crowns from nine adults in the Neolithic cemetery with neat holes drilled in life, probably with flint-tipped bow drills – the earliest known evidence of dentistry, about 7,500–9,000 years old.

alternatives.label: Local origin
alternatives.text: Jarrige argued that farming at Mehrgarh developed with a strong local background rather than arriving fully formed from the Near East.

alternatives.label: Imported package
alternatives.text: Others emphasise similarities with Neolithic sites in Iran and Mesopotamia and see a spread of crops and animals from the west.

alternatives.label: Dating debate
alternatives.text: The founding date of about 7000 BCE comes from the excavators; later radiocarbon dating of teeth by Mutin and Zazzo placed the first period at about 5250–4650 BCE, which is disputed.

entries.title: The lost Sarasvati: a holy river of the Rigveda that dried up?
entries.dateNote: Rigveda composed c. 1500–1200 BCE (conventional dating); Ghaggar-Hakra decline c. 2000 BCE
entries.mainstream: The Rigveda praises the Sarasvati as a great, holy river, placed in one hymn between the Yamuna and the Sutlej; it was later personified as the goddess Sarasvati, and Hindu tradition says the river now flows invisibly underground to meet the Ganges and Yamuna at Prayagraj. Since the 19th century many scholars have identified it with the Ghaggar-Hakra, a now seasonal river system of north-west India and eastern Pakistan along whose dry course many Indus Civilisation sites lie. A 2012 study (Giosan et al.) concluded that the Ghaggar-Hakra was fed by monsoon rains rather than Himalayan glaciers in Harappan times, and that the Sutlej had abandoned this channel thousands of years before the Harappans, with the river declining as monsoons weakened about 4,000 years ago.

alternatives.label: Memory of a real river
alternatives.text: Some scholars argue the early Rigvedic hymns preserve a memory of a once-mighty river, and that later texts describing it disappearing in the desert at Vinashana match the drying Ghaggar-Hakra.

alternatives.label: "Sindhu-Sarasvati Civilisation"
alternatives.text: Some Indian writers rename the Indus Civilisation the Sarasvati or Indus-Sarasvati civilisation and argue it was Vedic; most international scholars reject equating the two because the Rigveda is usually dated after the Harappan decline.

alternatives.label: Another river entirely
alternatives.text: Other scholars identify the early Rigvedic Sarasvati with the Helmand (Harakhvaiti) in Afghanistan, or treat the river as partly mythical.

sources.title: Fluvial landscapes of the Harappan civilization

entries.title: The Rakhigarhi genome: DNA from an Indus city
entries.mainstream: Rakhigarhi in Haryana, India, is one of the largest cities of the Indus (Harappan) Civilisation. In 2019 a team including Vasant Shinde and David Reich published in Cell the first genome from a Harappan city, from a skeleton buried there in the mature Harappan period. Despite poor preservation, it showed a mix of ancestry related to ancient Iranians (splitting from them before farming began) and to ancient hunter-gatherers of South Asia, and no detectable ancestry from steppe pastoralists or Anatolian farmers. The same pattern matched outlier individuals found in Central Asia, suggesting trade or migration between the Indus and Central Asia.

alternatives.label: Supports later steppe arrival
alternatives.text: Many geneticists read the result as consistent with Indo-European (Indo-Aryan) languages arriving in South Asia with steppe-related people after the Harappan period, since steppe ancestry is found in living South Asians.

alternatives.label: Supports continuity
alternatives.text: Some Indian commentators and members of the team emphasised that Harappans were ancestral to modern South Asians and that farming developed locally, rejecting any "Aryan invasion"; the paper itself does not resolve the languages question.

alternatives.label: One person
alternatives.text: Critics stress that a single, poorly preserved genome cannot represent a whole civilisation of millions.

sources.title: An Ancient Harappan Genome Lacks Ancestry from Steppe Pastoralists or Iranian Farmers

entries.title: Patala: the seven jewelled underworlds of the Nagas
entries.dateNote: Puranic texts c. 4th–10th c. CE, drawing on older traditions
entries.mainstream: In Hindu cosmology, as described in the Puranas, below the earth lie seven subterranean realms (lokas), collectively called Patala, each ruled by daityas, danavas or Nagas – serpent beings, sons of Kadru. The Vishnu Purana tells how the sage Narada visited Patala and found it more beautiful than heaven (Svarga), lit by the jewels on the Nagas' hoods; the Bhagavata Purana calls the lower realms bila-svargas, "subterranean heavens". The lowest, Nagaloka, is ruled by the serpent king Vasuki, and the whole cosmos rests on the thousand-headed serpent Shesha. Similar Naga underworld traditions spread with Buddhism and Hinduism through Southeast Asia.

alternatives.label: Cosmological symbolism
alternatives.text: Scholars read Patala as part of a symbolic vertical cosmos of upper and lower worlds, not as a physical place.

alternatives.label: Hidden peoples (speculative)
alternatives.text: Some modern alternative writers link Patala and the Nagas to hidden underground civilisations, reptilian beings or the Americas (as the land on the opposite side of the earth); these ideas have no evidential basis.

alternatives.label: Cross-cultural pattern
alternatives.text: Comparisons are drawn with other serpent or dragon kingdoms beneath the earth or water, such as Chinese dragon-king palaces and the Mesoamerican underworld.

entries.title: Sigiriya: the lion rock of a parricide king
entries.mainstream: Sigiriya is a 180 m granite rock in central Sri Lanka crowned with palace ruins. According to the Culavamsa chronicle, King Kashyapa I (reigned c. 477–495 CE) seized the throne by killing his father Dhatusena and built his capital on the rock, approached through a gateway shaped as a giant lion (only its paws remain), with water gardens below. Halfway up are frescoes of gracefully painted women and the "mirror wall", once polished so smooth the king could see his reflection; visitors from the 8th to 10th centuries scratched more than 1,500 poems on it, 685 of which were deciphered by Senarath Paranavitana. Kashyapa was defeated by his brother Moggallana, and the site became a Buddhist monastery.

alternatives.label: Fortress-palace
alternatives.text: The chronicle tradition presents Sigiriya as the fortified palace of a king fearing revenge.

alternatives.label: Monastery first
alternatives.text: Some scholars argue the site was mainly a Buddhist monastic complex, with the palace story exaggerated by later chroniclers; alternative traditions credit King Dhatusena with starting it.

alternatives.label: Who are the ladies?
alternatives.text: The fresco women have been interpreted as celestial nymphs (apsaras), court ladies, or goddesses; their identity is debated.

entries.title: Gwion Gwion (Bradshaw) paintings and the "lost race" claim
entries.dateNote: Most figures c. 12,000 years ago (2020 study); recorded 1891
entries.mainstream: In the north-west Kimberley of Western Australia, thousands of rock shelters bear finely painted, slender human figures with tassels, sashes and elaborate headdresses, now mostly a deep mulberry colour. Pastoralist Joseph Bradshaw recorded them in 1891 and they long carried his name; local Aboriginal names include Gwion Gwion and Kiro Kiro, and some Aboriginal accounts attribute them to a bird, Kujon, or to spirits. A 2020 study dating mud-wasp nests over and under the paintings concluded that most of the figures were made about 12,000 years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age; one experimental date suggests some may be older.

alternatives.label: Aboriginal ancestors
alternatives.text: Archaeologists, the Australian Archaeological Association and Aboriginal communities hold that the paintings were made by ancestors of today's Aboriginal people; there is no archaeological break in occupation.

alternatives.label: A vanished earlier people (rejected)
alternatives.text: Amateur researcher Grahame Walsh, who recorded thousands of sites from 1977, proposed an "Erudite Epoch" in which a non-Aboriginal people, perhaps from Indonesia, made the art before being displaced; scholars reject this and critics called it a racist stereotype.

alternatives.label: Change with climate
alternatives.text: Some researchers link the shift from Gwion to Wandjina-style art to environmental change at the end of the Ice Age; others say it was a normal stylistic change.

sources.title: 12,000-Year-old Aboriginal rock art from the Kimberley region, Western Australia

entries.title: Tycho's new star (1572): the day the heavens changed
entries.mainstream: In November 1572 a brilliant new star appeared in Cassiopeia; by 11 November, when the young Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe noticed it, it was brighter than Jupiter, and around 16 November it peaked about as bright as Venus. It was recorded in Europe, China and Korea, and stayed visible to the naked eye until early 1574. Tycho measured it carefully and found it showed no parallax and did not move against the stars, so it lay far beyond the Moon. In De nova stella (1573) he argued that the heavens – held since Aristotle to be perfect and unchanging – could change. Modern astronomers identified its remnant in 1952 and, from a light echo measured in 2008, showed it was a Type Ia supernova: an exploding white dwarf.

alternatives.label: Omen
alternatives.text: Many contemporaries read the star as an omen – of religious upheaval, war or the end times; Queen Elizabeth I consulted the astrologer Thomas Allen about it.

alternatives.label: Scientific revolution
alternatives.text: Historians of science see the 1572 star, the 1577 comet and SN 1604 as key blows to the Aristotelian cosmos that prepared the way for Kepler and Galileo.

alternatives.label: Shakespeare's star (speculative)
alternatives.text: Some researchers have argued that the "star that's westward from the pole" in Hamlet refers to Tycho's star; this is a literary hypothesis.

entries.changed: Before 1572: the heavens beyond the Moon held to be unchanging. 1573: Tycho shows the new star lies among the fixed stars. 1952: radio remnant found. 2008: light echo confirms a Type Ia supernova.

entries.title: Eyam: the village that shut itself in with the plague
entries.mainstream: In late summer 1665 a bundle of cloth from London reached the tailor's house in Eyam, Derbyshire, England; his assistant George Viccars opened the damp bundle and soon died of plague. As deaths mounted, the rector William Mompesson and the ejected Puritan minister Thomas Stanley persuaded villagers, from May 1666, to accept a voluntary quarantine: no one would leave, families buried their own dead, and church services moved outdoors. Neighbouring villages left food at boundary stones, where coins were left in holes filled with vinegar. The plague ran for 14 months; one account says at least 260 villagers died, leaving 83 survivors of 350, though other estimates give about 430 survivors from some 800.

alternatives.label: Heroic sacrifice
alternatives.text: The traditional story presents Eyam as a model of self-sacrifice that protected the surrounding region.

alternatives.label: Did it work?
alternatives.text: Some historians question whether the quarantine increased deaths within the village by keeping people together, and note that the heroic story was elaborated in the 19th century with commemorations and "plague tourism".

alternatives.label: Genetic resistance (speculative)
alternatives.text: Geneticist Stephen O'Brien suggested that the CCR5-Δ32 mutation, which protects against HIV, was more common among descendants of survivors and might have helped them; this is debated, especially since plague and HIV enter cells differently.

media.title: The English town that stopped the plague | BBC Global

entries.title: The Beast of Gévaudan
entries.mainstream: Between 30 June 1764 and 19 June 1767, a man-eating animal or animals attacked people – mostly women and children herding livestock – in the province of Gévaudan in south-central France, killing perhaps 60 to 100 and injuring many more. Witnesses described a creature "like a wolf, yet not a wolf", reddish with dark stripes, a long tufted tail and no fear of humans. King Louis XV sent soldiers and professional wolf hunters; his arquebus bearer François Antoine shot a very large grey wolf in September 1765 and was rewarded, but attacks resumed. On 19 June 1767 local hunter Jean Chastel shot an animal that the royal notary's report described as an extraordinary wolf, and the killings stopped.

alternatives.label: Wolves
alternatives.text: Most historians and zoologists attribute the attacks to one or more unusually large or bold wolves, at a time when wolf attacks were common in France; a 2021 proposal suggested an Italian wolf.

alternatives.label: Exotic animal or hybrid
alternatives.text: Others suggest an escaped striped hyena or lion from a menagerie, or a wolf–dog hybrid, based on the strange descriptions; no remains survive to test this.

alternatives.label: Human killer or werewolf
alternatives.text: Some writers have proposed a serial killer using a trained animal, and contemporary rumour spoke of a loup-garou (werewolf) or divine punishment, as a local bishop preached; these remain speculative.

entries.title: The Lisbon earthquake of All Saints' Day, 1755
entries.mainstream: At about 9:40 on the morning of 1 November 1755 – All Saints' Day, when churches were full and candles lit – a great earthquake, probably magnitude 8.5–9 with an epicentre in the Atlantic south-west of Portugal, destroyed much of Lisbon. About 40 minutes later a tsunami surged up the Tagus, and fires burned for days. The disaster struck Portugal, Spain and Morocco; tsunamis reached Cornwall, the Caribbean and Brazil. Estimates of the dead in Portugal, Spain and Morocco range from about 40,000 to 50,000 or more. The chief minister, later Marquis of Pombal, organised relief ("bury the dead and heal the living"), rebuilt the Baixa with early earthquake-resistant designs and sent a questionnaire to every parish, an early step towards scientific seismology.

alternatives.label: Divine punishment
alternatives.text: Many clergy interpreted the earthquake as God's judgement on Lisbon's sins; the Jesuit Gabriel Malagrida preached this and was later executed under Pombal. A Sebastianist prophet had predicted in 1752 that an earthquake would destroy Lisbon on All Saints' Day, and converts to Sebastianism surged afterwards.

alternatives.label: Philosophical shock
alternatives.text: Voltaire's Poem on the Lisbon Disaster and Candide used it to attack the optimistic belief that this is "the best of all possible worlds"; Rousseau replied that human choices, such as crowded cities, made the disaster worse.

alternatives.label: Natural science
alternatives.text: Pombal's survey and later studies made it the first earthquake investigated systematically, contributing to modern seismology; the exact fault remains debated.

media.title: The earthquake that changed history – BBC REEL

entries.title: The War of the Worlds broadcast (1938): the panic that mostly wasn't
entries.mainstream: On the evening of 30 October 1938, Orson Welles's Mercury Theatre on the Air broadcast an adaptation of H. G. Wells's novel over CBS radio, written by Howard Koch as a series of realistic news bulletins: explosions on Mars, a "meteorite" landing at Grovers Mill, New Jersey, Martians with heat rays, and gas spreading over New York. Next morning newspapers across the US reported a nationwide panic, with people fleeing homes and jamming phone lines. In 1940 Princeton psychologist Hadley Cantril estimated that about six million heard the show and over a million were frightened. Many later historians argue the panic was greatly exaggerated by newspapers.

alternatives.label: Mass panic
alternatives.text: The traditional account, built on newspaper reports and Cantril's study, holds that the broadcast caused widespread hysteria, and it became a classic example of media power.

alternatives.label: Newspaper myth
alternatives.text: Media historians Jefferson Pooley and Michael Socolow (2013) and W. Joseph Campbell argue that the audience was small (one ratings survey found about 2% of those polled were listening), that most callers were checking facts, and that newspapers, losing advertising to radio, sensationalised a few cases; no hospital admissions for shock were found.

alternatives.label: Real fear for some
alternatives.text: Letters to Welles and the FCC show some listeners were genuinely frightened, many thinking of a German attack in the tense weeks after the Munich crisis; a 1949 Spanish version in Quito, Ecuador, reportedly caused panic and a riot in which the radio station was attacked.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)

media.title: Orson Welles: The 'alien invasion' that fooled America - BBC News

entries.title: The Philadelphia Experiment: the warship that vanished
entries.mainstream: According to the legend, in October 1943 the US Navy used theories from Einstein's unfinished unified field theory to make the destroyer escort USS Eldridge invisible at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard; it vanished in a green fog, teleported to Norfolk, Virginia, and back, and some sailors were fused into the ship's hull or went mad. The story began in 1955–56, when a man calling himself Carlos Miguel Allende (Carl Meredith Allen) sent letters to UFO author Morris K. Jessup and an annotated copy of his book reached the Office of Naval Research. It grew through books such as The Philadelphia Experiment (1979) by William Moore and Charles Berlitz and a 1984 film.

alternatives.label: Secret teleportation (speculative)
alternatives.text: Believers, including Alfred Bielek who claimed in 1989 to have been aboard, link it to later secret projects such as the alleged "Montauk Project"; no documentary evidence supports these claims.

alternatives.label: Degaussing confused
alternatives.text: Researchers suggest the legend grew from real wartime degaussing work, which made ships "invisible" to magnetic mines, and other naval experiments; Jacques Vallée found a veteran who described degaussing aboard a nearby ship.

alternatives.label: Records contradict it
alternatives.text: The Navy says no such experiment took place; Eldridge's logs place it elsewhere at the time, and veterans said in 1999 it never docked in Philadelphia. Allen admitted writing all the annotations "to scare the hell out of Jessup".

entries.title: The Flatwoods monster (1952)
entries.mainstream: On the evening of 12 September 1952, in Flatwoods, West Virginia, brothers Edward and Fred May and their friend Tommy Hyer saw a bright object cross the sky and apparently land on a farm. A group including their mother Kathleen May and National Guardsman Eugene Lemon went up the hill and reported a pulsing red light, a pungent mist that made them sick, and a towering figure about 3 m tall with a glowing spade-shaped head, a pleated skirt-like body and claw-like hands, which hissed and glided towards them. A local newspaper man reported "skid marks" and a gummy residue the next day. It became one of the classic cases of the 1952 UFO wave.

alternatives.label: Alien visitor (speculative)
alternatives.text: Some ufologists consider it an encounter with an alien being or robot in a landed craft, pointing to the physical symptoms witnesses reported.

alternatives.label: Meteor, beacon and owl
alternatives.text: Investigator Joe Nickell (2000) concluded the light was a meteor seen over three states that night, the red light an aircraft beacon, and the "monster" a barn owl on a branch, its shape and hiss matching an owl seen in the dark by frightened people.

alternatives.label: Local legend
alternatives.text: The "Braxie" has become a tourism symbol for Braxton County, with a museum and giant chairs shaped like the creature.

entries.title: The Lonnie Zamora incident: Project Blue Book's unsolved landing (1964)
entries.mainstream: On 24 April 1964 at about 5:45 pm, police sergeant Lonnie Zamora of Socorro, New Mexico, was chasing a speeding car when he heard a roar and saw a flame in the sky. He drove to a gully and said he saw a shiny, egg-shaped object on legs and two small figures in white overalls beside it; as he approached, the object rose with a roar and a blue-orange flame and flew away. Investigators found scorched brush and depressions in the ground. Astronomer J. Allen Hynek investigated for the US Air Force, and Project Blue Book listed the case as "unknown" – one of its best-documented unexplained sightings.

alternatives.label: Craft of unknown origin
alternatives.text: Many ufologists regard Zamora, a respected officer, as a highly credible witness and the case as strong evidence for an unexplained landed craft.

alternatives.label: Test vehicle
alternatives.text: Some researchers suggest a test of a lunar-lander prototype or other experimental craft from nearby White Sands, though no such flight has been documented for that day.

alternatives.label: Hoax
alternatives.text: Sceptic Robert Sheaffer proposed a prank by New Mexico Tech students, and Philip Klass claimed it was a tourism scheme by local officials; no hoaxer has been identified.

entries.title: The Kecksburg "acorn": Pennsylvania's Roswell (1965)
entries.mainstream: On 9 December 1965 a brilliant fireball was seen across six US states and Ontario, and residents of Kecksburg, Pennsylvania, reported something falling into nearby woods. Some locals later said they had seen an acorn-shaped object about the size of a Volkswagen Beetle, with a band of writing like hieroglyphs, which soldiers removed under guard. In 2005 NASA said experts had examined fragments from the area and found they came from a re-entering Soviet satellite, but that the records had been lost in the 1980s; after a Freedom of Information lawsuit by journalist Leslie Kean, a court ordered NASA in 2007 to search again, and NASA reported missing boxes of papers.

alternatives.label: Soviet probe
alternatives.text: One explanation is debris from the Soviet Venus probe Kosmos 96, launched in November 1965; NASA's later statements are less supportive of this link.

alternatives.label: Meteor
alternatives.text: Astronomers who calculated the fireball's path concluded it was a natural meteor that descended steeply and probably ended near the north-western shore of Lake Erie, far from Kecksburg, implying no object landed there.

alternatives.label: Secret recovery (speculative)
alternatives.text: Ufologists suggest an alien craft or a classified US spy re-entry capsule was recovered by the military; no documents confirming a recovery have been released.

entries.title: Mothman and the Silver Bridge (1966–67)
entries.mainstream: On 15 November 1966 two young couples near Point Pleasant, West Virginia, told police that a large grey or black creature with glowing red eyes and huge wings had followed their car near the "TNT area", a former World War II munitions plant. The Point Pleasant Register reported "Couples See Man-Sized Bird" the next day, and more sightings followed over the next year. On 15 December 1967 the Silver Bridge over the Ohio River collapsed at rush hour, killing 46 people; the bridge failure was traced to a cracked eyebar. Writer John Keel's The Mothman Prophecies (1975) linked the creature to the disaster, UFO sightings, men in black and premonitions.

alternatives.label: Harbinger of disaster (speculative)
alternatives.text: In the Keel tradition, Mothman is an omen or messenger appearing before tragedies; later reports connect it with other disasters worldwide.

alternatives.label: Misidentified birds
alternatives.text: Local Sheriff George Johnson suggested an unusually large heron; others propose a sandhill crane far outside its range or a barred or snowy owl, whose eyeshine in headlights could explain glowing eyes.

alternatives.label: Folklore and tourism
alternatives.text: Folklorists see Mothman as a modern legend that grew through retelling and books, now celebrated with a statue, museum and annual festival in Point Pleasant.

entries.title: Jebel Sahaba: the Nile cemetery of the oldest known war
entries.dateNote: Best estimate c. 13,400–13,700 years ago (older estimates up to c. 18,600)
entries.mainstream: Jebel Sahaba (Site 117) is a Late Pleistocene cemetery on the Nile near the Sudan–Egypt border, found in 1964 by a team led by Fred Wendorf during the rescue campaigns before Lake Nasser flooded the valley; the site now lies under the lake. It held the remains of 61 people of both sexes and all ages. A 2021 re-examination (Crevecoeur and colleagues) found healed and unhealed injuries on 41 of them (about two-thirds), many caused by stone-tipped arrows or spears, and a best date estimate of roughly 13,400–13,700 years ago. It is often cited as the oldest known evidence of repeated, organised violence between groups.

alternatives.label: One massacre
alternatives.text: The original interpretation saw the cemetery as the result of a single battle or massacre.

alternatives.label: Recurrent raids
alternatives.text: The 2021 study argues that the mix of healed and fresh wounds points instead to sporadic, repeated raids and ambushes over a person's lifetime.

alternatives.label: Climate stress
alternatives.text: Since Hoffman (1993), researchers have linked the violence to competition for scarce resources as the climate and the Nile changed at the end of the last Ice Age; this remains a hypothesis rather than proven.

alternatives.label: How old is war?
alternatives.text: The site is a key data point in the wider debate over whether organised warfare is ancient and widespread among hunter-gatherers or arose mainly with farming and states.

entries.changed: 1964: cemetery found during the Nubian rescue campaign. 1960s–90s: read as a single battle. 2021: re-analysis argues for repeated violence and a younger date.

sources.title: New insights on interpersonal violence in the Late Pleistocene based on the Nile valley cemetery of Jebel Sahaba
