entries.title: The Garamantes: a Saharan kingdom that mined fossil water
entries.dateNote: Kingdom c. 500 BCE – c. 700 CE (roots earlier)
entries.mainstream: The Garamantes lived in the Fezzan region of south-west Libya, in the middle of the Sahara, and are mentioned by Herodotus in the 5th century BCE as "a very great nation" who used four-horse chariots to hunt "Troglodyte Ethiopians". Their capital Garama (modern Germa) was excavated from the 1960s. They built an extensive network of underground channels (foggaras) to tap groundwater stored from wetter millennia, supporting farms, towns and trans-Saharan trade with the Roman world. Their state declined in late antiquity; most researchers connect the decline with falling groundwater levels among other factors.

alternatives.label: Herodotus's wonders
alternatives.text: Herodotus also tells of Garamantian oxen that grazed walking backwards because their horns curved forward; scholars debate how much of his account is reliable report and how much traveller's tale. Some read the chariot raids on "Troglodytes" as early slave raiding, others as a speculative tale.

alternatives.label: Why the decline?
alternatives.text: Explanations include depletion of non-renewable fossil water, shifting trade routes, and political changes in late antiquity and after the Arab conquests of the 7th century; the weighting is debated.

alternatives.label: Lessons for today
alternatives.text: The Garamantes are often cited in discussions of modern "fossil water" use, including Libya's Great Man-Made River project; this is an analogy, not a historical claim.

entries.title: The Carthage Tophet: child sacrifice, or a cemetery for infants?
entries.mainstream: The Tophet of Salammbô at Carthage (in modern Tunisia) is a sacred precinct used from about the 8th century BCE until the Roman destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE. It contains thousands of urns holding the cremated remains of infants and young animals, many marked by stone stelae with dedications to the god Baal Hammon and the goddess Tanit recording a vow, often using the term mlk (molk). Greek and Roman writers such as Diodorus Siculus describe Carthaginians sacrificing children, especially in crises, and the Hebrew Bible condemns child sacrifice at a "Topheth" near Jerusalem.

alternatives.label: Ritual sacrifice
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists and historians argue that the inscriptions, the classical texts and the age profile of the remains together show that children were offered to the gods in fulfilment of vows (Smith and colleagues, Xella and others).

alternatives.label: Cemetery for the very young
alternatives.text: An osteological study by Schwartz and colleagues (2010) argued that many of the infants died before or around birth, suggesting a special burial ground for children who died naturally, possibly with rituals attached.

alternatives.label: Enemy propaganda?
alternatives.text: Because most written accounts come from Carthage's enemies (Greeks, Romans) or from biblical polemic, some scholars see them as exaggerated; others reply that the Punic inscriptions themselves describe offerings.

sources.title: Skeletal Remains from Punic Carthage Do Not Support Systematic Sacrifice of Infants
Bones, teeth, and estimating age of perinates: Carthaginian infant sacrifice revisited
Two tales of one city: data, inference and Carthaginian infant sacrifice

entries.title: Akhenaten: the pharaoh who replaced the gods, and was erased
entries.mainstream: Amenhotep IV came to the Egyptian throne around 1353 BCE, renamed himself Akhenaten ("effective for the Aten") and promoted the worship of the Aten, the sun disc, above or instead of Egypt's other gods. He founded a new capital, Akhetaten (modern Amarna), and art of his reign showed the royal family with elongated faces, skulls and bellies. After his death the court returned to the old gods; his son Tutankhaten became Tutankhamun, Amarna was abandoned, and later rulers erased Akhenaten's name, calling him "the enemy". Much of what is known was recovered only from the 19th century onwards, including the Amarna diplomatic letters found in the 1880s.

alternatives.label: First monotheist?
alternatives.text: Some scholars see Atenism as the first known monotheism; others call it henotheism or a royal cult centred on the king as the Aten's sole intermediary. Sigmund Freud (Moses and Monotheism, 1939) speculated that Moses was an Atenist priest; most historians reject this as unsupported.

alternatives.label: Art or illness?
alternatives.text: His unusual portraits have been explained as religious artistic convention, or as signs of a medical condition such as Marfan syndrome; DNA and CT studies of the Tutankhamun family (2010) reported no evidence of Marfan syndrome in the mummy from tomb KV55, whose identification as Akhenaten is itself debated.

alternatives.label: Alien-hybrid claims (speculative)
alternatives.text: Some popular writers have claimed the elongated depictions show a non-human or alien lineage; there is no evidence for this, and Egyptologists attribute the style to Amarna art conventions.

sources.title: Ancestry and Pathology in King Tutankhamun's Family
The Amarna Project (University of Cambridge-linked excavation)

entries.title: The curse of Tutankhamun: a newspaper legend tested by statistics
entries.mainstream: Howard Carter's team opened Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings in November 1922. When the expedition's sponsor Lord Carnarvon died in Cairo in April 1923 – from blood poisoning after an infected mosquito bite was nicked while shaving – newspapers spread the idea of a pharaoh's curse. The novelist Marie Corelli had published a warning shortly before, and Arthur Conan Doyle suggested "elementals" guarding the tomb. Each later death linked to the excavation fed the story. No curse inscription was found in the tomb.

alternatives.label: Curse
alternatives.text: The legend holds that disturbing the tomb brought death on those involved; it became a fixture of films and fiction.

alternatives.label: Statistical test
alternatives.text: A 2002 BMJ cohort study by Mark Nelson compared Westerners present at key openings with those who were not, and found no significant difference in survival; Carter himself lived until 1939.

alternatives.label: Natural hazards
alternatives.text: Some have suggested moulds or bacteria in sealed tombs could harm visitors; there is no evidence that this caused Carnarvon's death.

alternatives.label: Media creation
alternatives.text: Historians note that the curse story was amplified by rivalry between newspapers, after Carnarvon sold exclusive rights to The Times.

sources.title: The mummy's curse: historical cohort study

media.title: King Tut’s Curse Could Cure Cancer

entries.title: The Taung Child: Africa's first ape-man, rejected because of a hoax
entries.dateNote: c. 2.8 million years ago; found 1924, described 1925
entries.mainstream: In 1924 quarry workers at the Buxton Limeworks at Taung, South Africa, found a small fossil skull that reached anatomist Raymond Dart in Johannesburg. In 1925 Dart described it in Nature as Australopithecus africanus, a small-brained, upright ancestor linking apes and humans, and argued that humanity originated in Africa. Leading British scientists, including Arthur Keith, rejected his claims, partly because they expected an early large brain like that of Piltdown Man – later exposed (1953) as a hoax. Further finds by Robert Broom and others from the 1930s–40s vindicated Dart. The child is now thought to be roughly 2.8 million years old.

alternatives.label: Dart vindicated
alternatives.text: Today Australopithecus is accepted as a hominin genus and Africa as the birthplace of humankind; the Taung case is a textbook example of how expectations shaped the reception of evidence.

alternatives.label: Killed by an eagle
alternatives.text: In 2006 Lee Berger and Ron Clarke argued, from puncture marks in the eye sockets, that the child was killed by a large bird of prey; this is widely accepted though still discussed.

alternatives.label: Asia-first theories
alternatives.text: Before Taung many researchers favoured an Asian origin for humans; that view persisted until more African fossils accumulated in the mid-20th century.

entries.changed: 1925: Dart names Australopithecus and is widely rejected. 1940s: further finds turn opinion. 1953: Piltdown exposed. 2006: eagle-predation hypothesis.

sources.title: Australopithecus africanus The Man-Ape of South Africa

entries.title: San rock art: trance, rain-animals and the spirit world of southern Africa
entries.dateNote: Tradition spans thousands of years into the 19th century; start date indicative
entries.mainstream: Tens of thousands of rock paintings and engravings across southern Africa – in the Drakensberg, the Cederberg, Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe – were made by the ancestors of San hunter-gatherers over thousands of years, with some made into the 19th century. Common subjects include eland, human figures, dances and part-human, part-animal beings. In the 1870s Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd recorded extensive testimony from /Xam San informants in Cape Town, which later scholars used to interpret the images, including accounts of rain-making in which trance specialists "captured" a rain-animal whose blood and milk became rain.

alternatives.label: Trance and the spirit world
alternatives.text: From the 1970s–80s David Lewis-Williams and others argued that much of the art depicts the experiences of healers in trance dances – sensations, transformations into animals and journeys to the spirit world – an interpretation now widely influential.

alternatives.label: Myth and narrative
alternatives.text: Other scholars (for example Anne Solomon) argue the trance model is over-applied and that many images depict myths, the spirits of the dead or narrative scenes.

alternatives.label: Shared human patterns (debated)
alternatives.text: The neuropsychological model has been extended to European Ice Age caves, suggesting common human trance imagery; critics question applying southern African ethnography to such distant times and places.

sources.title: Rock Art Research Institute, University of the Witwatersrand

entries.title: The Agojie: the women soldiers of Dahomey
entries.dateNote: At least 18th century – 1894 (traditions trace them to the 17th)
entries.mainstream: The Kingdom of Dahomey (in present-day Benin) maintained an all-female military corps, called Agojie or Mino ("our mothers") in Fon, from at least the 18th century until the kingdom was conquered by France in 1894. Traditions trace the corps to King Houegbadja or to a corps of female elephant hunters (gbeto) and palace guards. At its height it may have numbered several thousand; the women were formally married to the king and lived in the palace. They fought neighbouring states, including the Egba at Abeokuta, and the French in 1890–92. A woman named Nawi, interviewed in 1978 and thought to be the last veteran, died in 1979.

alternatives.label: Origins debated
alternatives.text: Explanations include a shortage of men after wars and slave raids, the king's need for loyal guards inside the palace, and older traditions of women hunters.

alternatives.label: Amazons named by outsiders
alternatives.text: European visitors called them "Amazons" after Greek myth, shaping how they were described; Fon terms and oral histories give a different picture.

alternatives.label: Role in the slave trade
alternatives.text: Dahomey was deeply involved in the Atlantic slave trade, and the Agojie took part in raids that captured people for sale; this was debated publicly around the 2022 film The Woman King.

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine: The Real History Behind The Woman King

entries.title: Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba: diplomat, warrior and legend
entries.mainstream: Nzinga Mbande (c. 1583–1663) ruled the Mbundu kingdoms of Ndongo (from 1624) and Matamba (from 1631) in present-day Angola. As envoy to the Portuguese governor in Luanda in 1622 she negotiated a peace treaty; a famous story says that, offered only a mat while the Portuguese sat on chairs, she had an attendant kneel to form a seat. She later allied with the Dutch West India Company, fought the Portuguese for decades, and made peace in 1656, dying in 1663. She is a national heroine in Angola.

alternatives.label: Diplomat and strategist
alternatives.text: Historians emphasise her use of baptism, alliances (including with Imbangala war bands) and negotiation to keep her kingdoms independent.

alternatives.label: Hostile sources
alternatives.text: Much of her life is known from Capuchin missionaries such as Antonio Cavazzi, whose accounts include lurid stories of cruelty and of a male harem dressed as women; scholars treat these with caution as possibly shaped by European prejudice.

alternatives.label: Symbol
alternatives.text: After independence (1975) she became a symbol of resistance to colonial rule; some critics note that, like many rulers of the time, she also took part in the slave trade.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba

entries.title: Nongqawuse and the Xhosa cattle-killing: a prophecy that the dead would rise
entries.mainstream: In April 1856 Nongqawuse, a Xhosa girl of about 15 living near the mouth of the Gxarha River (in the present Eastern Cape, South Africa), said she had met the spirits of ancestors. Her message, relayed by her uncle Mhlakaza and accepted by the paramount chief Sarili, was that if the people killed their cattle and destroyed their crops the dead would rise, healthy new cattle would appear and the colonists would be swept into the sea. The Xhosa were already suffering land loss after frontier wars and an epidemic of bovine lungsickness. Over 1856–57 some 300,000–400,000 cattle were killed; when the prophesied day passed, famine killed about 40,000 people, and the colonial governor Sir George Grey used the crisis to seize land and recruit labour.

alternatives.label: Millenarian movement
alternatives.text: Historian Jeff Peires (The Dead Will Arise, 1989) interprets the movement as a rational response within Xhosa belief to disease and colonial pressure, comparable to other movements expecting the return of the dead.

alternatives.label: Conspiracy explanations
alternatives.text: A belief that Grey or missionaries engineered the prophecy to destroy the Xhosa has circulated; historians generally find no evidence of a plot, though Grey clearly exploited the aftermath.

alternatives.label: Believers and unbelievers
alternatives.text: Communities split between believers and "amagogotya" (unbelievers) who refused; the failure was blamed on them, a pattern seen in other prophecy movements.

entries.title: The Great Pyramid of Cholula: the world's largest pyramid, hidden under a hill and a church
entries.dateNote: Built c. 3rd century BCE – 9th century CE
entries.mainstream: The Great Pyramid of Cholula, or Tlachihualtepetl ("made mountain" in Nahuatl), in Puebla, Mexico, is the largest pyramid known by volume. It was built in successive stages from about the 3rd century BCE to the 9th century CE and was later dedicated to Quetzalcoatl. By the Spanish conquest it was overgrown and looked like a natural hill; in 1594 the Spanish built the church of Nuestra Señora de los Remedios on top. Tunnels dug by archaeologists from the 1930s revealed the inner structures.

alternatives.label: A giant's tower to the sky
alternatives.text: A tradition recorded in the 1560s by the Dominican friar Pedro de los Ríos (Codex Vaticanus A) and popularised by Alexander von Humboldt says that after a great flood one of seven surviving giants, Xelhua, built the pyramid in memory of the mountain that saved them; the gods, angered that it would reach the clouds, hurled fire and halted the work.

alternatives.label: Babel echo?
alternatives.text: Humboldt and later writers noted the parallel with the Tower of Babel. Many historians suspect the colonial versions mixed native tradition with biblical stories taught by missionaries; others hold that a pre-conquest core existed.

alternatives.label: Hidden in plain sight
alternatives.text: The pyramid's burial under earth and vegetation, and the church on its summit, are interpreted variously as natural overgrowth, deliberate concealment, or Christian appropriation of a sacred place.

sources.title: Humboldt, Vues des Cordillères (1810), chapter on the pyramid of Cholula (Wikisource, French)
Elementos (BUAP): Cholula, gigantes y Xelhua – exégesis de una placa conmemorativa

entries.title: Eagle on a cactus: the founding of Tenochtitlan
entries.mainstream: According to Mexica tradition, the people migrating from Aztlan were told by their god Huitzilopochtli to settle where they saw an eagle perched on a prickly-pear cactus (nopal) growing from a rock. They found the sign on an island in Lake Texcoco and founded Tenochtitlan there, traditionally in 1325 (the date 13 March 1325 was fixed in 1925 for a 600th-anniversary celebration). Tenochtitlan grew into a city of perhaps 200,000 people before the Spanish conquest of 1521; Mexico City was built over it and the lake was largely drained. The eagle and cactus are on Mexico's flag.

alternatives.label: Founding myth
alternatives.text: The story follows a widespread pattern of a divinely guided migration ending at a promised sign.

alternatives.label: The serpent question
alternatives.text: In the best-known modern image the eagle devours a serpent. Some early depictions, such as the Codex Mendoza, show the eagle on the cactus without a snake; scholars suggest the serpent may reflect a later reading of the Aztec war glyph atl-tlachinolli (water and fire), or a blending with European symbolism.

alternatives.label: History behind the myth
alternatives.text: Archaeologists and historians debate the real founding date and whether the island was already settled; the official story was also shaped by later Mexica rulers who reportedly rewrote their history.

media.title: The Rise and Fall of the Aztec Civilization

entries.title: La Llorona: the weeping woman of the waters
entries.mainstream: La Llorona ("the weeping woman") is a ghost of Mexican and wider Latin American folklore: a woman who drowned her children and now wanders by rivers and lakes at night crying for them, and who may seize anyone who hears her. Versions are found from the American Southwest to South America and are often used as warnings to children. Earlier roots are often traced to the Florentine Codex (compiled by Bernardino de Sahagún in the 16th century), which lists among the omens before the Spanish conquest a woman heard weeping at night for her children.

alternatives.label: Aztec roots
alternatives.text: Many folklorists connect her with the goddess Cihuacoatl and with Mexica beliefs about women who died in childbirth, whose spirits wandered at crossroads.

alternatives.label: La Malinche
alternatives.text: She is sometimes conflated with Malintzin (La Malinche), the Nahua interpreter and mother of a son of Hernán Cortés, making the legend an allegory of conquest and betrayal.

alternatives.label: European parallels
alternatives.text: Others note similarities with European tales of white ladies and water spirits, and see the modern legend as a colonial blend.

entries.title: Spiro Mounds: the looting of "America's King Tut's tomb"
entries.mainstream: Spiro, in eastern Oklahoma, was a major centre of the Mississippian world from about 800 to 1450 CE, with a ceremonial complex of earthen mounds. In 1936 a group of men leased the site and formed the Pocola Mining Company, tunnelling into Craig Mound, where they found an unusual hollow chamber with extraordinarily preserved objects – engraved shells, copper plates, textiles, pearls, effigy pipes and ceremonial weapons. They sold the finds to collectors around the world, and the looting prompted Oklahoma to pass an antiquities law; professional excavations followed. Craig Mound has been called "an American King Tut's tomb".

alternatives.label: Lost knowledge
alternatives.text: Archaeologists consider the looting one of the worst in North American archaeology, because the context that would explain the objects was destroyed; objects are scattered across many museums.

alternatives.label: Descendant communities
alternatives.text: The Caddo and Wichita nations are regarded as descendants of Spiro's people; their perspectives on the site and its objects are part of modern interpretation.

alternatives.label: Myths in shell
alternatives.text: The engraved shell art, with winged beings, horned serpents and birdmen, is studied as a record of Mississippian cosmology; readings of specific figures differ.

sources.title: Oklahoma Historical Society: Spiro Mounds Archaeological Center

entries.title: Skin-walkers: a Navajo belief and a ranch of strange claims
entries.mainstream: In Navajo (Diné) tradition a yee naaldlooshii ("by means of it, it goes on all fours") is one kind of malevolent witch, believed able to transform into or disguise themselves as animals; the term is never used for healers. Traditional Navajo people are reluctant to discuss this lore with outsiders. In 1996 claims about strange lights, cattle mutilations and creatures on the Sherman Ranch in Utah's Uintah Basin – later called Skinwalker Ranch – were published in the Deseret News; Robert Bigelow bought the ranch that year to study them, and it has since been the subject of books, US government-funded research contracts and television series.

alternatives.label: Cultural belief
alternatives.text: For many Navajo, skin-walkers are part of a living religious and moral tradition; some, including Native writers, object to outsiders' commercial and fictional use of it.

alternatives.label: Paranormal hot spot
alternatives.text: Researchers associated with the ranch report unexplained lights, animal deaths and other phenomena, and describe it as a site of interest for UFO and paranormal study.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Critics note the lack of verifiable evidence and suggest misperception, predators, folklore and the incentives of publicity and television; no claim has been independently confirmed.

entries.title: The Ghost Dance: a vision during an eclipse, and Wounded Knee
entries.mainstream: On 1 January 1889, during a solar eclipse, the Northern Paiute spiritual leader Wovoka (Jack Wilson) in Nevada had a vision. He taught that performing a circle dance and living peacefully and honestly would reunite the living with the spirits of the dead, restore the land and end white expansion. The Ghost Dance spread rapidly among Plains peoples. Among the Lakota, the movement – with "ghost shirts" rumoured to stop bullets – alarmed US authorities; the attempt to suppress it led to the killing of Sitting Bull and, on 29 December 1890, the Wounded Knee massacre, in which US soldiers killed some 250–300 Lakota, many of them women and children. An earlier Ghost Dance had arisen among the Paiute around 1870.

alternatives.label: Religious revival
alternatives.text: Anthropologist James Mooney (1896) and later scholars describe it as a revitalisation movement responding to loss of land, bison and population.

alternatives.label: A threat?
alternatives.text: Officials at the time portrayed it as a war movement; historians mostly see the panic as a misreading of a largely peaceful religion, with the ghost-shirt belief a Lakota development.

alternatives.label: A global pattern
alternatives.text: Scholars compare it with other movements that promised the return of the dead or of ancestors, such as the Xhosa cattle-killing and Melanesian cargo cults.

entries.title: White Sands footprints: people in North America 21,000 years ago?
entries.mainstream: Human footprints preserved in former lake-shore sediments of Lake Otero in White Sands National Park, New Mexico, were identified from 2009 onwards. In 2021 Matthew Bennett and colleagues reported in Science that seeds of the aquatic plant Ruppia in layers above and below the prints dated them to about 21,000–23,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum – thousands of years before the long-favoured Clovis-first date of about 13,000 years. The tracks, mostly of teenagers and children, appear alongside those of mammoths and giant ground sloths; one set shows a person carrying a small child. A 2023 study using conifer pollen and quartz luminescence dates supported the older ages.

alternatives.label: An early arrival
alternatives.text: If correct, people were south of the ice sheets during the height of the Ice Age, implying an even earlier entry into the Americas.

alternatives.label: Dating sceptics
alternatives.text: Critics argued that the aquatic seeds may have absorbed old carbon from groundwater, making them seem too old, and questioned the stratigraphy; debate continues on some of these points.

alternatives.label: Wider debate
alternatives.text: White Sands joins other contested early sites (such as Monte Verde and Chiquihuite Cave) in debates over when and how the Americas were first peopled.

entries.changed: 2009: tracks recognised. 2021: dated to 21,000–23,000 years ago. 2022: reservoir-effect critiques. 2023: independent dates support the older age.

sources.title: Evidence of humans in North America during the Last Glacial Maximum
Independent age estimates resolve the controversy of ancient human footprints at White Sands

media.title: These Ancient Footprints Rewrite Human History

entries.title: The Piasa: a painted monster on the Mississippi bluffs
entries.dateNote: Described 1673; original destroyed in the 19th century
entries.mainstream: In 1673 the French explorers Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet, travelling down the Mississippi near present-day Alton, Illinois, described two painted monsters on the river bluffs, with horns like a deer, red eyes, a human-like face and beard, a scaly body and a long tail ending in a fish's fin. Sketches from 1678 and 1682 survive. The bluff face carrying the painting was quarried away in the 19th century (around 1846–47 according to one account); a modern reconstruction now stands nearby.

alternatives.label: Underwater panther
alternatives.text: Many scholars relate the image to the underwater panther or horned serpent of regional Native traditions and to Mississippian iconography from nearby Cahokia.

alternatives.label: A 19th-century legend
alternatives.text: The popular story of the "Piasa bird" that devoured people until the chief Ouatoga offered himself as bait was published by John Russell in 1836; later researchers concluded it was largely Russell's literary invention rather than recorded folklore.

alternatives.label: Dragon or bird?
alternatives.text: The creature has been redrawn over time as a winged dragon-like bird, illustrating how a lost image can change as it is copied.

entries.title: The Tărtăria tablets: the world's oldest writing, or not writing at all?
entries.mainstream: In 1961 the archaeologist Nicolae Vlassa found three small clay tablets incised with symbols at Tărtăria in Transylvania, Romania, in a pit with burnt human bones and figurines. They belong to the world of the Vinča culture of south-eastern Europe, whose pottery and figurines carry a repertoire of signs (the Vinča symbols). If the tablets date to around 5300 BCE, as indirect dating of the associated layers suggests, they are older than the earliest Mesopotamian proto-writing.

alternatives.label: Not writing
alternatives.text: Most linguists and archaeologists regard the Vinča signs as symbols, marks of ownership or religious notation rather than a system that recorded language.

alternatives.label: Proto-writing ("Danube script")
alternatives.text: Researchers such as Harald Haarmann and Marco Merlini argue the signs form an early writing or proto-writing system of "Old Europe".

alternatives.label: Dating dispute
alternatives.text: Because the tablets were baked to conserve them, they cannot be dated directly, and the excavation's stratigraphy has been questioned; early on, some scholars instead compared them with Mesopotamian tablets of around 3000 BCE.

entries.title: Cucuteni–Trypillia: Europe's first giant settlements, burned and rebuilt
entries.mainstream: The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture flourished from roughly 5000 to 3000 BCE (estimates vary; recent ones give c. 5050–2950 BCE) in what are now Romania, Moldova and Ukraine. Around 4100–3600 BCE some of its settlements, such as Talianki and Maidanetske in Ukraine, grew into "mega-sites" covering more than 100 hectares – Talianki around 335 hectares – with up to a few thousand houses arranged in concentric ovals, among the largest settlements in the world at the time and earlier than the first Mesopotamian cities. A striking feature is that many houses were burned, apparently in a repeated cycle, and settlements were then rebuilt.

alternatives.label: Deliberate burning
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists think houses were burned on purpose, perhaps as a ritual at the end of a house's life or a settlement cycle.

alternatives.label: Accident or war
alternatives.text: Others suggest accidental fires or attacks; experiments show burning a wattle-and-daub house so thoroughly requires extra fuel, which supports the deliberate view but does not settle the reason.

alternatives.label: Cities without kings?
alternatives.text: The mega-sites show little sign of palaces, temples or a ruling elite, and are debated as possible early "egalitarian" or low-hierarchy cities, or as seasonal gathering places rather than permanent towns.

alternatives.label: Old Europe
alternatives.text: Marija Gimbutas saw the culture as part of a peaceful, goddess-centred "Old Europe" overrun by steppe peoples; this view is influential but widely criticised as too idealised.

sources.title: Proto-Cities or Non-Proto-Cities? On the Nature of Cucuteni–Trypillia Mega-Sites

entries.title: Kitezh: the Russian city that sank to escape the Mongols
entries.dateNote: Legend set in 1238 (Mongol invasion); text late 18th century
entries.mainstream: The legend of Kitezh tells of a city founded by Grand Prince Georgy (Yuri) II of Vladimir that, when the army of Batu Khan attacked during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century, was saved by being submerged in, or made invisible beneath, Lake Svetloyar near Nizhny Novgorod. Only the righteous can see it; pilgrims report hearing its church bells and singing from under the water. The legend survives mainly in the "Kitezh Chronicle", copied by Old Believers in the late 18th century, and inspired Rimsky-Korsakov's opera The Legend of the Invisible City of Kitezh (1907).

alternatives.label: Sacred lake
alternatives.text: Folklorists see the story as part of Russian Orthodox and Old Believer tradition of a hidden holy city, and pilgrims still walk around the lake on its shores at night.

alternatives.label: Real ruins?
alternatives.text: Expeditions have searched Svetloyar; geological studies suggest the lake formed long before, and no submerged city has been found, though some local traditions point to older settlement remains in the area.

alternatives.label: Sunken-city pattern
alternatives.text: Kitezh is often called the "Russian Atlantis" and is compared with Ys in Brittany and other drowned cities whose bells are heard under the water.

entries.title: Baba Yaga: the witch in the hut on chicken legs
entries.dateNote: First clear mention 1755; folk roots older
entries.mainstream: Baba Yaga is one of the best-known figures of Slavic folklore: an old woman who lives deep in the forest in a hut standing on chicken legs, flies in a mortar steered with a pestle and sweeps away her tracks with a broom. In folk tales she may eat children, or test and help heroes and heroines who come to her. The first clear written mention is in Mikhail Lomonosov's Russian Grammar of 1755; most tales were collected in the 19th century, notably by Alexander Afanasyev.

alternatives.label: Initiation figure
alternatives.text: The folklorist Vladimir Propp interpreted Baba Yaga and her hut as memories of initiation rites and of the boundary between the living and the dead.

alternatives.label: Goddess remnant?
alternatives.text: Some scholars see her as a survival of a pre-Christian goddess of death, birth or nature; others caution that there is no early evidence for such a cult.

alternatives.label: Ambiguity
alternatives.text: Her double nature as dangerous ogress and wise helper is widely discussed and has made her a popular figure in modern fiction.

entries.title: Arnold Paole: the Serbian vampire case that alarmed Europe
entries.mainstream: Arnold Paole was a Serbian hajduk (soldier) in the village of Medveđa, then under Habsburg rule, who said he had once been troubled by a vampire and had protected himself by eating earth from its grave. After he died from a fall from a hay wagon around 1726, villagers blamed him for several deaths; his body was exhumed, said to look undecayed with fresh blood, and staked. In 1731–32, after further deaths, Austrian military doctors including Johann Flückinger investigated and their report, Visum et Repertum, dated 26 January 1732, described exhumed bodies that seemed uncorrupted. It was widely published and helped make the word "vampire" known across Western Europe.

alternatives.label: Folk belief
alternatives.text: Villagers interpreted the deaths through Balkan beliefs in the restless dead who return to drain the living.

alternatives.label: Decomposition explained
alternatives.text: Researchers such as Paul Barber (Vampires, Burial and Death, 1988) argue that the signs described – bloated bodies, blood at the mouth, apparent growth of nails, sounds when staked – match normal processes of decomposition.

alternatives.label: Epidemic
alternatives.text: The cluster of deaths has been attributed to an infectious disease; which one is unknown.

entries.title: Anna Anderson: the woman who claimed to be Grand Duchess Anastasia
entries.mainstream: In 1920 a young woman was pulled from a canal in Berlin after a suicide attempt and later claimed to be Grand Duchess Anastasia, youngest daughter of Tsar Nicholas II, who was said to have survived the 1918 killing of the Romanov family. As Anna Anderson she drew supporters and opponents among Russian émigrés and royalty; a 1927 investigation identified her as Franziska Schanzkowska, a Polish factory worker who had disappeared in Berlin. A German court case lasting decades ended without a ruling that she was Anastasia. She later lived in Charlottesville, Virginia, and died in 1984. After the Romanov remains were found, DNA tests in 1994 on preserved tissue showed she was not a Romanov and matched a relative of Schanzkowska; the remains of the last two missing children were identified in 2008–09.

alternatives.label: Survival legend
alternatives.text: Rumours that one or more of the tsar's children escaped circulated for decades, encouraged by the secrecy over the burial site and by many claimants.

alternatives.label: DNA verdict
alternatives.text: Scientists regard the DNA evidence as conclusive that Anderson was not Anastasia and that all of the family died in 1918.

alternatives.label: Lingering doubts
alternatives.text: A few supporters questioned the chain of custody of the tested samples; tests on several independent samples gave the same result.

sources.title: Identification of the remains of the Romanov family by DNA analysis
Mystery Solved: The Identification of the Two Missing Romanov Children Using DNA Analysis

entries.title: The House of Wisdom: Baghdad's translation movement
entries.mainstream: The Bayt al-Hikma, or House of Wisdom, was a library and centre of learning in Abbasid Baghdad, associated with the caliphs Harun al-Rashid and especially al-Ma'mun (reigned 813–833). It was linked to the Graeco-Arabic translation movement, in which works of Greek philosophy, medicine, mathematics and astronomy, along with Persian, Indian (Sanskrit) and Syriac texts, were translated into Arabic. Scholars connected to the movement include al-Khwarizmi, whose name gave us "algorithm", and the translator Hunayn ibn Ishaq. Baghdad was sacked by the Mongols in 1258, and later accounts say the Tigris ran black with the ink of destroyed books.

alternatives.label: Golden-age academy
alternatives.text: A popular modern image presents the House of Wisdom as a great university or academy that preserved ancient learning and launched an Islamic scientific golden age.

alternatives.label: A palace library?
alternatives.text: Historians such as Dimitri Gutas argue that the translation movement was driven by many patrons across Baghdad's elite, and that the Bayt al-Hikma itself was probably a palace library on a Sasanian model rather than a research institution; its role has been mythologised.

alternatives.label: Lost libraries
alternatives.text: The story of the 1258 destruction is often paired with that of the Library of Alexandria as a symbol of knowledge lost to war; scholars note that both stories have been dramatised.

media.title: A day in the life of a teenager in medieval Baghdad - Birte Kristiansen and Petra Sijpesteijn

entries.title: Ibn Fadlan meets the Rus: a ship burning on the Volga
entries.mainstream: Ahmad ibn Fadlan was a member of an embassy sent in 921 by the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir from Baghdad to the king of the Volga Bulgars, arriving in May 922. His account (the Risala) describes the peoples he met, including traders he called the Rus, generally identified as Scandinavians (Vikings). It contains a vivid description of the funeral of a Rus chieftain, in which an enslaved girl is killed and burned with him in his ship. A fuller manuscript was found in Mashhad, Iran, in 1923. Michael Crichton drew on it for his novel Eaters of the Dead (1976), filmed as The 13th Warrior (1999).

alternatives.label: Rare eyewitness
alternatives.text: Historians value the Risala as one of very few outsider accounts of Viking-age Scandinavians abroad, matching archaeological finds of ship burials.

alternatives.label: Outsider bias
alternatives.text: Others caution that Ibn Fadlan observed through the lens of his own culture and may have misunderstood rituals; whether the Rus he met were Scandinavian, Slavic or mixed is debated.

alternatives.label: Fiction blending
alternatives.text: Crichton's novel mixed the real account with the Beowulf story, and the film version has sometimes been taken as history by audiences.

entries.title: The Seven Sleepers of Ephesus: a cave sleep of centuries
entries.dateNote: Set c. 250 CE; texts from 5th–7th centuries
entries.mainstream: A legend told by Christians and Muslims says that during the persecution of the Roman emperor Decius (around 250 CE) a group of young Christian men hid in a cave near Ephesus and fell into a miraculous sleep, waking centuries later – Christian versions place it under the Christian emperor Theodosius II – to find their faith triumphant. Early versions in Syriac appear in the 5th–6th centuries, and the story is told in the Qur'an (Surah 18, al-Kahf, "The Cave"), which includes their dog and says they stayed "three hundred years, and add nine".

alternatives.label: Faith and resurrection
alternatives.text: In Christian tradition the story was read as proof of bodily resurrection; in Islam, as a sign of God's power and of protection for believers.

alternatives.label: Many caves
alternatives.text: Several places claim the cave, including Ephesus in Turkey, a site near Amman in Jordan and Tarsus; each has become a place of pilgrimage.

alternatives.label: Time-slip pattern
alternatives.text: The story belongs to a widespread family of tales in which a person sleeps or visits another world and returns after long years, such as Japan's Urashima Tarō, Ireland's Oisín and Washington Irving's Rip Van Winkle.

entries.title: The roc and the elephant bird: a giant bird of legend and a real one
entries.mainstream: The roc is a gigantic bird of Middle Eastern legend, said to carry off elephants; it appears in the voyages of Sinbad in the One Thousand and One Nights. Marco Polo, around 1298, reported that the bird lived on islands south of Madagascar and that Kublai Khan had been shown a giant roc feather. Madagascar was home to the real elephant birds (Aepyornithidae), flightless birds up to about 3 metres tall that laid the largest eggs known; they died out within roughly the last thousand years, after people arrived. Huge eggs from Madagascar reached the French Academy of Sciences in 1851.

alternatives.label: Memory of real birds
alternatives.text: Some writers think the roc legend grew from sailors' reports of elephant-bird eggs and bones, or of Madagascar's now-extinct giant eagles.

alternatives.label: Older myth
alternatives.text: Others trace the roc to older traditions such as the Indian Garuda, the Persian Simurgh and the Arabian anqa, and note that a giant flightless bird cannot carry elephants.

alternatives.label: A real feather?
alternatives.text: The "roc feathers" shown in China are often thought to have been fronds of the raffia palm; this is a plausible guess rather than documented.

sources.title: Unexpected diversity within the extinct elephant birds (Aves: Aepyornithidae) and a new identity for the world's largest bird

entries.title: Wolfe Creek crater (Kandimalal): where the evening star fell
entries.dateNote: Impact less than c. 120,000 years ago (2019 estimate)
entries.mainstream: Wolfe Creek Crater in the Kimberley region of Western Australia is a well-preserved meteorite impact crater about 875 metres across. It was brought to scientists' attention after being spotted during an aerial survey in 1947 and was described in 1949. It was long thought to be about 300,000 years old, but a 2019 study estimated it to be less than 120,000 years old. Small iron meteorites and iron-rich "shale balls" have been found around it. The local Djaru (Jaru) people call it Kandimalal and have several Dreaming stories about its origin.

alternatives.label: Dreaming stories
alternatives.text: One story says the round crater was made by a rainbow snake emerging from the earth; another, told by an Elder, says that the evening star passed close to the crescent moon, became so hot that it fell to the ground with a great explosion, flash and dust cloud, and that people long feared to go near the place.

alternatives.label: Memory of an impact?
alternatives.text: Some writers suggest the falling-star story may preserve a memory of the impact, since people have lived in Australia for perhaps 50,000–65,000 years; others note the story could have arisen after people saw the crater and that the impact's precise age is uncertain.

alternatives.label: Science and culture
alternatives.text: The crater is a site of interest both for impact science and for discussions of how Aboriginal knowledge records landscape features.

entries.title: The Mahogany Ship: a lost wreck in the dunes of Victoria
entries.mainstream: The Mahogany Ship is a supposed old shipwreck said to lie buried in sand dunes in the Armstrong Bay area west of Warrnambool, Victoria, Australia. 19th-century settlers and whalers told of a wreck of dark timber; the "1836 Hopkins River incident", in which shipwrecked sealers reportedly saw an old wreck, became the story's foundation and was popularised by George Dunderdale's The Book of the Bush (1898). A Portland newspaper of 1847 described a wreck in the hummocks near Warrnambool. Searches since the 1980s, and symposia in 1981, 1987 and 2005, have found no conclusive evidence that such a wreck exists.

alternatives.label: Portuguese caravel
alternatives.text: In 1977 Kenneth McIntyre argued that it was a caravel from a secret Portuguese voyage under Cristóvão de Mendonça around 1522, part of his theory that the Portuguese reached Australia before the Dutch.

alternatives.label: Folklore
alternatives.text: Researcher Jenny Fawcett and others argue that the accounts are inconsistent second-hand recollections and that the legend grew in retelling; some suggest a later wreck was misidentified.

alternatives.label: Other origins
alternatives.text: Spanish, Dutch and Chinese origins have also been proposed; none has been confirmed.

entries.title: The Great Moon Hoax: bat-people seen through a telescope
entries.mainstream: Beginning on 25 August 1835, the New York newspaper The Sun published a series of six articles claiming that the astronomer Sir John Herschel, working at the Cape of Good Hope, had used a powerful new telescope to discover life on the Moon, including bison, unicorn-like goats, beavers walking upright and winged humanoids ("Vespertilio-homo", bat-men) living beside temples. The supposed author, Dr Andrew Grant, was fictitious. The series was widely believed and reprinted, and boosted The Sun's circulation. On 16 September 1835 the paper admitted the articles were a hoax, and the reporter Richard Adams Locke publicly admitted authorship in 1840.

alternatives.label: Satire and its times
alternatives.text: Historians link the series to popular speculative science of the day, such as the Reverend Thomas Dick's claims that the Moon was inhabited by billions of beings, and some read it partly as satire; many readers took it literally.

alternatives.label: Media lesson
alternatives.text: It is often cited as an early example of mass-media hoaxing and of how scientific authority (here, Herschel's name) can lend credibility to invented claims.

alternatives.label: Poe's claim
alternatives.text: Edgar Allan Poe claimed the story plagiarised his own moon-voyage tale, "Hans Pfaall", published shortly before.

media.title: The 'Great Moon Hoax' that fooled the world – BBC REEL

entries.title: The phantom airships of 1896–97: UFOs before aircraft
entries.mainstream: From 17 November 1896, starting in Sacramento, California, and continuing through mid-1897 across the Midwest and Texas, thousands of people in the United States reported seeing mysterious lighted airships in the night sky, years before the first successful powered aeroplane flights. Some newspaper reports described cigar-shaped craft with wings, propellers and searchlights, and encounters with pilots who claimed to be inventors. One of the most famous stories, published in April 1897, said an airship had crashed into a windmill at Aurora, Texas, and that its pilot, "not an inhabitant of this world", was buried in the town cemetery.

alternatives.label: Hoaxes and misperception
alternatives.text: Historians and sceptics attribute most reports to newspaper hoaxes, tall tales, misidentified stars and planets (such as Venus), balloons and the excitement of a period anticipating flight; the Aurora story is widely considered a hoax.

alternatives.label: Secret inventors
alternatives.text: Some at the time believed a secret inventor had built a working airship; no evidence of such a craft has been found.

alternatives.label: Early UFO wave
alternatives.text: UFO researchers regard the wave as an early example of unexplained aerial sightings and note how the objects matched the technology people then expected – airships – just as later sightings resembled rockets and saucers.

entries.title: The Fox sisters: knocking spirits and the birth of Spiritualism
entries.mainstream: In March 1848 in Hydesville, New York, the young sisters Kate and Margaretta (Maggie) Fox reported rapping sounds in their home, which they said were messages from a spirit, later identified as a murdered peddler. Managed by their elder sister Leah, they became famous mediums, and their séances helped launch the Spiritualist movement, which spread across the US and Europe. In 1851 doctors from Buffalo concluded the raps were made by cracking joints. In October 1888 Maggie publicly confessed at the New York Academy of Music, demonstrating how she made the sounds with her toe joints, and the confession was published in the New York World; in 1889 she retracted it.

alternatives.label: Fraud
alternatives.text: Most historians accept the 1888 confession and the earlier investigations as showing that the raps were produced by the sisters.

alternatives.label: Spiritualist view
alternatives.text: Spiritualists argued that the confession was given for money (a reporter had offered a fee) and pointed to Maggie's retraction.

alternatives.label: The bones in the cellar
alternatives.text: In 1904 human remains were reportedly found behind a fallen cellar wall of the house; supporters saw it as proof of the murdered peddler, while sceptics note that no investigation confirmed whose bones they were or how they got there.

entries.title: Ignaz Semmelweis: the doctor who said wash your hands, and was rejected
entries.mainstream: In 1847, at the Vienna General Hospital, the Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that women giving birth in the clinic staffed by doctors and medical students died of childbed (puerperal) fever far more often than those in the clinic staffed by midwives. After his colleague Jakob Kolletschka died of a similar illness following a scalpel cut during an autopsy, Semmelweis concluded that "cadaverous particles" on doctors' hands were transmitting the disease, and introduced handwashing in a chlorinated lime solution, which sharply reduced deaths. His ideas were widely rejected; he became increasingly angry, was committed to an asylum in 1865 and died there of an infected wound about two weeks later. The work of Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister on germs later vindicated him.

alternatives.label: Rejected pioneer
alternatives.text: He is often presented as a martyr of science whose evidence was ignored because it contradicted established theories and implied that doctors were killing patients.

alternatives.label: A more mixed story
alternatives.text: Historians note that Semmelweis was slow to publish his findings in full and could offer no theoretical explanation before germ theory, which contributed to their rejection; some of his students did publicise the results, so the "lone genius" narrative is simplified.

alternatives.label: Semmelweis reflex
alternatives.text: The term "Semmelweis reflex" is used for the tendency to reject new evidence that contradicts established norms.

media.title: The surprising history of hand-washing - BBC REEL

entries.title: The canals of Mars: a civilisation seen through a telescope
entries.mainstream: During the close approach of Mars in 1877 the Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli mapped the planet and named long straight features canali, meaning "channels" (the word had been used for Mars by Angelo Secchi in 1858). In English this was often read as "canals", implying construction. The American Percival Lowell founded an observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, in 1894 and promoted the idea that Martians had built a vast irrigation network to carry water from the polar caps. Better telescopes in the early 20th century showed the canals were optical illusions, and spacecraft from Mariner 4 (1965) onward found no such features, with the possible exception of the canyon Valles Marineris.

alternatives.label: Intelligent Martians
alternatives.text: Lowell and his followers argued the regular network could only be artificial; the idea shaped science fiction, from H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds onward.

alternatives.label: Optical illusion
alternatives.text: Astronomers such as E. M. Antoniadi showed that the human eye tends to join faint, scattered markings into lines at the limit of visibility.

alternatives.label: Lasting pattern
alternatives.text: The episode is sometimes compared with later claims of artificial structures on Mars, such as the "Face on Mars", as examples of the mind finding patterns in ambiguous images.

entries.title: N-rays: a new radiation that existed only in the eye of the beholder
entries.mainstream: In 1903 the respected French physicist Prosper-René Blondlot, at the University of Nancy, announced a new form of radiation, which he called N-rays, detected by slight brightening of a spark or a phosphorescent screen. Many other scientists reported confirming it and many papers were published, though leading physicists such as Lord Kelvin and William Crookes failed to replicate it. In 1904 the American physicist Robert W. Wood visited Blondlot's laboratory and, in the dark, secretly removed an essential prism from the apparatus; the experimenters still reported seeing the effect. Wood's account in Nature effectively ended belief in N-rays.

alternatives.label: Experimenter bias
alternatives.text: N-rays are a classic case of observers seeing what they expect, and are cited by Irving Langmuir as an example of "pathological science".

alternatives.label: Why many confirmed it
alternatives.text: Writers on the episode point to the subjective nature of judging faint brightness changes by eye, the prestige of Blondlot and the excitement after the discovery of X-rays (1895) as reasons why many researchers reported seeing the effect.

entries.title: Krakatoa 1883: the loudest sound in history and a blood-red sky
entries.mainstream: On 26–27 August 1883 the volcanic island of Krakatoa in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra (in present-day Indonesia) erupted catastrophically. A series of huge explosions on 27 August, heard as far as Rodrigues near Mauritius about 4,800 km away, is considered the loudest sound in recorded history; barometers around the world recorded the pressure wave circling the globe more than three times. Tsunamis devastated nearby coasts, and at least 36,417 deaths are attributed to the eruption. Volcanic aerosols produced vivid red sunsets worldwide for months and cooled global temperatures. A new island, Anak Krakatau ("Child of Krakatoa"), emerged from the sea in 1927.

alternatives.label: The Scream
alternatives.text: Some researchers have argued that the red sky in Edvard Munch's The Scream (1893) reflects his memory of Krakatoa sunsets in Norway; others suggest nacreous (mother-of-pearl) clouds or simply artistic expression.

alternatives.label: Global event
alternatives.text: The eruption was among the first natural disasters reported worldwide almost immediately via the telegraph network.

alternatives.label: Recorded skies
alternatives.text: The British artist William Ascroft made thousands of colour sketches of the strange sunsets seen in London after the eruption, now a record of its atmospheric effects.

entries.title: The Devil's Footprints: hoof-marks across the snow of Devon
entries.mainstream: On the night of 8–9 February 1855, after heavy snow, trails of hoof-like marks appeared around the Exe Estuary in Devon, England, covering an estimated 40 to 100 miles in total. The prints, about 4 inches long and mostly in a single line, were reported to pass over roofs and walls and through obstacles, and some locals attributed them to the Devil. The event was reported in the Illustrated London News and other newspapers.

alternatives.label: Animal tracks
alternatives.text: Proposed explanations include wood mice or other small animals hopping in the snow, badgers, donkeys and ponies, and birds; Mike Dash concluded there was no single source and that some trails were probably hoaxes.

alternatives.label: A runaway balloon
alternatives.text: Author Geoffrey Household suggested an experimental balloon released from Devonport Dockyard trailing shackles on its mooring ropes; critics doubt it could have followed such a course without snagging.

alternatives.label: Exaggeration
alternatives.text: Sceptics such as Joe Nickell argue that no one followed the whole trail, and that separate tracks were combined into one story by excited reports.

entries.title: Halley's Comet 1910: comet pills and the poison-tail panic
entries.mainstream: In February 1910 astronomers at Yerkes Observatory reported that the spectrum of Halley's Comet showed cyanogen, a poisonous gas, and it was known that Earth would pass through the comet's tail in May. The French astronomer and popular writer Camille Flammarion was reported as saying the gas could "impregnate the atmosphere and possibly snuff out all life on the planet". Although most astronomers explained that the tail was far too thin to cause harm, people in several countries bought "anti-comet pills", gas masks and comet umbrellas, sealed their homes, and held comet parties. Earth passed through the tail around 18–19 May 1910 without any effect. Mark Twain, born in the comet year of 1835, had predicted he would "go out with it"; he died on 21 April 1910, the day after the comet's perihelion.

alternatives.label: Science misread
alternatives.text: Historians use the episode as a case study in how a real scientific finding, amplified by newspapers, can turn into public panic.

alternatives.label: Ancient fear
alternatives.text: Comets have been seen as omens of disaster in many cultures, including Halley's appearance before the Norman Conquest of 1066, so the 1910 panic drew on a very old tradition.

alternatives.label: Coincidence
alternatives.text: Twain's death is often told as an uncanny fulfilment; sceptics note that he was 74 and in poor health.

sources.title: Science History Institute: The Comet Panic of 1910, Revisited
Library of Congress: Halley's Comet – Topics in Chronicling America

entries.title: Kaspar Hauser: the boy from the dark cell, and the lost-prince theory
entries.mainstream: On 26 May 1828 a teenage boy was found in Nuremberg, Bavaria, carrying two letters and barely able to speak. As Kaspar Hauser he said he had spent his whole childhood alone in a dark cell, fed bread and water by an unseen man. He became a European sensation, was wounded in mysterious attacks, and on 14 December 1833 came home in Ansbach with a deep stab wound, saying a stranger had attacked him in the Court Garden; he died on 17 December. A rumour spread that he was the hereditary prince of Baden, born in 1812 and supposedly switched at birth. DNA tests reported in 1996 and a 2024 study of several samples attributed to him found that his mitochondrial DNA did not match the House of Baden line.

alternatives.label: Lost prince
alternatives.text: For nearly two centuries supporters argued he was the Baden heir hidden for dynastic reasons and murdered to keep the secret; the 2024 genetic study is widely seen as ruling this out.

alternatives.label: Impostor
alternatives.text: Sceptics at the time and since have argued that he exaggerated or invented his story and inflicted his own wounds, possibly including the fatal one by accident; a 1928 medical study supported self-infliction, while a 2005 forensic analysis was inconclusive.

alternatives.label: Feral child
alternatives.text: Others see him as a genuinely neglected or abused child whose true origins remain unknown; he is often discussed alongside other "feral children".

entries.title: Zarathustra (Zoroaster): a prophet nobody can date
entries.dateNote: Proposed dates range from c. 1500 BCE to the 6th century BCE
entries.mainstream: Zarathustra (Greek Zoroaster) is the prophet of Zoroastrianism, the ancient religion of Iran centred on the wise lord Ahura Mazda and a cosmic struggle between truth (asha) and the lie (druj). The oldest texts attributed to him are the Gathas, hymns in Old Avestan preserved in the Avesta. Almost nothing about his life can be confirmed independently, and his date is one of the widest-ranging in the history of religion. Because the language of the Gathas is very close to that of the Rigveda, many linguists place him somewhere around 1500–1000 BCE; a later Zoroastrian tradition dates him "258 years before Alexander", i.e. around the 6th century BCE. Zoroastrianism became the main religion of the Achaemenid, Parthian and Sasanian empires and survives today among Parsis and Iranian Zoroastrians.

alternatives.label: Early date
alternatives.text: Many Iranists (for example Mary Boyce) place him in the late 2nd millennium BCE, among pastoral peoples of Central Asia, based on the archaic language and the society described in the Gathas.

alternatives.label: Late date
alternatives.text: Others follow the traditional "258 years before Alexander" figure and place him in the 7th–6th century BCE, close to the rise of the Persian Empire.

alternatives.label: Fabulous antiquity
alternatives.text: Some Greek writers, quoted by Pliny the Elder, placed Zoroaster thousands of years before Plato; scholars regard these figures as legendary.

alternatives.label: Influence on other religions
alternatives.text: Scholars debate how far Zoroastrian ideas such as a final judgement, resurrection, a saviour figure and heaven and hell influenced post-exilic Judaism, Christianity and Islam; some see strong influence, others parallel development.

entries.title: Yima's Var: the Persian shelter built against a world-ending winter
entries.dateNote: Text date uncertain (Avestan oral tradition, written down in the Sasanian era); story older
entries.mainstream: In the Vendidad (Videvdad), a Zoroastrian text in the Avesta, the god Ahura Mazda warns Yima, the first king, that terrible winters are coming that will destroy most life. He tells Yima to build a var, an enclosure, and to bring into it the seeds of the best men and women, animals, plants and fires, so that they can repopulate the world afterwards. Yima, who presides over a golden age without death or sickness, is the same figure as Jamshid in later Persian tradition, celebrated in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (c. 1010 CE) as a great king who fell through pride. He is linguistically cognate with Yama, the first mortal and king of the dead in Indian tradition.

alternatives.label: Ark parallel
alternatives.text: Many writers note the similarity to Noah, Utnapishtim and Manu: a chosen survivor saves living things from a world-ending disaster; here the disaster is cold rather than water.

alternatives.label: Ice Age memory?
alternatives.text: Bal Gangadhar Tilak's The Arctic Home in the Vedas (1903) used the Vendidad's winters to argue for an Arctic homeland of the early Indo-Europeans; this idea is not accepted by mainstream scholars and is regarded as speculative.

alternatives.label: Mythic winter
alternatives.text: Scholars usually read the var as a mythic paradise or a cosmological story rather than a memory of a specific climate event; comparisons are drawn with the Norse Fimbulwinter before Ragnarök.

entries.title: The Cyrus Cylinder: the "first charter of human rights"?
entries.mainstream: The Cyrus Cylinder is a clay cylinder inscribed in Akkadian cuneiform, made after Cyrus the Great of Persia captured Babylon in 539 BCE. It was found in 1879 by Hormuzd Rassam at Babylon and is in the British Museum. In the traditional style of Mesopotamian building inscriptions, it condemns the previous king Nabonidus, presents Cyrus as chosen by the god Marduk, and describes him restoring temples and returning deported peoples and their gods to their homes. In 2010 the British Museum identified fragments of copies of the same text on tablets in its collection. The Hebrew Bible (Ezra) also credits Cyrus with allowing exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple, although the cylinder does not mention Jews.

alternatives.label: Human-rights charter
alternatives.text: In 1971 the Shah of Iran promoted the cylinder as "the first charter of human rights", and a replica is displayed at the United Nations; this view remains popular in Iran and elsewhere.

alternatives.label: Royal propaganda
alternatives.text: Most historians see it as a skilful piece of Mesopotamian royal propaganda in a long-established genre, legitimising a foreign conqueror; it does not set out universal rights.

alternatives.label: Biblical connection
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether the cylinder's general policy of repatriation supports the Bible's account of a decree for the Jews (Ezra 1 and 6) or only shows that such a policy was plausible.

entries.changed: 1879: found at Babylon. 1971: promoted as a human-rights charter. 2010: further copies of the text identified.

media.title: A new beginning for the Middle East: The Cyrus Cylinder and Ancient Persia

entries.title: The lost army of Cambyses: 50,000 men swallowed by the desert?
entries.mainstream: According to Herodotus (Histories 3.26), the Persian king Cambyses II, after conquering Egypt, sent 50,000 soldiers from Thebes to attack the Ammonians of the Siwa oasis and burn the oracle of Amun. The army reached an oasis seven days' march into the desert, then vanished: the Ammonians said a great southern wind buried it under sand. No trace of the army has been confirmed, and the story has become one of the desert's best-known mysteries.

alternatives.label: Buried by a sandstorm
alternatives.text: The traditional view takes Herodotus at face value. In 2009 Italian explorers Angelo and Alfredo Castiglioni announced finds of bones, weapons and other objects they linked to the army; these claims were widely reported but not confirmed in peer-reviewed archaeology, and Egyptian authorities were sceptical.

alternatives.label: Defeated, not buried
alternatives.text: Egyptologist Olaf Kaper (Leiden) argued in 2014 that the army was in fact defeated by an Egyptian rebel leader, Petubastis III, and that the sandstorm tale was later Persian face-saving; this is a hypothesis based on inscriptions from the Dakhla oasis.

alternatives.label: Exaggeration
alternatives.text: Other historians suggest that the size of the army, or the whole episode, may be exaggerated in Herodotus, who wrote around 70 years later and portrays Cambyses as mad.

entries.title: Alamut and the Assassins: hashish gardens and the Old Man of the Mountain
entries.mainstream: In 1090 the Ismaili missionary Hasan-i Sabbah took the mountain fortress of Alamut in northern Iran and founded the Nizari Ismaili state, a network of castles in Iran and Syria that survived until the Mongols took Alamut in 1256. Facing far larger Seljuk armies, the Nizaris used targeted killings of political and military leaders, which made them notorious. Their enemies called them hashishiyya, a term of abuse that reached Europe through the Crusaders as "Assassins". The Mongols destroyed Alamut's famous library, though the historian Juvayni saved some works first.

alternatives.label: Hashish and paradise legend
alternatives.text: Marco Polo (c. 1300) and Crusader writers described the "Old Man of the Mountain" drugging young men and placing them in a secret garden of paradise so they would die for him; tales also told of followers leaping to their deaths on command.

alternatives.label: Legends of enemies
alternatives.text: Modern historians of the Ismailis, notably Farhad Daftary, argue that these "Assassin legends" were invented or embellished by hostile Sunni and Crusader writers and that there is no evidence the Nizaris used hashish.

alternatives.label: Lasting myth
alternatives.text: The legends shaped the word "assassin" in European languages and modern fiction; the Nizari Ismaili community continues today under the Aga Khan.

entries.title: Jikji: the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, 78 years before Gutenberg
entries.mainstream: Jikji (in full Baegun Hwasang Chorok Buljo Jikji Simche Yojeol) is a Korean anthology of Zen (Seon) Buddhist teachings printed with movable metal type at Heungdeok temple near Cheongju in 1377, during the Goryeo dynasty. It is the oldest existing book printed with movable metal type, about 78 years older than the Gutenberg Bible. Only the second of its two volumes survives; it was acquired in Korea in the late 19th century by the French diplomat Victor Collin de Plancy and is held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France, where the Korean scholar Park Byeong-seon identified its significance in 1972. It was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2001.

alternatives.label: East Asian priority
alternatives.text: Movable type itself was invented earlier in China by Bi Sheng (c. 1040, ceramic type), and Korean records describe metal-type printing in the 13th century, but no earlier metal-type books survive.

alternatives.label: Did it reach Europe?
alternatives.text: Some writers have suggested that knowledge of East Asian printing reached Gutenberg through trade or travellers; there is no direct evidence, and most historians see European printing as an independent development. This connection remains speculative.

alternatives.label: Ownership
alternatives.text: Korea has sought the return of Jikji; France holds it as legally acquired. The dispute is part of a wider debate about cultural heritage held abroad.

entries.title: Korea's egg-born kings: Jumong, Bak Hyeokgeose and Kim Suro
entries.mainstream: Korean founding legends repeatedly describe kings hatched from eggs. Jumong (Dongmyeong), founder of Goguryeo (traditionally 37 BCE), was born from an egg laid by Lady Yuhwa, daughter of the river god Habaek, after she was touched by sunlight. Bak Hyeokgeose, founder of Silla (traditionally 57 BCE), hatched from a large egg found beside a well where a white horse knelt. Kim Suro, founder of Geumgwan Gaya (traditionally 42 CE), came from one of six golden eggs lowered from the sky in a box. The stories are recorded in the Samguk sagi (1145) and Samguk yusa (late 13th century); the Gwanggaeto Stele of 414 CE already states that Goguryeo's founder came out of an egg.

alternatives.label: Sacred kingship
alternatives.text: Scholars read the eggs as markers of heavenly origin that legitimised royal lineages, linking rulers to the sun or sky; similar motifs appear in Manchurian and other north-east Asian traditions.

alternatives.label: Wider pattern
alternatives.text: Egg births are widespread in world myth: the cosmic egg of Pangu, the Hindu Hiranyagarbha, the Orphic egg, Leda's eggs in Greek myth; whether these reflect diffusion or independent invention is debated.

alternatives.label: Historical kernel
alternatives.text: Historians accept that Goguryeo, Silla and Gaya were real states, but the traditional founding dates, especially Silla's early date, are considered unreliable.

entries.title: Shahr-e Sukhteh, the "Burnt City": an artificial eye and a 5,000-year-old animation?
entries.mainstream: Shahr-e Sukhteh ("Burnt City") in Sistan and Baluchestan, south-east Iran, was a large Bronze Age urban settlement occupied from about 3200 BCE until roughly 2000 BCE, and burned several times during its history. Excavations since the 1960s (Italian and later Iranian teams) found evidence of crafts, long-distance trade with Mesopotamia, Central Asia and the Indus, and well-preserved organic remains. Famous finds include an artificial eyeball found in 2006 with the skeleton of a tall woman, dated about 2900–2800 BCE, a game board with dice, and an earthenware goblet painted with a series of images of a goat leaping towards a tree. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.

alternatives.label: First animation?
alternatives.text: When the goblet's five images are viewed in sequence they appear to show the goat leaping; Iranian archaeologists have called it the earliest known animation. Others think the repetition is decorative and that calling it animation is a modern reading.

alternatives.label: Ancient surgery
alternatives.text: Excavators have reported a child's skull with signs of surgery, presented as early brain surgery; these claims are discussed mainly in Iranian publications and press reports and are less widely examined in international literature.

alternatives.label: Lost civilisation?
alternatives.text: Together with Jiroft, Shahr-e Sukhteh is cited as evidence of a sophisticated eastern Iranian Bronze Age culture largely unknown before the late 20th century; it is a lost civilisation in the sense of being forgotten, not mysterious.

entries.title: The Behistun inscription: a king's cliff boast that unlocked cuneiform, and the impostor he killed
entries.mainstream: At Mount Behistun (Bisotun) in western Iran, about 100 metres up a limestone cliff above an ancient road, Darius I of Persia had a relief and a long inscription carved around 520 BCE in three languages and scripts: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian (Akkadian). It tells how Darius came to power after defeating Gaumata, a Magian priest who, he says, had pretended to be Bardiya (Smerdis), the brother of the previous king Cambyses. Copied at great risk by Henry Rawlinson between 1835 and 1847, the trilingual text became the key to deciphering cuneiform, much as the Rosetta Stone was for Egyptian hieroglyphs. In 1857 the Royal Asiatic Society asked four scholars (Rawlinson, Edward Hincks, Julius Oppert and William Henry Fox Talbot) to translate a newly found Assyrian text independently; their versions agreed closely, convincing the public that Akkadian could be read.

alternatives.label: Darius's account
alternatives.text: Darius says the real Bardiya had been secretly killed by Cambyses and that Gaumata was an impostor; Herodotus tells a similar story of a false Smerdis.

alternatives.label: Usurper's propaganda?
alternatives.text: Many historians suggest that Darius himself may have killed the genuine Bardiya and invented the impostor story to justify a usurpation; the evidence allows both readings.

alternatives.label: Decipherment
alternatives.text: The 1857 translation test is often described as one of the first deliberate tests of a decipherment; the convergence of the four versions is still cited as evidence that cuneiform was really understood.

entries.changed: c. 520 BCE: carved. 1835–47: copied by Rawlinson. 1857: independent translation test confirms cuneiform decipherment.

entries.title: Qanats: Persia's underground rivers and their world-wide spread
entries.dateNote: Early 1st millennium BCE onwards; still in use
entries.mainstream: A qanat is a gently sloping underground tunnel that taps groundwater at the foot of hills and carries it by gravity, sometimes for tens of kilometres, to fields and towns, with a line of vertical shafts for digging and maintenance. Developed in Iran in the early 1st millennium BCE (or possibly earlier), the technique spread under the Persian empires and later Islamic and other states, from Oman (aflaj) and North Africa (foggaras) to Spain and the Turpan oasis in China (karez). The Qasabeh qanat at Gonabad, said to date from c. 700–500 BCE, has 427 wells and a total length of about 33 km. Eleven Iranian qanats were inscribed by UNESCO as "The Persian Qanat" in 2016.

alternatives.label: Where invented?
alternatives.text: Most scholars credit Iran, but some archaeologists argue that similar systems in south-east Arabia (the UAE and Oman) date to the early Iron Age and may have developed independently or earlier; the dating evidence is debated.

alternatives.label: Water and empire
alternatives.text: Historians link qanats to Achaemenid policy: Polybius records that the Persians granted tax privileges to those who brought water to dry land, and Persian engineers built qanats in Egypt's Kharga oasis.

alternatives.label: Fossil water
alternatives.text: Like the Garamantes' foggaras in the Sahara, qanats can deplete ancient groundwater; many have dried up in recent decades as deep pumped wells lower the water table.

entries.title: Turtle ships: Korea's armoured warships and the "first ironclad" debate
entries.dateNote: Mentioned 1413; famous in the Imjin War 1592–1598
evidenceTypes: textual (Joseon annals, Yi Sun-sin's war diary)
entries.mainstream: The geobukseon (turtle ship) was a Korean warship with a covered deck, often shown with spikes and a dragon head at the bow. Ships called gwiseon are mentioned in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty in 1413 and 1415. An improved design was used by Admiral Yi Sun-sin against the Japanese invasions of 1592–1598 ordered by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, beginning at the Battle of Sacheon in 1592, alongside the main panokseon warships. Yi's fleet won a series of victories that cut Japanese supply lines. No original turtle ship survives, and searches for wrecks have so far not found one.

alternatives.label: First ironclad
alternatives.text: Popular accounts in Korea and elsewhere describe the turtle ship as the world's first ironclad, with a roof of iron plates.

alternatives.label: Uncertain evidence
alternatives.text: Many historians note that Yi Sun-sin's own reports and other contemporary Korean sources do not clearly describe iron plating; later illustrations show hexagonal plates that could be iron or wood. The armour question is unresolved.

alternatives.label: Lost wrecks
alternatives.text: Several surveys of the seabed near battle sites have reported possible remains, but none has been confirmed as a turtle ship.
