entries.title: Himiko, the shaman queen of Yamatai: Japan's lost kingdom
entries.dateNote: Reigned c. 189 – c. 248 CE (per Chinese sources)
entries.mainstream: The Chinese Records of Wei (Wei zhi, part of the Records of the Three Kingdoms compiled by Chen Shou in the late 3rd century) describe the land of Wa (Japan) as unified under Himiko, an unmarried queen of Yamatai who "occupied herself with magic and sorcery" (kidō), lived secluded with a thousand female attendants and was served by her younger brother. In 238 or 239 CE she sent envoys to the Wei court, which gave her the title "Queen of Wa, friendly to Wei", a gold seal and a hundred bronze mirrors. When she died around 248, a large mound was raised and, the text says, over a hundred attendants followed her in death. Japan's own chronicles, the Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720), do not name her.

alternatives.label: Kinai (Nara) location
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists place Yamatai in the Nara basin and link Himiko to the Makimuku site and the Hashihaka kofun, an early keyhole tomb dated to the mid-3rd century; the tomb is managed by the Imperial Household Agency and cannot be excavated freely.

alternatives.label: Kyushu location
alternatives.text: Others place Yamatai in northern Kyushu, pointing to the Wei zhi's itinerary and to large moated settlements such as Yoshinogari; taken literally, the itinerary's distances lead into the ocean, so both camps must correct it.

alternatives.label: Identity
alternatives.text: The Nihon Shoki quotes the Wei zhi in its section on Empress Jingū, and some scholars link Himiko with figures such as Yamatototohimomosohime; none of these identifications is proven.

entries.title: Kitsune and Tamamo-no-Mae: the nine-tailed fox and the Killing Stone
entries.dateNote: Set in the 12th century; tale written down from the 14th–17th centuries; stone split 2022
entries.mainstream: In Japanese folklore, kitsune are foxes with magical powers that grow more tails as they age, up to nine, and can take human form, often as beautiful women; some are benevolent messengers of the rice deity Inari, others tricksters. The idea draws on Chinese huli jing (fox spirit) lore. The most famous tale is Tamamo-no-Mae, a brilliant courtesan of a 12th-century emperor (Konoe or Toba, depending on the version) who fell mysteriously ill; the diviner Abe no Yasuchika exposed her as a nine-tailed fox, and warriors killed her on the plain of Nasu. Her body became the Sesshō-seki (Killing Stone), a rock in a volcanic area of Tochigi where poisonous gases rise. The poet Bashō visited it in 1689. On 5 March 2022 the stone was reported to have split in two, probably through weathering, and a ceremony was held to appease the spirit.

alternatives.label: Volcanic origin of the legend
alternatives.text: Volcanic gases (such as hydrogen sulphide) at Nasu really do kill small animals near the stone; many see the "killing" legend as an explanation of this natural hazard.

alternatives.label: Fox possession
alternatives.text: Kitsunetsuki (fox possession) was a widely reported belief in Japan into the 20th century; psychiatrists and anthropologists have studied it as a culture-bound way of describing illness or social conflict.

alternatives.label: Shared Asian motif
alternatives.text: The nine-tailed fox spirit appears in Chinese, Korean (kumiho) and Japanese tradition; the Tamamo story itself links to Chinese tales of fox consorts who ruined kings.

entries.title: The Takeuchi documents and the "Tomb of Christ" in northern Japan
entries.mainstream: The Takeuchi documents are texts promoted in the 1920s–30s by Takeuchi Kiyomaro (Kyōmaro), founder of the Kōso Kōtai Jingū religious group, who claimed they were ancient family records written in "divine characters". They describe a vast prehistory in which Japan was the centre of the world and figures such as Moses, the Buddha and Jesus came to Japan to serve its emperors. In 1935 Takeuchi identified a grave mound in the village of Herai (now Shingō, Aomori) as the tomb of Christ: according to the story, Jesus studied in Japan, returned to Judea, escaped crucifixion while his brother Isukiri died in his place, and returned to Japan to live to 106. The village has held a "Christ festival" every June since 1964, and the site is a tourist attraction.

alternatives.label: Modern forgery
alternatives.text: Historian Kanō Kōkichi examined five of the documents in the 1930s and concluded they were modern forgeries; mainstream historians and linguists agree, citing anachronistic language and lack of any earlier provenance.

alternatives.label: Believers
alternatives.text: A small number of followers continue to treat the documents as genuine; the shrine says the originals and sacred treasures are kept privately. The originals have not been made available for independent study.

alternatives.label: A wider pattern
alternatives.text: Stories that Jesus survived or lived abroad also appear elsewhere, for example claims of his tomb at Roza Bal in Srinagar, Kashmir, and Nicolas Notovitch's 1894 "Life of Saint Issa" set in Tibet; these too are rejected by mainstream historians.

entries.changed: 1935: tomb announced. 1930s: documents examined and judged forgeries. 1964 onwards: annual festival at the site.

entries.title: Tsunami stones: Japan's warnings carved in rock
entries.dateNote: Many erected after 1896 and 1933; some much older
entries.mainstream: Along Japan's north-east coast stand hundreds of stone markers, some said to be over 600 years old, that record past tsunamis, list the dead or warn people where not to build. Most were set up after the 1896 Meiji Sanriku earthquake and tsunami, which killed about 22,000 people, and the 1933 Shōwa Sanriku tsunami. The stone at Aneyoshi in Miyako, Iwate, reads in part: "High dwellings are the peace and harmony of our descendants. Remember the calamity of the great tsunamis. Do not build any homes below this point." In the Tōhoku tsunami of 11 March 2011 the water at Aneyoshi stopped short of the stone, and the hamlet's houses, built above it, survived; elsewhere many towns had spread below old markers, trusting sea walls.

alternatives.label: Generational forgetting
alternatives.text: Tohoku University disaster researcher Fumihiko Imamura has observed that "it takes about three generations for people to forget"; the stones are studied as an attempt to beat that forgetting.

alternatives.label: Messages to the future
alternatives.text: Researchers compare tsunami stones with other long-term warnings, such as European "hunger stones" in river beds and proposals for markers at nuclear-waste sites meant to last 10,000 years.

alternatives.label: Limits
alternatives.text: Many stones were ignored, moved or eroded; after 2011 some argued that ruined buildings should be preserved as warnings in the same way.

entries.title: Namazu: the giant catfish that shakes Japan
entries.dateNote: Belief older; namazu-e prints flourished after the 1855 Edo earthquake
entries.mainstream: In Japanese folk belief, earthquakes are caused by Ōnamazu, a giant catfish living in the mud beneath the islands. The god Kashima (Takemikazuchi) keeps it pinned down with a great stone, the kaname-ishi, which visitors can still see at Kashima Shrine in Ibaraki; when the god's attention lapses, the catfish thrashes. After the Ansei Edo earthquake of 11 November 1855, which devastated Edo (Tokyo), hundreds of popular woodblock prints called namazu-e appeared, showing the catfish being punished by townspeople, apologising, or, in some prints, as an agent of "world renewal" (yonaoshi) that redistributed wealth from the rich to the builders and labourers who profited from reconstruction.

alternatives.label: Animal precursors
alternatives.text: The belief that catfish behave strangely before earthquakes has prompted scientific study in Japan; animal-behaviour precursors remain unproven, and no reliable prediction method based on them exists.

alternatives.label: Social commentary
alternatives.text: Historians such as Gregory Smits read the namazu-e as political and economic commentary in late-Tokugawa Japan, expressing hopes and fears about social change.

alternatives.label: World-supporting creatures
alternatives.text: Many cultures explain earthquakes by a creature carrying or under the earth, such as the Hindu world-elephants or the Greek god Poseidon "Earth-shaker"; namazu is the Japanese form of this pattern.

entries.title: Lucy (Dinkinesh): the skeleton that walked upright 3.2 million years ago
entries.mainstream: On 24 November 1974, at Hadar in the Afar region of Ethiopia, Donald Johanson and Tom Gray found the first bones of a partial skeleton (AL 288-1) of Australopithecus afarensis, about 40 percent complete and dated to about 3.2 million years ago. That night the team played the Beatles' "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds", and the skeleton was nicknamed Lucy; in Amharic she is Dinkinesh, "you are marvellous". Her pelvis and leg bones show she walked upright, while her brain was ape-sized, settling a major debate: upright walking came long before big brains. She is kept at the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa.

alternatives.label: Fall from a tree
alternatives.text: A 2016 study (Kappelman and colleagues) proposed that compressive fractures in Lucy's bones show she died after falling from a tall tree; Johanson and others replied that such breaks commonly occur during fossilisation.

alternatives.label: Tree climber too?
alternatives.text: Researchers debate how much time A. afarensis spent in trees: curved finger bones and strong arms suggest climbing, while the feet and hips were adapted for walking.

alternatives.label: Ancestor or cousin
alternatives.text: Lucy's species is often presented as a likely ancestor of Homo, but newer finds (for example Australopithecus deyiremeda and Kenyanthropus) show several hominin species lived at the same time, making the family tree bushier and the direct line uncertain.

entries.changed: 1974: found. 1978: species Australopithecus afarensis named. 2007–2013: toured the USA. 2016: tree-fall hypothesis published.

entries.title: Laas Geel: the painted cattle of Somaliland
entries.mainstream: Laas Geel is a group of rock shelters on the outskirts of Hargeisa in Somaliland whose walls are covered with vivid painted figures, mainly of humped and long-horned cattle with decorated necks and what look like ceremonial robes, together with people with raised arms, dogs and wild animals. A French archaeological team led by Xavier Gutherz documented them in 2002–2003, although local people had known of the site for centuries. The paintings are estimated to be about 5,500 to 4,500 years old and belong to an "Ethiopian-Arabian" rock-art style found across the Horn of Africa and southern Arabia. They are among the earliest evidence of cattle herding in the Horn.

alternatives.label: Cattle cult
alternatives.text: Archaeologists interpret the decorated cattle and worshipping figures as evidence of a pastoral society in which cattle had religious as well as economic importance, a pattern also seen among later herders of East Africa and in ancient Egypt.

alternatives.label: Arabian links
alternatives.text: The shared style with southern Arabian rock art is read as evidence of contacts across the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden in the 4th–3rd millennia BCE; the direction and nature of the contact are debated.

alternatives.label: Dating uncertainty
alternatives.text: The paintings have not been dated directly; the estimates come from style and regional context, so the age could change with new evidence.

entries.title: The settlement of Madagascar: voyagers from Borneo to Africa's great island
entries.dateNote: Main settlement 1st millennium CE (earlier dates debated)
entries.mainstream: Madagascar was one of the last large landmasses settled by people. Its language, Malagasy, is Austronesian, and in 1951 the linguist Otto Dahl showed that its closest relative is Ma'anyan, spoken in south-east Borneo, more than 7,000 km away across the Indian Ocean. Genetic studies show that Malagasy people have roughly mixed Southeast Asian (Austronesian) and East African (Bantu) ancestry; one study (Cox and colleagues, 2012) estimated that the Asian maternal lineages trace back to a small founding group of perhaps about 30 women. Most evidence points to substantial settlement during the 1st millennium CE, followed by the extinction of the island's megafauna, including elephant birds and giant lemurs.

alternatives.label: Much earlier visitors?
alternatives.text: A 2018 study (Hansford and colleagues) reported cut marks on elephant-bird bones dated to around 10,500 years ago, suggesting a much older human presence; other researchers question whether the marks were made by people. The question is open.

alternatives.label: How did they come?
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether settlers sailed directly across the ocean, followed the coasts of the Indian Ocean via India and Arabia, or came in multiple waves; Austronesian outrigger technology made long voyages possible.

alternatives.label: Accidental or planned
alternatives.text: Some suggest that the founding group may have been small and partly accidental (for example drifting boats); others see deliberate trade-linked voyages. Malagasy oral traditions about the first inhabitants, the Vazimba, add another layer.

sources.title: A small cohort of Island Southeast Asian women founded Madagascar
Early Holocene human presence in Madagascar evidenced by exploitation of avian megafauna

entries.title: The Vazimba and the kalanoro: Madagascar's first people and the little forest folk
entries.dateNote: Undated tradition; refers to the first settlers
entries.mainstream: In popular Malagasy tradition, the Vazimba were the island's first inhabitants, often described as small people who lived in the forests before later arrivals, knew no iron or rice farming, and kept cattle without eating them; their graves and the spirits of Vazimba are still honoured or feared at sacred sites, especially in the central highlands. Malagasy folklore also tells of the kalanoro, small hairy forest beings with long nails and backward-pointing feet, sometimes said to steal children, sometimes to serve people as spirit helpers and healers who speak through mediums.

alternatives.label: Memory of first settlers
alternatives.text: Some historians think Vazimba stories preserve memories of earlier waves of Austronesian settlers, absorbed by later arrivals; the idea that they were a distinct short-statured people has not been proven.

alternatives.label: Ancestors and land
alternatives.text: Anthropologists emphasise the Vazimba's role as original "owners of the land" whose spirits must be respected, a role found in many cultures' stories of first peoples.

alternatives.label: Cryptid or spirit
alternatives.text: Cryptozoology programmes have searched for the kalanoro as an unknown primate; mainstream researchers treat it as a folklore being, possibly influenced by memories of extinct giant lemurs. A parallel often drawn is Hawaiʻi's menehune.

entries.title: Lepenski Vir: fish-faced stone heads of the Danube's Iron Gates
entries.mainstream: Lepenski Vir is a Mesolithic and early Neolithic settlement on the Serbian bank of the Danube in the Iron Gates gorge, occupied in phases from about 9500 to about 6000 BCE. It was excavated from 1965 by Dragoslav Srejović and, because the Đerdap dam would flood it, the site was moved about 30 metres higher in 1971. Its inhabitants, mainly fishers and foragers, built houses with trapezoidal floor plans and hearths, buried some of the dead beneath the floors, and carved large river boulders into sculptures with bulging eyes and fish-like mouths. Ancient DNA studies (for example Mathieson et al., Nature 2018) show that the Iron Gates foragers met and mixed with incoming farmers whose ancestry came from Anatolia.

alternatives.label: Fish-people
alternatives.text: The sculptures are often described as human-fish hybrids; interpretations include river spirits, ancestors, or deities linked to the Danube's fish (such as sturgeon) on which the community depended.

alternatives.label: Sacred geometry
alternatives.text: Some writers argue the trapezoidal houses encode deliberate geometry or astronomy aligned with the nearby trapezoid-shaped mountain Treskavac; archaeologists generally see the shape as practical and symbolic rather than evidence of advanced mathematics.

alternatives.label: Contact zone
alternatives.text: The site is studied as one of the clearest places in Europe where hunter-gatherers and the first farmers met, traded and intermarried rather than one simply replacing the other.

sources.title: The genomic history of southeastern Europe

entries.title: The Saqqara Bird: an ancient Egyptian model glider?
entries.mainstream: The Saqqara Bird is a small model made of sycamore wood, with a wingspan of about 18 centimetres, found in 1898 during excavation of the tomb of Pa-di-Imen at Saqqara, Egypt, and dated to about 200 BCE. It is kept in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. It has a bird's head with painted eyes and a beak, straight outstretched wings and a vertical tail. In 1972 Egyptian physician Khalil Messiha, a model-aircraft enthusiast, argued that its shape resembles a glider and that it might be a scale model of an ancient flying machine.

alternatives.label: Glider model
alternatives.text: Messiha and later ancient-astronaut and lost-technology writers argue the wings and fuselage resemble aircraft design and that the bird may be evidence of ancient knowledge of flight.

alternatives.label: Bird toy or ornament
alternatives.text: Egyptologists see it as a bird figure, possibly a toy, a votive object or a weather vane. Bird figures are common in Egyptian art, and the model has no horizontal tailplane.

alternatives.label: Replica tests
alternatives.text: Glider replicas have been built and tested; they reportedly flew only poorly or after a horizontal tailplane (which the original lacks) was added, so the tests have not settled the question for supporters.

entries.title: The Abydos "helicopter" hieroglyphs
entries.mainstream: On a ceiling beam in the Temple of Seti I at Abydos, Egypt (built about 1290–1279 BCE), a group of carved hieroglyphs looks like a helicopter, a submarine and a jet plane. Photographs spread widely online from the 1990s onwards, and the carving became a famous example in ancient-astronaut circles. Egyptologists explain it as a palimpsest: the beam was first carved with a royal title of Seti I, then the hollows were filled with plaster and recarved with a title of his son Ramesses II. Over the centuries the plaster fell out, leaving the two sets of signs overlapping, and the combined shapes happen to resemble modern machines.

alternatives.label: Ancient aircraft
alternatives.text: Supporters argue the shapes are too close to modern vehicles to be accidental and that they show technology seen or remembered by the ancient Egyptians.

alternatives.label: Recarving explanation
alternatives.text: Egyptologists can read both inscriptions and point out that the recarving of earlier kings' names was common; the same kind of overlap is visible elsewhere in Egyptian monuments.

alternatives.label: Retouched photos
alternatives.text: Some widely shared images of the panel were digitally edited to sharpen the machine-like shapes, which made the resemblance look stronger than it is on the stone.

entries.title: Hatshepsut: the woman who ruled as pharaoh, and the attempt to erase her
entries.mainstream: Hatshepsut was a ruler of Egypt's 18th Dynasty who reigned from about 1479 to 1458 BCE. First regent for her young stepson Thutmose III, she then took the full titles of a pharaoh and was often portrayed with the traditional male regalia, including a false beard. Her reign was prosperous: she built the temple at Deir el-Bahari and sent a famous trading expedition to Punt. Some decades after her death, many of her statues and images were smashed or chiselled out and her name was left off later king lists. In 2007 a mummy from tomb KV60 was identified as hers, in part because a loose molar in a box bearing her name fitted a gap in its jaw.

alternatives.label: Revenge
alternatives.text: An older view held that Thutmose III erased her out of hatred for a usurping stepmother; because the destruction happened late in his reign, perhaps 20 years after her death, many historians now doubt this.

alternatives.label: Succession politics
alternatives.text: A widely held explanation is that the erasure was meant to secure the succession for Thutmose III's son Amenhotep II and to remove a precedent for female kingship.

alternatives.label: Mummy identification
alternatives.text: The 2007 identification via the tooth and CT scans was widely reported; some specialists consider it plausible but not conclusive, as it is not based on DNA results that have been fully published.

media.title: The pharaoh that wouldn't be forgotten - Kate Green

entries.title: Pompeii and Herculaneum: frozen moments, re-read by new science
entries.mainstream: In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the Roman towns of Pompeii, Herculaneum and others under ash and pyroclastic flows. Pliny the Younger described the eruption and the death of his uncle Pliny the Elder in letters to the historian Tacitus. Excavations from the 18th century onwards revealed streets, houses, graffiti and paintings; from 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into the cavities left by bodies, creating the famous casts. New methods continue to change the story. A charcoal inscription found in 2018 dated to the 16th day before the Kalends of November supports an eruption in October rather than the traditional 24 August. Ancient DNA from the casts (2024) showed that some long-told stories were wrong. Since 2023 the Vesuvius Challenge has used X-ray scans and machine learning to read carbonised scrolls from Herculaneum without unrolling them.

alternatives.label: The eruption date
alternatives.text: The 24 August date comes from manuscript copies of Pliny's letter. Autumn fruits found in the ruins, warm clothing and the 2018 inscription point to October; some scholars still defend August.

alternatives.label: Stories in the casts
alternatives.text: Guides long described the casts as mothers with children or sisters embracing. The 2024 DNA study (Pilli et al.) found, for example, that an adult holding a child was an unrelated man, showing how modern assumptions had shaped the stories.

alternatives.label: Lost library
alternatives.text: Hundreds of carbonised papyri from the Villa of the Papyri, largely Epicurean philosophy (e.g. Philodemus), are being read for the first time; many hope that lost classical works will turn up as more scrolls are read.

entries.changed: 1863: plaster casts. 2018: October inscription. 2023–24: first words and passages read from unopened Herculaneum scrolls. 2024: DNA overturns cast stories.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD
Ancient DNA challenges prevailing interpretations of the Pompeii plaster casts

entries.title: The Eleusinian Mysteries: a secret kept for a thousand years, and a psychedelic theory
entries.dateNote: Attested from c. 7th–6th century BCE; ended c. 392–396 CE
entries.mainstream: The Eleusinian Mysteries were secret initiation rites held at Eleusis near Athens in honour of Demeter and her daughter Persephone, whose descent to the underworld and return explained the seasons. They are described in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (about 7th–6th century BCE) and drew initiates from across the Greek and later Roman world, including emperors. Initiates fasted, drank a barley drink called kykeon, and saw something in the Telesterion hall that they were forbidden to reveal; ancient writers said it removed the fear of death. The secret was kept so well that what exactly happened is still unknown. The rites ended in the late 4th century CE, after Theodosius I's measures against pagan cults and the sack of Eleusis by Alaric's Goths in 396.

alternatives.label: Ergot hypothesis
alternatives.text: In The Road to Eleusis (1978) R. Gordon Wasson, Albert Hofmann (who synthesised LSD) and Carl Ruck proposed that the kykeon contained ergot, a fungus on barley with LSD-like alkaloids. Brian Muraresku's The Immortality Key (2020) revived the idea. There is no direct chemical evidence from Eleusis.

alternatives.label: Ritual drama
alternatives.text: Many classicists think the experience came from fasting, a night procession, darkness and sudden light, and a dramatic re-enactment of the myth, without needing drugs; the toxicity of ergot is an objection to the drug theory.

alternatives.label: Origins
alternatives.text: Some scholars trace the cult back to the Mycenaean period (2nd millennium BCE); the evidence for its early origins is debated.

entries.title: Sutton Hoo: the ghost ship of an Anglo-Saxon king
entries.mainstream: Sutton Hoo, near Woodbridge in Suffolk, England, is a cemetery of early 7th-century burial mounds. In 1939 the landowner Edith Pretty asked the self-taught local archaeologist Basil Brown to dig the mounds; in Mound 1 he found the impression of a ship about 27 metres long, its wood rotted away but its rivets still in place. The burial chamber held the richest treasure known from Anglo-Saxon England, including the Sutton Hoo helmet, a gold belt buckle, shoulder clasps with garnet cloisonné, silver from the Byzantine Empire and coins from Merovingian Gaul. No body was found because the acidic soil dissolved bone. The story was dramatised in the 2021 film The Dig.

alternatives.label: Rædwald
alternatives.text: The most widely accepted identification is Rædwald, king of East Anglia (died about 624), who according to Bede kept both a Christian and a pagan altar. The dating of the coins fits this.

alternatives.label: Other kings
alternatives.text: Other candidates include his successors Eorpwald and Sigeberht; no inscription names the dead person.

alternatives.label: Body or cenotaph?
alternatives.text: Because no remains were found, some thought the ship was a memorial without a body; phosphate tests in the 1960s supported the presence of a body that has since dissolved.

alternatives.label: Rewriting the Dark Ages
alternatives.text: The find showed that early Anglo-Saxon England had sophisticated crafts and connections reaching to Byzantium, contradicting older views of a primitive Dark Age, and gave context to the poem Beowulf with its ship funeral.

entries.changed: 1939: excavated by Basil Brown; treasure given to the British Museum by Edith Pretty.

media.title: The Sutton Hoo ship burial: excavation

entries.title: Berserkers: Norse warriors in a frenzy, mushrooms, henbane or myth?
entries.dateNote: Earliest mention in Hrafnsmál (late 9th century); sagas 13th century
entries.mainstream: In Old Norse sources, berserkers were warriors who fought in a trance-like fury. The skaldic poem Hrafnsmál, about the battle of Hafrsfjord (late 9th century), mentions berserkers and ulfheðnar ("wolf-skins") in King Harald Fairhair's army. Snorri Sturluson's Ynglinga saga (13th century) says Odin's warriors went without mail, were mad as dogs or wolves, bit their shields, and could not be hurt by fire or iron. Medieval Icelandic law (the Grágás) made berserk frenzy an offence. Some of the 12th-century Lewis chessmen show warders biting their shields, which is often read as a depiction of berserkers.

alternatives.label: Fly agaric
alternatives.text: In 1784 the Swedish priest Samuel Ödman suggested that berserkers ate fly agaric mushrooms (Amanita muscaria). The idea became popular, but critics note that the mushroom usually causes nausea and drowsiness.

alternatives.label: Henbane
alternatives.text: A 2019 paper by Karsten Fatur in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology argued that henbane (Hyoscyamus niger) fits the described symptoms better; he presents it as speculation.

alternatives.label: Ritual and psychology
alternatives.text: Many historians see the berserk state as a ritual or cultic warrior identity linked to bear and wolf animal cults and to Odin, possibly with self-induced rage, rather than drug use.

alternatives.label: Literary exaggeration
alternatives.text: Since most detailed accounts are written centuries later, some scholars think the saga berserkers are partly literary stock characters, villains or bullies, rather than descriptions of real fighters.

sources.title: Sagas of the Solanaceae: Speculative ethnobotanical perspectives on the Norse berserkers

entries.title: The Uffington White Horse: a Bronze Age figure kept alive for 3,000 years
entries.mainstream: The Uffington White Horse is a highly stylised figure of a horse, about 110 metres long, cut into the chalk hillside below an Iron Age hillfort in Oxfordshire, England. It was long thought to be Iron Age, Anglo-Saxon or even 17th-century. In the 1990s, excavations by the Oxford Archaeological Unit dated the silt layers of the figure using optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) to between about 1380 and 550 BCE, making it the oldest known hill figure in Britain. It survived only because local communities regularly cleaned it ("scouring"), a custom that by the 18th century was accompanied by fairs and games.

alternatives.label: Horse or dragon?
alternatives.text: Local tradition links the figure to nearby Dragon Hill, where St George is said to have killed the dragon, and some have suggested the figure represents a dragon rather than a horse.

alternatives.label: Tribal or sun symbol
alternatives.text: Archaeologists suggest it may have been a tribal emblem or connected to a sun cult; similar horse designs appear on Iron Age coins. Its meaning is unknown.

alternatives.label: Chain of memory
alternatives.text: It is an unusual case of a monument that only exists because people kept maintaining it for perhaps 3,000 years, through changes of language, religion and population.

entries.title: Ulfberht swords: Viking blades made of steel from the East?
entries.mainstream: Around 170 medieval swords found mainly in northern Europe, dated from the 9th to the 11th century, carry the inlaid inscription +VLFBERH+T or similar variants. The name is Frankish, and the blades may have originated in a Rhineland workshop or brand. Metallurgical studies, notably by Alan Williams, found that some of them are made of unusually pure, high-carbon steel with very little slag, comparable to crucible steel, while others are ordinary iron, with differently spelled inscriptions, possibly copies or counterfeits. The swords were popularised by the 2012 PBS documentary Secrets of the Viking Sword.

alternatives.label: Steel from the East
alternatives.text: One hypothesis is that the crucible steel came from Central Asia or Iran (where crucible steel was produced) via the Volga trade route with which the Vikings were connected; this would make the best Ulfberhts a product of a long-distance trade.

alternatives.label: European production
alternatives.text: Others argue that the high-quality blades could have been produced in Europe by skilled smiths using carefully selected or refined iron, without imported crucible steel.

alternatives.label: Medieval counterfeits
alternatives.text: The variation in spelling and quality suggests that the name was a mark of quality that was imitated, an early example of brand counterfeiting.

entries.title: The "Battle of Los Angeles": the night the city fired at the sky
entries.mainstream: On the night of 24–25 February 1942, less than three months after Pearl Harbor and one day after a Japanese submarine shelled an oil field near Santa Barbara, air-raid sirens sounded across Los Angeles. Searchlights swept the sky and anti-aircraft batteries fired about 1,400 shells for roughly an hour at reported enemy aircraft. No bombs fell and no aircraft were shot down; five deaths were attributed to the event (traffic accidents and heart attacks), and falling shell fragments damaged buildings. Navy Secretary Frank Knox called it a false alarm caused by "jittery nerves"; the Army maintained that unidentified aircraft had been present. A widely reproduced Los Angeles Times photograph shows searchlights converging on an object.

alternatives.label: War nerves
alternatives.text: The mainstream explanation is a false alarm in a tense wartime atmosphere, possibly triggered by a stray weather balloon, after which gun flashes and shell bursts were themselves reported as aircraft.

alternatives.label: UFO
alternatives.text: From the 1980s onwards UFO writers presented the event as an encounter with an extraterrestrial craft, citing the searchlight photograph.

alternatives.label: A retouched photo
alternatives.text: The newspaper photograph was heavily retouched before publication, as was common at the time; the darkroom work makes the "object" look more solid than in the original negative.

entries.title: The 1919 eclipse: the day starlight proved Einstein right, or did it?
entries.mainstream: General relativity, published by Albert Einstein in 1915, predicted that the Sun's gravity would bend starlight twice as much as Newtonian physics suggested. During the total solar eclipse of 29 May 1919, British expeditions led by Arthur Eddington on the island of Príncipe and by Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson at Sobral in Brazil photographed stars near the darkened Sun. On 6 November 1919, the Astronomer Royal Frank Dyson announced that the results supported Einstein, and the story made Einstein world-famous overnight. Later eclipse and radio-astronomy measurements have confirmed the light bending predicted by general relativity with much higher precision.

alternatives.label: Selected data?
alternatives.text: In 1980 philosophers John Earman and Clark Glymour argued that Eddington and Dyson had favoured the data that fitted Einstein, discarding a set of Sobral plates that gave a Newton-like value; the episode is often cited as an example of confirmation bias.

alternatives.label: Vindicated
alternatives.text: A 1979 re-measurement of the Sobral plates with modern methods, and later historical analyses, concluded that the 1919 judgement was reasonable and that the discarded plates had a known focus problem.

alternatives.label: Science and politics
alternatives.text: Historians note that the expedition by British scientists to test a German theory just after the First World War had symbolic importance for international science.

entries.changed: 1919: confirmed light bending. 1980: data selection questioned. 1979 and later re-analyses: result stands.

entries.title: The Face on Mars
entries.mainstream: On 25 July 1976 NASA's Viking 1 orbiter photographed the Cydonia region of Mars. One image showed a mesa about 2 kilometres across which, at low resolution and with shadows falling in a particular way, looked like a human face. NASA itself mentioned the resemblance in a press release, describing it as a trick of light and shadow. Writers such as Richard C. Hoagland argued it was an artificial monument, part of a complex of ruins including pyramid-shaped hills. Higher-resolution images from Mars Global Surveyor (1998 and 2001), Mars Express (2006) and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showed an eroded hill with no facial features.

alternatives.label: Artificial monument
alternatives.text: Hoagland and others argued that the Face and nearby "pyramids" were built by an ancient civilisation, possibly linked to Earth, and that NASA was hiding the evidence; some still argue the later images were processed to hide features.

alternatives.label: Pareidolia
alternatives.text: Scientists explain it as pareidolia, the tendency of human vision to see faces in random patterns, combined with low resolution and lighting; it is a common textbook example.

alternatives.label: Cultural legacy
alternatives.text: The Face became a pop-culture icon in books, films and television and helped draw public interest to Mars exploration.

entries.changed: 1976: Viking image. 1998, 2001, 2006: high-resolution images show an eroded mesa.

entries.title: The Black Knight satellite: a 13,000-year-old alien probe?
entries.mainstream: The Black Knight satellite is a modern legend that an alien spacecraft has been orbiting Earth in a near-polar orbit for about 13,000 years and that NASA is covering it up. As the Armagh Planetarium put it, it is a jumble of unrelated stories: Nikola Tesla's 1899 radio signals (probably natural), long-delayed radio echoes heard from 1928, a 1954 newspaper claim by UFO writer Donald Keyhoe about secret satellites, a dark object detected in 1960 that was identified as part of a US Discoverer satellite, and Scottish writer Duncan Lunan's 1973 speculation about an alien probe from Epsilon Boötis, which he later withdrew. The best-known photograph, taken during the 1998 Space Shuttle mission STS-88, is catalogued by NASA as space debris and is explained as a thermal blanket lost during a spacewalk.

alternatives.label: Alien probe
alternatives.text: Believers see the photographs and radio stories as pieces of evidence for a single ancient artificial satellite.

alternatives.label: Conflation of stories
alternatives.text: Sceptics such as James Oberg and Brian Dunning show how independent, well-documented events were combined online, mostly after the 1998 photographs appeared; none of the original stories used the name Black Knight.

alternatives.label: Myth-making in real time
alternatives.text: The case is studied as an example of how a modern legend is built by joining unrelated fragments, a process that may also have shaped some older myths.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Black Knight satellite conspiracy theory

entries.title: The faces of Bélmez
entries.mainstream: On 23 August 1971 María Gómez Cámara said that a human face had appeared on the concrete kitchen floor of her house in Bélmez de la Moraleda in Andalusia, Spain. Her family destroyed it and laid new concrete, but, they said, another face formed; the mayor forbade its destruction and the concrete was cut out for study. For about 30 years the family reported faces appearing and disappearing, and the "House of the Faces" attracted many visitors. It became one of the best-known paranormal cases in Spain.

alternatives.label: Paranormal
alternatives.text: Some parapsychologists claimed the faces were a "thoughtographic" phenomenon, images produced unconsciously by María Gómez Cámara's mind.

alternatives.label: Paint and hoax
alternatives.text: Sceptical investigators argue the faces were painted or chemically applied. In 1993 Luis Ruiz-Noguez, writing in the Journal of the Society for Psychical Research, discussed analyses showing lead, zinc and chromium consistent with paint pigments; sociologist Manuel Martín Serrano described the case as a hoax driven by money and tourism.

alternatives.label: Seeing faces
alternatives.text: Some faces are vague stains in which viewers recognise features, a pattern-seeking effect (pareidolia) that also played a part.

entries.title: The Hitler Diaries: the forgery that fooled a magazine and a historian
entries.mainstream: In April 1983 the German magazine Stern announced that it had obtained Adolf Hitler's secret diaries, 60 volumes reportedly rescued from a plane crash in 1945. Stern journalist Gerd Heidemann had paid about 9 million Deutschmarks for them through Konrad Kujau, a dealer in Nazi memorabilia. The British historian Hugh Trevor-Roper initially vouched for their authenticity, and The Sunday Times bought serialisation rights. Within two weeks, the West German Federal Archives found that the paper, bindings and glue contained substances that did not exist until after the war, and the content was copied from published sources. Kujau, who had written the diaries himself, and Heidemann were convicted in 1985.

alternatives.label: Why experts were fooled
alternatives.text: The rush to publish, the secrecy around the deal, the desire for a sensational find, and handwriting comparisons with documents that Kujau had also forged all contributed.

alternatives.label: Rewriting history
alternatives.text: Had they been accepted, the diaries would have presented a Hitler who did not know about the Holocaust; historians note the danger of forgeries that conveniently change the historical record.

alternatives.label: Lasting lesson
alternatives.text: The case is still used to teach journalists and historians to check the material provenance of documents, not just their content.

media.title: How fake Hitler diaries fooled the British press | BBC Global

entries.title: The Alien Autopsy film
entries.mainstream: In 1995 the London businessman Ray Santilli released black-and-white footage that he said showed the autopsy of an alien recovered from the 1947 Roswell crash, filmed by a US military cameraman. It was shown on television in many countries, including the Fox programme Alien Autopsy: Fact or Fiction?, and drew huge audiences. Pathologists, special-effects artists and UFO researchers raised many objections. In 2006 Santilli said the film was a "restoration": he claimed to have seen real footage in 1992 that had since deteriorated, and that he had recreated it in a London flat with a dummy made by the sculptor John Humphreys.

alternatives.label: Real footage remade
alternatives.text: Santilli still maintains that the original film existed and that his version only reproduces it; there is no independent evidence of the original film or the cameraman.

alternatives.label: Staged hoax
alternatives.text: Most consider the entire story a hoax, pointing to the dummy, the absence of the claimed military film and the commercial success of the project.

alternatives.label: Roswell legend
alternatives.text: The film became part of the Roswell legend and is an example of how a staged reconstruction can be accepted as documentary evidence.

entries.title: ALH84001: the Martian meteorite that seemed to contain fossils
entries.mainstream: ALH84001 is a meteorite found on 27 December 1984 in the Allan Hills of Antarctica. It is a piece of the Martian crust about 4 billion years old, blasted off Mars by an impact and landing on Earth about 13,000 years ago. In August 1996 a NASA team led by David McKay published a paper in Science stating that it contained possible signs of ancient Martian life: tiny worm-like structures, carbonate globules, magnetite crystals and organic molecules (PAHs). US President Bill Clinton spoke publicly about the discovery. Over the following years most researchers concluded that each feature could have been formed without life; a 2022 study (Steele et al.) found that its organic material probably formed through reactions between rock and water on early Mars.

alternatives.label: Fossil microbes
alternatives.text: McKay's team and some later researchers argued that the combination of features, especially the magnetite chains resembling those made by bacteria, was best explained by biology.

alternatives.label: Non-biological origin
alternatives.text: Critics argued that the structures are too small for known cells, that magnetite and carbonates form inorganically, and that some organics are terrestrial contamination.

alternatives.label: A turning point
alternatives.text: Regardless of the outcome, the debate shaped astrobiology and Mars exploration, including missions that are now looking for biosignatures in Martian rocks.

entries.changed: 1984: found. 1996: possible microfossils announced. 2022: organics explained by water–rock chemistry.

entries.title: The Richat Structure: the "Eye of the Sahara" as Atlantis?
entries.dateNote: Geological formation c. 100 million years ago; Atlantis claims from c. 2018
entries.mainstream: The Richat Structure (Guelb er Richât), near Ouadane in Mauritania, is a circular feature about 40 kilometres across, made of concentric rings of rock that are clearly visible from space. Geologists explain it as a deeply eroded dome, raised by an underground igneous intrusion about 100 million years ago (the carbonatite rocks date to roughly 94–104 million years) and later shaped by erosion of harder and softer rock layers. It is not an impact crater. The area contains exceptional quantities of Acheulean (Lower Palaeolithic) stone tools, showing that early humans used it long ago. It is listed among the IUGS's 100 most important geological heritage sites.

alternatives.label: Atlantis
alternatives.text: Since about 2018, online videos have proposed that the rings match Plato's description of Atlantis as a city of concentric rings of land and water, pointing to its size and its location relative to the Atlantic.

alternatives.label: Geology and archaeology
alternatives.text: Geologists note that the rings are natural rock layers, and that there is no evidence of a large city, harbour or Bronze Age settlement; the region's archaeology is Palaeolithic tools and later Neolithic sites.

alternatives.label: Ring-shaped patterns
alternatives.text: The case is an example of how a striking natural shape seen from space can be matched to an ancient description.

entries.title: Havana syndrome: an invisible weapon or something else?
entries.mainstream: From late 2016, US diplomats and intelligence officers in Havana, Cuba, and later in China, Europe and elsewhere, reported sudden sensations of pressure or loud sounds followed by headaches, dizziness, hearing problems and cognitive difficulties. The US government calls these "anomalous health incidents". Early studies suggested brain changes, and a 2020 National Academies report considered directed pulsed radiofrequency energy to be the most plausible mechanism for some cases. In March 2023 most US intelligence agencies judged it "very unlikely" that a foreign adversary was responsible. In 2024, studies by the US National Institutes of Health published in JAMA found no evidence of brain injury in MRI scans or biomarkers of affected people compared with controls, although the symptoms were real.

alternatives.label: Directed-energy weapon
alternatives.text: Some affected officials, journalists and investigators (for example a 2024 report linking the incidents to the Russian GRU unit 29155) argue that a foreign weapon was used and that the evidence is being underestimated.

alternatives.label: Mixed causes
alternatives.text: Many researchers think the cases have several ordinary causes, including existing illnesses, environmental factors and stress; recordings of one Havana sound were matched to the call of a cricket.

alternatives.label: Mass psychogenic illness
alternatives.text: Some experts have proposed that a shared fear spread through diplomatic communities, a pattern seen in earlier collective episodes; others strongly reject this as dismissive.

sources.title: Neuroimaging Findings in US Government Personnel and Their Family Members Involved in Anomalous Health Incidents

entries.title: The Tuatha Dé Danann: Ireland's gods who arrived in dark clouds and went into the hills
entries.dateNote: Text compiled 11th century CE; legendary setting before c. 1000 BCE
entries.mainstream: The Lebor Gabála Érenn ("Book of the Taking of Ireland"), compiled by Christian monks in the 11th century from older material, tells Ireland's history as a series of invasions: Cessair before the Flood, then Partholón, Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the Tuatha Dé Danann ("peoples of the goddess Danu") and finally the Milesians, ancestors of the Gaels. The Tuatha Dé arrive in dark clouds, bringing four treasures (the Stone of Fál, the spear of Lugh, the sword of Nuada and the Dagda's cauldron). Defeated by the Milesians, they withdraw into the síde, the ancient mounds such as Newgrange, and become the aos sí, the fairy folk of later Irish belief. Most scholars see them as the pre-Christian gods of Ireland, recast by monastic writers as a human or semi-human people so they could fit into a biblical history of the world.

alternatives.label: Gods made human
alternatives.text: The mainstream reading is euhemerism: the monks turned the old gods (Lugh, the Dagda, the Morrígan, Brigid) into early kings and magicians and dated them alongside Noah and Moses.

alternatives.label: Memory of real invasions
alternatives.text: 19th-century antiquarians tried to match the invasions to real peoples (for example the Fir Bolg to the Belgae); modern archaeology and genetics show real population changes in Ireland, but they do not map onto the medieval scheme, so this remains speculative.

alternatives.label: Sky arrival
alternatives.text: Some ancient-astronaut writers read the arrival "in dark clouds" or in ships through the air as a description of aircraft; this is speculative, and other versions simply say they burned their ships on landing so the smoke hid the sun.

entries.title: The voyage of Saint Brendan: Irish monks across the Atlantic in a leather boat?
entries.dateNote: Brendan lived c. 484–577; the Navigatio was written c. 800–1000 CE
entries.mainstream: Brendan of Clonfert (c. 484 – c. 577) was a real Irish abbot. The Navigatio Sancti Brendani Abbatis ("Voyage of Saint Brendan the Abbot"), a Latin text probably written in the 9th or 10th century, tells how he and a group of monks sailed a hide-covered boat (a currach) for seven years in search of the Promised Land of the Saints. They celebrate Easter on the back of a huge fish, Jasconius, which they first take for an island, pass a floating crystal column, and are pelted with burning rocks by smiths on a dark island. It was hugely popular in medieval Europe, and 'Saint Brendan's Island' appeared on Atlantic charts for centuries. Irish hermits (papar) really did reach the Faroes and Iceland before the Norse, according to the Irish scholar Dicuil (825) and the Icelandic Íslendingabók.

alternatives.label: A real crossing
alternatives.text: In 1976–77 the explorer Tim Severin built a leather currach and sailed from Ireland to Newfoundland via the Hebrides, Faroes and Iceland, showing that such a voyage was technically possible; some readers see the crystal column as an iceberg and the smiths' island as an Icelandic eruption.

alternatives.label: Religious allegory
alternatives.text: Most medievalists read the Navigatio as a spiritual allegory built around the monastic calendar, drawing on the older Irish immram (voyage) tales; possibility is not evidence that Brendan himself reached America.

alternatives.label: Pre-Columbian claims
alternatives.text: The story is often cited alongside Vinland in debates about pre-Columbian Atlantic crossings; there is no archaeological trace of Irish monks in North America.

entries.title: Hy-Brasil: the phantom island west of Ireland that stayed on maps for 500 years
entries.mainstream: Hy-Brasil is a phantom island said to lie in the Atlantic west of Ireland. Irish tradition described it as hidden in mist except for one day every seven years, when it can be seen but not reached. An island called "Bracile" appears west of Ireland on Angelino Dulcert's portolan chart of about 1325 and on the Catalan Atlas (c. 1375); later charts usually drew it as a circle split by a channel. Expeditions sailed from Bristol to look for it in 1480 and 1481. In 1674 a Captain John Nisbet supposedly landed there and found giant black rabbits and a magician in a stone castle, but the account was a literary invention by the Irish writer Richard Head. It kept appearing on charts south-west of Galway Bay until 1865, by which time it had shrunk to "Brasil Rock". The name may come from the Irish Uí Breasail (a clan name) or be linked to the medieval red dye brasile; the country Brazil was later named after brazilwood.

alternatives.label: Misread shoals or mirages
alternatives.text: Suggested real origins include the Porcupine Bank, a shallow area west of Ireland, or optical effects such as fata morgana that can make distant land appear over the horizon.

alternatives.label: Otherworld island
alternatives.text: Folklorists link it to the Irish otherworld islands such as Tír na nÓg, where time runs differently, and to the immram voyage tales.

alternatives.label: Found America first?
alternatives.text: A letter written shortly after John Cabot's 1497 voyage reports that the land Cabot found had been "discovered in the past by the men from Bristol who found Brasil"; some historians suggest Bristol sailors searching for the island reached Newfoundland before John Cabot's 1497 voyage, while others think the letter refers only to the search. The question is unresolved.

entries.title: The Gundestrup cauldron: a horned god, a giant dipping men into a cauldron, and elephants in a Danish bog
entries.mainstream: The Gundestrup cauldron is a richly decorated silver vessel found in 1891 by peat cutters in a bog near Gundestrup in Himmerland, Denmark, where it had been taken apart and deposited, probably as an offering. It is the largest known piece of European Iron Age silverwork (about 69 cm across) and is usually dated between about 150 BCE and 1 BCE. Its panels show a seated antlered figure holding a torc and a ram-horned serpent, often identified with the Gaulish god Cernunnos; a giant figure plunging a man head-first into a vat while warriors march past; wheel-holding deities; and exotic animals including elephants and lion-like beasts. The workmanship resembles Thracian silverwork from south-east Europe, while much of the imagery looks Celtic, so it is a meeting point of several cultures. It is in the National Museum of Denmark.

alternatives.label: Sacrifice or rebirth
alternatives.text: The vat scene has been read as a human sacrifice by drowning (a later commentary on the Roman poet Lucan says victims were drowned for the god Teutates) or as soldiers being brought back to life in a cauldron of rebirth, as in the Welsh Mabinogion.

alternatives.label: Who made it
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether Thracian silversmiths made it for Celtic patrons, whether it was booty, or whether it was made in Gaul; elephants suggest knowledge of the Mediterranean or the East.

alternatives.label: Shamanic imagery
alternatives.text: Some see the antlered figure as a shaman or a lord of animals comparable to images from India (the so-called Pashupati seal of the Indus civilisation); such links are speculative.

media.title: Curators choose their favourite object: the Gundestrup cauldron

entries.title: Ogham: Ireland's notched alphabet, invented by a god, and the ogham claims in America
entries.mainstream: Ogham is an early medieval alphabet made of groups of strokes and notches cut along a central line, usually the edge of a standing stone. About 400 inscriptions survive, mostly in Ireland and also in Wales, Scotland, the Isle of Man and Cornwall; the oldest are usually dated from about the 4th to the 6th centuries CE. Most record a personal name in the form "X son of Y", probably marking land boundaries or graves. Medieval Irish texts such as the Auraicept na nÉces say ogham was invented by Ogma, one of the Tuatha Dé Danann, and name its letters after trees. Scholars think it was designed by people who knew the Latin alphabet and Latin grammar, and adapted to the sounds of Primitive Irish.

alternatives.label: Divine invention
alternatives.text: In Irish tradition Ogma created ogham to give learned men a secret script; the stories also describe it being used for magical messages carved on wood.

alternatives.label: Ogham in America
alternatives.text: In America B.C. (1976) the marine biologist Barry Fell claimed that markings on rocks in West Virginia and elsewhere were ogham left by ancient Irish or Celtic visitors; archaeologists and Celtic scholars reject these readings as natural or later scratches interpreted through wishful thinking.

alternatives.label: Older origins?
alternatives.text: A few writers suggest ogham grew out of an older tally or sign system; there is no surviving evidence of ogham before the Roman-influenced period.

entries.title: The Giant's Causeway: a road built by Fionn mac Cumhaill, or cooling lava?
entries.dateNote: Basalt formed c. 50–60 million years ago; legend recorded in modern folklore
entries.mainstream: The Giant's Causeway on the north coast of County Antrim, Northern Ireland, is made of about 40,000 interlocking basalt columns, most of them hexagonal. They formed about 50–60 million years ago, when thick lava flows cooled slowly and contracted, cracking into columns, during the volcanic activity that accompanied the opening of the North Atlantic. Similar columns appear across the sea at Fingal's Cave on Staffa in Scotland. In legend, the giant Fionn mac Cumhaill (Finn McCool) built the causeway to reach his Scottish rival Benandonner; when Benandonner came across, Fionn's wife Oonagh disguised Fionn as a baby, and the Scot fled, tearing up the causeway behind him. It was announced to the Royal Society in 1693, and Susanna Drury's paintings (1739) made it famous; in 1768 the French geologist Nicolas Desmarest, captioning engravings of it, suggested in print for the first time that such columns were volcanic, part of a long argument over whether basalt formed from lava or precipitated from water.

alternatives.label: Too regular to be natural?
alternatives.text: Its geometric regularity long fed the feeling that such columns must be built; the same intuition still drives claims about other columnar basalt sites, such as Nan Madol or Gunung Padang.

alternatives.label: Physics of cracking
alternatives.text: Laboratory work and modelling show that cooling lava naturally cracks into polygons, with hexagons favoured because they release stress efficiently; column size depends on the cooling rate.

alternatives.label: Giant's road
alternatives.text: The Fionn story is a comic folktale rather than a creation myth; it links two landscapes across the sea that really do share the same geology.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Giant's Causeway and Causeway Coast

entries.title: The druids: what we really know, and the forgers who reinvented them
entries.dateNote: Classical accounts c. 58 BCE – 1st century CE; antiquarian revival 17th–19th centuries
entries.mainstream: The druids were the learned priestly class of the Iron Age Celtic-speaking peoples of Gaul and Britain. Almost everything known about them comes from outsiders: Julius Caesar (Gallic War, book 6, 50s BCE) says they judged disputes, taught young men orally for up to twenty years, believed souls passed into new bodies after death and met yearly in the land of the Carnutes; he and other writers claim they presided over human sacrifices, including burning victims in huge wicker figures. Pliny the Elder describes them cutting mistletoe from an oak with a golden sickle, and Tacitus describes the Roman attack on their stronghold on Anglesey (Mona) in 60 or 61 CE. The druids left no writing of their own. From the 17th century antiquarians such as John Aubrey and William Stukeley credited them with Stonehenge and Avebury, which are in fact thousands of years older, and in 1792 the Welsh poet Iolo Morganwg founded the Gorsedd, supported partly by manuscripts he had forged.

alternatives.label: Roman propaganda?
alternatives.text: Many historians caution that accounts of druidic human sacrifice came from enemies conquering their lands and may be exaggerated; others point to archaeological evidence of ritual killing, such as Lindow Man (found 1984), though linking such bodies to druids is debated.

alternatives.label: Keepers of lost wisdom
alternatives.text: Romantic and modern pagan traditions see druids as guardians of ancient astronomical and spiritual knowledge; much of this tradition was created in the 18th and 19th centuries.

alternatives.label: Revived druidry
alternatives.text: Modern druid orders openly describe their practice as a revival inspired by fragments of history and folklore rather than an unbroken tradition.

media.title: Ancient Celtic Religion, Druids and Funerary Beliefs

entries.title: Selkies: seal-people of the northern isles, and families who claimed seal ancestry
entries.dateNote: Collected mainly 18th–19th centuries; older oral tradition
entries.mainstream: Selkies are shapeshifters of the folklore of Orkney, Shetland, the Hebrides, Ireland, Iceland and the Faroe Islands: seals that can shed their skins and walk ashore as humans. In the commonest story, a man steals and hides a seal-woman's skin so she must stay and marry him; years later she or one of her children finds the skin, and she returns to the sea, sometimes still watching over her family. Some families were said to descend from selkies, such as the MacCodrums of North Uist, the 'MacCodrums of the seals'. The Faroese tale of Kópakonan (the seal woman) of Mikladalur is commemorated by a bronze statue in the village. The word comes from Scots selch, a grey seal. Collected mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries, the stories are much older.

alternatives.label: Explaining difference
alternatives.text: Folklorists suggest such stories explained unusual traits: the MacCodrum descent story has been linked to webbed fingers (syndactyly) in the family.

alternatives.label: Kayaking strangers
alternatives.text: The antiquarian David MacRitchie (1890s) argued that the stories remembered real people in skin boats, perhaps Sámi or Inuit; there are 17th–18th century reports of lone 'Finnmen' in kayaks off Orkney and a kayak kept in Aberdeen. Most historians think any such visitors were Inuit taken to Europe by whalers rather than an ancient seafaring people, and the idea remains debated.

alternatives.label: Human-animal marriage worldwide
alternatives.text: The seal-wife tale belongs to the international 'swan maiden' type, in which a hidden animal skin or feather cloak binds a supernatural wife; similar tales exist in Japan, Siberia and North America.

entries.title: Cantre'r Gwaelod: the drowned kingdom of Cardigan Bay and its forest of stumps
entries.dateNote: Legendary setting c. 5th–6th century CE; forest drowned c. 4,000–5,000 years ago
entries.mainstream: Cantre'r Gwaelod ("the lowland hundred") is a legendary kingdom said to lie under Cardigan Bay in west Wales. In the oldest version, a poem in the 13th-century Black Book of Carmarthen, a maiden called Mererid lets a well overflow and the land is drowned. In the better-known later version, the drunken Seithennin neglects the sluice gates of the sea wall during a storm and sixteen towns are lost; their bells are said to ring under the water. At Borth and Ynyslas, storms periodically uncover the stumps of a submerged prehistoric forest of oak, pine and birch, thought to have been submerged about 4,000–5,000 years ago as sea levels rose after the Ice Age. Long stony ridges called sarnau, such as Sarn Badrig, run out into the bay; they are glacial deposits left by retreating ice sheets, though legend called them the kingdom's roads.

alternatives.label: Memory of rising seas
alternatives.text: Some researchers suggest the legend preserves a very long memory of land lost to rising sea levels after the last Ice Age, comparable to Aboriginal Australian stories; others think the stories were inspired by the visible stumps and ridges rather than remembered from prehistory.

alternatives.label: Moral tale
alternatives.text: The legend blames a human failing (neglect or drunkenness) for the flood, a theme shared with Ys in Brittany and the biblical flood.

alternatives.label: Medieval storms
alternatives.text: Another view links the legend to real medieval coastal flooding in the 13th–14th centuries, when the story first appears in writing.

entries.title: Ys: the Breton city drowned when a princess stole the key to the sea gates
entries.dateNote: Legendary setting c. 5th–6th century CE; first written versions 15th–17th centuries
entries.mainstream: Ys (Breton Kêr-Is) is a legendary city on the coast of Brittany, in or near the Bay of Douarnenez, built by King Gradlon below sea level and protected by a dyke whose gates only the king could open. In the best-known version, his daughter Dahut, who lived a life of pleasure, stole the key from her sleeping father for a lover (sometimes the Devil in disguise) and opened the gates; the sea poured in. Gradlon escaped on horseback, but Saint Gwénnolé told him to cast off Dahut, who fell into the waves and became a mermaid (a morgen). The story is attested from the 15th–16th centuries, and Albert Le Grand's lives of the Breton saints (17th century) contain the first known mention of Dahut. It became famous through the Breton song collection Barzaz Breiz (1839). A popular folk etymology said Paris was named Par-Is, 'equal to Ys'.

alternatives.label: Sunken Roman town?
alternatives.text: Some local historians have searched for real remains under the bay, citing Roman roads that run into the sea near Douarnenez; no submerged city has been found.

alternatives.label: Rising seas
alternatives.text: As with Cantre'r Gwaelod in Wales and Lyonesse in Cornwall, some suggest a folk memory of coastal land lost to the sea; the Breton coast has submerged prehistoric sites, but none linked to a city.

alternatives.label: Christian vs pagan
alternatives.text: Scholars read the tale as a story of the Christian saint triumphing over a pagan, sensual princess, a reworking of older water-fairy beliefs.

entries.title: Kaali: a Bronze Age meteorite strike on an Estonian island, and a sacred lake
entries.dateNote: Impact shortly after c. 1530–1450 BCE (other estimates differ)
entries.mainstream: Kaali, on the Estonian island of Saaremaa, is a group of nine meteorite craters. The largest is about 110 m across and 22 m deep and holds a small round lake; the other eight are 12–40 m wide and all lie within a kilometre. The latest estimates date the impact to shortly after 1530–1450 BCE, when the island was already inhabited. The impact released energy roughly comparable to the Hiroshima bomb (about 20 kilotons of TNT) and burned forest for several kilometres around. Until the 1930s some thought the crater was volcanic or a sinkhole; Ivan Reinvald showed in 1928–1937 that it was made by a meteorite. Excavations in 1976–79 found a fortified settlement and a stone wall around the lake, with animal bones (horses, dogs, sheep, pigs, oxen) that may be sacrifices, mostly from the pre-Roman Iron Age, so the lake seems to have been a cult site for centuries.

alternatives.label: Remembered in myth
alternatives.text: Scholars such as Karl Kello and the writer Lennart Meri suggested that Estonian and Finnish poems about a sun or fire falling from the sky, including the Kalevala episode (runes 47–49) in which a spark of the new Sun falls from the sky, preserve a memory of the impact; this is plausible but cannot be proven.

alternatives.label: Ultima Thule
alternatives.text: In his book Hõbevalge (Silverwhite, 1976), Meri, later Estonia's president, speculated that the classical name Thule, the land 'where the sun goes to sleep', came from the Kaali story; most historians place Thule elsewhere (Shetland, Iceland or Norway).

alternatives.label: Dating debate
alternatives.text: Published estimates of the impact date have varied by about 6,000 years, from roughly 6400 BCE to 400 BCE; the Bronze Age date is now most widely accepted.

entries.title: The Sampo: the Finnish magic mill that made grain, salt and gold, and the theft that broke it
entries.dateNote: Runic songs are older; collected from 1817; Kalevala published 1835 and 1849
entries.mainstream: In Finnish and Karelian runic songs the Sampo is a mysterious object of plenty forged by the smith Ilmarinen, originally a sky god who had also forged the sky. In Elias Lönnrot's Kalevala (1835; expanded 1849), compiled from songs he and others collected, Ilmarinen makes it for Louhi, the mistress of the dark northern land Pohjola, as a bride-price; it grinds out flour, salt and gold. The heroes Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen and Lemminkäinen steal it back, Louhi pursues them, and in the battle at sea the Sampo is smashed; its fragments wash ashore and bring prosperity to Finland. The songs never describe clearly what it looks like, and it has 'a lid of many colours' (kirjokansi).

alternatives.label: World pillar
alternatives.text: Uno Harva and others argued that the Sampo was originally a world pillar or world tree holding up the sky, like the Estonian Sammas or the Norse Yggdrasil.

alternatives.label: Many interpretations
alternatives.text: It has also been read as the Sun, a compass, a treasure chest, a Byzantine coin die, a decorated shield or a Christian relic; Lönnrot himself made it a mill, perhaps influenced by the Norse magic mill Grótti.

alternatives.label: Cosmic machine
alternatives.text: In Hamlet's Mill (1969), Giorgio de Santillana and Hertha von Dechend argued that the Sampo and similar mills encode ancient knowledge of the precession of the equinoxes; most scholars see this as speculative.

media.title: The myth of the Sampo— an infinite source of fortune and greed - Hanna-Ilona Härmävaara

entries.title: Lithuania: the last pagan state in Europe
entries.mainstream: While the rest of Europe had become Christian, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania kept its old religion, with gods such as the thunder god Perkūnas, into the late 14th century, despite crusades by the Teutonic Knights. King Mindaugas was baptised in the 1250s, but the country went back to the old ways after his death. Lithuania officially converted in 1387, after Grand Duke Jogaila married the Polish queen Jadwiga and became king of Poland; nobles and peasants were baptised in and around Vilnius. Samogitia in the west, long held by the Teutonic Order, was the last region to convert: Grand Duke Vytautas baptised the first Samogitians in 1413, after the Battle of Grunwald, and the diocese of Samogitia was founded in 1417. Pagan customs survived among country people for much longer.

alternatives.label: Holy groves and fires
alternatives.text: Chronicles describe sacred groves, holy snakes and eternal fires; how organised the pagan religion was (for example whether there was a high priest, the 'Krivis') is debated because much comes from hostile Christian writers.

alternatives.label: Temple under the cathedral
alternatives.text: A tradition going back to the 15th-century historian Jan Długosz linked Vilnius Cathedral with an earlier building later used for pagan worship; modern archaeologists and historians question this interpretation.

alternatives.label: Revival
alternatives.text: Romuva, a modern revival of Baltic pagan religion, began in the 20th century and draws on folklore and these medieval accounts.

entries.title: Sámi drums: the shaman drums burned by missionaries, and the one that came home after 300 years
entries.dateNote: Drum persecution 17th–18th centuries; Lars Nilsson executed 1693; drum returned 2023
entries.mainstream: Sámi noaidi (shamans) used drums painted with figures of gods, animals, people and the landscape to enter trance, contact the spirit world and foretell the future. During the 17th and 18th centuries the Swedish and Danish-Norwegian authorities and church tried to wipe out the old Sámi religion: drums were confiscated and burned, and owners were tried. In Arjeplog, Sweden, Lars Nilsson was tried in 1691 for keeping his drum and his old faith and was burned at the stake in 1693. About 70 drums survive, mostly in museums across Europe. One of the best documented, Freavnantjahke gievrie (the Folldal drum), was taken by the missionary Thomas von Westen in 1723, passed through Copenhagen and ended up in Meiningen, Germany; the Meiningen Museum decided to return it in June 2023 and handed it over to the South Sámi museum Saemien Sijte in October 2023.

alternatives.label: What the symbols mean
alternatives.text: Only a few drums were explained by their owners; later scholars such as Ernst Manker interpreted the figures as gods and spirits, while some contemporary explanations relate them to weather, animals and daily life, so readings remain uncertain.

alternatives.label: Witchcraft rumours
alternatives.text: During the Thirty Years' War rumours spread that Swedish armies won with the help of Sámi sorcery, part of the background to the state's interest in Sámi religion.

alternatives.label: Living tradition
alternatives.text: Many Sámi today see the drums as living cultural heritage rather than museum objects, which is why their return matters.

entries.title: The Amber Road: Baltic "tears of the sun" in Mycenae and Tutankhamun's tomb
entries.dateNote: Baltic amber in the Mediterranean from the 2nd millennium BCE
entries.mainstream: Amber, fossilised tree resin washed up on the shores of the Baltic and North Seas, was traded south for thousands of years along routes now called the Amber Road. Heinrich Schliemann found amber beads at Mycenae that spectroscopic analysis showed to be Baltic, and a breast ornament of Tutankhamun (c. 1333–1324 BCE) contains large Baltic amber beads. Amber was also sent as an offering to the temple of Apollo at Delphi. In the Roman period a route ran from the Baltic coast to Aquileia on the Adriatic. Greek myth explained amber as the hardened tears of the Heliades, the sisters of Phaethon, who wept after he crashed the sun's chariot. A Lithuanian legend first written down in 1842 tells of the sea goddess Jūratė, whose amber palace under the Baltic was shattered by the thunder god Perkūnas because she loved a mortal fisherman, Kastytis; the pieces of amber on the shore are its ruins.

alternatives.label: Old myth or modern tale
alternatives.text: Because Jūratė does not appear in older Lithuanian mythology, scholars think the legend is largely a 19th-century literary creation, although it uses older gods such as Perkūnas.

alternatives.label: Magic and medicine
alternatives.text: Amber was widely believed to have protective and healing powers, which helps explain why it travelled so far; amber and other exotic materials in elite graves show long-distance networks long before written records.

alternatives.label: Wider contacts
alternatives.text: Some writers use amber finds to argue for direct Bronze Age voyages between the Baltic and the Mediterranean; most archaeologists think the amber moved through many hands in stages.

entries.title: Areni-1 cave: the world's oldest leather shoe and oldest winery, next to the dead
entries.dateNote: Winery c. 4100–4000 BCE; shoe c. 3600–3500 BCE
entries.mainstream: Areni-1 is a three-chambered cave by the Arpa River in Vayots Dzor, southern Armenia. Excavations by an Armenian, Irish and American team (Boris Gasparyan, Ron Pinhasi, Gregory Areshian) from 2007 to 2010 found remarkably preserved remains from the Late Chalcolithic, protected by the cave's dry, cool air and layers of sheep dung. In 2008 Diana Zardaryan found a complete one-piece leather shoe, about 5,500 years old (c. 3600–3500 BCE), stuffed with grass and laced, the oldest leather shoe known. The cave also held the oldest known winery, from about 4100–4000 BCE: a clay basin used as a press, a 60 cm fermentation vat, storage jars, grape seeds and skins, with traces of the red-wine pigment malvidin. The winery sat among burials, and a human brain preserved in a skull was reported in 2009.

alternatives.label: Wine for the dead
alternatives.text: Because the press and vat were found among graves, the excavators suggested that wine was made for funeral rituals, linking the beginnings of wine with religion rather than everyday drinking.

alternatives.label: Cradle of wine
alternatives.text: The South Caucasus (Armenia and Georgia) and eastern Anatolia have produced the earliest evidence of grape wine; Georgian sites have traces from around 6000 BCE, earlier than Areni's winery but without a press installation.

alternatives.label: Same shoe for thousands of years
alternatives.text: The shoe resembles one-piece leather shoes known from Europe and the traditional Irish pampootie, suggesting a very long-lived design.
