entries.title: Zorats Karer (Carahunge): Armenia's "Stonehenge" of holed stones, observatory or necropolis?
entries.dateNote: Tombs mainly Middle Bronze to Iron Age (c. 2000–800 BCE); observatory dating claims up to c. 5500 BCE
entries.mainstream: Zorats Karer, also called Carahunge or Karahunj, is a site on a plateau at about 1,770 m near Sisian in Syunik, southern Armenia. It contains stone settings, burial cists and 223 numbered standing stones of basalt, up to 3 m tall and up to 10 tons. About 80 stones have a circular hole bored through them, and the wind can make them whistle, which fits the popular explanation of the name Carahunge as 'speaking stones'. In 1984 the archaeologist Onik Khnkikyan drew attention to possible astronomical meaning, and from 1985 the astrophysicist Elma Parsamyan and later the radiophysicist Paris Herouni proposed that it was an ancient observatory, with some stones aligned on solstice sunrises and lunar extremes. In 2004 the Armenian government officially named the site the Karahunj Observatory.

alternatives.label: Necropolis and later wall
alternatives.text: A German team from LMU Munich led by Stephan Kroll identified the site as a necropolis mainly from the Middle Bronze Age to the Iron Age, with large tombs, and suggested that the lines of stones were remains of a later, possibly Hellenistic, wall.

alternatives.label: Very ancient observatory
alternatives.text: Herouni argued that the alignments dated the site to about 5500 BCE, making it older than Stonehenge; archaeoastronomers such as Clive Ruggles have called such claims speculative and poorly supported.

alternatives.label: Holes not prehistoric?
alternatives.text: The insides of the holes are much less weathered than the stone surfaces, so some of them may be much later than the stones; conclusions about their use remain provisional.

entries.title: Amirani: the Georgian Prometheus chained in the Caucasus
entries.dateNote: Oral epic; core possibly 1st–2nd millennium BCE; recorded from the 19th century
entries.mainstream: Amirani is the hero of a Georgian epic known in many oral versions. Son of Dali, a Caucasian goddess of the hunt, he is a giant-slaying hero who defies God (in some versions by bringing the use of metal to humanity) and is punished by being chained to a stake or beneath a mountain rock in the Caucasus with his winged dog Q'ursha. In some versions an eagle eats his liver, which heals each night. The dog licks the chains until they are about to break, but then blacksmiths strike their anvils and the chains regain their strength; once a year the mountain opens and Amirani may see the sky for a single night.

alternatives.label: Source of Prometheus?
alternatives.text: The Greek Prometheus, who brings fire and is chained in the Caucasus with an eagle eating his liver, is strikingly similar; many scholars think the Greeks took the setting, and perhaps elements of the story, from Caucasian peoples.

alternatives.label: Very old roots
alternatives.text: The core of the legend has been traced to the 3rd–2nd millennia BCE and the beginning of metalworking; this is hard to prove because the epic was written down only in modern times.

alternatives.label: The hero who will return
alternatives.text: Like King Artavazd in the Armenian tradition recorded by Movses Khorenatsi, chained in a cave of Mount Masis (Ararat) whose chains smiths strengthen by striking their anvils, Amirani is a bound hero whose escape is feared or awaited.

entries.title: The Golden Fleece: Colchis, Jason and the sheepskins used to catch gold
entries.dateNote: Legendary voyage set before the Trojan War (traditional c. 13th century BCE); fullest text 3rd century BCE
entries.mainstream: In Greek myth Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis, at the eastern end of the Black Sea in what is now western Georgia, to take the Golden Fleece of a flying ram from King Aeëtes, son of the Sun; the king's daughter, the sorceress Medea, helped him. The story is told most fully by Apollonius of Rhodes in the 3rd century BCE, though it is much older. Colchis really was rich in gold: the Greek geographer Strabo (1st century CE) wrote that in the country of the Soani (Svans) gold was carried down by mountain torrents and caught with perforated troughs and fleecy skins, and suggested this was the origin of the myth. Archaeologists have found rich gold jewellery in Colchian graves such as those at Vani.

alternatives.label: Gold-washing fleece
alternatives.text: The mainstream rational explanation follows Strabo: sheepskins laid in streams trapped gold dust, a method reportedly used in Svaneti into modern times.

alternatives.label: Real voyages
alternatives.text: Some historians see the myth as a memory of early Greek trading or exploring voyages into the Black Sea; in 1984 Tim Severin rowed a replica Bronze Age galley from Greece to Georgia to show it was possible.

alternatives.label: Other readings
alternatives.text: The fleece has also been read as a symbol of kingship, a sun symbol, a record of writing on parchment, or alchemical gold; these are interpretations rather than evidence.

media.title: The myth of Jason, Medea, and the Golden Fleece - Iseult Gillespie

entries.title: Vishap stones: Armenia's fish- and bull-shaped dragon stelae high in the mountains
entries.dateNote: Two vishaps at Tirinkatar dated c. 4200–4000 BCE; others undated
entries.mainstream: Vishapakar ('dragon stones') are tall stone stelae found in the Armenian Highlands, mostly near springs, streams, ancient irrigation channels and mountain lakes, including on the slopes of Mount Aragats and in the Gegham mountains. About 150 are known, 90 of them in Armenia, and the largest is just over 5 m tall. Most are carved as a fish, often like a catfish, with eyes, gills and tail; others show the stretched hide of a bull or ram, sometimes with water flowing from its mouth, and long-legged birds. Armenian folklore calls them vishaps, water dragons. Their age is hard to establish because they stand far from settlements; one was reused for an inscription of the Urartian king Argishti I (8th century BCE), and later ones were carved with Christian crosses, so they are older than both.

alternatives.label: Water cult
alternatives.text: In the 1920s–30s Ashkharbek Kalantar linked them to irrigation and a cult of water; a 2025 statistical study of 115 stones by Vahe Gurzadyan and Arsen Bobokhyan found larger stones at high altitudes where little time was available for work, which they took as support for a strong cult motive.

alternatives.label: 6,000 years old
alternatives.text: Excavations since 2012 at Tirinkatar on Mount Aragats, at about 2,700–3,100 m, radiocarbon-dated the erection of two vishaps to about 4200–4000 BCE; the excavators say this cannot automatically be extended to all vishaps, which were also reused in later periods.

alternatives.label: Dragons and water
alternatives.text: The idea of a water-holding dragon or serpent appears in many cultures, from the Vedic Vritra to Chinese rain dragons, which some see as a shared motif and others as independent responses to the importance of water.

sources.title: Vishap stelae as cult dedicated prehistoric monuments of Armenian Highlands: data analysis and interpretation

entries.title: The Shigir Idol: a 5-metre wooden god carved by hunter-gatherers 11,500 years ago
entries.dateNote: Carved c. 11,500 years ago (c. 9500 BCE); found 1890
entries.mainstream: The Shigir Idol is the oldest known monumental wooden sculpture. Gold prospectors' workers found it on 24 January 1890 at a depth of 4 m in the Shigir peat bog on the eastern slope of the Middle Urals, near Kirovgrad, about 100 km from Yekaterinburg. It was carved with stone tools from a single larch trunk at least 159 years old, and pulled out in ten pieces. Its flat body is covered in zigzags and lines and carries several human faces, with a head at the top. Professor D. I. Lobanov reassembled it to 2.8 m; in 1914 the archaeologist Vladimir Tolmachev used extra fragments to propose an original height of 5.3 m, though some of those pieces were later lost and survive only in his drawings. Radiocarbon dates in the 1990s gave about 9,500 years, and later German AMS dating pushed it back to about 11,500 years ago, at the very start of the Holocene, roughly twice the age of the Great Pyramid. It is in the Sverdlovsk Regional Museum of Local Lore in Yekaterinburg.

alternatives.label: Hunter-gatherer monument
alternatives.text: The dating means people who lived by hunting, fishing and gathering made monumental, symbolic art, like the contemporary carved pillars of Göbekli Tepe in Turkey; this challenges the older idea that complex ritual art came only after farming.

alternatives.label: Too old to believe
alternatives.text: When the first radiocarbon date came back, some scholars thought it must be wrong because they did not believe hunter-gatherers could make such an object; later dating proved it even older.

alternatives.label: Coded meanings
alternatives.text: The faces and zigzags have been read as spirits, a creation myth, a boundary marker or a map; there is no way to test these ideas, and the researchers note that wooden art of this age is almost never preserved.

entries.title: Deer stones: Mongolia's tattooed warriors in stone with flying deer
entries.mainstream: Deer stones are carved standing stones of granite or greenstone, found mainly in Mongolia and southern Siberia; of more than 1,500 known, over 1,300 are in Mongolia, and a few scattered examples reach as far west as the Kuban, Ukraine, Bulgaria and the Elbe. Most date from about 1400 to 700 BCE, the Late Bronze and Early Iron Age. Most are over 0.9 m tall (some reach 4.6 m), their 'face' usually turns east, and they often stand near khirigsuurs, large stone burial mounds. Each stone is a stylised human body: a belt hung with weapons and tools such as a bow case, a shield on the back, earrings and a necklace, and sometimes a face. The body is covered with elegant 'flying deer' with long beak-like snouts and swept-back antlers. The work required suggests the first complex, hierarchical societies on the Mongolian steppe, ancestors of later nomadic states.

alternatives.label: Tattooed bodies
alternatives.text: The flying deer may show tattoos: similar deer tattoos were found on frozen bodies of the later Pazyryk culture in the Altai, so the stones may represent real tattooed leaders.

alternatives.label: Spirit journeys
alternatives.text: Some scholars connect the flying deer to beliefs in deer carrying souls to the sky, later seen in Siberian shamanism; this is an interpretation.

alternatives.label: Cut by machine?
alternatives.text: A few stones show cuts that the Wikipedia summary describes as possibly made with a primitive mechanical drill, and the tops of some were deliberately smashed; these details are unexplained but not anomalous for metal-using societies.

media.title: Protecting and Preserving Mongolian Culture: the Deer Stone Project

entries.title: King Gesar of Ling: the world's longest epic, still sung, and a hero who will return
entries.dateNote: Core formed by c. 12th century CE; oral tradition still alive
entries.mainstream: The Epic of King Gesar tells of Gesar, a divine being sent to earth to become the fearless king of Ling and to defeat demons and enemy kings, and to bring order to the land. Its classic form probably took shape by about the 12th century, and it spread from Tibet to Mongolia, Buryatia, Ladakh, Baltistan, Hunza and the Kalmyks. It is still performed: about 100 bards remain active in the 'Gesar belt' of China. There is no single text; a Chinese compilation of Tibetan versions fills about 120 volumes and more than a million verses, so it is often called the longest epic in the world. The first printed version was a Mongolian text published in Beijing in 1716. Instead of dying, Gesar departs to a hidden realm from which he may return to save his people.

alternatives.label: Caesar in Tibet?
alternatives.text: Some scholars have proposed that the name Gesar comes from the Roman title Caesar, passed via the Byzantine and Turkic world (kaiser), or via the 8th-century Turkic ruler of Kabul called Fromo Kesaro ('Caesar of Rome'); a king Phrom Ge-sar appears in some Tibetan versions. This is debated.

alternatives.label: Prophecy
alternatives.text: Gesar's withdrawal to a hidden realm, ready to come back, ties him to the worldwide pattern of sleeping or returning heroes such as Arthur; in some later Buddhist writings he is linked to the hidden kingdom of Shambhala.

entries.title: The Denisovan gene that lets Tibetans breathe at altitude, and a jaw found by a meditating monk
entries.dateNote: Xiahe jaw c. 160,000 years old; found 1980, identified 2019
entries.mainstream: Denisovans are an extinct group of archaic humans first identified in 2010 from DNA in a finger bone from Denisova Cave in Siberia. In 2014 geneticists showed that many Tibetans carry a version of the gene EPAS1, which helps the body cope with low oxygen, that matches the Denisovan genome; the variant probably entered modern humans through interbreeding and then spread because it helped people live on the high plateau. In 1980 a Tibetan Buddhist monk meditating in Baishiya Karst Cave, a Buddhist sanctuary high on the north-east edge of the Tibetan Plateau, found half of a human lower jaw. In 2019, analysis of ancient proteins in its teeth identified it as Denisovan, about 160,000 years old: the first Denisovan fossil found outside Denisova Cave and proof that archaic humans lived at high altitude long before modern humans. The cave is said in tradition to have been an abode of Padmasambhava.

alternatives.label: Inherited adaptation
alternatives.text: The mainstream view is that this is an example of adaptive introgression: modern humans picked up a useful gene from people already adapted to the environment.

alternatives.label: Hidden people in myths
alternatives.text: Some writers link Denisovans and other archaic humans to legends of wild men, giants and yeti-like beings in Asia; there is no evidence connecting specific legends to them.

alternatives.label: A face for the Denisovans
alternatives.text: In 2025, proteins and DNA linked the Harbin skull (Homo longi) to the Denisovans, which may finally show what they looked like; research is ongoing.

sources.title: Altitude adaptation in Tibetans caused by introgression of Denisovan-like DNA

entries.title: Terma: Tibetan treasure texts hidden by Padmasambhava for the future
entries.dateNote: Terma tradition from c. 10th–11th centuries; Bardo Thodol revealed 14th century
entries.mainstream: In the Nyingma school of Tibetan Buddhism and in Bon, terma ('hidden treasures') are teachings believed to have been hidden in the 8th century by the master Padmasambhava and his consort Yeshe Tsogyal, to be found centuries later by treasure revealers (tertöns) when the time was right. A terma may be a physical object, such as a scroll or ritual tool buried in the ground or hidden in rocks, water or trees, or a 'mind treasure' that arises in the revealer's mind; a few symbolic letters can trigger the revealer's memory of a whole text. The most famous terma outside Tibet is the Bardo Thodol, popularly called the Tibetan Book of the Dead, revealed by Karma Lingpa in the 14th century. Similar ideas of hidden teachings recovered later exist in India, such as Nagarjuna's recovery of a sutra from the realm of the nagas.

alternatives.label: Continuous revelation
alternatives.text: Within the tradition, terma are genuine teachings, timed for when people are ready, and are tested by elaborate procedures; believers see this as a way the teaching stays alive.

alternatives.label: New texts with old authority
alternatives.text: Historians see terma as a way that new religious texts could be accepted by attributing them to an ancient master; Tibetan critics themselves sometimes questioned particular revelations.

alternatives.label: Global pattern
alternatives.text: Hidden scriptures recovered at the right moment appear in many traditions, from the Book of the Law 'found' in the Jerusalem Temple under King Josiah to Joseph Smith's golden plates.

entries.title: Kimpa Vita: the Kongolese prophetess who said Jesus was born in Kongo
entries.mainstream: Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita (1684 – 2 July 1706) was a young noblewoman of the Kingdom of Kongo, in today's Angola and DR Congo, which had been officially Catholic since the 16th century. Kongo had been torn by civil war since the Battle of Mbwila in 1665, and the old capital São Salvador (Mbanza Kongo) had been abandoned. In 1704, during an illness, she said she had died and been possessed by Saint Anthony, who sent her to reunite Kongo under one king. Her movement, Antonianism, taught that Jesus and other holy figures were Kongolese, adapted Catholic prayers, and attacked both traditional charms (nkisi) and the European missionaries; thousands of followers resettled the ruined capital. Accused of heresy, she was burned at the stake on 2 July 1706 on the orders of King Pedro IV, after he consulted Italian Capuchin friars including Bernardo da Gallo. Her movement's years are among the best documented in Kongo's history.

alternatives.label: African Christianity
alternatives.text: Historians such as John Thornton (The Kongolese Saint Anthony, 1998) see her as part of a long tradition of Kongolese Christianity that made the faith local; she is often compared with later Congolese prophetic movements such as Kimbanguism.

alternatives.label: Political prophet
alternatives.text: Some today honour her as a heroine of African resistance to European religious and colonial power; others stress that she was above all a religious reformer within Kongo's civil wars.

alternatives.label: Sainthood and doubt
alternatives.text: She reportedly came to doubt her own mission after becoming pregnant despite preaching chastity; the main sources are hostile Capuchin accounts, so her own voice survives only through them.

entries.title: Senegambian stone circles: the world's largest concentration of stone circles
entries.dateNote: Built between c. 3rd century BCE and 16th century CE
entries.mainstream: Across an area about 350 km long and 100 km wide in the Gambia and central Senegal, along the Gambia River, stand more than 1,000 stone circles and burial mounds, the largest concentration of stone circles in the world. The four main sites, Sine Ngayène and Wanar in Senegal and Wassu and Kerr Batch in the Gambia, together have around 29,000 stones in about 17,000 monuments. The stones are pillars of laterite, cut with iron tools, arranged in circles and double circles; others stand apart, usually to the east (frontal stones), and pairs of connected parallel rows of frontal stones are called lyre stones. Burials, pottery and iron objects are found in and around them. They were built over a long period, generally put between the 3rd century BCE and the 16th century CE. They were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006.

alternatives.label: Who built them
alternatives.text: There are no written records; archaeologists link them to ancestors of local peoples and to iron-using societies with chiefs or elites honoured by large funerary monuments.

alternatives.label: Astronomy and sacred space
alternatives.text: Some have suggested astronomical alignments, as for European stone circles; most researchers see them as funerary monuments marking a sacred landscape used for more than 1,500 years.

alternatives.label: Parallel worlds
alternatives.text: They are often compared with British and Breton stone circles, which are thousands of years older; the similarity is in form, not in time or culture.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Stone Circles of Senegambia

entries.title: Lake Bosumtwi: Ghana's sacred crater lake, where souls say farewell to the Earth goddess
entries.dateNote: Crater formed c. 1.07 million years ago
entries.mainstream: Lake Bosumtwi (Bosomtwe), about 30 km south-east of Kumasi, is Ghana's only natural lake. It lies in a meteorite impact crater about 10.5 km across, formed about 1.07 million years ago; tektites (glassy impact debris) thrown out by it are found in neighbouring Côte d'Ivoire. The Asante consider it sacred: in traditional belief the souls of the dead come here to bid farewell to the Earth goddess Asase Ya, and it has been considered proper to fish in the lake only from wooden planks. About 30 villages, with some 70,000 people, lie around the lake.

alternatives.label: Legend confirmed by science
alternatives.text: Local tradition held that the lake was once much smaller; sediment cores show that a period of low water, when forest grew in the basin, lasted until about 300 years ago.

alternatives.label: Impact memory?
alternatives.text: The impact happened long before modern humans, so the sacredness of the lake cannot be a memory of it; its unusual round shape and lack of outlets are enough to explain why it was seen as special.

media.author: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Adam Voi

entries.title: Nsibidi: the secret sign-writing of the leopard societies that crossed to Cuba and Haiti
entries.dateNote: Age uncertain; documented from c. 1900; possibly centuries older
entries.mainstream: Nsibidi is a system of symbols, often called proto-writing, from the Cross River region of south-eastern Nigeria and south-western Cameroon, usually attributed to the Ejagham (Ekoi) people. Hundreds of pictographic and abstract signs were drawn on walls, calabashes, brass, leaves, swords, textiles and as tattoos. Its fullest and most secret forms were kept by the Ekpe (Egbo) and Mgbe 'leopard' societies, men's associations that acted as governments and courts among the Efik, Ejagham, Igbo and their neighbours; a simpler public version could be used by women. Through the Atlantic slave trade nsibidi reached Cuba and Haiti, where it developed into the anaforuana signs of the Cuban Abakuá society (which descends from Ekpe) and influenced Haitian veve symbols. The Ikom monoliths of Cross River, about 300 carved stones possibly from around 200 CE, carry designs that some researchers think may be related.

alternatives.label: Writing or symbols
alternatives.text: It is usually classed as pictographic; scholars debate whether some signs worked as logograms or syllabic signs, which would make it a true writing system.

alternatives.label: How old
alternatives.text: Its age is unknown; claims that it is many centuries or even more than a thousand years old depend mainly on links to the Ikom monoliths, which are themselves poorly dated.

alternatives.label: Secret societies across the ocean
alternatives.text: The survival of Ekpe/Abakuá and its signs in Cuba is one of the clearest cases of an African institution re-created in the Americas, and part of a wider pattern of secret knowledge passed through initiation.

entries.title: Treasures under Lake Titicaca: the Khoa reef offerings and the Island of the Sun
entries.dateNote: Tiwanaku offerings 8th–10th centuries CE; Inca pilgrimages 15th–16th centuries
entries.mainstream: Lake Titicaca, on the border of Peru and Bolivia, was sacred in Andean belief. In Inca tradition the Sun hid under a crag on the Island of the Sun during a great flood and emerged there to light the world again, and the Incas built a pilgrimage complex on the island. Divers and local people had long recovered objects from the lake, fuelling stories of sunken temples and treasure. Systematic underwater excavations around the Khoa reef, near the Island of the Sun, recovered thousands of objects: ceramic puma-shaped incense burners, remains of sacrificed young llamas, and gold, shell and stone ornaments. A 2019 study by Christophe Delaere, José Capriles and Charles Stanish showed that many of these offerings were made by the Tiwanaku state between the 8th and 10th centuries CE, centuries before the Incas, as repeated state rituals.

alternatives.label: Religion and the first states
alternatives.text: The authors argue that dramatic shared rituals helped Tiwanaku consolidate power and cooperation, making the reef evidence for how religion and state formation went together.

alternatives.label: Sunken city
alternatives.text: Some expeditions have claimed underwater walls and a submerged temple or city; archaeologists accept that lake levels changed and drowned some structures, but the dramatic 'lost city' claims are not supported by published evidence.

alternatives.label: Flood stories
alternatives.text: The Inca story of the Sun rising from the lake after a flood belongs to the global pattern of origin-after-flood myths, and Lake Titicaca's water level really has risen and fallen dramatically in the past.

sources.title: Underwater ritual offerings in the Island of the Sun and the formation of the Tiwanaku state

entries.title: Greek fire: the Byzantine liquid fire whose recipe was lost
entries.dateNote: Invented c. 672 CE; used until about the 14th century
entries.mainstream: Greek fire was an incendiary weapon used by the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire from the 7th to the 14th centuries. It could keep burning on water, and was sprayed from tubes (siphons) on ships or thrown in grenades. The chronicler Theophanes the Confessor credits its invention, around 672, to Kallinikos, an architect who had fled to Constantinople from Heliopolis in Syria, then overrun by the Muslim conquests. It helped defend Constantinople against Arab fleets, and was later used with devastating effect against Rus' raids on the Bosporus in 941 and 1043. The recipe was a closely guarded state secret: Emperor Constantine VII (r. 945–959) told his son never to reveal it, since it had been 'shown and revealed by an angel' to Constantine the Great. The formula has been lost; rivals tried and failed to copy it.

alternatives.label: Petroleum napalm
alternatives.text: Most modern scholars think it was based on crude oil (petroleum) mixed with resins, similar to napalm; the pressurised pumping system may have been as secret as the liquid itself.

alternatives.label: Other recipes
alternatives.text: Older theories proposed quicklime, which ignites with water, or saltpetre, as in gunpowder; these are now generally rejected.

alternatives.label: Divine secret
alternatives.text: Byzantine writers described it as a gift from heaven; this is one of many cases where a powerful technology was protected by secrecy and given a sacred origin.

media.title: How Greek Fire was Used to Target Enemy Ships

entries.title: The Plague of Justinian: the first great plague pandemic
entries.dateNote: First wave 541–549 CE; recurrences until c. 750
entries.mainstream: In 541 CE an epidemic reached the Egyptian port of Pelusium and spread across the Mediterranean, Europe and the Near East, hitting both the Byzantine and the Sasanian Persian empires. The historian Procopius described it in Constantinople, where at its height in 542 it killed about a fifth of the city's population; Emperor Justinian himself caught it and survived. Waves continued until 549, and the disease kept returning in the region for about two centuries. In 2013–2014 DNA from 6th-century skeletons confirmed earlier suspicions that it was caused by Yersinia pestis, the same bacterium behind the Black Death eight centuries later. The ancestor of this strain is related to strains found in the Tian Shan mountains of Central Asia, suggesting it came from there. It struck just a few years after the volcanic 'year without summer' of 536.

alternatives.label: How deadly
alternatives.text: Historians disagree on the scale: some see it as a turning point that weakened Rome's attempt to reconquer the West and helped open the way for the early Islamic conquests; Lee Mordechai and Merle Eisenberg argue the sources exaggerate its long-term demographic impact, a view others criticise.

alternatives.label: Climate and disease
alternatives.text: Some researchers link it to the cold years after the volcanic eruptions of the 530s and 540s, which may have stressed populations and rodents; this connection is still debated.

alternatives.label: God's punishment
alternatives.text: Contemporary writers, including the church historian John of Ephesus, often understood it in religious terms, as a sign of divine anger and the end times, like many other plagues in history.

sources.title: Yersinia pestis and the Plague of Justinian 541–543 AD: a genomic analysis

media.title: The past, present, and future of the bubonic plague - Sharon N. DeWitte

entries.title: The Marble Emperor: the last Byzantine emperor, turned to stone to await his return
entries.dateNote: Died 29 May 1453; legend developed under Ottoman rule
entries.mainstream: Constantine XI Palaiologos (1404–1453) was the last Byzantine emperor. He died fighting on 29 May 1453 when the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, ending an empire that traced its origins to Constantine the Great's founding of the city in 330. Accounts of the details of his death differ. In later Greek folklore he became the Marmaromenos Vasilias, 'the emperor turned into marble'. In the legend, an angel rescued him at the moment of defeat and turned him into marble, hiding him beneath the Golden Gate of Constantinople, where he waits for God's call to come back to life and retake the city and the empire. People also noted that the city was founded by one Constantine and lost under another, just as Rome had been founded by a Romulus and lost under Romulus Augustulus.

alternatives.label: National hope
alternatives.text: Under Ottoman rule the legend expressed Greek hopes of liberation and of one day regaining Constantinople.

alternatives.label: Sleeping king
alternatives.text: The story follows a pattern found across Europe and Asia, where a lost leader sleeps in a hidden place until the moment of greatest need, like Arthur, Frederick Barbarossa or King Gesar.

alternatives.label: Historical figure
alternatives.text: Historians see Constantine XI mainly as a capable soldier in an impossible position; the legend says more about later memory than about him.

entries.title: The Donation of Constantine: the forgery that gave popes an empire
entries.dateNote: Forged probably 8th century; exposed by Lorenzo Valla 1439–1440
entries.mainstream: The Donation of Constantine is a forged Roman imperial decree in which Emperor Constantine the Great supposedly gave Pope Sylvester I and his successors authority over Rome, Italy and the western provinces of the empire, along with imperial insignia and the Lateran Palace, in gratitude for curing his leprosy through baptism. It was probably composed in the 8th century, built on the 5th-century legend of Sylvester (which also has him defeating a dragon in Rome). It was included in the 9th-century Pseudo-Isidorean Decretals and used, especially in the 13th century, to support papal claims to political power. Its authenticity had been challenged since 1001, but in 1439–1440 the Italian humanist Lorenzo Valla proved it a forgery using philology: its Latin used words and forms that did not exist in Constantine's time. It also names the wrong consul for its date.

alternatives.label: A founding forgery
alternatives.text: Historians see it as one of the most influential forgeries in history; its exposure is a classic early example of textual criticism, the same methods later used on many other documents.

alternatives.label: Who forged it
alternatives.text: The forger is unknown; it was probably produced in Rome or in the Frankish world in the 8th century, perhaps linked to papal alliances with the Frankish kings.

alternatives.label: Belief and power
alternatives.text: For centuries many accepted it in good faith; it shows how a document can shape real politics long before anyone checks it.

entries.title: John Dee, Edward Kelley and the angels' language
entries.mainstream: John Dee (1527 – 1608/9) was an English mathematician, astronomer, astrologer and adviser to Elizabeth I, who promoted English voyages of exploration and is credited with coining the term 'British Empire'. From 1582 he worked with the scryer Edward Kelley, who gazed into a 'shew-stone' and reported messages from angels. Dee recorded these sessions in detail: the angels dictated several books, some in a special angelic language now called Enochian, with its own alphabet. The two travelled in central Europe, meeting Emperor Rudolf II in Prague and King Stephen Báthory of Poland. In 1587 Kelley said the angel Uriel had ordered them to share everything, including their wives; Dee was distressed but apparently obeyed. Dee died in poverty at Mortlake. The British Museum holds objects linked to him, including an Aztec obsidian mirror, though the link of the mirror to Dee rests on Horace Walpole's later claim.

alternatives.label: A made-up language?
alternatives.text: The linguist Donald Laycock found that Enochian's sounds and grammar closely resemble English, with nothing beyond what a person could invent; most scholars think Kelley produced it, consciously or not.

alternatives.label: Real spirits
alternatives.text: Méric Casaubon, who published the diaries in 1659, believed the spirits were real but evil, deceiving Dee; later occultists adopted Enochian magic as a working system.

alternatives.label: Scientist and magician
alternatives.text: Historians stress that in Dee's time mathematics, astronomy, astrology and angelic magic were not clearly separated; he hoped the angels would reveal the secrets of nature.

entries.title: The dodo: a real bird that people later thought was a myth
entries.mainstream: The dodo was a flightless bird about 62–75 cm tall that lived only on Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. It belonged to the pigeon family; its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon, and its closest relative overall was the also-extinct Rodrigues solitaire. Dutch sailors first recorded it in 1598, and the last widely accepted sighting was in 1662, after hunting and animals introduced by people (such as rats, pigs and monkeys) destroyed it. Its extinction went unnoticed at first, and some later came to think the bird was a myth. Only drawings, paintings and written accounts show what it looked like, and they differ. In 1848 Hugh Strickland and Alexander Melville used the preserved head and foot in Oxford to show it was a real, pigeon-related bird, and large numbers of bones were later dug from the Mare aux Songes swamp. Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) made it famous.

alternatives.label: Fat and clumsy?
alternatives.text: The old image of a fat, stupid bird comes partly from overfed captive birds and artists' imagination; modern studies suggest it was well adapted to its island.

alternatives.label: Symbol of extinction
alternatives.text: The dodo became the world's best-known symbol of human-caused extinction; there are now projects that aim to 'de-extinct' it with genetic engineering, which many scientists question.

alternatives.label: From fact to myth and back
alternatives.text: Its story shows how quickly a real animal can be doubted, and is often compared with creatures like the okapi or giant squid that moved from legend to science.

media.title: The Real Story Of The Dodo Bird's (Current) Extinction

entries.title: The 774 CE cosmic-ray spike and the 'red crucifix' in the sky
entries.mainstream: In 2012 the Japanese physicist Fusa Miyake and colleagues reported a sudden jump in radioactive carbon-14 in the annual rings of Japanese cedars for the year 774/775 CE. It was soon found in trees worldwide, and matching spikes of beryllium-10 and chlorine-36 appear in ice cores. Such 'Miyake events' are now known for 7176 BCE, 5259 BCE, 664–663 BCE, 774 CE and 993 CE, with other candidates including a huge one around 12,350 BCE. Most scientists think they were caused by extreme storms of particles from the Sun, much stronger than any recorded in the modern age; a similar event today could severely damage satellites, communications and power grids. For 774 the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle recorded 'a red crucifix, after sunset', and 'wonderful serpents' seen in Sussex.

alternatives.label: What was the red crucifix
alternatives.text: Some have suggested the Chronicle's red cross was an aurora caused by the same solar storm, or a supernova; no supernova remnant of the right age is known, and the link is uncertain.

alternatives.label: Cosmic time-stamps
alternatives.text: Because the spikes fall in exact years, they can date wood precisely: wood from the Viking site at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland carries the 993 spike, showing the trees were cut in 1021 CE, proving Europeans were in the Americas that year.

alternatives.label: Other causes
alternatives.text: A gamma-ray burst from a distant star was proposed for 774, but is considered unlikely because the event also left beryllium and chlorine traces typical of solar particles.

sources.title: A signature of cosmic-ray increase in ad 774–775 from tree rings in Japan
Evidence for European presence in the Americas in ad 1021

entries.title: Shimabara and Japan's hidden Christians: a boy messiah and 250 years of secret faith
entries.mainstream: Christianity spread in Japan after Jesuit missionaries arrived in the 16th century, but the Tokugawa shogunate banned it. In December 1637, in the Shimabara and Amakusa region of Kyushu, heavy taxes and violent persecution under the lord Matsukura Katsuie sparked a rebellion of peasants and masterless samurai, many of them Catholics. Their leader was a teenager, Amakusa Shirō, known to followers as 'Heaven's messenger', to whom miraculous powers were attributed. The rebels held Hara Castle for months against a shogunate army of more than 125,000, which was helped by Dutch gunpowder, cannon and a Dutch ship. In April 1638 the castle fell; Shirō and an estimated 37,000 rebels and sympathisers were killed, and Japan tightened its seclusion and anti-Christian laws. Many Christians went underground for about 250 years, as Kakure Kirishitan ('hidden Christians'): they disguised the Virgin Mary as the Buddhist Kannon ('Maria Kannon') and passed down prayers orally, with Latin, Portuguese and Spanish words. When the ban was lifted in 1873, about 30,000 came out of hiding.

alternatives.label: Religious or economic
alternatives.text: It is often told as a Christian uprising, but the academic consensus is that it was driven mainly by peasant anger at misrule, with Christian identity becoming central as it spread.

alternatives.label: Prophecy and messiah
alternatives.text: Shirō's role as a charismatic youth with miraculous powers fits a worldwide pattern of messianic leaders in rebellions against overwhelming power.

alternatives.label: Faith that changed
alternatives.text: Some hidden-Christian communities, the Hanare Kirishitan, chose not to rejoin the Catholic Church, because their own tradition had become a distinct religion over centuries of secrecy.

media.title: The hidden religion banned in Japan for 200 years - BBC REEL

entries.title: Henderson Island: a Polynesian island whose people vanished
entries.dateNote: Settled possibly from c. 800 CE; abandoned before the 1600s
entries.mainstream: Henderson Island is an uninhabited raised coral island of about 37 km² in the Pitcairn group in the South Pacific, with poor soil, little fresh water and cliffs. Polynesians settled it, possibly from around 800 CE, and lived there for about 600 years, but by the 1600s it was empty. When the Portuguese captain Pedro Fernandes de Queirós, sailing for Spain, sighted it in 1606, no one lived there; Captain Henderson of the Hercules rediscovered it in 1819. The next year survivors of the whaleship Essex, sunk by a sperm whale (the inspiration for Moby-Dick), landed there. Its small community seems to have depended on trade with Pitcairn and with Mangareva for stone and other basics; when those links broke, the people disappeared. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1988) and, ironically, one of the places most polluted by plastic waste on Earth, carried by the South Pacific Gyre.

alternatives.label: Collapse of a network
alternatives.text: The mainstream explanation, popularised by Jared Diamond, is that Henderson and Pitcairn were at the end of a trade chain from Mangareva; when Mangareva's forests and society declined, the outlying islands could not survive alone.

alternatives.label: Moving on
alternatives.text: Some researchers suggest the people may have moved on rather than died out, noting links between Henderson, Pitcairn and Easter Island in language, tools and skulls.

alternatives.label: Mystery islands
alternatives.text: Henderson is one of several Pacific islands found empty by Europeans but with traces of earlier Polynesian life, a pattern that once fed theories of lost peoples.

media.title: Island's rubbish density 'world's worst' - BBC News

entries.title: Two-million-year-old DNA: mastodons in a warm Greenland forest
entries.dateNote: Sediments c. 2 million years old; DNA published 2022
entries.mainstream: The Kap København Formation is a set of sediments at the northern tip of Greenland. In 2022 a team led by Kurt Kjær and Eske Willerslev published DNA extracted from these sediments, collected in 2006: about two million years old, it was by far the oldest DNA ever sequenced. The DNA, bound to minerals in the sediment, revealed an open forest of poplar, birch and willow with avens and bilberry, animals including mastodons, hares, geese and reindeer, and, in the nearby sea, horseshoe crabs and corals. Average minimum temperatures were more than 10 °C warmer than today. The mastodon DNA showed that these elephant relatives once ranged much further north than anyone knew. Nothing like this ecosystem exists anywhere on Earth today.

alternatives.label: A window on warm climates
alternatives.text: The researchers see it as a guide to how life adapted to a much warmer Arctic, useful for understanding future climate change.

alternatives.label: How DNA survived
alternatives.text: Scientists had assumed DNA could not last this long; the team found that DNA bound to clay and quartz minerals can survive far longer than free DNA, especially in cold conditions.

alternatives.label: Lost worlds
alternatives.text: The finding is a real example of a 'lost world' in the far north, though from long before humans, so unrelated to legends of Hyperborea or lost polar civilisations.

sources.title: A 2-million-year-old ecosystem in Greenland uncovered by environmental DNA

entries.title: Enūma Eliš: Marduk splits the sea-dragon Tiamat to make heaven and earth
entries.dateNote: Composed c. 18th–12th century BCE; surviving copies mostly 7th century BCE
entries.mainstream: The Enūma Eliš ("When on high"), named after its opening words, is the Babylonian creation epic, written on seven clay tablets. Copies were found in the 19th century in the ruins of the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh; the composition is usually dated between the 18th and the 12th century BCE, with many scholars favouring the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I (c. 1100 BCE). It begins with the mingling of two primordial waters, Apsû (fresh water) and Tiamat (salt water). Younger gods are born, conflict follows, and Tiamat raises an army of monsters. The young god Marduk agrees to fight her if he is made king of the gods; he kills her, splits her body in two like a dried fish, and makes the sky from one half and the earth from the other, then creates humans from the blood of her general Kingu so that they can serve the gods. The poem was recited at the Babylonian New Year (Akitu) festival and served to justify Marduk's, and Babylon's, supremacy.

alternatives.label: Political theology
alternatives.text: Most Assyriologists read the epic as a statement of Babylon's rise: an older storm-god combat story was retold with Babylon's city god Marduk as the hero. In Assyrian copies Marduk was sometimes replaced by the Assyrian god Ashur.

alternatives.label: Genesis parallels
alternatives.text: The ordered creation, the dividing of the waters above from the waters below, and the Hebrew word tehom ("the deep"), possibly related to Tiamat, have led many scholars to see a Mesopotamian background to Genesis 1; others stress the differences, since Genesis has no divine battle.

alternatives.label: Chaos-dragon pattern
alternatives.text: The theme of a storm god defeating a sea serpent recurs in Ugaritic Baal and Yam, Hittite Tarhunz and Illuyanka, and biblical Leviathan; whether this reflects shared ancestry, borrowing, or a common human way of picturing order defeating chaos is debated.

alternatives.label: Ancient-astronaut reading
alternatives.text: Zecharia Sitchin read Tiamat as a former planet destroyed in a collision with the hypothetical planet Nibiru; astronomers and Assyriologists reject this as unsupported by the texts or by planetary science (speculative).

media.author: editor Austen Henry Layard , drawing by L. Gruner
