entries.title: Sargon of Akkad: the first empire and the baby in the reed basket
entries.dateNote: Reign c. 2334–2279 BCE (middle chronology); the basket legend is known from 7th-century BCE copies
entries.mainstream: Sargon of Akkad founded what is often called the first empire, uniting the Sumerian city-states of southern Mesopotamia and campaigning as far as Syria and Elam; his traditional dates are c. 2334–2279 BCE (middle chronology). His capital, Akkad (Agade), has never been located. His dynasty made Akkadian the language of administration and his daughter Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon god at Ur, is the earliest author known by name. Much later, a Neo-Assyrian text known as the 'Legend of Sargon' (7th century BCE) has Sargon say that his mother, a high priestess, bore him in secret, placed him in a basket of rushes sealed with bitumen and set him on the river, where he was found and raised by Akki, a water-drawer, before the goddess Ishtar loved him and he became king.

alternatives.label: Founding-hero pattern
alternatives.text: The basket story closely resembles the infancy of Moses in Exodus 2 and recalls other exposed-infant tales (Romulus and Remus, Cyrus the Great in Herodotus, Karna in the Mahabharata). Folklorists such as Otto Rank grouped these as a common "myth of the birth of the hero".

alternatives.label: Who borrowed from whom
alternatives.text: Some biblical scholars think the Moses story drew on the Sargon legend, which was well known in the Assyrian period; others see independent use of a widespread motif. Neither can be proven from the surviving texts.

alternatives.label: Real usurper
alternatives.text: Historians generally read the legend as propaganda explaining how a man of humble or uncertain birth (Sargon's name, Sharru-kin, means "the king is legitimate") came to rule, rather than as biography.

media.title: Sargon of Akkad: History's First Emperor?

entries.title: The Hittites: a forgotten empire rediscovered in 1906
entries.mainstream: Until the late 19th century the Hittites were known almost only as a minor people mentioned in the Hebrew Bible (Uriah the Hittite, the sons of Heth). In 1906 Hugo Winckler began excavating at Boğazköy in central Anatolia and found a royal archive of thousands of clay tablets, including a copy of the peace treaty between the Hittite king Hattusili III and Ramesses II of Egypt that had been known from Egyptian temple walls: the site was Hattusa, capital of a great Bronze Age empire (c. 1650–1180 BCE). In 1915 the Czech scholar Bedřich Hrozný showed that the Hittite language was Indo-European, the oldest attested member of that family. The Hittites fought Egypt at Kadesh (c. 1274 BCE) and corresponded with a land called Ahhiyawa, probably Mycenaean Greeks. Hattusa was abandoned around 1180 BCE during the Late Bronze Age collapse.

alternatives.label: Kumarbi and Kronos
alternatives.text: The Hittite 'Kingship in Heaven' myth, adapted from Hurrian sources, has the god Kumarbi overthrow and castrate the sky god Anu before being overthrown in turn by the storm god; scholars widely see this as a forerunner of Hesiod's story of Ouranos, Kronos and Zeus, showing myths travelled from Anatolia to Greece.

alternatives.label: Troy connection
alternatives.text: Hittite letters mention Wilusa and its ruler Alaksandu, which many scholars equate with (W)ilios/Troy and Alexandros (Paris); this identification is widely accepted but not certain.

alternatives.label: Why the collapse
alternatives.text: Explanations for the fall of the Hittite state include drought and famine (tree-ring and pollen evidence), internal conflict, disruption of trade and the 'Sea Peoples'; most researchers favour a combination.

entries.changed: Before 1906 the Hittites were an obscure biblical people; the Boğazköy archive and Hrozný's decipherment (1915) revealed a major Bronze Age empire and the oldest written Indo-European language.

media.title: The Entire History Of The Hittites / Ancient History Documentary

entries.title: Ugarit: the city of the first alphabet and the Baal Cycle
entries.mainstream: In 1928 a farmer ploughing near Ras Shamra on the Syrian coast broke into an ancient tomb, and excavations from 1929 under Claude Schaeffer uncovered Ugarit, a wealthy port city destroyed around 1185 BCE. Its archives held texts in several languages and a local cuneiform alphabet of about 30 signs, one of the earliest alphabets, with abecedaries that list the letters in an order close to the later Phoenician, Hebrew and Greek alphabets. Among the tablets is the Baal Cycle, in which the storm god Baal defeats Yam (Sea), gets a palace, and is swallowed by Mot (Death) before returning to life. The poems call a sea monster Lotan, the 'twisting serpent', with almost the same words that Isaiah 27:1 uses for Leviathan, and they refer to El as father of the gods with his divine council. Letters from the last days describe enemy ships on the coast just before the city fell.

alternatives.label: Bible background
alternatives.text: Ugaritic texts transformed biblical studies by showing the Canaanite religious language (El, Baal, Asherah, Leviathan, the divine council) that the Hebrew Bible both drew on and polemicised against; scholars debate how much early Israelite religion overlapped with Canaanite religion.

alternatives.label: Dying and rising god
alternatives.text: Baal's death and return have been read as a seasonal myth of drought and rain; the broader idea of a common 'dying and rising god' type (from James Frazer) is contested by many modern historians of religion.

alternatives.label: The final letters
alternatives.text: Letters such as one from the king of Ugarit to the king of Alashiya (Cyprus) describe enemy ships burning towns; they were long said to have been found in a kiln, never sent, but later re-examination of the excavation records questioned that find context, a reminder of how dramatic stories attach to finds.

media.title: 2. The Bronze Age Collapse - Mediterranean Apocalypse

entries.title: Did Phoenicians sail around Africa c. 600 BCE? Herodotus and the sun on the wrong side
entries.dateNote: Reported by Herodotus c. 430 BCE; voyage set in the reign of Necho II (610–595 BCE)
entries.mainstream: In his Histories (Book 4.42), written in the 5th century BCE, the Greek historian Herodotus says that the Egyptian pharaoh Necho II (reigned 610–595 BCE) sent Phoenician sailors south down the Red Sea with orders to return through the 'Pillars of Heracles' (the Strait of Gibraltar). Each autumn they landed, sowed grain and waited for the harvest, and in the third year they arrived back in Egypt. Herodotus adds that he does not believe one detail of their report: that as they sailed westward around the south of Libya (Africa) they had the sun on their right, that is, to the north. No other ancient source independently confirms the voyage, and no archaeology has been found.

alternatives.label: The disbelieved detail as evidence
alternatives.text: Many modern historians point out that south of the equator the midday sun really does stand to the north, so the detail Herodotus rejected is exactly what a real crossing would report; for them this makes the voyage plausible.

alternatives.label: Sceptical view
alternatives.text: Other scholars argue the voyage would have been very hard against the currents and winds off West Africa, that the story could be built from geographical speculation, and that the sun detail could have been reasoned out or added; they classify it as unproven.

alternatives.label: Later attempts
alternatives.text: Herodotus also tells of a Persian, Sataspes, who failed to sail around Africa, and the Carthaginian Hanno is said to have explored the West African coast; the first documented European rounding of the Cape was by Bartolomeu Dias in 1488.

entries.title: The Library of Ashurbanipal and the 1872 discovery of a flood story older than Noah's
entries.mainstream: Ashurbanipal, king of Assyria (668–c. 631 BCE), collected or had copied thousands of tablets on divination, medicine, magic, literature and history into royal libraries at Nineveh; he boasted that he could read and write. When Nineveh was sacked in 612 BCE the fire baked many of the clay tablets hard, preserving them. Austen Henry Layard and Hormuzd Rassam excavated them from 1849 onward and about 30,000 fragments went to the British Museum. In 1872 George Smith, a self-taught former banknote engraver working on them, recognised part of the Epic of Gilgamesh in which Utnapishtim survives a flood in a boat, sends out birds and offers a sacrifice. When Smith presented this to the Society of Biblical Archaeology in December 1872 it caused a sensation, because it showed that a Mesopotamian flood story very like Genesis existed in an older written tradition.

alternatives.label: Borrowing or shared memory
alternatives.text: Most scholars think the biblical flood narrative drew on Mesopotamian flood tradition (Atrahasis, Gilgamesh XI), probably during or before the Babylonian exile; some argue both preserve memory of real, very large local floods in Mesopotamia, as found in flood deposits at Ur, Kish and Shuruppak.

alternatives.label: Literal flood view
alternatives.text: Some religious readers take the Mesopotamian versions as distorted memories of a single real global flood that Genesis records accurately; geologists find no evidence of a single worldwide flood in human times.

alternatives.label: A library that burned to survive
alternatives.text: Unlike the Library of Alexandria, whose papyrus books were lost, this library survived because of its destruction: fire hardened clay.

entries.changed: The 1872 identification of the Gilgamesh flood tablet changed debates about the originality and sources of Genesis.

entries.title: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon: the Wonder no one can find
entries.mainstream: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon are one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Greek and Roman writers such as Berossus (via Josephus), Diodorus Siculus, Strabo and Quintus Curtius Rufus describe terraced gardens raised on vaults and watered by machinery, usually attributing them to Nebuchadnezzar II (reigned 605–562 BCE) for a wife homesick for the green mountains of Media. However, no Babylonian text, including Nebuchadnezzar's own detailed building inscriptions, mentions them, and Herodotus, who describes Babylon, does not mention them. Robert Koldewey, who excavated Babylon from 1899, proposed that a vaulted building in the Southern Palace was their base, but it is now thought to have been a storehouse or administrative building.

alternatives.label: They were at Nineveh
alternatives.text: The Assyriologist Stephanie Dalley (2013) argued that the gardens were built by the Assyrian king Sennacherib (c. 700 BCE) at Nineveh, watered by his aqueducts and Archimedes-screw-like devices described in his inscriptions, and that later Greeks confused the two cities; this has support but is not accepted by everyone.

alternatives.label: Lost to the river
alternatives.text: Some think the gardens did exist at Babylon but were destroyed and their remains lie under the shifting Euphrates or unexcavated ground.

alternatives.label: Literary invention
alternatives.text: Others suggest the gardens were a romantic idea built up by Greek writers from reports of Mesopotamian royal parks, and never existed in the form described.

entries.title: The Ebla tablets: an unknown Syrian kingdom and the battle over biblical names
entries.mainstream: In 1964 an Italian team led by Paolo Matthiae began digging at Tell Mardikh in northern Syria; in 1968 an inscribed statue identified the site as Ebla, a city known from Mesopotamian texts, and in 1974–76 they found a palace archive of about 17,000 tablets and fragments from around 2400–2300 BCE, written in Sumerian and in a previously unknown Semitic language now called Eblaite. Ebla was a major trading kingdom that was destroyed and rebuilt several times. The archive's first epigrapher, Giovanni Pettinato, initially reported that the tablets mentioned names like Sodom and Gomorrah, Abraham-like personal names and a god 'Ya', apparently linking them to the Bible. These claims caused a worldwide stir, a dispute within the team and political sensitivity, and were later rejected or withdrawn after closer reading by other epigraphers such as Alfonso Archi.

alternatives.label: Mainstream outcome
alternatives.text: Scholars now agree that the archive is extremely important for early Syrian history, language and trade, but that it contains no references to biblical people or places.

alternatives.label: Suppression claims
alternatives.text: During the controversy some writers claimed the biblical evidence was being suppressed for political reasons; specialists attribute the reversal to misreadings of early cuneiform signs, which were corrected as study progressed.

alternatives.label: Lesson about sensational finds
alternatives.text: The episode is often cited as an example of how early readings of new texts can be shaped by what researchers and the public hope to find.

entries.title: Inanna's descent to the underworld: a goddess hung on a hook for three days
entries.dateNote: Surviving tablets c. 1900–1600 BCE; the tradition is probably older
entries.mainstream: The Sumerian poem known as the Descent of Inanna into the Underworld survives on tablets mostly from the Old Babylonian period (c. 1900–1600 BCE). Inanna, queen of heaven, decides to visit the underworld ruled by her sister Ereshkigal. At each of seven gates she must give up a piece of her regalia until she arrives naked, is judged, killed, and her corpse is hung on a hook. After three days and nights her servant Ninshubur seeks help, and the god Enki creates two beings who revive her with the food and water of life. But no one may leave the underworld without a substitute, and Inanna chooses her husband Dumuzi, who did not mourn her; in the end Dumuzi and his sister Geshtinanna share the underworld for half the year each. A later Akkadian version tells of Ishtar's descent.

alternatives.label: Seasonal myth
alternatives.text: Many scholars connect Dumuzi's half-year in the underworld with the agricultural or pastoral year and with annual mourning rites for Dumuzi (Tammuz), which Ezekiel 8:14 mentions women performing at the Jerusalem temple.

alternatives.label: Comparative patterns
alternatives.text: The story has been compared with Persephone's half-year in Hades, with Orpheus, and, controversially, with Christian resurrection imagery (the three days); scholars disagree about whether such parallels reflect any historical connection.

alternatives.label: Initiation reading
alternatives.text: Some psychologists and modern spiritual writers read the descent as a model of an inner journey of loss and renewal; this is an interpretive, not historical, reading.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Descent of Inanna into the Underworld

entries.title: Oannes and the seven Apkallu: fish-men who taught humanity civilisation
entries.dateNote: Berossus wrote c. 290–278 BCE; apkallu imagery is attested from at least the 9th century BCE
entries.mainstream: Mesopotamian tradition held that before the Flood seven sages, the apkallu, were sent by the wise god Enki (Ea) to teach humans the arts of civilisation, each serving a king. Around 290–278 BCE the Babylonian priest Berossus, writing in Greek for the Seleucid king Antiochus I, described the first of them, Oannes, as a creature with the body of a fish and a human head and feet that came out of the Erythraean Sea, spent the days among people teaching writing, mathematics, laws, building, agriculture and the founding of temples, and returned to the sea at night. Berossus's work survives only in quotations by later authors. Assyrian palace reliefs and figurines show apkallu as men wearing fish cloaks, as bird-headed beings, or as winged genies carrying a bucket and cone, often in protective scenes.

alternatives.label: Mythological reading
alternatives.text: Assyriologists see the apkallu as mythic culture-bringers who legitimise civilisation as a divine gift and connect antediluvian kings to later scholars, who traced their learning back to the sages.

alternatives.label: Ancient-astronaut reading
alternatives.text: Robert Temple (The Sirius Mystery, 1976) and others linked Oannes to the amphibious Nommo of Dogon tradition and proposed visitors from the Sirius system; scholars reject both the Dogon interpretation and the alien hypothesis as unsupported (speculative).

alternatives.label: Lost-civilisation reading
alternatives.text: Some alternative writers read the sages who emerge from the sea after or before a flood as memories of survivors of an earlier seafaring culture teaching others; there is no archaeological evidence for this (speculative).

alternatives.label: Biblical echoes
alternatives.text: Scholars compare the antediluvian sages with the long-lived patriarchs of Genesis 5 and with the Watchers of the Book of Enoch, who also teach forbidden arts before the Flood.

entries.title: The Nag Hammadi library: buried Gnostic gospels found in a jar in 1945
entries.dateNote: Codices copied 4th century CE; found December 1945
entries.mainstream: In December 1945 farmers digging for fertile soil near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt found a sealed jar containing thirteen leather-bound papyrus codices. According to the account later gathered from one of them, Muhammad Ali al-Samman, some pages were burned as kindling before the books were sold. The codices, written in Coptic in the 4th century CE and translated from Greek originals, contain 52 texts, most previously unknown, including the Gospel of Thomas (114 sayings attributed to Jesus), the Gospel of Philip, the Apocryphon of John and the Gospel of Truth. Many reflect Gnostic thought: salvation through secret knowledge (gnosis), and a lower creator god distinct from the true, hidden God. They are now in the Coptic Museum in Cairo; a full English translation edited by James M. Robinson appeared in 1977.

alternatives.label: Hidden from the authorities?
alternatives.text: A widely repeated idea is that monks of the nearby Pachomian monastery hid the books after Bishop Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 CE listed the accepted biblical books and condemned others; this is plausible but not proven, and some scholars think the books were buried with a burial or by private owners.

alternatives.label: Early or late?
alternatives.text: Some scholars argue that parts of the Gospel of Thomas preserve sayings as early as those in the canonical gospels; others date it to the 2nd century and see it as dependent on them.

alternatives.label: Suppressed Christianity
alternatives.text: Popular books, notably Elaine Pagels's The Gnostic Gospels (1979), present the texts as voices of early Christian diversity later suppressed by an emerging orthodoxy; other historians caution that 'Gnosticism' itself is a modern umbrella term covering very different groups.

entries.title: The Gospel of Judas: the betrayer as hero, from a codex that rotted in a bank vault
entries.dateNote: Text probably 2nd century; codex c. 280 CE; published 2006
entries.mainstream: The Gospel of Judas is a Gnostic text in which Jesus shares secret teachings with Judas Iscariot and tells him that he will 'exceed' the other disciples by sacrificing 'the man that clothes me'. A gospel of that name was condemned by Bishop Irenaeus of Lyon around 180 CE, but no copy was known until a Coptic codex, later called Codex Tchacos, surfaced on the antiquities market after being found in Egypt in the 1970s. It spent years in poor conditions, including a safe-deposit box in New York, and crumbled badly before it was bought by the Maecenas Foundation, restored and published by the National Geographic Society in 2006. Radiocarbon dating placed the codex around 280 CE (±60 years).

alternatives.label: Judas as hero
alternatives.text: The first published interpretation presented Judas as the favoured disciple who helped Jesus escape his body.

alternatives.label: Judas as demon
alternatives.text: Other Coptic scholars, notably April DeConick (2007), argued the translation was mistaken in key places and that the text actually calls Judas the 'thirteenth daemon' and condemns him; the meaning remains debated.

alternatives.label: Provenance problems
alternatives.text: Because the codex was looted and traded without a clear record, scholars use it with caution and the case is cited in debates about the ethics of publishing unprovenanced manuscripts.

entries.title: The 'Gospel of Jesus's Wife': a papyrus scrap that fooled Harvard
entries.mainstream: In September 2012 the Harvard historian Karen L. King announced a business-card-sized papyrus fragment in Coptic containing the words 'Jesus said to them, "My wife..."'. She was careful to say it did not show the historical Jesus was married, but that some early Christians discussed it; the media dubbed it the Gospel of Jesus's Wife. Coptic scholars quickly raised doubts: the text appeared to copy words and even a typographical error from an online edition of the Gospel of Thomas. Lab tests in 2014 dated the papyrus to the early medieval period and found the ink consistent with ancient ink, which did not settle the question. In 2016 the journalist Ariel Sabar traced the fragment's owner, Walter Fritz, a former Egyptology student who had run adult websites, and showed the provenance documents were doubtful. King then said the evidence 'tips the balance' toward forgery.

alternatives.label: Scholarly consensus
alternatives.text: The fragment is now generally regarded as a modern forgery written on a genuine old piece of papyrus.

alternatives.label: Owner's position
alternatives.text: Fritz denied forging the text in interviews with Sabar, and no court finding exists; the forgery conclusion rests on textual, documentary and journalistic evidence.

alternatives.label: Wider debate
alternatives.text: The case showed that scientific testing of materials cannot by itself authenticate a text, and fed into a broader debate about unprovenanced manuscripts such as the Museum of the Bible's forged 'Dead Sea Scroll' fragments.

entries.changed: Announced 2012 as a possible ancient text; by 2016 even the scholar who announced it accepted it was probably forged.

sources.title: “Jesus said to them, ‘My wife . . .'”: A New Coptic Papyrus Fragment

entries.title: The Knights Templar: arrested on Friday 13 October 1307
entries.mainstream: The Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon were founded in Jerusalem around 1119 to protect pilgrims, and named after their headquarters in the al-Aqsa mosque, believed to be the Temple of Solomon. They grew into a rich international order of warrior monks with an early form of banking. After the loss of the Holy Land in 1291 they lost their purpose. At dawn on Friday 13 October 1307 King Philip IV of France, who owed them money, had all Templars in France arrested on charges of heresy, spitting on the cross, idolatry (worshipping a head called Baphomet) and sodomy; many confessed under torture. Pope Clement V dissolved the order in 1312 and the last Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, was burned in Paris in March 1314 after retracting his confession. The Chinon Parchment, rediscovered in the Vatican Secret Archives in 2001, shows that Clement had privately absolved the leaders in 1308.

alternatives.label: Mainstream view
alternatives.text: Most historians think the charges were fabricated or extracted under torture and that Philip's motives were largely financial and political.

alternatives.label: Secret survival
alternatives.text: Legends from the 18th century onward claim the Templars survived in secret, passing their knowledge to the Freemasons or to Scotland (Rosslyn Chapel), or that they held the Holy Grail, the Ark of the Covenant or the Shroud of Turin; historians find no documentary support (speculative).

alternatives.label: Friday the 13th
alternatives.text: The idea that the arrest is the origin of Friday the 13th as an unlucky day is popular but unsupported; that superstition is not documented before the 19th century.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Trials of the Knights Templar

entries.title: The Holy Grail: from a mysterious dish in a 12th-century romance to bloodline theories
entries.mainstream: The Grail first appears in Chrétien de Troyes' unfinished romance Perceval, the Story of the Grail (c. 1180–1190), as a precious dish carried in a procession at the castle of a wounded Fisher King; Perceval fails to ask the question that would heal him. Soon afterwards Robert de Boron made it the cup of the Last Supper in which Joseph of Arimathea caught Christ's blood and which was brought to Britain, while Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (c. 1210) made it a stone that fell from heaven. In the 13th-century Vulgate Cycle, the pure knight Galahad achieves the Grail quest. Several real vessels are venerated as the Grail, including the Holy Chalice in Valencia Cathedral.

alternatives.label: Celtic roots
alternatives.text: Some scholars trace the Grail to Celtic magic vessels such as the cauldron of plenty of the Dagda or the cauldrons of Welsh tales; others see it as mainly a Christian creation of the 12th century linked to Eucharistic devotion.

alternatives.label: Bloodline theory
alternatives.text: The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail (1982) argued that san graal (holy grail) should be read sang real (royal blood) and that Jesus's descendants survived in France, protected by a Priory of Sion; the Priory documents were shown to be forgeries created by Pierre Plantard in the 1960s, and historians reject the theory.

alternatives.label: Psychological reading
alternatives.text: Jungian writers read the quest as a symbol of spiritual wholeness; this is interpretation rather than historical claim.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail

media.title: Galahad, Perceval, and the Holy Grail: Crash Course World Mythology #28

entries.title: Pope Joan: the female pope who supposedly gave birth in a procession
entries.dateNote: Legend first recorded c. 1250; set c. 855–857 CE
entries.mainstream: According to a legend first recorded in the mid-13th century (by the Dominican Jean de Mailly, and spread widely by Martin of Opava's chronicle), a learned woman disguised as a man rose through the Church to become pope, reigning for just over two years in the 9th century, often placed between Leo IV (died 855) and Benedict III. She was exposed when she gave birth during a procession between St Peter's and the Lateran, and died soon afterwards. The story was widely believed in the late Middle Ages: a bust of 'Johannes VIII, a woman from England' stood among papal busts in Siena Cathedral, and later Protestant writers used her against the papacy. Historians find no contemporary evidence for her and no gap in the papal succession where she could fit.

alternatives.label: Debunked by a Protestant
alternatives.text: The French Protestant scholar David Blondel argued in 1647 that the story was false, showing the chronology does not allow it; most historians since agree.

alternatives.label: Origins of the legend
alternatives.text: Suggested sources include Roman street names and a statue near the Lateran misread as a woman and child, satire about the influence of women such as Marozia over 10th-century popes, and the use of a pierced chair in papal ceremonies, which later stories claimed was for checking a pope's sex.

alternatives.label: A real hidden woman?
alternatives.text: A minority of writers, including the novelist Donna Woolfolk Cross, argue that records could have been erased; there is no documentary support for this.

entries.title: The Children's Crusade of 1212: a march to the sea that would not part
entries.mainstream: In 1212 two popular movements, one led by a shepherd boy, Stephen of Cloyes, in France, and one by a youth called Nicholas in the Rhineland, gathered thousands of young people and poor folk who set off to recover Jerusalem, believing that the sea would part for them. Nicholas's followers crossed the Alps to Italy, where the Mediterranean did not open; many dispersed, stayed in Italy or struggled home. Later chroniclers, writing decades afterwards, added that merchants offered them ships and sold them into slavery in North Africa. The contemporary chronicles are short and sometimes contradictory.

alternatives.label: Not really children
alternatives.text: The historian Peter Raedts (1977) and others argued that the Latin pueri used by chroniclers meant the poor, landless or young people in general, so the movement was a popular crusade of the poor rather than of children; this view is widely accepted.

alternatives.label: Myth growth
alternatives.text: The slavery and shipwreck episodes appear in later sources and are thought to be legendary embellishment.

alternatives.label: Pied Piper link
alternatives.text: Some writers connect the loss of Hamelin's children in 1284 to similar movements of young people (to crusades or eastern colonisation); this is one of several speculative explanations of the Pied Piper legend.

entries.title: Joan of Arc: the voices that led a peasant girl to command an army
entries.mainstream: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431), a peasant girl from Domrémy in north-eastern France, said that from about the age of 13 she heard the voices of Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret telling her to help the dauphin Charles drive the English out of France. In 1429, aged about 17, she persuaded Charles to send her with the army to relieve the siege of Orléans, which was lifted within nine days, and she was present when Charles was crowned at Reims. Captured in 1430, she was tried for heresy by a pro-English church court at Rouen, partly for wearing men's clothing, and burned on 30 May 1431. A retrial authorised by the pope annulled the verdict in 1456, and she was canonised in 1920. The detailed transcripts of both trials survive, making her one of the best-documented people of the Middle Ages.

alternatives.label: Religious explanation
alternatives.text: For believers, including the Catholic Church, her voices were genuine divine communications.

alternatives.label: Medical hypotheses
alternatives.text: Modern doctors have proposed conditions such as idiopathic partial epilepsy with auditory features, migraine or psychiatric illness; others point out that diagnosing a person dead for six centuries from trial testimony is speculative.

alternatives.label: Survival story
alternatives.text: In 1436 a woman, Jeanne (Claude) des Armoises, appeared claiming to be Joan, escaped from execution, and was accepted by some, including reportedly Joan's brothers, before being exposed as an impostor; a modern fringe theory that Joan survived has no support among historians.

media.title: Joan of Arc: Martyr and a Patron Saint of France

entries.title: The Wild Hunt: a ghostly army seen riding across the sky in 1091 and 1127
entries.dateNote: Medieval accounts from 1091 and 1127; named by Grimm in 1835
entries.mainstream: Across Europe, folklore told of a ghostly procession of the dead, hunters or warriors that rushed across the night sky or along roads, often in winter, led by a figure such as Odin/Wodan, Herne, King Arthur, Herodias or the devil; seeing it could foretell death or disaster. Some of the earliest descriptions are in medieval chronicles. The Norman monk Orderic Vitalis records that on 1 January 1091 a priest named Walchelin met the 'household of Herlechin', a vast column of suffering dead, including people he knew. The Peterborough version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle reports that in 1127, after an unpopular abbot arrived, many people saw and heard huntsmen, black and huge, riding on black horses with hounds through the deer park and woods. Jacob Grimm, in his Deutsche Mythologie (1835), coined the term 'wild hunt' (Wilde Jagd) and linked it to a pre-Christian Wodan cult.

alternatives.label: Pagan survival
alternatives.text: Grimm and later writers saw the Hunt as a survival of beliefs about Odin leading the dead; modern scholars think this is partly right but warn that the medieval stories were shaped mainly by Christian ideas of purgatory and penance.

alternatives.label: Natural phenomena
alternatives.text: Possible natural triggers include the calls of migrating geese at night, storms and wind in forests, and auroras; this explains some reports but not the detailed visions.

alternatives.label: Collective experience or rumour
alternatives.text: The 1127 report is often read as political satire on the abbot or as rumour amplified by fear; believers in the paranormal treat such accounts as genuine sightings.

entries.title: The Cathars: a dualist church destroyed by a crusade, and the legend of their treasure
entries.mainstream: From the 12th century, groups of Christians in Languedoc (southern France) and northern Italy, called Cathars or Albigensians by their opponents, taught a dualist faith in which the material world was created by an evil principle, and a class of 'Perfect' (perfecti) lived strict ascetic lives. In 1209 Pope Innocent III launched the Albigensian Crusade against them and the southern nobles who protected them. At Béziers the crusaders massacred the inhabitants; the monk Caesarius of Heisterbach, writing some years later, attributes to the papal legate Arnaud Amalric the words 'Kill them all; God will know his own', although whether he said them is uncertain. The crusade ended in 1229, and the Inquisition, founded partly to deal with the Cathars, continued the repression. In 1244 more than 200 Perfect who would not recant were burned below the mountain fortress of Montségur.

alternatives.label: A real counter-church
alternatives.text: The traditional view, based on inquisition records and Cathar texts such as the Book of the Two Principles, is that Catharism was an organised dualist church with links to the Bogomils of the Balkans.

alternatives.label: Constructed by opponents
alternatives.text: Historians such as R. I. Moore and Mark Gregory Pegg argue that the idea of a unified Cathar church was largely constructed by churchmen and inquisitors from local religious diversity; this revisionist view is debated.

alternatives.label: Treasure and Grail
alternatives.text: A legend says that a few Perfect escaped from Montségur on the night before the surrender carrying the Cathar 'treasure'. In the 1930s Otto Rahn, later an SS officer, claimed it was the Holy Grail; there is no evidence for this (speculative).

entries.title: The Mechanical Turk: the chess-playing machine that beat Napoleon
entries.mainstream: In 1770 the Hungarian inventor Wolfgang von Kempelen presented to Empress Maria Theresa a life-size figure dressed in Ottoman robes seated at a cabinet, which appeared to play chess by itself. Before each game the doors were opened to show clockwork inside. For 84 years the Turk toured Europe and America, first with Kempelen and after 1804 with Johann Nepomuk Maelzel, defeating many challengers; a game against Napoleon in 1809 is the best-known story, and it is said to have played Benjamin Franklin in Paris. In reality a skilled human chess player hid inside the cabinet, sliding on a seat as the doors were opened and moving the pieces with a pantograph-like arm while following the game through magnets under the board. Edgar Allan Poe's essay 'Maelzel's Chess-Player' (1836) argued it must be human-operated. The machine was destroyed in a fire at the Chinese Museum in Philadelphia in 1854, and the son of its last owner published its secret in 1857.

alternatives.label: Hoax and showmanship
alternatives.text: The Turk is a classic illusion: audiences saw the machinery they expected and filled in the rest, which made it a much-cited example in debates on automata and mind.

alternatives.label: Did it really beat Napoleon?
alternatives.text: The Napoleon and Franklin games are reported in later accounts and some details are uncertain; historians accept that it played many notable people but treat individual anecdotes with caution.

alternatives.label: Legacy
alternatives.text: Its name was taken by Amazon Mechanical Turk (2005), a platform where hidden human workers do tasks that appear automated, a modern echo of the original deception.

media.title: Making Marvels—Reproduction of the Chess Player (The Turk)

entries.title: Mesmerism and the 1784 Franklin commission: one of the first blind trials
entries.mainstream: The German physician Franz Anton Mesmer (1734–1815) claimed that an invisible fluid, 'animal magnetism', flowed through all living things and that illness came from its obstruction. In Paris from 1778 he treated wealthy patients, often in groups around a tub (baquet) filled with magnetised water and iron rods, and many fell into convulsive 'crises' and reported cures. In 1784 King Louis XVI appointed commissions including Benjamin Franklin, the chemist Antoine Lavoisier, the astronomer Jean-Sylvain Bailly and the physician Joseph-Ignace Guillotin. They ran tests in which subjects were blindfolded or deceived about whether they were being magnetised: effects appeared when people believed they were being treated, whether or not they were, and did not appear when they were magnetised without knowing. The commission concluded that the fluid did not exist and the effects came from imagination.

alternatives.label: Scientific landmark
alternatives.text: Historians of medicine often cite the 1784 tests as one of the earliest uses of blinding and placebo-like controls, a method now central to clinical trials.

alternatives.label: Forerunner of hypnosis
alternatives.text: Mesmer's followers, such as the Marquis de Puységur, discovered trance states; the Scottish surgeon James Braid later reinterpreted them as 'hypnotism' (1841), which is now studied scientifically.

alternatives.label: Believers' view
alternatives.text: Mesmer and his supporters held that the commission had tested the wrong things; ideas of a vital energy field continued in later spiritualism and in some alternative medicine, which mainstream science does not support.

entries.title: Spring-heeled Jack: the leaping fire-breather of Victorian England
entries.mainstream: From late 1837, reports spread around the outskirts of London of a figure that could leap great heights and attacked or frightened people, usually women. In January 1838 the Lord Mayor of London, Sir John Cowan, publicly read out a letter about the attacks. In February 1838 Jane Alsop told magistrates that a man in a cloak had come to her family's door in Bow claiming to be a policeman, then vomited blue and white flames into her face, had eyes like red balls of fire and tore at her clothes with metallic claws. Sightings continued sporadically for decades, from the Midlands to Aldershot army camp, where sentries in 1877 reported a figure that leapt over them, and to Liverpool in 1904. Spring-heeled Jack became a stock villain of penny dreadfuls and stage plays.

alternatives.label: Pranksters
alternatives.text: The Marquess of Waterford, a notorious aristocratic prankster, was rumoured at the time to be responsible, but there is no proof; imitators probably caused some later incidents.

alternatives.label: Mass panic and folklore
alternatives.text: Many historians see Spring-heeled Jack as a moral panic or urban legend: a few real assaults and hoaxes, fed by newspapers and fiction, grew into a supernatural figure.

alternatives.label: Paranormal and alien readings
alternatives.text: Some modern writers have suggested a demon, a ghost, or an alien visitor, pointing to the leaping and glowing eyes; there is no evidence for these ideas (speculative).

entries.title: The Missoula floods: the geologist laughed at for proposing a giant Ice Age flood
entries.dateNote: Floods c. 18,000–15,000 years ago; proposed 1923; accepted by the 1960s–70s
entries.mainstream: In 1923 the geologist J Harlen Bretz proposed that the strange Channeled Scablands of eastern Washington state, with dry waterfalls, giant ripple marks and huge boulders, had been carved by a single catastrophic flood. At a time when geologists favoured slow, gradual change (uniformitarianism), the idea was treated as a throwback to biblical catastrophism and was publicly challenged at a meeting in Washington D.C. in 1927. The source of the water was identified by Joseph Pardee: Glacial Lake Missoula, a vast lake dammed by a lobe of the Cordilleran ice sheet in Montana, which repeatedly broke the ice dam and drained across Idaho, Washington and Oregon to the Pacific. Aerial photographs and Pardee's 1940s work on giant ripples convinced most geologists, and in 1979, aged 96, Bretz received the Penrose Medal. The floods happened between about 18,000 and 15,000 years ago.

alternatives.label: One flood or many
alternatives.text: Bretz first argued for one flood; work by Richard Waitt and others from about 1980 indicates dozens of separate floods as the ice dam repeatedly re-formed and failed.

alternatives.label: Younger Dryas impact link
alternatives.text: Supporters of the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis, including the writer Graham Hancock, have connected late Ice Age megafloods to a cosmic impact on the ice sheet; most geologists explain the floods by ice-dam failure alone and see no need for an impact.

alternatives.label: Lesson for science
alternatives.text: The case is often cited as an example of a correct idea rejected for decades because it conflicted with the prevailing paradigm.

entries.changed: Bretz's 1923 flood hypothesis was rejected by many geologists in the 1920s–30s; evidence from Pardee and later aerial imagery led to its acceptance, honoured with the Penrose Medal in 1979.

entries.title: Trinity: the first nuclear explosion, 16 July 1945
entries.mainstream: At 5:29 am on 16 July 1945, scientists of the Manhattan Project detonated a plutonium implosion device, nicknamed 'the Gadget', on a 30-metre tower in the Jornada del Muerto desert of New Mexico. The blast, equivalent to roughly 20–25 kilotons of TNT, was seen hundreds of kilometres away and turned desert sand into a green glass later called trinitite. The official cover story was that an ammunition dump had exploded. Less than a month later, similar weapons destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The laboratory director J. Robert Oppenheimer later recalled (in a 1965 television interview) that a line from the Bhagavad Gita came to his mind: 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.' Trinity marks the start of the Atomic Age, and the radioactive fallout from atmospheric tests later became a global marker layer proposed for the start of the 'Anthropocene'.

alternatives.label: Ancient nuclear war claims
alternatives.text: Some alternative writers have claimed that Indian epics such as the Mahabharata describe ancient atomic weapons, or that vitrified forts and desert glass show nuclear blasts in prehistory; scholars explain the texts as poetic descriptions of divine weapons and the glass as volcanic, impact or fire effects, and find no radioactive signature (speculative).

alternatives.label: Atomic age and UFOs
alternatives.text: The first modern wave of UFO reports began in 1947, two years after Trinity, and some early cases were near nuclear sites such as Roswell and Los Alamos; sceptics attribute this to Cold War anxiety and secret military projects, while some ufologists argue that nuclear activity attracted non-human attention (speculative).

alternatives.label: Downwinders
alternatives.text: Residents of nearby communities, many of them Hispanic and Native American, were not warned or evacuated; their health claims were largely ignored for decades.

entries.title: Photo 51 and the double helix: the woman whose data revealed DNA's structure
entries.dateNote: Photo taken May 1952; double helix published 25 April 1953
entries.mainstream: In May 1952 Raymond Gosling, a PhD student working under Rosalind Franklin at King's College London, took an X-ray diffraction photograph of the 'B' form of DNA, later known as Photo 51, whose X-shaped pattern indicated a helix. In January 1953 Maurice Wilkins showed the photograph to James Watson without Franklin's knowledge, and Watson and Francis Crick in Cambridge also saw an unpublished report summarising her measurements. On 25 April 1953 Nature published Watson and Crick's double-helix model alongside papers by Wilkins and colleagues and by Franklin and Gosling, presented as supporting evidence. Franklin moved to work on viruses and died of ovarian cancer in 1958, aged 37. Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962; the Nobel Prize is not awarded posthumously.

alternatives.label: Wronged heroine
alternatives.text: Watson's memoir The Double Helix (1968) portrayed Franklin unflatteringly; later biographers, starting with Anne Sayre (1975), presented her as a pioneer whose data was used without credit.

alternatives.label: Equal collaborator
alternatives.text: In 2023 the historians Matthew Cobb and Nathaniel Comfort, using newly studied documents, argued in Nature that Franklin was not a victim who failed to understand her data but an equal member of a competitive collaboration.

alternatives.label: Scientific debate
alternatives.text: Historians still debate how decisive Photo 51 itself was compared with Franklin's numerical measurements and the model-building of Watson and Crick.

entries.title: The echo of the Big Bang found by mistake: the cosmic microwave background (1965)
entries.mainstream: In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs were using a large horn antenna in Holmdel, New Jersey, for radio astronomy when they found a faint, steady microwave hiss coming from every direction, equivalent to a temperature of about 3 kelvins. They removed nesting pigeons and cleaned out what they called 'white dielectric material' (droppings), but the noise remained. Meanwhile a Princeton group under Robert Dicke was building an instrument to look for the predicted afterglow of a hot early universe; when Penzias called, Dicke reportedly told his team 'Boys, we've been scooped.' The two groups published side by side in 1965. The cosmic microwave background (CMB) was decisive evidence for the Big Bang model over the rival steady-state theory; Penzias and Wilson shared the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics. Satellites (COBE, WMAP, Planck) later mapped its tiny fluctuations.

alternatives.label: Earlier predictions
alternatives.text: Ralph Alpher, Robert Herman and George Gamow had predicted a relic radiation of a few kelvins in the late 1940s, a prediction that had been largely forgotten by 1964.

alternatives.label: Alternative cosmologies
alternatives.text: Fred Hoyle and colleagues proposed that the radiation could be starlight thermalised by dust in a steady-state or quasi-steady-state universe; most cosmologists regard the CMB's near-perfect blackbody spectrum as strongly against this.

alternatives.label: Remaining puzzles
alternatives.text: Some features of the CMB maps, such as the 'cold spot' and large-scale alignments sometimes called the 'axis of evil', are discussed as statistical flukes or as possible signs of new physics.

entries.title: LGM-1: the radio pulse first nicknamed 'Little Green Men' (1967)
entries.mainstream: In August 1967 the Cambridge PhD student Jocelyn Bell, checking kilometres of chart paper from a new radio telescope, noticed a small 'bit of scruff'. Follow-up showed a pulse repeating every 1.337 seconds with extraordinary regularity. Because no natural source was known to keep such precise time, the team half-seriously labelled it LGM-1, for 'Little Green Men', and briefly considered whether it might be an artificial signal. After Bell found a second similar source elsewhere in the sky, an alien origin became very unlikely, and the discovery was published in Nature in February 1968. The sources were soon explained as pulsars: rapidly spinning neutron stars sweeping beams of radio waves past Earth like a lighthouse. The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics went to her supervisor Antony Hewish (with Martin Ryle), not to Bell, which drew criticism; Bell Burnell herself said she was not upset. In 2018 she received the Breakthrough Prize and gave the $3 million to fund physics scholarships for under-represented students.

alternatives.label: Signal from aliens?
alternatives.text: The episode is a case study in how scientists test for artificial signals: the team looked for planetary orbital motion (Doppler shifts) that would be expected from a transmitter on a planet and did not find it.

alternatives.label: Credit debate
alternatives.text: Many scientists, including Fred Hoyle, criticised the Nobel decision; others argue that prizes routinely went to project leaders at the time.

alternatives.label: Pulsars as cosmic beacons
alternatives.text: The Pioneer plaques and Voyager Golden Record later used pulsars as a map to locate the Sun for any alien finder, turning the 'Little Green Men' signal into a message to them.

sources.title: Observation of a Rapidly Pulsating Radio Source

entries.title: The Voyager Golden Record: a message for whoever finds it
entries.mainstream: When NASA launched Voyager 1 and 2 in 1977, each carried a 12-inch gold-plated copper phonograph record intended as a message from Earth for any intelligent beings who might find it. A committee chaired by Carl Sagan, including Frank Drake, Ann Druyan, Timothy Ferris, Linda Salzman Sagan and Jon Lomberg, chose 115 encoded images, greetings in 55 languages, sounds of Earth such as wind, rain, whales and a heartbeat, and 90 minutes of music from Bach and Beethoven to Chuck Berry, Javanese gamelan and Navajo night chant. The cover shows how to play the record and, using 14 pulsars, where the Sun is. Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause into interstellar space in 2012, and Voyager 2 in 2018; they will not come within about 1.6 light-years of another star for some 40,000 years.

alternatives.label: Symbolic message
alternatives.text: Sagan himself said the chances of the record being found were small and that it mattered more as a statement to humanity about itself.

alternatives.label: Risk of contact
alternatives.text: Some scientists, notably Stephen Hawking, warned in general that announcing our presence to unknown civilisations could be dangerous, a debate also linked to the Fermi paradox; others reply that our radio and TV leakage already travels further than the probes.

alternatives.label: Reverse of the ancient-astronaut idea
alternatives.text: Writers have noted that the record is exactly the kind of artefact that ancient-astronaut theorists propose other civilisations may have left on Earth; no such artefact has been confirmed.

entries.title: The Laschamp excursion: when Earth's magnetic field nearly vanished 41,000 years ago
entries.mainstream: About 41,000 years ago Earth's magnetic field briefly reversed direction and fell to a small fraction of its present strength, an event named after the Laschamp lava flows in France's Massif Central where it was first identified in the 1960s. The reversal itself lasted only a few centuries. With the shield weakened, more cosmic rays reached the atmosphere, producing peaks of beryllium-10 in Greenland and Antarctic ice and of carbon-14 in the record. In 2021 Alan Cooper, Chris Turney and colleagues published in Science a precisely dated radiocarbon record from an ancient New Zealand kauri tree spanning the event and argued that the weakest phase, about 42,000 years ago, which they named the 'Adams event', caused ozone loss, climate shifts and higher ultraviolet levels.

alternatives.label: Wide-ranging effects
alternatives.text: Cooper and Turney suggested the event may have contributed to megafauna extinctions in Australia, the final decline of Neanderthals and a rise in cave art and red ochre use as sunscreen; these links are speculative and disputed.

alternatives.label: Sceptical response
alternatives.text: Other researchers, including archaeologists and palaeoclimatologists, argued that the proposed connections are not supported by the timing or by other climate records, and that previous excursions had no comparable effects.

alternatives.label: Future reversals
alternatives.text: The present field has weakened by about 9% in the past two centuries, and the South Atlantic Anomaly is growing; geophysicists say this does not necessarily mean a reversal is imminent.

sources.title: A global environmental crisis 42,000 years ago

entries.title: Unkulunkulu and the chameleon: the Zulu story of how death came into the world
entries.dateNote: Oral tradition of unknown age; recorded by Callaway 1868–70
entries.mainstream: In Zulu tradition as recorded in the 19th century, Unkulunkulu ('the very old one', or 'the great-great-one') was the first ancestor, who came forth from a bed of reeds (uhlanga) and brought out people, cattle and all things. He sent the chameleon to tell humans that they would not die, but the chameleon dawdled, stopping to eat. Unkulunkulu then sent the lizard (intulo) with the message that people would die; the lizard ran fast and arrived first, and so death came into the world. The best-known record is the Anglican missionary Henry Callaway's The Religious System of the Amazulu (1868–70), which printed testimonies in isiZulu with English translation; Callaway's informants differed among themselves, and some distinguished Unkulunkulu from a sky god, uMvelinqangi.

alternatives.label: Widespread African pattern
alternatives.text: Versions of the 'failed message' myth, in which a slow messenger with news of immortality is overtaken by a faster one bringing death, are recorded across much of sub-Saharan Africa (often with a chameleon, hare, dog or lizard); folklorists see it as one of the continent's most widespread myths.

alternatives.label: Missionary filter
alternatives.text: Historians note that Callaway and other missionaries asked questions shaped by Christian ideas of a creator, and that answers given in a colonial context may not reflect pre-colonial belief exactly.

alternatives.label: Ancestor or god
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether Unkulunkulu was understood as a creator god or as the first ancestor of humans, honoured within the wider ancestor (amadlozi) tradition.

entries.title: Shaka and the rise of the Zulu kingdom: history, legend and the 'mfecane' debate
entries.mainstream: Shaka kaSenzangakhona (c. 1787–1828) became chief of the small Zulu clan in about 1816 and within a decade built a powerful kingdom in what is now KwaZulu-Natal, through warfare, alliances and the reorganisation of age-regiments (amabutho). He is credited in tradition with introducing the short stabbing spear (iklwa) and the 'bull's horns' encircling formation, though some historians think these innovations were older or shared with neighbours such as the Mthethwa under Dingiswayo. In 1828 Shaka was assassinated by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana. Much of what was written about him came from a few European traders at Port Natal, especially Nathaniel Isaacs and Henry Francis Fynn, whose accounts portrayed him as a bloodthirsty tyrant, and from oral traditions later collected by James Stuart.

alternatives.label: The mfecane
alternatives.text: The traditional view holds that Zulu expansion set off the mfecane ('crushing'), a chain of wars and migrations across southern Africa in the 1820s–30s that produced states such as the Ndebele, Sotho and Gaza.

alternatives.label: Cobbing's challenge
alternatives.text: In 1988 the historian Julian Cobbing argued that the mfecane was a myth used as a colonial 'alibi', and that slave-raiding and labour demands from the Cape Colony and Delagoa Bay caused much of the upheaval; the debate that followed led many to see a more complex picture with multiple causes.

alternatives.label: National hero or tyrant
alternatives.text: Shaka is remembered as a founding hero and military genius (Shaka Day, 24 September, is Heritage Day in South Africa), while traders' tales of mass killings may have been exaggerated to attract settlers or to justify intervention.

entries.changed: From the 1980s, historians re-examined European trader sources and the idea of a Zulu-driven mfecane, giving more weight to colonial slave-raiding and environmental pressures.

entries.title: Nyai Roro Kidul: the Queen of the Southern Sea who married Java's kings
entries.dateNote: Linked to Senopati of Mataram (late 16th century); the belief is older
entries.mainstream: In Javanese and Sundanese belief, Nyai Roro Kidul (also Kanjeng Ratu Kidul) is the spirit queen of the Indian Ocean south of Java, ruling an undersea palace with an army of spirits. According to the Babad Tanah Jawi, a Javanese chronicle, Panembahan Senopati, founder of the Mataram Sultanate in the late 16th century, meditated on the southern shore and entered into a spiritual marriage with her, gaining her support for his dynasty; his successors, the sultans of Yogyakarta and the Susuhunans of Surakarta, are held to renew this bond. The sacred Bedhaya Ketawang dance at the Surakarta court is said to honour her, and offerings are made at the beach of Parangkusumo. Popular belief warns against wearing green on south-coast beaches, as she may take swimmers, and a room at a hotel in Pelabuhan Ratu is kept for her.

alternatives.label: Political theology
alternatives.text: Historians read the marriage as a way for Mataram's rulers to anchor Islamic kingship in older Javanese ideas of sacred power over land and sea.

alternatives.label: Natural danger
alternatives.text: The south coast of Java has powerful rip currents and dangerous surf; the warnings attached to her may encode real hazards, a pattern seen in other water-spirit traditions.

alternatives.label: Living belief
alternatives.text: For many Javanese she is a real spiritual being; for some Muslim reformers her cult is un-Islamic; and she is a popular figure of horror films and folklore.

entries.title: Majapahit: the Javanese empire born from a trick on Kublai Khan's fleet
entries.mainstream: In 1293 a Mongol-Chinese fleet sent by Kublai Khan landed in Java to punish King Kertanegara of Singhasari, who had insulted his envoy. Kertanegara had already been killed by a rebel, and his son-in-law Raden Wijaya allied with the Mongols to defeat the rebel, then turned on them and drove them out, founding the kingdom of Majapahit with its capital near present-day Trowulan in East Java. Under King Hayam Wuruk and his chief minister Gajah Mada, who according to the Pararaton swore the Palapa oath (c. 1336) not to taste spices until he had united the archipelago, Majapahit became the dominant power in maritime Southeast Asia. The court poem Nagarakretagama (1365) by Mpu Prapanca lists dozens of 'tributary' lands across modern Indonesia and beyond. Majapahit declined in the 15th century and ended around 1527 as Islamic sultanates such as Demak rose.

alternatives.label: How big was it?
alternatives.text: Indonesian nationalists from the 20th century presented Majapahit as a forerunner of a unified Indonesia; many historians think its direct control was limited mainly to Java, Bali and Madura, and that the Nagarakretagama's list mixes trade partners and claimed vassals.

alternatives.label: Gajah Mada mystery
alternatives.text: Gajah Mada's origins and death are unknown, which has fed legends; a terracotta face from Trowulan popularly said to be his portrait has no firm identification.

alternatives.label: Hindu-Buddhist legacy
alternatives.text: After Majapahit fell, tradition holds that nobles and priests fled to Bali, which preserved its Hindu culture; this is broadly supported though simplified.

entries.title: The Ifugao rice terraces: 2,000 years old, or built in response to the Spanish?
entries.dateNote: Traditional estimate 2,000+ years; radiocarbon evidence suggests major expansion after c. 1600 CE
entries.mainstream: The rice terraces of the Ifugao people in the Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon in the Philippines climb steep slopes up to about 1,500 m, fed by forest water channelled down the hills; they became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995. For much of the 20th century they were said to be 2,000–3,000 years old, an estimate popularised by the anthropologist H. Otley Beyer, who assumed the very slow growth needed for such large works. From 2012 the Ifugao Archaeological Project, led by Stephen Acabado with Ifugao community partners, excavated at Old Kiyyangan village and dated terrace and settlement layers by radiocarbon. Their results indicate that wet-rice terracing in the area expanded rapidly after about 1600 CE, around the time Spanish colonial power reached the lowlands.

alternatives.label: Recent and resistant
alternatives.text: Acabado and colleagues argue that the Ifugao intensified rice farming and built terraces to support a growing population of people moving uphill to stay out of Spanish control, so the terraces are a monument of resistance rather than of extreme antiquity.

alternatives.label: Older origins
alternatives.text: Other scholars and many local voices maintain that some terraces are much older; the new dates apply to particular sites, and earlier small-scale terracing could have existed elsewhere in the Cordillera.

alternatives.label: National identity
alternatives.text: The debate matters because the 2,000-year figure became part of Philippine national pride and school textbooks; supporters of the new dating stress that a recent origin makes the achievement no less remarkable.

entries.changed: Beyer's 20th-century estimate of 2,000–3,000 years was challenged from the 2010s by radiocarbon results suggesting expansion after c. 1600 CE.

entries.title: The Birdman cult of Rapa Nui: a swimming race for the first sooty tern egg
entries.dateNote: Practised from at least the 18th century until the 1860s
entries.mainstream: After the era of moai statue building, the people of Rapa Nui (Easter Island) developed a ritual centred on the stone village of Orongo on the rim of the Rano Kau volcano. Each spring, competitors representing chiefs or warrior groups climbed down the cliffs and swam through shark-inhabited water to the islet of Motu Nui to wait for the first egg of the manutara (sooty tern). The first to bring an egg back intact won for his sponsor the title of tangata manu (birdman), who lived in seclusion for a year as a sacred figure associated with the creator god Makemake. Hundreds of petroglyphs of bird-headed men are carved on the rocks at Orongo. The cult is thought to have operated from at least the 18th century until the 1860s, when Peruvian slave raids, disease and the arrival of Catholic missionaries ended it.

alternatives.label: Response to crisis
alternatives.text: A traditional view held that the birdman cult replaced moai-building after social collapse and war; recent researchers argue the island's population was more stable before European contact than the 'ecocide' story suggests, and that the cult reflects religious change rather than collapse.

alternatives.label: Egg and origin
alternatives.text: The cult belongs to a wider Pacific pattern in which birds and eggs symbolise creation and rebirth; some writers compare it with egg-born origin myths elsewhere, which may be coincidental.

alternatives.label: Hoa Hakananai'a
alternatives.text: The basalt moai Hoa Hakananai'a, taken from Orongo by the crew of HMS Topaze in 1868 and now in the British Museum, has birdman carvings on its back; Rapa Nui have asked for its return.

media.title: Could You Survive the Birdman Competition

entries.title: Hōkūleʻa's 1976 voyage: testing Polynesian navigation without instruments
entries.mainstream: In the mid-20th century some scholars, notably Andrew Sharp in 1956, argued that Polynesians could not have navigated deliberately across thousands of kilometres of ocean and that islands were settled by accidental drift, while Thor Heyerdahl argued for settlement from South America. To test deliberate voyaging, the Polynesian Voyaging Society, founded in 1973 by the anthropologist Ben Finney, the artist Herb Kawainui Kāne and the sailor Charles Tommy Holmes, built Hōkūleʻa, a replica double-hulled voyaging canoe. In 1976 it sailed about 4,000 km from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti, navigated without compass, charts or instruments by Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Satawal in Micronesia, using stars, swells, winds and birds. Huge crowds greeted the canoe in Papeete. Hōkūleʻa's voyages helped spark a Hawaiian cultural renaissance, and the Hawaiian navigator Nainoa Thompson later revived wayfinding; in 2014–17 it sailed around the world.

alternatives.label: Tested by experiment
alternatives.text: The voyage showed that intentional navigation between distant islands with traditional methods was possible; together with computer simulations and archaeology, it led most researchers to reject the accidental-drift theory.

alternatives.label: Proof versus possibility
alternatives.text: Critics noted that a successful modern voyage proves feasibility rather than what ancient voyagers actually did; genetics and linguistics, rather than the voyage, establish Polynesian origins in Island Southeast Asia and Near Oceania.

alternatives.label: Living knowledge
alternatives.text: Mau Piailug's willingness to teach non-Micronesians was controversial in his community, but helped save a tradition then close to disappearing.

entries.title: Terra preta: the Amazon's man-made black earth
entries.dateNote: Most sites c. 450 BCE – 950 CE and later
entries.mainstream: Terra preta de índio ('Indian black earth') is very fertile dark soil found in patches across the Amazon basin, often along rivers and bluffs, in a region where natural soils are typically thin and poor. It contains large amounts of charcoal, pottery fragments, bone and other organic waste, and remains fertile centuries after its formation. Most terra preta sites date from roughly 450 BCE to 950 CE and later, and they are associated with long-term settlements. Soil scientists regard it as anthropogenic, created by people through the accumulation of household waste and low-temperature burning, whether deliberately or as a by-product of daily life. Its high stable carbon content has inspired modern research into 'biochar' as a soil improver and a way to store carbon.

alternatives.label: Large populations
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists see terra preta as evidence that parts of Amazonia supported large, settled populations before European contact, challenging the old view of the rainforest as a 'counterfeit paradise' too poor to sustain complex societies (Betty Meggers, 1971).

alternatives.label: Deliberate or accidental
alternatives.text: Researchers debate whether the soils were deliberately engineered for farming or built up gradually as midden; both processes may have occurred.

alternatives.label: El Dorado link
alternatives.text: Supporters of the idea that 16th-century reports of dense riverside populations (by the Orellana expedition, 1542) were accurate point to terra preta and earthworks as confirmation; others caution that the soils span many centuries and do not show their size at any one time.

entries.title: Percy Fawcett and the Lost City of Z: vanished in the Amazon, 1925
entries.mainstream: Colonel Percy Harrison Fawcett (1867–c. 1925) was a British army officer and surveyor who mapped borders in Bolivia and Brazil for the Royal Geographical Society. He became convinced that a lost city, which he called 'Z', lay in the unexplored forests of Mato Grosso, partly inspired by Manuscript 512, a Portuguese document of 1753 in the National Library of Brazil describing a ruined city found by bandeirantes. In 1925 he set off with his son Jack and Jack's friend Raleigh Rimell; his last letter, dated 29 May 1925 from 'Dead Horse Camp', said they were about to enter unknown territory. They were never seen again. Dozens of later expeditions searched for them, and several searchers also died or disappeared. Bones produced in 1951 by the Kalapalo leader Izarari, said to be Fawcett's, were judged by experts not to be his.

alternatives.label: Killed by local people
alternatives.text: The most common explanation is that the party were killed by one of the Indigenous groups of the upper Xingu, or died of starvation or disease; the Kalapalo oral tradition names another group as responsible.

alternatives.label: Living as a mystic
alternatives.text: Rumours that Fawcett stayed in the forest by choice, as a chief or as the founder of a theosophical commune (he was interested in spiritualism and occultism), circulated for decades without evidence.

alternatives.label: Z partly vindicated
alternatives.text: From the 1990s Michael Heckenberger and Kuikuro colleagues documented large pre-Columbian settlements with roads, ditches and plazas in the upper Xingu (Kuhikugu), suggesting that Fawcett's idea of complex Amazonian societies was not baseless, even if no stone city has been found.

entries.title: The Bighorn Medicine Wheel: a stone circle aligned to the solstice sunrise?
entries.dateNote: Age uncertain; often placed c. 1200–1700 CE
entries.mainstream: High in the Bighorn Mountains of Wyoming, at about 2,940 m, lies a ring of limestone boulders about 25 m across, with a central cairn and 28 spokes radiating to the rim, and six smaller cairns. It is one of the best-known of the 'medicine wheels' of the northern Plains, mostly in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Montana, some of which date back thousands of years. Its age is uncertain; dates of a few hundred years to around 1,500 years have been suggested, and it may have been built in stages. The site is sacred to many Plains nations, including the Crow, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Lakota and Shoshone, and is still used for ceremonies. It is now a National Historic Landmark managed in consultation with tribes.

alternatives.label: Astronomical alignment
alternatives.text: In 1974 the solar astronomer John Eddy argued in Science that lines between some cairns point to the summer solstice sunrise and sunset and to the rising of the bright stars Aldebaran, Rigel and Sirius around 1200–1700 CE.

alternatives.label: Sceptical response
alternatives.text: Critics have noted that with many cairns, some alignments will occur by chance, that the high site is snow-covered for much of the year, and that the dating needed for the star alignments is uncertain.

alternatives.label: Indigenous interpretations
alternatives.text: Tribal traditions variously connect the wheel to the Crow figure Burnt Face, to vision quests, or to the lodge of the Sun; for many Native Americans it is a living sacred place rather than an observatory.

entries.title: The Rigveda and the 'Aryan' debate: who brought Sanskrit to India?
entries.mainstream: The Rigveda, a collection of 1,028 hymns in Vedic Sanskrit, is among the oldest texts in any Indo-European language. Most scholars date its composition to about 1500–1200 BCE in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent (the Punjab). It was handed down orally for more than two thousand years with remarkable precision before being written down; manuscripts of the Rigveda are on UNESCO's Memory of the World register. Because Sanskrit is related to Persian, Greek, Latin and the Germanic languages, most linguists conclude that Indo-Aryan speakers entered South Asia from Central Asia in the 2nd millennium BCE, after the Indus civilisation had declined. A 2019 ancient-DNA study (Narasimhan et al., Science) found steppe-related ancestry arriving in South Asia in the early-to-mid 2nd millennium BCE, which most researchers read as support for this migration.

alternatives.label: Indo-Aryan migration
alternatives.text: The mainstream view combines linguistics, the Rigveda's own geography and ancient DNA: a gradual movement of steppe-derived pastoralists, not a single violent 'invasion', mixing with existing populations.

alternatives.label: Indigenous Aryans / Out of India
alternatives.text: A minority of scholars, mostly in India, argue that Vedic culture developed within South Asia, perhaps identical with the Indus civilisation, and that Indo-European languages spread outward from India. They point to the Rigveda's praise of a mighty Sarasvati river, which some identify with the now-dry Ghaggar-Hakra. Most linguists and geneticists consider this view inconsistent with the evidence.

alternatives.label: Astronomical dating
alternatives.text: Some writers, from B. G. Tilak (The Arctic Home in the Vedas, 1903) onwards, have read astronomical references in the Vedas as pointing to dates of 4000 BCE or much earlier; these interpretations are not accepted by most Indologists (speculative).

alternatives.label: Politics of the debate
alternatives.text: Since the colonial era, when 'Aryan' was misused in European race theories, the question has been entangled with nationalism and identity, which both sides accuse the other of letting shape their conclusions.

entries.title: The Mahabharata and the Kurukshetra war: a remembered battle or an ancient nuclear war?
entries.dateNote: Tradition: 3102 BCE; historians who accept a kernel: c. 1000 BCE; text composed c. 400 BCE–400 CE
entries.mainstream: The Mahabharata, at around 100,000 verses one of the longest poems ever composed, tells of the war at Kurukshetra between two branches of the Kuru royal family, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, and contains the Bhagavad Gita. The text grew over many centuries, roughly 400 BCE to 400 CE, and is traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa. Tradition places the war at the start of the Kali Yuga, 3102 BCE. Historians who accept a historical kernel usually link it to the Kuru kingdom of the early first millennium BCE (Painted Grey Ware culture), perhaps c. 1000 BCE; others regard the war as essentially literary. The epic describes divine weapons such as the brahmastra, which can destroy whole armies.

alternatives.label: Historical kernel
alternatives.text: Many historians think a real conflict among Iron Age Kuru-Panchala clans may lie behind the story, greatly magnified by later poets; there is no direct archaeological evidence of the battle itself.

alternatives.label: Traditional and astronomical dates
alternatives.text: Hindu tradition dates the war to 3102 BCE; various writers have used planetary positions described in the epic to propose dates from c. 5500 to 1500 BCE, with little agreement between them.

alternatives.label: Ancient nuclear war claim
alternatives.text: From the 1960s–70s, writers such as Charles Berlitz and David Davenport claimed that the brahmastra descriptions recall nuclear blasts and that skeletons at Mohenjo-daro show signs of a sudden catastrophe or radiation. Archaeologists note that no unusual radioactivity has been reported, that the skeletons came from different periods, and that George Dales argued in 1964 that the 'massacre' at Mohenjo-daro was a misreading (speculative).

alternatives.label: Modern echo
alternatives.text: Robert Oppenheimer famously recalled a line of the Bhagavad Gita, 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds', after the 1945 Trinity test, which has helped link the epic to nuclear imagery in popular culture.

entries.title: The edicts of Ashoka: a forgotten emperor read again after 2,000 years
entries.mainstream: Ashoka, emperor of the Maurya dynasty (r. c. 268–232 BCE), ruled most of the Indian subcontinent. After his bloody conquest of Kalinga (c. 261 BCE) he turned to Buddhism and had edicts carved on rocks and polished stone pillars across his empire, mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script, but also in Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic. They speak of remorse for the war, tolerance between religious groups, care for animals and the sending of envoys to Hellenistic kings. Over the following centuries the Brahmi script was forgotten. In 1837 the British scholar James Prinsep deciphered it, but the king called 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' ('Beloved of the gods, of gracious mien') was only firmly identified with the Ashoka of Buddhist chronicles when an edict naming him was found at Maski in 1915.

alternatives.label: A model ruler?
alternatives.text: Buddhist texts such as the Ashokavadana portray a cruel king transformed into an ideal Buddhist monarch who built 84,000 stupas. Historians debate how much of his 'dhamma' policy was personal conviction and how much was a political tool for holding together a vast, diverse empire.

alternatives.label: Secret society legend
alternatives.text: Talbot Mundy's 1923 novel The Nine Unknown claimed that Ashoka founded a secret society of nine men to guard dangerous knowledge; the story is fiction, though it is sometimes repeated as fact.

alternatives.label: Rediscovery
alternatives.text: The rediscovery is often cited as an example of how a major ruler can largely vanish from historical memory and be restored by decipherment; Ashoka's lion capital is now India's national emblem.

media.title: Chandragupta, Ashoka and the Maurya Empire  | World History | Khan Academy

entries.title: Nalanda: the great Buddhist university and the fire that burned for months
entries.mainstream: Nalanda, in Bihar, India, was a large Buddhist monastic centre of learning from about the 5th century CE, under the Gupta kings, to around 1200 CE. Pilgrim-scholars such as Xuanzang (7th century) and Yijing described thousands of monks studying Buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar and medicine. Nalanda declined and was sacked around 1200, usually attributed to troops of the Turkic general Bakhtiyar Khalji, and was abandoned. Its ruins were identified in the 19th century and excavated by the Archaeological Survey of India from 1915; the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016, and a new Nalanda University opened nearby in 2014.

alternatives.label: Destroyed by Khalji
alternatives.text: The common account holds that Khalji's forces killed the monks and burned the libraries, which were said to have smouldered for months. The nearest contemporary Persian chronicle (Minhaj-i-Siraj) describes the sacking of a fortified monastery that most scholars identify as Odantapuri or Vikramashila, not Nalanda by name.

alternatives.label: Tibetan accounts
alternatives.text: Later Tibetan sources, including Taranatha (17th century), describe further destruction and a fire attributed to hostile non-Buddhist ascetics, and say teaching continued in a reduced way for a time after the raid.

alternatives.label: Long decline
alternatives.text: Some historians stress that Buddhist institutions in India were already declining from loss of royal patronage and competition with Hindu devotional movements, so the raid was the end of a longer process. The story remains politically sensitive in modern India.
