entries.title: The churning of the ocean: gods and demons pull the serpent Vasuki for the nectar of immortality
entries.dateNote: Texts c. 400 BCE–1000 CE; mythic time
entries.mainstream: In a Hindu myth told in the Mahabharata, the Ramayana and the Puranas, the gods (devas) and their rivals the asuras cooperate to churn the cosmic ocean of milk to obtain amrita, the nectar of immortality. They use Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent king Vasuki as the rope, while Vishnu, as the tortoise Kurma, supports the mountain. The churning first releases a deadly poison, halahala, which Shiva drinks, turning his throat blue, and then treasures including the goddess Lakshmi. Vishnu, disguised as the enchantress Mohini, tricks the asuras out of the nectar. The asura Rahu sneaks a sip and is beheaded; his immortal head chases the Sun and Moon, causing eclipses. Drops of nectar falling to earth are linked to the four sites of the Kumbh Mela. A famous 12th-century relief at Angkor Wat depicts the scene.

alternatives.label: Religious meaning
alternatives.text: Within Hinduism the story teaches cosmic cooperation and the need to endure poison before reward, and explains rituals and festivals including the Kumbh Mela, one of the largest gatherings of people on Earth.

alternatives.label: Eclipse explanation
alternatives.text: The Rahu episode is a mythic explanation of eclipses; in Indian astronomy Rahu and Ketu became the names of the lunar nodes, the points where eclipses occur.

alternatives.label: Precession reading
alternatives.text: In Hamlet's Mill (1969), Giorgio de Santillana and Hertha von Dechend argued that churning and mill myths worldwide encode knowledge of the precession of the equinoxes; most scholars of myth and astronomy consider this unproven (speculative).

alternatives.label: Elixir pattern
alternatives.text: Comparativists note parallels with other drinks of immortality, such as Greek ambrosia, Norse mead and the Vedic soma, debated as shared Indo-European inheritance or independent invention.

entries.title: Lothal: the oldest dockyard in the world, or a water tank?
entries.mainstream: Lothal, in Gujarat, India, was a town of the Harappan (Indus) civilisation, occupied roughly 2400–1900 BCE and excavated by S. R. Rao of the Archaeological Survey of India in 1955–60. It had a planned grid, drains, a bead-making factory and evidence of long-distance trade, including a Persian Gulf-type seal. Its most famous feature is a large brick-lined basin, about 214 by 36 m, connected by channels to an old course of the Sabarmati river.

alternatives.label: Tidal dockyard
alternatives.text: Rao interpreted the basin as the world's oldest known dockyard, able to take ships at high tide, with a nearby wharf and warehouse; this view is promoted by the Indian government and a national maritime heritage complex is being built at the site.

alternatives.label: Reservoir or tank
alternatives.text: Other archaeologists, beginning with L. S. Leshnik in 1968, argued that the basin was a freshwater reservoir for irrigation and drinking, noting its distance from the sea and the lack of clear evidence of ships entering it.

alternatives.label: Wider significance
alternatives.text: Either way, Lothal shows Harappan expertise in hydraulic engineering and maritime trade with Mesopotamia and the Gulf (Dilmun and Magan), which is attested in cuneiform texts.

entries.title: The Bakhshali manuscript and the birth of zero
entries.dateNote: Radiocarbon dates of leaves range from 224–383 to 885–993 CE
entries.mainstream: The Bakhshali manuscript is an Indian mathematical text written on 70 leaves of birch bark, found by a farmer in 1881 in a field at Bakhshali, near Peshawar (now Pakistan), and held by the Bodleian Library, Oxford, since 1902. It uses a dot as a placeholder zero in a decimal place-value system, the ancestor of the zero used worldwide. In 2017 the Bodleian announced radiocarbon dates showing that different leaves date from 224–383 CE, 680–779 CE and 885–993 CE, and publicised the manuscript as containing the oldest recorded use of the zero symbol. The first known written rules for calculating with zero as a number are in Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE).

alternatives.label: Earliest zero
alternatives.text: Supporters of the 2017 result argue that the oldest leaves push the dot-zero back by several centuries, before the 876 CE Gwalior inscription that was long cited as the earliest Indian zero.

alternatives.label: Doubts about the dates
alternatives.text: Historians of mathematics such as Kim Plofker and colleagues pointed out that a single coherent text spread over leaves six centuries apart is implausible, and suggested the dating needs re-examination; many date the text itself to around the 8th–12th century.

alternatives.label: Wider story
alternatives.text: Placeholders for zero also existed in Babylonian and Maya mathematics; the Indian contribution is usually seen as treating zero as a number in its own right, transmitted through the Islamic world to Europe.

media.title: A Big Zero: Research uncovers the date of the Bakhshali manuscript

entries.title: Soma: the lost sacred drink of the Vedas
entries.mainstream: In the Rigveda, soma is both a god and a drink pressed from a plant, offered in rituals and drunk by priests; an entire book (Mandala 9) praises it for bringing inspiration, strength and a sense of immortality. The Iranian Avesta describes the same drink as haoma. By the later Vedic period the original plant seems to have been replaced by substitutes, and its identity is not known.

alternatives.label: Ephedra
alternatives.text: Many scholars favour ephedra, a stimulant shrub still called hum or homa in parts of Iran and Afghanistan and used in Zoroastrian haoma rituals; Viktor Sarianidi reported traces of ephedra in vessels at Bactria-Margiana (BMAC) sites, although the identification has been questioned.

alternatives.label: Fly agaric mushroom
alternatives.text: In 1968 the banker and ethnomycologist R. Gordon Wasson argued that soma was the hallucinogenic mushroom Amanita muscaria, used by Siberian shamans; this was popular but is rejected by many Vedic specialists.

alternatives.label: Other candidates
alternatives.text: Proposals include Syrian rue (Peganum harmala), cannabis, opium poppy, honey and various psychoactive plants; some scholars argue the drink may not have been psychoactive at all, its effects being religious rather than chemical.

entries.title: The red rain of Kerala: alien cells or algae?
entries.mainstream: From 25 July to 23 September 2001, red-coloured rain fell sporadically over Kerala, southern India, staining clothes pink; yellow, green and black rain was also reported. A study commissioned by the Indian government (Centre for Earth Science Studies and Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute) concluded that the colour came from spores of a locally abundant lichen-forming green alga of the genus Trentepohlia. Similar 'blood rain' events had been recorded in Kerala before and have occurred elsewhere, often caused by dust or algae.

alternatives.label: Algae
alternatives.text: The mainstream explanation is that large quantities of Trentepohlia spores were lifted into the air and washed out by rain, although exactly how so many spores became airborne at once is not fully explained.

alternatives.label: Extraterrestrial cells
alternatives.text: In 2006 physicists Godfrey Louis and Santhosh Kumar published a paper in Astrophysics and Space Science suggesting the particles were cells lacking DNA that might have come from a disintegrating comet or meteor, supporting panspermia; Chandra Wickramasinghe also promoted the idea. Most biologists reject this, and later work reported DNA consistent with algae (speculative).

alternatives.label: Blood rain tradition
alternatives.text: Red rain has been read as an omen since antiquity, from Homer's Iliad to medieval chronicles; modern cases are generally traced to Saharan dust or microorganisms.

entries.title: Konark Sun Temple: a stone chariot whose wheels tell the time
entries.mainstream: The Sun Temple at Konark, Odisha, India, was built around 1250 CE by King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. It was designed as a colossal chariot of the sun god Surya, with 24 elaborately carved stone wheels pulled by seven horses. The main tower, perhaps 70 m tall, collapsed by the 19th century; the surviving assembly hall was filled with sand by British engineers in 1903 to stabilise it. European sailors used the temple as a landmark and called it the 'Black Pagoda'. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Sundial wheels
alternatives.text: Guides and some scholars describe the wheels as working sundials, with the spokes' shadows marking the time of day; it is unclear whether this function was intended by the builders or is a later interpretation.

alternatives.label: Lodestone legend
alternatives.text: A popular legend says that a huge magnet at the top held the iron-joined structure together and disturbed ships' compasses, so sailors removed it, causing the collapse. There is no historical evidence for this; engineers attribute the collapse to foundations, weathering and possibly an unfinished structure.

alternatives.label: Boy architect legend
alternatives.text: Another local legend says 1,200 craftsmen could not set the crowning stone until Dharmapada, the 12-year-old son of the chief architect, succeeded and then leapt into the sea to save the workers from the king's anger.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Sun Temple, Konârak

entries.title: Fu Hao: a Shang queen, general and priestess, found in an unlooted tomb
entries.mainstream: Fu Hao was one of the wives of King Wu Ding of the Shang dynasty (c. 1250–1192 BCE). Oracle-bone inscriptions from the Shang capital at Anyang record her leading military campaigns, including one said to involve 13,000 troops, conducting sacrifices and being the subject of divinations about childbirth and illness. In 1976 the archaeologist Zheng Zhenxiang excavated her tomb at Anyang, one of the very few Shang royal tombs found intact. It held over 1,600 objects, including about 468 bronzes, 755 jades, some 7,000 cowrie shells, bronze weapons and the remains of 16 sacrificed people and six dogs.

alternatives.label: Warrior queen
alternatives.text: Many historians present Fu Hao as one of the earliest documented female military commanders, and her tomb weapons support her martial role.

alternatives.label: One woman or several?
alternatives.text: Some scholars note that 'Fu' may be a title and that oracle-bone references across many years might concern more than one person, so the unified biography could be partly a modern construction.

alternatives.label: Religious role
alternatives.text: Her role in sacrifices and divination suggests royal women could hold ritual authority; she was later worshipped as an ancestor.

media.title: The All-Female Shang-Era Troops Led by Queen Fu Hao | Smithsonian Channel

entries.title: Zhang Heng's dragon-and-toad seismoscope (132 CE)
entries.mainstream: Zhang Heng (78–139 CE), an Eastern Han astronomer, mathematician, poet and inventor, is credited in the Book of the Later Han with building in 132 CE a bronze vessel that detected distant earthquakes. Eight dragons around its outside each held a bronze ball; when the ground shook, a ball dropped from one dragon's mouth into the mouth of a bronze toad below, supposedly indicating the direction of the quake. The text says it once signalled an earthquake that was not felt in the capital Luoyang, and messengers later arrived reporting a quake in Longxi (Gansu), several hundred kilometres away. The original device is lost and only this short description survives.

alternatives.label: Working pendulum
alternatives.text: Most historians accept that some kind of earthquake indicator existed and propose a pendulum mechanism inside; modern Chinese reconstructions (1951 and 2005) have been built and tested.

alternatives.label: Doubts about direction
alternatives.text: Seismologists point out that a simple pendulum could not reliably show the direction of the epicentre, and some suspect the account may idealise the device's performance; the reconstructions are informed guesses.

alternatives.label: Wider context
alternatives.text: Whatever its exact performance, it is often cited as the world's first seismoscope, more than 1,500 years before comparable European instruments.

entries.title: The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom: Jesus's 'younger brother' and one of history's deadliest wars
entries.mainstream: Hong Xiuquan, a Hakka villager from Guangdong, failed the imperial civil-service examinations several times. During a long illness in 1837 he had visions of a heavenly father and an elder brother who charged him with destroying demons. After reading a Christian missionary tract in 1843 he concluded that he was the younger brother of Jesus. His God Worshipping Society grew into the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, which rose against the Qing dynasty in 1850–51, captured Nanjing in 1853 and held much of southern China until 1864. Taiping ideology banned opium, foot-binding and idol worship and proclaimed shared property and equality of the sexes in principle. The war and the famines and epidemics that went with it are estimated to have killed 20–30 million people or more.

alternatives.label: Religious movement
alternatives.text: Many historians stress Hong's sincere, if unorthodox, Christian-inspired theology; Western missionaries initially welcomed the movement and then rejected it as heretical.

alternatives.label: Medical explanations
alternatives.text: Some writers have suggested Hong's visions reflected a psychological or neurological illness during his breakdown; this cannot be tested and others caution against diagnosing historical figures.

alternatives.label: Political readings
alternatives.text: Chinese Communist historiography long portrayed the Taiping as a peasant revolution and forerunner of socialism, while other historians emphasise Han resistance to the Manchu Qing or the social crisis of overpopulation and economic distress.

media.title: Asian Responses to Imperialism: Crash Course World History #213

entries.title: The Yellow Emperor: inventor, sage-king and ancestor of the Chinese
entries.mainstream: Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor, is a legendary ruler traditionally said to have reigned 2697–2597 BCE (dates calculated much later). The Han-dynasty historian Sima Qian placed him first among the Five Emperors. He is credited with defeating his rival Chiyou at the Battle of Zhuolu, and he and his court are credited with inventing silk-making (his wife Leizu), writing (his scribe Cangjie), the calendar, medicine (the Huangdi Neijing, actually compiled around the Han period) and the south-pointing chariot. Daoists revered him as an immortal who ascended to heaven on a dragon. In the early 20th century he was promoted as the common ancestor of the Chinese nation, and he is still honoured at a mausoleum in Shaanxi.

alternatives.label: Deified culture hero
alternatives.text: Historians of the 1920s 'Doubting Antiquity' school, led by Gu Jiegang, argued that the Yellow Emperor was a deity or later invention whose 'history' grew richer the later the sources were; this is widely accepted among scholars.

alternatives.label: Memory of a real chief
alternatives.text: Some Chinese scholars and the state-backed tradition hold that the legends preserve memories of real Neolithic leaders of the Yellow River valley; there is no direct evidence for an individual.

alternatives.label: Sky-ascent readings
alternatives.text: His ascent to heaven on a dragon has been read by some ancient-astronaut writers as a memory of flying machines; mythologists see it as a standard motif of Daoist immortality (speculative).

entries.title: Xuanzang: the real pilgrim behind Journey to the West
entries.mainstream: The Chinese Buddhist monk Xuanzang (c. 602–664) left the Tang capital Chang'an in 629, against an imperial travel ban, and travelled overland via Central Asia to India, where he studied at Nalanda. He returned in 645 with 657 Buddhist texts, which he spent the rest of his life translating, and dictated an account of the lands he had seen, the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (646). In the 19th century British archaeologists including Alexander Cunningham used his detailed distances and descriptions to locate Buddhist sites such as Nalanda, Sarnath and Kushinagar. His journey became the basis of the 16th-century novel Journey to the West, in which the monk is escorted by the Monkey King Sun Wukong, a pig and a river spirit.

alternatives.label: Reliable guide
alternatives.text: His travel records proved accurate enough to guide excavations, making them an example of an ancient text later confirmed by archaeology.

alternatives.label: Monkey King origins
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether Sun Wukong was inspired by the Hindu monkey god Hanuman (argued by Hu Shih) or developed from Chinese folk traditions (argued by Lu Xun); both influences may be involved.

alternatives.label: Fact and fantasy
alternatives.text: The novel turned a scholarly pilgrimage into a fantastic quest with 81 trials, and is counted among the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Records of the Western Regions

entries.title: The Dunhuang Library Cave: a sealed room of 50,000 manuscripts
entries.mainstream: In 1900 Wang Yuanlu, a Daoist caretaker of the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang on the Silk Road, found a walled-up chamber, now Cave 17, packed with tens of thousands of manuscripts, paintings and printed items from the 4th to early 11th centuries, in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit, Khotanese, Sogdian, Old Uyghur, Hebrew and other languages. Among them is a copy of the Diamond Sutra dated 868 CE, the oldest dated printed book in the world (now in the British Library). In 1907–08 the explorers Aurel Stein and Paul Pelliot acquired large parts of the collection cheaply, and the rest was dispersed to Beijing, St Petersburg, Japan and elsewhere. The International Dunhuang Project now reunites them digitally.

alternatives.label: Hidden from invaders
alternatives.text: A common explanation is that the monks sealed the cave in the early 11th century to protect its contents from an expected invasion, by the Tanguts (Xi Xia) or by the Muslim Karakhanids who had conquered Buddhist Khotan in 1006.

alternatives.label: Sacred waste store
alternatives.text: Others, following Fujieda Akira, propose that the cave was a repository for worn-out or obsolete sacred texts that could not be destroyed, which would explain the many fragments and duplicates.

alternatives.label: Rescue or looting?
alternatives.text: Stein and Pelliot are seen by some as having saved the material for scholarship and by others, especially in China, as having taken national treasures; the episode remains part of debates on the return of cultural property.

entries.title: The Hongshan jade dragons: the first Chinese dragon?
entries.mainstream: The Hongshan culture (c. 4700–2900 BCE) of Inner Mongolia and Liaoning, north-east China, is known for finely worked jades, including curled 'pig-dragons' (zhulong) and a 26 cm C-shaped jade dragon found at Sanxingtala in 1971. At Niuheliang, archaeologists found a 'Goddess Temple' with clay statues and large stone burial mounds. Even earlier, a dragon and a tiger made of mussel shells flank a burial at Xishuipo (Puyang, Henan, c. 4000 BCE). The dragon later became a central symbol of rain, water, emperors and good fortune in Chinese culture.

alternatives.label: Animal origins
alternatives.text: Scholars have proposed many models for the Chinese dragon: pigs, snakes, alligators, fish, silkworms or a combination of clan totems; the curled Hongshan jades look to some like embryos or larvae.

alternatives.label: Fossil inspiration
alternatives.text: For centuries Chinese apothecaries sold fossil bones and teeth as 'dragon bones'; some writers argue that fossils influenced dragon legends, as folklorist Adrienne Mayor has argued for Greek monsters, though this is hard to prove for the earliest Chinese images.

alternatives.label: Lost-civilisation claims
alternatives.text: Some popular writers present Hongshan as a lost early civilisation or the single source of Chinese culture; archaeologists see it as one of several interacting Neolithic cultures that contributed to later Chinese civilisation.

entries.title: The Great Wall of China and the myth that it can be seen from space
entries.mainstream: The 'Great Wall' is really many walls built by different Chinese states and dynasties from around the 7th century BCE to the 17th century CE to guard against northern peoples. The first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, linked earlier walls after 221 BCE; most of the brick-and-stone wall visible today was built by the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). A 2012 Chinese survey measured all wall sections at about 21,196 km. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Visible from space?
alternatives.text: A widely repeated claim, already in print in the 1930s, says the wall is the only human-made structure visible from the Moon or from space. NASA and astronauts, including China's first astronaut Yang Liwei in 2003, say it is not visible to the naked eye from the Moon and is very hard to see even from low Earth orbit, because it is narrow and similar in colour to its surroundings.

alternatives.label: Meng Jiangnu legend
alternatives.text: A famous folk tale says that Lady Meng Jiang's husband died as a forced labourer on the Qin wall, and her weeping was so bitter that a section of the wall collapsed to reveal his bones; it expresses popular memory of the suffering of wall builders.

alternatives.label: Bodies in the wall
alternatives.text: The common claim that workers' bodies were buried inside the wall is not supported by archaeological evidence, though many labourers certainly died during construction.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: The Great Wall

media.title: What makes the Great Wall of China so extraordinary - Megan Campisi and Pen-Pen Chen

entries.title: The Jews of Kaifeng: a Jewish community in imperial China
entries.mainstream: A Jewish community lived in Kaifeng, the capital of the Northern Song dynasty, probably from around the 10th–11th centuries. A stele of 1489 says Jews arrived during the Song, bringing cotton goods from the 'Western regions', and built a synagogue in 1163. In 1605 the Jesuit Matteo Ricci met a Kaifeng Jew, Ai Tian, who had come to Beijing, bringing the community to European attention. Through intermarriage, Chinese education and the loss of rabbis, the community gradually assimilated; the synagogue, repeatedly damaged by Yellow River floods, was not rebuilt after the mid-19th century. A few hundred to around a thousand people in Kaifeng today identify as descendants, and some have emigrated to Israel.

alternatives.label: Silk Road merchants
alternatives.text: Most historians think the founders were Persian-speaking Jewish merchants who came via the Silk Road or by sea; the community's texts include Persian words.

alternatives.label: Earlier origins
alternatives.text: A stele of 1663 claims an arrival as early as the Han dynasty, and other claims connect them to the Lost Tribes of Israel; these are not supported by firm evidence (speculative).

alternatives.label: Identity today
alternatives.text: Chinese authorities do not recognise the descendants as a separate ethnic group or Judaism as an official religion, and their status remains sensitive.

entries.title: The hanging coffins of China: how were they placed on sheer cliffs?
entries.dateNote: Oldest c. 3,000 years old; practice into the Ming dynasty
entries.mainstream: In southern China, notably in the Wuyi Mountains (Fujian), the Three Gorges and the Bo people's homeland in Gongxian, Sichuan, wooden coffins were placed in caves or on wooden beams driven into sheer cliff faces, sometimes more than 100 m above the ground. The oldest are thought to be around 3,000 years old, and the practice continued in some places into the Ming dynasty. The Bo, who used the custom, largely disappear from records after a Ming military campaign against them in 1573. Similar cliff burials exist at Sagada in the Philippines and among the Toraja of Sulawesi.

alternatives.label: How they were raised
alternatives.text: Proposed methods include lowering coffins by ropes from the cliff top, building scaffolding or plank walkways, or floating them up on high water; researchers have demonstrated rope-and-winch methods, but no contemporary description survives.

alternatives.label: Why so high
alternatives.text: Explanations include protecting the dead from animals and robbers, bringing the dead closer to heaven, and showing filial piety; the meaning probably differed between cultures.

alternatives.label: Vanished people
alternatives.text: The fate of the Bo has been the subject of speculation; most scholars think survivors assimilated into neighbouring populations after 1573.

entries.title: The mustatils of Arabia: 7,000-year-old monuments older than Stonehenge
entries.mainstream: More than 1,600 large rectangular stone structures, called mustatils (Arabic for 'rectangle'), have been recorded across north-western Saudi Arabia, mainly through aerial and satellite surveys in the AlUla and Khaybar regions. Some are over 500 m long. Excavations published by Melissa Kennedy and colleagues in Antiquity (2021) found chambers with deposits of cattle, goat and gazelle horns and skulls, interpreted as offerings, and radiocarbon dates of about 5300–5000 BCE, making them older than Stonehenge or the Egyptian pyramids. They were built when the Arabian interior was wetter and greener than today. Earlier observers had called them 'gates'.

alternatives.label: Ritual monuments
alternatives.text: The excavators interpret mustatils as places of ritual, perhaps linked to a cattle cult among Neolithic herders, built over a relatively short period across a wide region.

alternatives.label: Changing picture
alternatives.text: The discoveries are part of a growing recognition that Neolithic Arabia had monumental traditions comparable to those elsewhere, overturning older views of the interior as marginal.

alternatives.label: Popular speculation
alternatives.text: Their age and scale have prompted online claims of a lost advanced civilisation; archaeologists note that they are dry-stone walls well within the abilities of mobile herding groups.

sources.title: The mustatils: cult and monumentality in Neolithic north-western Arabia

entries.title: Dilmun: the Sumerian paradise and the island of burial mounds
entries.mainstream: Dilmun, centred on the island of Bahrain and nearby eastern Arabia, was a trading civilisation of the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE, a link between Mesopotamia, Magan (Oman) and the Indus civilisation, with its capital at Qal'at al-Bahrain and temples at Barbar. In Sumerian literature Dilmun is a pure, holy land without sickness or death, the setting of the myth of Enki and Ninhursag, and the place where the flood hero Ziusudra was granted eternal life. Bahrain contains tens of thousands of burial mounds built c. 2200–1750 BCE, part of which became the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Dilmun Burial Mounds' in 2019.

alternatives.label: Island of the dead
alternatives.text: Early researchers suggested Bahrain was a sacred burial ground to which people from Mesopotamia brought their dead; excavations have shown that the mounds belong mainly to the local population.

alternatives.label: Garden of Eden
alternatives.text: Assyriologist Samuel Noah Kramer suggested that Dilmun's paradise myth influenced the biblical Eden; others, notably archaeologist Juris Zarins, proposed that Eden traditions relate to a now-submerged Persian Gulf basin flooded after the Ice Age (speculative).

alternatives.label: Freshwater springs
alternatives.text: The myth of Enki bringing fresh water to Dilmun matches Bahrain's real freshwater springs, including undersea springs, which made the island an oasis.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Dilmun Burial Mounds

entries.title: The Great Dam of Marib and the Flood of the Dam
entries.dateNote: c. 8th century BCE to c. 570 CE
entries.mainstream: The Great Dam of Marib in Yemen, built by the kingdom of Saba (Sheba) across the Wadi Dhana, was one of the great engineering works of the ancient world, irrigating a large oasis around the Sabaean capital. Its earliest structures go back at least to the 8th century BCE, and South Arabian inscriptions record repeated breaches and repairs, including by Himyarite rulers and the Aksumite-backed ruler Abraha in the 5th–6th centuries CE. The dam failed for the last time around 570 CE. The Qur'an (Surah Saba, 34:15–16) describes the people of Saba being punished for ingratitude with the 'flood of the dam' (sayl al-'arim), their gardens turned to bitter plants.

alternatives.label: Divine punishment
alternatives.text: In Islamic tradition the collapse is a sign of God's judgement on a prosperous people who turned away from him.

alternatives.label: Tribal dispersal
alternatives.text: Arab genealogical tradition links the collapse to the migration of South Arabian tribes such as the Azd, Ghassanids and the Aws and Khazraj of Medina; historians think such migrations were real but spread over a longer period.

alternatives.label: Long decline
alternatives.text: Historians generally see the final failure as a symptom of wider decline, including shifting incense trade routes, wars, plague and loss of central authority, rather than a single sudden cause.

entries.title: Hegra (Mada'in Salih): Nabataean tombs and the doomed people of Thamud
entries.mainstream: Hegra (al-Hijr, also called Mada'in Salih), in north-western Saudi Arabia, was the southern city of the Nabataean kingdom, whose capital was Petra. Its 111 monumental tombs, carved into sandstone outcrops between about 1 BCE and 75 CE, carry inscriptions naming their owners and cursing anyone who disturbs them. It was Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site (2008) and opened to tourism in 2020. Islamic tradition associates al-Hijr with the people of Thamud, who carved houses out of rock and were destroyed for rejecting the prophet Salih and killing a miraculous she-camel.

alternatives.label: Cursed place
alternatives.text: Because of a hadith in which Muhammad urged his followers to pass the ruins quickly and not use their water, many local people long avoided the site.

alternatives.label: Thamud and the Nabataeans
alternatives.text: Historians distinguish the Nabataean tombs from the Thamud, an Arabian people attested in Assyrian records (8th century BCE) and in a Greek-Nabataean inscription at Ruwafa (2nd century CE); tradition merged the visible ruins with the older story.

alternatives.label: Archaeology
alternatives.text: Excavations since 2001 by a French-Saudi team have revealed the city's residential areas, wells and evidence of a Roman military presence after Nabataea was annexed in 106 CE.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Hegra Archaeological Site (al-Hijr / Mada'in Salih)

media.title: The mysterious 'other Petra' of Saudi Arabia - BBC REEL

entries.title: The jinn: beings of smokeless fire
entries.mainstream: In pre-Islamic Arabia the jinn were invisible spirits of the desert, linked to inspiration (poets and soothsayers were said to have a jinn companion) and to danger. The Qur'an, which has a chapter named after them (Surah 72, al-Jinn), describes them as beings created from smokeless fire, with free will, who can be believers or unbelievers and will be judged. Folklore across the Muslim world tells of jinn living in ruins, wells and wild places, taking animal shapes and possessing people, and of King Solomon commanding them. The English word 'genie' comes via Antoine Galland's French translation of the Thousand and One Nights (1704–1717).

alternatives.label: Religious belief
alternatives.text: For many Muslims the existence of jinn is part of faith, and practices such as ruqya (Qur'anic healing recitation) are used against believed jinn affliction.

alternatives.label: Psychological readings
alternatives.text: Psychiatrists and anthropologists have studied how experiences such as sleep paralysis, epilepsy and mental illness are interpreted as jinn affliction in different communities, without necessarily dismissing the cultural meaning.

alternatives.label: Folklore parallels
alternatives.text: Folklorists compare jinn to fairies, elves and other hidden peoples; Jacques Vallee's Passport to Magonia (1969) compared modern UFO encounter reports with older fairy and spirit lore, and some writers have equated jinn with UFO entities (speculative).

entries.title: Hezarfen Ahmed Celebi: did an Ottoman fly across the Bosphorus?
entries.mainstream: The Ottoman travel writer Evliya Celebi, in his Seyahatname (Book of Travels), records that around 1630–1632 a scholar named Hezarfen ('thousand sciences') Ahmed Celebi practised flying with wings, then leapt from the Galata Tower in Istanbul and glided across the Bosphorus to land at Dogancilar in Uskudar. Sultan Murad IV is said to have rewarded him with gold but then exiled him to Algeria as too dangerous. Evliya also describes Lagari Hasan Celebi rising into the air on a gunpowder rocket in 1633 and landing in the sea. Evliya's account is the only source for both stories.

alternatives.label: Possible feat
alternatives.text: Supporters argue that a glide of several kilometres from a tall tower with favourable winds is not impossible with well-designed wings; Hezarfen is celebrated in Turkey as an aviation pioneer, and Hezarfen Airfield in Istanbul is named after him.

alternatives.label: Literary embellishment
alternatives.text: Historians note that Evliya Celebi's Book of Travels mixes reliable observation with entertaining exaggeration, and no other contemporary source mentions the flights, so the details at least are doubtful.

alternatives.label: Tower jumpers
alternatives.text: The story fits a long tradition of tower-jumping flight attempts, from Abbas ibn Firnas in Cordoba in the 9th century to Eilmer of Malmesbury in the 11th, most of which ended in injury.

entries.title: Sabbatai Zevi: the messiah who converted to Islam
entries.mainstream: In 1665 Sabbatai Zevi, a Jewish mystic from Smyrna (Izmir), was proclaimed the Messiah by his prophet Nathan of Gaza. News spread across the Jewish world, from Yemen to Amsterdam and Poland; people sold their property in expectation of the return to the Holy Land, and 1666 was widely expected to bring redemption. In 1666 he was arrested by the Ottoman authorities and, brought before the Sultan's court at Edirne, chose conversion to Islam over death. Most followers were devastated, but some believed his apostasy was a hidden part of his mission; a group of followers who converted with him became the Donme of Salonica.

alternatives.label: Messianic expectation
alternatives.text: Historians, notably Gershom Scholem, link the movement's explosive spread to Lurianic Kabbalah and to the trauma of the 1648–1657 massacres of Jews in Ukraine.

alternatives.label: Mental illness
alternatives.text: Some biographers have suggested Sabbatai suffered from bipolar disorder, alternating between ecstatic states and depression; this is a retrospective diagnosis.

alternatives.label: Lasting influence
alternatives.text: Secret Sabbatean groups persisted for centuries, and the Frankist movement in 18th-century Poland drew on his legacy; the Donme later became the subject of conspiracy theories in Turkey, which historians reject.

media.title: Sabbateanism: The Rise and Fall of a Messiah

entries.title: The huldufolk: Iceland's hidden people
entries.dateNote: Folk tradition; collected from the 19th century
entries.mainstream: In Icelandic folklore the huldufolk ('hidden people') are human-like beings who live in rocks, hills and cliffs, in a parallel world usually invisible to humans. Stories collected by Jon Arnason in the 19th century tell of hidden people who seek human midwives, lure people away and reward or punish humans. In modern Iceland, news reports regularly describe road and building projects being disrupted or rerouted after objections that they would disturb elf rocks. Surveys by the University of Iceland (2006–2007) and an earlier 1974 survey found that many Icelanders would not rule out the existence of elves.

alternatives.label: Living belief
alternatives.text: For some Icelanders, especially those who report seeing them, the hidden people are real; others respect elf rocks as cultural heritage without belief.

alternatives.label: Folklore explanation
alternatives.text: Folklorists see the stories as a way to explain the landscape, to talk about taboo matters such as illegitimate children or abandoned infants, and to reflect isolation in a harsh environment.

alternatives.label: Media exaggeration
alternatives.text: Sceptics note that disputed projects are usually also opposed on environmental or engineering grounds, and that foreign media can overstate the role of elf belief in planning decisions.

media.title: Iceland's magical world of elves | BBC Ideas

entries.title: The Viking sunstone: navigating by polarised light?
entries.mainstream: Some Old Norse texts, such as the saga of Saint Olaf, mention a sólarsteinn (sunstone) used to locate the sun in cloudy weather. Researchers have proposed that this was a crystal such as Iceland spar (calcite), which splits light into two images depending on polarisation, allowing a skilled user to find the sun's direction even when it is hidden. In 2011 a study in the Proceedings of the Royal Society A showed experimentally that calcite could be used to locate the sun to within a few degrees, and a calcite crystal was found among navigation equipment on a 1592 English shipwreck off Alderney.

alternatives.label: Real navigation tool
alternatives.text: Supporters argue that sunstones would have helped Norse sailors cross the open North Atlantic to Iceland, Greenland and Vinland.

alternatives.label: Unproven
alternatives.text: Sceptics note that no sunstone has been found in a Viking-Age context, and the saga references may describe a ritual or symbolic object; Norse navigators may have relied on other cues such as birds, whales and swells.

alternatives.label: Experiments
alternatives.text: Later studies have tested how accurately sunstone navigation would work in different sky conditions, with mixed but generally positive results in laboratory and model settings.

sources.title: A depolarizer as a possible precise sunstone for Viking navigation by polarized skylight

media.title: Did Vikings Use These Crystals To Navigate?

entries.title: The Trundholm sun chariot
entries.mainstream: In 1902 a farmer ploughing a bog at Trundholm on Zealand, Denmark, found a bronze statue of a horse pulling a large disc on wheels. The disc is gilded on one side and plain on the other, which is usually interpreted as showing the sun's bright journey across the day sky and dark return at night. It dates to around 1400 BCE, the Nordic Bronze Age, and is now in the National Museum of Denmark. It was probably deliberately placed in the bog as an offering.

alternatives.label: Sun religion
alternatives.text: Archaeologists see the chariot as evidence of a Bronze Age sun cult in Scandinavia, in which the sun was carried across the sky by a horse by day and a boat or fish by night, as depicted on rock carvings and razors.

alternatives.label: Later myth
alternatives.text: Some scholars connect it with the later Norse myth of the sun goddess Sol, whose chariot is pulled by horses chased by wolves, though more than 2,000 years separate them.

alternatives.label: Calendar
alternatives.text: Some researchers have proposed that the spiral patterns on the disc encode a calendar or astronomical count, an idea that remains speculative.

entries.title: Sputnik 1 and the start of the space age
entries.mainstream: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a 58 cm polished metal sphere weighing about 84 kg, into Earth orbit on an R-7 rocket from what is now the Baikonur Cosmodrome. Its radio beeps were picked up by amateurs and scientists around the world. It transmitted for about three weeks and burned up in the atmosphere in January 1958. A month later Sputnik 2 carried the dog Laika. In the United States the launch caused the 'Sputnik crisis', a public fear of falling behind the Soviets, leading to the creation of NASA and DARPA in 1958, increased science education funding and the space race.

alternatives.label: Cold War shock
alternatives.text: Historians note that US leaders knew a Soviet satellite was possible; the public shock was amplified by the media and by the fact that the same rocket could carry nuclear warheads across continents.

alternatives.label: Sky-watching boom
alternatives.text: Sputnik and later satellites encouraged large numbers of people to watch the night sky, which some researchers link to waves of UFO reports in the late 1950s.

alternatives.label: Unidentified satellites
alternatives.text: Its success contributed to later legends of unknown objects in orbit, such as the Black Knight satellite, which experts attribute to misidentified debris and early tracking errors.

media.title: Sputnik
media.channel: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

entries.title: Starfish Prime: the nuclear bomb exploded in space
entries.mainstream: On 9 July 1962 the United States detonated a 1.4-megaton thermonuclear warhead about 400 km above Johnston Atoll in the Pacific, as part of Operation Fishbowl. The explosion created an artificial aurora visible from Hawaii, about 1,450 km away, where its electromagnetic pulse was blamed for knocking out streetlights and damaging telephone equipment. High-energy electrons trapped in Earth's magnetic field formed an artificial radiation belt that damaged or disabled several satellites, including Telstar 1, the first commercial communications satellite. A 2026 study in the Journal of Geophysical Research used Starfish data to examine how such artificial belts limit themselves.

alternatives.label: Science and warfare
alternatives.text: The test was meant to study how nuclear explosions affect radar, communications and missile defence; it remains a key data source on electromagnetic pulse (EMP) and space radiation.

alternatives.label: Lasting effects
alternatives.text: The artificial radiation belt faded only slowly; in 1968 it was reported that some Starfish electrons had remained for five years. The 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty later banned nuclear tests in outer space.

alternatives.label: UFO connections
alternatives.text: Some UFO writers claim that nuclear tests attract UFOs or link Cold War tests to unexplained sightings; there is no evidence connecting Starfish Prime to UFO reports.

entries.title: The Malmstrom missile shutdown: UFO or secret test?
entries.mainstream: On 16 March 1967 all ten Minuteman nuclear missiles of Echo Flight, an underground complex controlled from Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, shut down nearly simultaneously with 'No-Go' indications. An Air Force report said rumours of UFOs in the area had been disproven. In 1996 former Air Force officer Robert Salas went public with claims that guards had seen a glowing red object over a launch facility just before missiles went offline. The story became a pillar of ufology. In 2025 a Pentagon report, as reported by the Wall Street Journal, stated that the incident had been caused by a classified test of an electromagnetic pulse device.

alternatives.label: UFO interference
alternatives.text: Salas and others argue that UFOs deliberately disabled nuclear missiles, a claim that later became central to the idea that aliens monitor nuclear weapons.

alternatives.label: Mundane explanations
alternatives.text: Sceptics point out that early accounts did not tie the Echo Flight fault to UFO reports, and that Salas's memories changed over time; a bright planet such as Mars has been suggested as the origin of light sightings.

alternatives.label: Secrets and disinformation
alternatives.text: The 2025 revelations suggest that secret military tests, and sometimes deliberate disinformation, helped feed UFO stories in the Cold War.

entries.title: The Belgian UFO wave: black triangles and F-16s
entries.mainstream: From 29 November 1989 to April 1990, many people in Belgium, starting in Eupen, reported large triangular objects with lights underneath flying slowly at low altitude. On the night of 30–31 March 1990, after ground reports and radar contacts, two Belgian Air Force F-16s were scrambled; they obtained brief radar locks but the pilots never saw anything. The Belgian Air Force released its report publicly. The most famous photograph of the wave, the Petit-Rechain photo of a dark triangle, was examined by several institutions without being identified. In 2011 its photographer, Patrick Maréchal, said it was a hoax made from painted polystyrene and lamps.

alternatives.label: Unexplained craft
alternatives.text: The Belgian UFO study group SOBEPS and physicist Auguste Meessen argued that the reports showed a real, unexplained phenomenon.

alternatives.label: Helicopters, radar and psychology
alternatives.text: Sceptics, including Brian Dunning, argue that the first report probably described a helicopter, that the F-16 radar locks were on each other or due to atmospheric interference, and that the wave grew through media coverage as a psychosocial phenomenon.

alternatives.label: Secret aircraft
alternatives.text: General Wilfried De Brouwer of the Belgian Air Staff initially thought the sightings could be experimental American craft; US authorities stated that no USAF stealth aircraft were operating in the area.

entries.title: Japan Air Lines Flight 1628: the pilot who saw a mothership
entries.mainstream: On 17 November 1986 a Japan Air Lines Boeing 747 cargo plane flying from Reykjavik to Anchorage over eastern Alaska reported three unidentified objects, described by captain Kenji Terauchi as 'two small ships and the mothership', one 'twice the size of an aircraft carrier', which followed the aircraft for several hundred kilometres. Ground radar initially appeared to show something, but on review military radar returns were dismissed as clutter, the FAA object was thought to be a split image of the aircraft, and nearby aircraft saw nothing. The FAA found the crew to be professional and rational.

alternatives.label: Credible witnesses
alternatives.text: UFO researchers see the case as important because of the experienced crew, the duration and the initial radar reports; it was widely reported in the press in early 1987.

alternatives.label: Planets
alternatives.text: Sceptic Philip J. Klass noted that Jupiter and Mars were bright in the direction where Terauchi saw lights, and that the pilot did not mention seeing the planets; he argued that the lights were celestial objects.

alternatives.label: Witness reliability
alternatives.text: The FAA noted that Terauchi had reported other UFO sightings, including one in January 1987 later explained as lights from villages, and sceptics such as Robert Sheaffer argue he was not an unbiased observer.

entries.title: The thylacine: extinct, surviving, or coming back?
entries.mainstream: The thylacine or Tasmanian tiger, a striped carnivorous marsupial, disappeared from mainland Australia and New Guinea thousands of years ago and survived in Tasmania until European settlement. Bounties paid by the Tasmanian government and the Van Diemen's Land Company encouraged hunting, and the species declined rapidly. Official protection came on 10 July 1936, 59 days before the last known thylacine died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936. The species was declared extinct in 1982 (IUCN) and 1986 (Tasmania). Its genome has been sequenced, and in 2022 the US company Colossal Biosciences announced a project to recreate a thylacine-like animal by editing the genome of a living marsupial relative.

alternatives.label: Still out there
alternatives.text: Hundreds of sightings have been reported in Tasmania and mainland Australia since 1936, and some researchers argue that the species may have survived for decades after its official extinction; none has been confirmed by a specimen, clear photograph or DNA.

alternatives.label: Extinct
alternatives.text: Most biologists consider the species extinct, noting that intensive searches and camera trapping have found no proof.

alternatives.label: De-extinction debate
alternatives.text: Supporters of de-extinction see a chance to restore a lost predator; critics argue that any animal produced would be a genetically modified proxy and that resources would be better spent on species still alive.

media.title: Secrets of the Tasmanian Tiger (Full Episode) | Lost Beasts Unearthed | Nat Geo Animals

entries.title: The Jersey Devil of the Pine Barrens
entries.dateNote: Legend set in 1735; panic in January 1909
entries.mainstream: The Jersey Devil, or Leeds Devil, is a legendary creature said to live in the Pine Barrens of southern New Jersey, usually described as a flying biped with hooves, wings, a horse- or goat-like head and a forked tail. The best-known story says that in 1735 a woman called Mother Leeds, pregnant with her 13th child, cursed it, and the baby turned into a monster and flew up the chimney into the pines. In January 1909 a wave of reported sightings and strange footprints across New Jersey and Pennsylvania caused panic, closed schools and was eagerly covered by newspapers. The creature is now the mascot of New Jersey's ice hockey team.

alternatives.label: Political origins
alternatives.text: Folklorists and historians link the legend to the Leeds family of Leeds Point, in particular almanac maker Daniel Leeds, who was attacked as a servant of the devil by Quaker opponents in the early 18th century, and to rivalry between almanacs.

alternatives.label: Real animal
alternatives.text: Some suggest that sightings of cranes, owls or other animals, and hoaxes such as the 1909 tracks, keep the legend alive; the 1909 wave also included deliberate hoaxes by showmen.

alternatives.label: Cryptid
alternatives.text: Cryptozoology enthusiasts continue to collect reports and investigate the Pine Barrens, treating the creature as a possible unknown animal.

entries.title: The mapinguari: Amazon monster or surviving giant sloth?
entries.mainstream: The mapinguari is a creature of Brazilian Amazonian folklore, described as a huge, hairy, foul-smelling being with hooked claws, backward-facing feet, a single eye, and sometimes a mouth in its belly. Similar beings appear in the traditions of Indigenous peoples such as the Matsigenka of Peru. Giant ground sloths, such as Megatherium and Eremotherium, lived in South America until the end of the last Ice Age, about 10,000 years ago.

alternatives.label: Surviving ground sloth
alternatives.text: Biologist David Oren, who collected testimonies from hunters and rubber tappers from the 1990s, proposed that the mapinguari could be a surviving ground sloth or a folk memory of one; searches have found no physical evidence.

alternatives.label: Forest spirit
alternatives.text: Anthropologists and folklorists such as Candace Slater see the mapinguari as a forest guardian figure related to other Amazonian beings such as the curupira, expressing fears and rules about the forest.

alternatives.label: Folk memory
alternatives.text: Some researchers suggest that early humans in South America encountered giant sloths, and stories might preserve a very distant memory, though this cannot be proven.

entries.title: The first detection of gravitational waves
entries.mainstream: On 14 September 2015 the two detectors of LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) in Louisiana and Washington state recorded a tiny ripple in space-time, named GW150914, produced by the merger of two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses about 1.3 billion light years away. The discovery, announced in February 2016, confirmed a prediction of Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity from 1916 and was the first direct observation of a binary black hole merger. Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics. Since then, hundreds of such events have been detected.

alternatives.label: New window on the universe
alternatives.text: Astronomers describe gravitational-wave astronomy as a new way of observing the cosmos, allowing the study of black holes and neutron stars that emit little light.

alternatives.label: Earlier false alarm
alternatives.text: In 2014 the BICEP2 team claimed to have detected primordial gravitational waves in the cosmic microwave background, but the signal was later attributed to galactic dust, a reminder of how carefully such claims are tested.

alternatives.label: Einstein's doubts
alternatives.text: Einstein himself was at times unsure whether gravitational waves were physically real and thought they would be too weak ever to detect.

entries.title: Phosphine on Venus: a sign of life in the clouds?
entries.mainstream: In September 2020 a team led by Jane Greaves reported in Nature Astronomy the detection of phosphine gas, about 20 parts per billion, in the clouds of Venus, using the JCMT and ALMA telescopes. On Earth phosphine is associated with anaerobic life and industrial processes, and the team said they could not identify any known non-biological process on Venus that could produce that amount. Subsequent studies disputed the detection, citing data-processing problems and suggesting the signal could be sulfur dioxide; reanalysis lowered the estimated amount. The question remains open, and new missions to Venus are planned.

alternatives.label: Possible biosignature
alternatives.text: Some scientists argue that microbes could survive in the temperate, acidic cloud layers of Venus, 50–60 km above the scorching surface, and that phosphine could be produced by them.

alternatives.label: Unknown chemistry or error
alternatives.text: Critics argue that the signal may be an artefact or misidentified sulfur dioxide, or that unknown volcanic or photochemical processes could produce phosphine.

alternatives.label: Lessons
alternatives.text: The episode is often compared to earlier claims of life signs on Mars, such as the 1996 ALH84001 meteorite, as an example of how extraordinary claims are tested in public.

entries.title: Sima de los Huesos: the 'pit of bones' at Atapuerca
entries.mainstream: Deep inside the Cueva Mayor at Atapuerca in northern Spain, a 13-metre shaft called the Sima de los Huesos ('pit of bones') has yielded the remains of at least 28-29 individuals dated to about 430,000 years ago, excavated from the 1980s onwards by teams led by Juan Luis Arsuaga, Eudald Carbonell and José María Bermúdez de Castro. When first reported in 1993 they made up most of the world's Middle Pleistocene human fossil record. They show a mix of Neanderthal and more archaic traits, and nuclear DNA recovered in 2016 (Meyer et al., Nature) placed them on the Neanderthal side of the split from Denisovans, making it the oldest human DNA then sequenced. A single finely made quartzite hand-axe, nicknamed 'Excalibur', was found among the bones. Nearby Atapuerca sites (Gran Dolina, Sima del Elefante) contain some of the oldest human fossils in western Europe, over 800,000 years old.

alternatives.label: Deliberate deposition
alternatives.text: Many of the excavators argue that bodies were deliberately dropped into the pit by other humans, which would be among the earliest evidence of funerary behaviour; the lone hand-axe has been read as a possible offering.

alternatives.label: Natural accumulation
alternatives.text: Other researchers suggest the bodies could have arrived through natural processes such as debris flows, carnivore activity or falls, and caution against reading symbolism into a single tool.

alternatives.label: Classification
alternatives.text: The fossils were once assigned to Homo heidelbergensis; since the DNA results most researchers treat them as early members of the Neanderthal lineage, which has reshaped debates over when Neanderthals and modern humans diverged.

entries.changed: Reported 1993 as pre-Neanderthals; mitochondrial DNA (2013) unexpectedly matched Denisovans; nuclear DNA (2016) showed they belong to the Neanderthal lineage.

entries.title: Tartessos: Iberia's lost kingdom, Tarshish, and Atlantis
entries.mainstream: Greek writers described Tartessos as a rich city and kingdom beyond the Pillars of Hercules, near the mouth of the Guadalquivir in south-western Spain, famous for silver, tin and copper; Herodotus tells of a long-lived Tartessian king, Arganthonios, who welcomed Phocaean Greek traders. Archaeology has identified a Tartessian culture in Andalusia and southern Portugal from the Late Bronze Age to about the 5th century BCE, shaped by intense contact with Phoenician colonists at Gadir (Cádiz). It is known for gold hoards such as the El Carambolo treasure (found 1958), the Southwest script with around a hundred inscriptions in an undeciphered language, and the burned and buried 5th-century BCE building at Casas del Turuñuelo (excavated from 2015). No capital city has ever been found.

alternatives.label: Tarshish
alternatives.text: Many biblical scholars have identified Tarshish, the distant source of metals for Solomon's and Tyre's ships in the Hebrew Bible, with Tartessos; others link Tarshish to Tarsus in Anatolia or elsewhere.

alternatives.label: Atlantis connection
alternatives.text: In 1922 the German archaeologist Adolf Schulten proposed that Tartessos was the real-world source of Plato's Atlantis, buried under the Doñana marshes. In 2011 a team led by Richard Freund claimed evidence in Doñana; Spanish researchers on the wider project described those claims as fanciful (speculative).

alternatives.label: A state or a culture?
alternatives.text: Archaeologists debate whether 'Tartessos' was a centralised kingdom with a lost capital or a looser network of communities that Greek writers summed up under one name.

media.title: How an advanced civilisation vanished 2,500 years ago – BBC News

entries.title: The Lady of Elche: Iberian masterpiece or forgery?
entries.mainstream: The Lady of Elche (Dama de Elche) is a painted limestone bust of a woman wearing an elaborate headdress with large wheel-shaped side ornaments, found in 1897 at La Alcudia near Elche in eastern Spain. Generally dated to the 4th century BCE, it is regarded as a masterpiece of Iberian sculpture showing Greek influence and may have served as a funerary urn, as it has a cavity in the back. It was sold to the Louvre within weeks of its discovery, returned to Spain in 1941 and is in the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid.

alternatives.label: Genuine Iberian work
alternatives.text: Most Spanish archaeologists accept the bust as ancient. A 2005 study by the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) of microscopic pigment traces found materials consistent with antiquity and no modern pigments.

alternatives.label: Forgery claim
alternatives.text: In 1995 the American art historian John F. Moffitt argued in 'Art Forgery: The Case of the Lady of Elche' that the bust was a 19th-century fake, perhaps by the restorer Francisco Pallás, citing stylistic differences from other Iberian sculpture. Doubts had first been raised in 1906. Experts in Iberian archaeology have rejected the claim.

alternatives.label: Goddess or noblewoman?
alternatives.text: Interpretations range from a portrait of a high-status woman to a priestess or a goddess associated with the Carthaginian Tanit.

entries.title: The tomb of St James at Santiago de Compostela
entries.mainstream: According to Compostela tradition, the hermit Pelagius saw mysterious lights over the Libredon forest in Galicia in the early 9th century (usually 814), and Bishop Theodemir identified a tomb there as that of the apostle James, son of Zebedee, who had been executed in Jerusalem around 44 CE. Medieval legend held that James had preached in Hispania and that his disciples brought his body by a stone boat to Galicia. King Alfonso II built a church, the cult grew rapidly, and the Way of St James became one of the great pilgrimage routes of medieval Europe; the Romanesque cathedral was begun in 1075. Excavations under the cathedral revealed a Roman-era necropolis, and the relics, hidden in 1589 against an English attack, were rediscovered in 1879 and declared authentic by Pope Leo XIII in 1884.

alternatives.label: Faith tradition
alternatives.text: The Catholic Church venerates the remains as those of the apostle; the pilgrimage revived strongly in the late 20th century and hundreds of thousands of people now walk the routes each year.

alternatives.label: Historical scepticism
alternatives.text: Most historians note that there is no early evidence that James ever went to Spain or was buried there, and see the 9th-century discovery as serving the Christian kingdom of Asturias in its struggle with al-Andalus; later legend made James 'Matamoros', the Moor-slayer, appearing at the (probably legendary) battle of Clavijo.

alternatives.label: Priscillian hypothesis
alternatives.text: Some writers have suggested that the tomb venerated at Santiago actually held Priscillian, a 4th-century Galician bishop executed for heresy at Trier in 385 whose body was returned to Galicia and revered as a martyr (speculative).

alternatives.label: Lights and stars
alternatives.text: The name Compostela is popularly explained as Campus Stellae, 'field of the star', after Pelagius' lights, and the route became linked with the Milky Way; many linguists prefer a derivation from a Latin word for a burial ground.

entries.title: Abbas ibn Firnas: the flying man of Córdoba
entries.mainstream: Abbas ibn Firnas (c. 810-887) was a polymath at the Umayyad court of Córdoba in al-Andalus: a poet, musician, astronomer and engineer credited with a planetarium-like device, a water clock and a method of cutting rock crystal and making glass. About seven centuries after his death the historian Ahmad al-Maqqari (d. 1632) wrote that Ibn Firnas covered himself in feathers, attached wings and launched himself from a height, flying 'a considerable distance' before landing badly and hurting his back, because he had not made himself a tail. A ninth-century verse quoted by al-Maqqari is the only earlier hint of the event.

alternatives.label: Early gliding attempt
alternatives.text: Many historians of flight accept that Ibn Firnas probably made some kind of gliding attempt, comparable to the reported jump of the English monk Eilmer of Malmesbury around 1000-1010; he is honoured by a statue at Baghdad International Airport, a bridge in Córdoba and a lunar crater.

alternatives.label: Late and thin evidence
alternatives.text: Others stress that the story rests on a single 17th-century source that does not cite its authority, so the details cannot be checked.

alternatives.label: 'Armen Firman' confusion
alternatives.text: Some modern books say Ibn Firnas was inspired by an earlier parachute-like jump by one 'Armen Firman' in Córdoba; this figure appears in no primary source and is probably a garbled Latinised form of Ibn Firnas' own name.

entries.title: The Guanches: Amazigh islanders of the Canaries
entries.mainstream: When Europeans reached the Canary Islands in the 14th-15th centuries they found them inhabited by peoples, collectively called Guanches (strictly, the people of Tenerife), who herded goats, grew barley, lived in caves and stone houses, and on Tenerife mummified some of their dead. Their languages were related to the Berber (Amazigh) languages of North Africa, and in 2017 the first ancient-genome study confirmed a North African origin, most similar to ancient and modern Amazigh populations. They probably arrived in the 1st millennium BCE or early 1st millennium CE, though how is unclear, since they appear to have had no seagoing boats at contact. The Castilian conquest (1402-1496) killed or enslaved many and the rest were assimilated; the Guanche languages died out by the 17th century, but traces survive, including Silbo Gomero, the whistled language of La Gomera.

alternatives.label: How they arrived
alternatives.text: Some researchers think the islands were settled by North Africans brought or encouraged by Phoenician-Punic or Roman traders; others suggest independent voyages with seafaring knowledge later lost.

alternatives.label: Atlantis and lost races
alternatives.text: From the 19th century some writers claimed the Guanches were survivors of Atlantis or a lost white race, partly because of reports of fair hair and the islands' remote position; genetics and linguistics place them firmly within North African populations (speculative claims rejected).

alternatives.label: Pyramids of Güímar
alternatives.text: Stepped stone platforms at Güímar on Tenerife were promoted by Thor Heyerdahl in the 1990s as possible links to ancient pyramid builders; archaeologists date them to the 19th century, when farmers cleared stones from their fields.

sources.title: Genomic Analyses of Pre-European Conquest Human Remains from the Canary Islands Reveal Close Affinity to Modern North Africans

entries.title: Dihya, 'al-Kahina': the Amazigh warrior-queen who fought the Umayyads
entries.mainstream: Dihya, known in Arabic sources as al-Kahina ('the priestess' or 'soothsayer'), was a 7th-century Amazigh (Berber) leader in the Aurès mountains of present-day Algeria. After the Umayyad general Hassan ibn al-Nu'man took Carthage, she defeated his army at the battle of the Meskiana (c. 698) and pursued him back into Libya, ruling much of the Maghreb for several years. Chroniclers say she then adopted a scorched-earth policy that alienated oasis and town dwellers, and that she was defeated and killed around 701-703 at a well still called Bir al-Kahina. Before the last battle she reportedly sent her sons to join the Arabs. Most details come from Arab historians writing centuries later, notably Ibn Khaldun.

alternatives.label: Religion
alternatives.text: Interpretations of her faith differ: some, reading Ibn Khaldun, have described her as Jewish or as leading Judaised Berber tribes; others, including the historians Mohamed Talbi and Gabriel Camps, think she was more probably Christian; still others see a traditional Amazigh religious role behind the title 'priestess'.

alternatives.label: Legend and history
alternatives.text: Her prophetic powers, her adoption of an Arab captive and her foreknowledge of her death are widely regarded as legendary embellishment, and some historians doubt parts of the chronology.

alternatives.label: Shifting symbol
alternatives.text: She has been claimed in turn as an Algerian national heroine, an Amazigh cultural icon, a Jewish heroine and a feminist symbol; a statue of her stands in Khenchela, Algeria.

entries.title: Tin Hinan: the ancestral queen of the Tuareg
entries.mainstream: Tuareg tradition in the Hoggar (Ahaggar) of southern Algeria holds that a noblewoman named Tin Hinan came from the Tafilalt oasis in Morocco with a companion, Takamat, and became the founding ancestress of the noble Tuareg lineages. A monumental stone tomb at Abalessa, opened in 1925 by the adventurer Byron Khun de Prorok with French military support and studied more carefully in 1933, contained the skeleton of a tall woman lying on a wooden bed, adorned with gold and silver bracelets and beads, together with a coin impression of the Roman emperor Constantine. She is usually dated to the 4th-5th century CE, and her remains are in the Bardo Museum in Algiers.

alternatives.label: Tomb of the legendary queen
alternatives.text: Many writers and the Tuareg themselves identify the Abalessa burial with the Tin Hinan of tradition, which would make it a rare case of an oral ancestress matched to a real grave.

alternatives.label: Unproven identification
alternatives.text: Archaeologists note that nothing in the tomb names its occupant; the link to the legend was made by its excavators, and the building may have been a fortified structure reused for the burial.

alternatives.label: Matrilineal society
alternatives.text: The legend is often connected with the relatively high status of women and matrilineal descent among the Tuareg.

entries.title: Taforalt: North Africa's oldest cemetery and its genetic surprise
entries.mainstream: Grotte des Pigeons at Taforalt in north-eastern Morocco holds what is probably the oldest known cemetery in North Africa: dozens of Iberomaurusian hunter-gatherers buried between about 15,100 and 14,000 years ago. Their teeth show unusually high rates of tooth decay, linked to a diet rich in starchy wild plants such as acorns and pine nuts, thousands of years before farming (Humphrey et al. 2014). In 2018 seven individuals produced the oldest nuclear genomes then known from Africa (van de Loosdrecht et al., Science): they carried a large Near Eastern-related component, most similar to the Natufians of the Levant, plus a component related to sub-Saharan Africans.

alternatives.label: Migration into Africa
alternatives.text: The original study suggested that the Near Eastern-related ancestry reflects movement of people into North Africa before the Holocene.

alternatives.label: Back-migration debate
alternatives.text: Other geneticists have modelled the data differently, arguing that Iberomaurusian-related ancestry contributed to the Natufians rather than the other way round, and that some 'Eurasian' and 'African' labels for lineages long present in North Africa are misleading. The direction of gene flow remains debated.

alternatives.label: Sahara as a barrier
alternatives.text: A 2025 study of 7,000-year-old Green Sahara individuals from Takarkori, Libya, found a separate, long-isolated North African lineage, suggesting the Green Sahara was not a major corridor between north and sub-Saharan Africa.

sources.title: Pleistocene North African genomes link Near Eastern and sub-Saharan African human populations
sources.authors: van de Loosdrecht, M. et al.

entries.title: Msoura: Morocco's stone circle and the tomb of the giant Antaeus
entries.mainstream: Msoura (Mzora), about 15 km south-east of Asilah in northern Morocco, is an oval ring of 167 standing stones surrounding a large burial mound about 58 by 54 metres; one stone, El Uted ('the peg'), is over 5 metres tall. It is usually dated to around the 4th-3rd century BCE and may relate to the beginnings of the Kingdom of Mauretania. Local legend calls it the tomb of the giant Antaeus, the Libyan wrestler defeated by Heracles in Greek myth; the Roman writer Plutarch reports that the general Sertorius dug open a tomb said to be that of Antaeus near Tingis (Tangier) and found a skeleton 60 cubits long, before reburying it. In January 2025 Morocco listed the site as national heritage.

alternatives.label: Mauretanian royal tomb
alternatives.text: Archaeologists generally interpret Msoura as a monumental tomb of a local elite or early royal family, with parallels to other North African tumuli.

alternatives.label: Antaeus and Sertorius
alternatives.text: Some writers suggest Msoura may be the tomb Sertorius opened; this cannot be confirmed, and stories of giant bones are common worldwide, often arising from fossil animal bones (speculative).

alternatives.label: Atlantic megalithic link
alternatives.text: Its circle of standing stones has led some to compare it with Atlantic European megaliths, which are thousands of years older; most archaeologists see it as a local North African tradition.

entries.title: Murujuga: a million petroglyphs and the world's largest rock-art gallery
entries.dateNote: Engravings span tens of thousands of years to the recent past
entries.mainstream: Murujuga, the Burrup Peninsula and Dampier Archipelago in the Pilbara of Western Australia, holds what is often described as the world's largest concentration of rock engravings: around a million petroglyphs at some 2,500 recorded sites, made over many millennia by the ancestors of today's custodians, the Yaburara, Ngarluma, Mardudhunera, Yindjibarndi and Wong-Goo-Tt-Oo peoples (many Yaburara people were killed in the Flying Foam massacre of 1868). The oldest are commonly estimated at tens of thousands of years (figures of 40,000-50,000 years are often cited, though direct dating of engravings is difficult). Images include human figures, faces, kangaroos, emus, marine animals and many depictions of the thylacine, which disappeared from mainland Australia about 3,000 years ago. The engravings also record environmental change as rising seas after the last Ice Age turned a coastal range into islands. In July 2025 the Murujuga Cultural Landscape was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

alternatives.label: Industry and preservation
alternatives.text: Since the 1960s port, iron-ore and gas developments have destroyed or moved many engravings, and scientists disagree with government and industry over whether industrial emissions are damaging the rock surfaces; a monitoring programme began in 2023.

alternatives.label: Deep-time record
alternatives.text: Many researchers see Murujuga as a continuous visual archive spanning from the Ice Age to the present, comparable in significance to European cave art; exact ages for individual motifs remain uncertain.

alternatives.label: Living tradition
alternatives.text: Traditional custodians emphasise that the engravings are part of living law and story, not only an archaeological record.

entries.title: Wurdi Youang: an Aboriginal stone arrangement aligned with the sun?
entries.dateNote: Age unknown; date shown is a placeholder for a pre-contact construction
entries.mainstream: Wurdi Youang, near Little River in Victoria, Australia, is an egg-shaped arrangement of about 100 basalt stones some 50 metres across, with three prominent waist-high stones at its highest, western end. It is on the traditional country of the Wathaurong people and was returned to the Wathaurong Aboriginal Co-operative in 2006. A 2013 study by Ray Norris, Duane Hamacher and colleagues argued that the arrangement's straight sides and outlying stones mark the setting points of the sun at the solstices and equinoxes, and that this is unlikely to be coincidence. Its age is unknown.

alternatives.label: Solar observatory
alternatives.text: Supporters argue that Wurdi Youang demonstrates sophisticated Aboriginal astronomical knowledge used for calendars and ceremony, consistent with recorded oral traditions of sky lore across Australia.

alternatives.label: Caution over alignments
alternatives.text: Sceptics note that with many stones, some alignments can arise by chance, that the site has been disturbed since European settlement, and that no oral tradition specifically describing its astronomical use was recorded.

alternatives.label: Claims of great age
alternatives.text: Popular reports have described it as possibly older than Stonehenge or even 11,000 years old, based on dates from other sites in the region; the arrangement itself has not been dated (speculative).

sources.title: Norris, R. P. et al. (2013) Wurdi Youang: an Australian Aboriginal stone arrangement with possible solar indications, Rock Art Research 30(1) (arXiv preprint)
