entries.title: The Emu in the Sky and Aboriginal astronomy
entries.dateNote: Traditions of great but unknown age; first written records 1840s-1850s
entries.mainstream: Across much of Australia, Aboriginal peoples recognise a constellation made not of stars but of the dark dust lanes of the Milky Way: the Emu in the Sky, whose head is the Coalsack nebula beside the Southern Cross and whose body stretches towards Scorpius. Its changing position through the year signals when emus lay eggs and when to collect them. Rock engravings in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park near Sydney include an emu in the same pose as the sky emu. Records of Aboriginal astronomy go back to the settler William Stanbridge, who in 1857 published star lore of the Boorong people of north-western Victoria. In 2010 astronomers Duane Hamacher and David Frew argued that a Boorong story about a star called Collowgulloric War records the 1840s outburst of the star Eta Carinae.

alternatives.label: Practical calendar
alternatives.text: Researchers emphasise that sky knowledge was tied to seasons, food resources, law and navigation, a practical and ceremonial system rather than abstract star-gazing.

alternatives.label: 'World's first astronomers'
alternatives.text: Some writers call Aboriginal Australians the world's first astronomers given the continuity of their cultures over tens of thousands of years; others caution that the antiquity of any particular sky story cannot be directly measured.

alternatives.label: Diversity of traditions
alternatives.text: The same dark shape is read differently in different nations; for the Wardaman, for example, the Coalsack is the head of a lawman, not an emu.

sources.title: Hamacher, D. W. & Frew, D. J. (2010) An Aboriginal Australian record of the Great Eruption of Eta Carinae, Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage (arXiv preprint)

media.title: Ancient astronomy and modern technology combine to tell stories of the night sky | ABC Australia

entries.title: The Kula ring: shell valuables that circle the islands
entries.mainstream: In the Massim islands of Milne Bay, Papua New Guinea, including the Trobriand Islands, men make long canoe voyages to exchange two kinds of ceremonial valuables: red shell-disc necklaces (soulava or veigun), which travel clockwise around a ring of island communities, and white shell armbands (mwali), which travel anticlockwise. The objects are not kept permanently but passed on, and their histories and the partnerships they create bring prestige. The anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski, who lived in the Trobriands in 1915-18, made the Kula famous in Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), asking why people would risk dangerous ocean voyages to give away apparently useless trinkets. The exchange continues today.

alternatives.label: Gift economy
alternatives.text: Marcel Mauss used the Kula in The Gift (1925) to argue that exchange creates social obligations, an idea that became central to anthropology and economics debates about non-market economies.

alternatives.label: Women and wealth
alternatives.text: Annette Weiner, revisiting the Trobriands in the 1970s, argued that Malinowski had overlooked women's wealth and exchanges, which were essential to the system.

alternatives.label: Antiquity
alternatives.text: Archaeologists have looked for the roots of the Kula in older Massim trade networks; when the ring as described by Malinowski took shape is uncertain.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Argonauts of the Western Pacific

entries.title: Teouma: the first Pacific islanders and their missing skulls
entries.mainstream: At Teouma on Efate island, Vanuatu, archaeologists found the oldest known cemetery in the Pacific Islands, used about 3,000-3,200 years ago by people of the Lapita culture, the first settlers of Remote Oceania. Many burials had their skulls removed after decomposition; some were replaced with cone-shell rings, and in one burial three skulls lay on the chest of a headless body. The site was found by chance in 2003 during earthworks for a prawn farm. Finely stamped Lapita pottery accompanied the dead, including a decorated pot holding a human skull, covered by an upturned flat-bottomed dish used as a lid. In 2016 ancient DNA from Teouma individuals (Skoglund et al., Nature) showed that the first settlers had almost entirely East Asian-related ancestry, with Papuan ancestry arriving in Vanuatu later.

alternatives.label: Skull rituals
alternatives.text: Archaeologists interpret skull removal as ancestor veneration, a practice known from later Melanesian societies and from other regions such as the Neolithic Near East.

alternatives.label: Population replacement debate
alternatives.text: The genetic results suggested that modern ni-Vanuatu largely descend from later Papuan-ancestry arrivals while keeping Austronesian languages; researchers continue to debate how this language and population turnover happened.

alternatives.label: Wider pattern
alternatives.text: Teouma has become a key site in tracing the rapid Lapita expansion from the Bismarck Archipelago to Tonga and Samoa within a few centuries.

sources.title: Genomic insights into the peopling of the Southwest Pacific

media.author: Rebecca Kinaston, Hallie Buckley, Frederique Valentin, Stuart Bedford, Matthew Spriggs, Stuart Hawkins, Estelle Herrsche

entries.title: Ghost ancestors in Papua: Denisovan DNA in Melanesians
entries.dateNote: Interbreeding c. 45,000 and possibly c. 30,000 years ago
entries.mainstream: The Denisovans, an archaic human group known mainly from DNA first read from a finger bone in Siberia's Denisova Cave in 2010, left their largest genetic legacy far away: in Papuans, Aboriginal Australians and other Near Oceanians, who carry several per cent Denisovan ancestry (Philippine Aeta groups carry even more). In 2019 Guy Jacobs and colleagues reported that Papuans carry DNA from at least two deeply divergent Denisovan populations, one of which may have interbred with modern humans as recently as about 30,000 years ago, suggesting Denisovans may have survived in or near New Guinea until surprisingly late. No Denisovan fossil has yet been found east of the Wallace Line.

alternatives.label: Wallacea or Sundaland?
alternatives.text: Some researchers think Denisovans crossed the deep-water Wallace Line, as Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis ancestors did; others suggest the mixing happened further west, in Sundaland, before modern humans crossed.

alternatives.label: Adaptive genes
alternatives.text: Studies suggest some Denisovan gene variants in Papuans affect immunity and possibly adaptation to different altitudes.

alternatives.label: Late survival
alternatives.text: A late date for interbreeding implies that a Denisovan population persisted after most other archaic humans had vanished; this is debated because dating methods based on DNA segment lengths carry large uncertainties.

sources.title: Multiple Deeply Divergent Denisovan Ancestries in Papuans

media.title: The Ancient Human Species With A Missing Body

entries.title: Kongamato: the 'boat-overwhelmer' of the Zambian swamps and living pterosaur claims
entries.mainstream: In his 1923 book In Witch-Bound Africa the British colonial official Frank Melland described the kongamato ('overwhelmer of boats'), a winged creature said to haunt the Jiundu swamps of north-western Zambia and to capsize canoes. He reported that local Kaonde men, shown pictures of a pterosaur, identified it as the kongamato. Later travellers added further reports from Zambia, Angola and the Congo, and cryptozoologists linked it to similar claims elsewhere, such as the ropen of Papua New Guinea, which some young-earth creationist writers promote as living pterosaurs.

alternatives.label: Misidentified birds or bats
alternatives.text: Sceptics, including the museum director Reay Smithers in 1957, suggested shoebills or saddle-billed storks, which can be aggressive near their nests; others proposed large fruit bats such as the hammer-headed bat.

alternatives.label: Fossil influence
alternatives.text: In 1928 the Swedish palaeontologist Carl Wiman suggested the stories might have been influenced by pterosaur fossils dug up in Tanganyika (at Tendaguru) before the First World War, as news of them travelled.

alternatives.label: Living pterosaur
alternatives.text: A few cryptozoologists have entertained the idea of a surviving pterosaur; palaeontologists note there are no pterosaur fossils younger than 66 million years (speculative).

entries.title: Toumaï: a 7-million-year-old skull from Chad, and the femur that went missing
entries.mainstream: In July 2001 a Franco-Chadian team found a distorted but nearly complete ape-like skull in the Djurab desert of northern Chad; President Idriss Déby nicknamed it Toumaï, 'hope of life' in the Daza language. Described by Michel Brunet and colleagues in Nature in 2002 as Sahelanthropus tchadensis, it is dated by associated animal fossils to about 7 million years ago, close to the time humans and chimpanzees are thought to have diverged, and far west of the East African Rift where most early hominin fossils come from. Its small canines and the forward position of the opening where the spinal cord enters the skull were taken as signs it was a hominin that walked upright.

alternatives.label: Earliest known hominin
alternatives.text: Brunet's team and supporters regard Sahelanthropus as the oldest known member of the human lineage; in 2022 Guillaume Daver and colleagues described a femur and ulnae from the site as showing habitual bipedalism combined with tree climbing.

alternatives.label: Ape, not hominin
alternatives.text: Other researchers argue it may be an ape outside the human lineage, perhaps related to gorillas. A femur found among the site's animal bones by Poitiers graduate student Aude Bergeret in 2004 was described by Roberto Macchiarelli and colleagues in 2020 as not consistent with habitual upright walking, and they criticised the delay in publishing it.

alternatives.label: A disturbed site
alternatives.text: Alain Beauvilain, who was present at the discovery, argued that the skull was found loose on the surface, not excavated, possibly after being reburied by nomads, which complicates dating.

sources.title: A new hominid from the Upper Miocene of Chad, Central Africa
Postcranial evidence of late Miocene hominin bipedalism in Chad

entries.title: The Happisburgh footprints: Britain's first people, washed away within weeks
entries.mainstream: In May 2013, waves at Happisburgh on the Norfolk coast of England stripped sand from the ancient Cromer Forest Bed and exposed around 50 human footprints pressed into estuarine mud. The team, led by Nick Ashton of the British Museum, recorded them with 3D photogrammetry before the tide destroyed them within about two weeks. Published in 2014, they date to roughly 850,000-950,000 years ago, making them the oldest known human footprints outside Africa. The prints seem to come from a group of adults and children, perhaps up to five people, at a time when Britain was joined to the continent by land (later Doggerland). Stone tools from Happisburgh are of similar age.

alternatives.label: Who made them?
alternatives.text: No bones have been found at Happisburgh; the most likely candidate is Homo antecessor, known from similarly old fossils at Gran Dolina, Atapuerca in Spain.

alternatives.label: Cold-climate pioneers
alternatives.text: The finds suggest early humans could survive in a cool, northern climate far earlier than once thought, raising questions about clothing, shelter and fire.

alternatives.label: Fragile evidence
alternatives.text: Because the prints no longer exist, all later analysis depends on the 3D records made in the field, a reminder of how chance exposure and erosion shape the archaeological record.

sources.title: Hominin Footprints from Early Pleistocene Deposits at Happisburgh, UK

media.title: The oldest human footprints in Europe | Natural History Museum

entries.title: Australopithecus sediba: the fossil found by a nine-year-old
entries.mainstream: On 15 August 2008, nine-year-old Matthew Berger, exploring near his father Lee Berger's research area at Malapa in South Africa's Cradle of Humankind, spotted a fossil collarbone in a rock. It belonged to a juvenile skeleton (MH1, nicknamed Karabo), and a partial adult female skeleton (MH2) was found soon after. Described in 2010 as a new species, Australopithecus sediba, the fossils are about 1.98 million years old and combine a small australopith brain and climbing arms with a more human-like face, teeth and hand, and an unusual way of walking. The cave may have been a natural death trap at the base of a vertical shaft.

alternatives.label: Ancestor of Homo?
alternatives.text: Berger and colleagues proposed that A. sediba, or something like it, could be close to the ancestry of our genus Homo.

alternatives.label: Late cousin
alternatives.text: Many others point out that fossils attributed to early Homo are older than Malapa, so sediba is more likely a late-surviving relative or a sister group of A. africanus, showing features evolved in parallel.

alternatives.label: Open science
alternatives.text: The Malapa team made casts and scans widely available and invited many early-career researchers, an approach Berger later repeated with Homo naledi.

sources.title: Australopithecus sediba : A New Species of Homo -Like Australopith from South Africa

entries.title: The hunebedden: 'giants' beds' of Drenthe
entries.mainstream: The hunebedden are megalithic passage graves in the north-east of the Netherlands, built from glacial boulders by people of the Western Group of the Funnelbeaker culture between about 3470 and 3250 BCE and used until about 2760 BCE. Of perhaps 100 original tombs, 54 survive, 52 of them in Drenthe, most along the Hondsrug ridge. They were reused by later Bronze Age peoples. The tombs attracted attention early: the first paper on them appeared in 1547, Titia Brongersma carried out the first known excavation in 1685, and in 1734 the government of Drenthe passed one of the earliest laws in Europe protecting antiquities.

alternatives.label: Built by giants
alternatives.text: The Dutch name is usually linked to old words for giants, and in 1660 the pastor Johan Picardt published a widely read book arguing that the tombs were built by giants who had come to Drenthe from the Holy Land via Scandinavia. The idea stayed popular in folklore and illustrations long after scholars dropped it.

alternatives.label: Ordinary farmers
alternatives.text: Already in Picardt's time some, mainly German, scholars attributed the tombs to ordinary people. Modern archaeology shows they were collective graves of early farming communities, part of a Funnelbeaker tradition that may have built tens of thousands of such tombs across northern Europe.

entries.title: The Flying Dutchman: the ghost ship of the Cape
entries.mainstream: The Flying Dutchman is a legendary ghost ship doomed never to make port and to sail the seas forever, usually off the Cape of Good Hope. The legend probably grew out of the Golden Age of the Dutch East India Company (VOC); the oldest known printed mention is in John MacDonald's travel memoir of 1790 ('the sailors said they saw the Flying Dutchman'). An 1821 story in Blackwood's Magazine named the captain Hendrick van der Decken, who swore he would round the Cape even if it took until the day of judgment, and added the motif of the ghostly crew offering letters to long-dead people. Heinrich Heine's 1833 retelling inspired Richard Wagner's opera The Flying Dutchman (1843).

alternatives.label: Real sightings
alternatives.text: Sailors continued to report the ship. The best known account is in the published log of the royal princes' cruise, recording that before dawn on 11 July 1881 off Australia a brig appeared in 'a strange red light as of a phantom ship all aglow' and then vanished; the young Prince George, the future King George V, was on board. In the legend, seeing the ship is an omen of doom.

alternatives.label: Mirage at sea
alternatives.text: The most widely accepted explanation for sightings is a superior mirage or Fata Morgana, in which ships beyond the horizon appear raised and distorted above the sea.

alternatives.label: Historical captain
alternatives.text: Some sources suggest the legend was modelled on the 17th-century Dutch captain Bernard Fokke, famous for the speed of his voyages to Java and suspected of being in league with the Devil.

entries.title: St Elizabeth's flood (1421): drowned villages and the cat in the cradle
entries.mainstream: During the night of 18-19 November 1421 a severe North Sea storm broke the dikes of the Grote Hollandse Waard, a large polder in what is now the Netherlands. A number of villages were swallowed and never rebuilt, and estimates of the dead range from 2,000 to 10,000. Much of the drowned land became tidal marsh; the area of today's Biesbosch National Park has been flooded ever since. The disaster also separated the rival cities of Dordrecht and Geertruidenberg, which had been fighting in the Hook and Cod wars.

alternatives.label: The cat and the cradle
alternatives.text: According to legend, after the flood people saw a cradle floating towards the dike with a cat leaping from side to side to keep it balanced; inside was a baby, still dry and asleep. The tale is linked to the name of Kinderdijk ('children's dike') and was painted by Lawrence Alma-Tadema in 1856.

alternatives.label: Legend and memory
alternatives.text: Historians treat the cradle story as folklore without contemporary evidence, while the flood itself is well recorded. Medieval sources also blamed neglect of the dikes during the civil wars for making the disaster worse.

entries.title: The 'great animal of Maastricht': the fossil that proved extinction
entries.mainstream: In 1778 a chalk quarry in the Sint-Pietersberg near Maastricht produced a huge fossil skull with rows of teeth, the second such find there; it attracted the attention of the local physician Johann Leonard Hoffmann, who thought it was a crocodile, while others took it for a whale. When French revolutionary armies took Maastricht in 1795, the skull was seized as a prize of war and sent to Paris. In 1808 Georges Cuvier concluded that it belonged to a giant marine lizard related to monitor lizards but unlike any living animal, an idea that helped establish that species could become extinct. William Conybeare named it Mosasaurus, 'lizard of the Meuse', in 1822. The species lived around 82-66 million years ago, and the largest reached about 12 metres or more.

alternatives.label: 600 bottles of wine
alternatives.text: In a 1799 account, Barthélemy Faujas de Saint-Fond wrote that the skull was retrieved for the French by twelve grenadiers in exchange for 600 bottles of wine; the story is often repeated but rests on this single account.

alternatives.label: Monsters and dragons
alternatives.text: Before Cuvier, fossils of large unknown creatures were widely read as remains of giants, dragons or animals killed in the biblical Flood. The Maastricht skull became a key piece of evidence that whole worlds of animals had vanished.

entries.title: The stolen Just Judges panel of the Ghent Altarpiece
entries.mainstream: The Just Judges is the lower left panel of the Ghent Altarpiece (Adoration of the Mystic Lamb), painted by Jan van Eyck and possibly his brother Hubert between about 1430 and 1432. During the night of 10 April 1934 it was stolen from St Bavo's Cathedral in Ghent. On 30 April the Bishop of Ghent received a ransom demand for one million Belgian francs; the Belgian government refused, and as a sign of good faith the thief returned the panel's reverse side, a grisaille of St John the Baptist. On 25 November 1934 Arsène Goedertier told his lawyer on his deathbed that he alone knew where the Mystic Lamb was, and that he would take the secret to his grave. Carbon copies of the ransom notes were found in his desk. The panel has never been found; it was replaced in 1945 by a copy made by Jef Van der Veken.

alternatives.label: Goedertier the thief
alternatives.text: The police concluded that Goedertier was the thief; one of his unsent notes said the panel rested in a place where neither he nor anyone else could take it away without attracting public attention.

alternatives.label: A wider plot
alternatives.text: There is speculation that Goedertier could not have acted alone and had inside help, possibly from one of the cathedral's custodians, and amateur and official searches continue to be proposed (speculative).

alternatives.label: The copy
alternatives.text: Van der Veken based his copy on a 16th-century copy by Michiel Coxie, and subtly marked it as a copy by giving one of the horsemen the face of King Leopold III.

entries.title: Han van Meegeren: the forger who fooled Göring
entries.mainstream: Han van Meegeren (1889-1947), a Dutch painter dismissed by critics, set out to prove his talent by forging Dutch Golden Age paintings. He mixed phenol formaldehyde resin (Bakelite) into his paints and baked the canvases so the paint would harden as if centuries old. In 1937 the leading expert Abraham Bredius hailed his The Supper at Emmaus as 'the masterpiece of Johannes Vermeer of Delft', and it was bought for the Museum Boijmans in Rotterdam. In 1942 one of his fake Vermeers, Christ with the Adulteress, was acquired by Hermann Göring in exchange for 137 looted paintings. After the war Van Meegeren was arrested for selling Dutch cultural property to the Nazis; to escape a possible death penalty he confessed to forgery, and between July and December 1945 painted a new 'Vermeer' before court-appointed witnesses. A scientific commission led by Paul Coremans found 20th-century resins in the paint. In November 1947 he was sentenced to one year for forgery and fraud, but died of heart failure on 30 December 1947.

alternatives.label: Folk hero
alternatives.text: A Dutch opinion poll in October 1947 ranked Van Meegeren among the most popular people in the country, seen as the trickster who had fooled the experts and Göring.

alternatives.label: Self-made legend
alternatives.text: The art historian Jonathan Lopez argued that this image was itself a forgery: Van Meegeren had written articles echoing Nazi and antisemitic rhetoric, and his trial defence, presenting the sale to Göring as a patriotic trick, was a masterpiece of self-invention.

alternatives.label: Doubters of the forgery
alternatives.text: In the 1950s the Belgian expert Jean Decoen and the collector Daniël van Beuningen insisted that some of the works, including the Emmaus, were genuine Vermeers; courts and later analyses, including radioactive dating of the lead white and a 1977 forensic study, confirmed they were modern.

media.title: The art forger who tricked the Nazis - Noah Charney

entries.title: Akbar's House of Worship and the 'Divine Faith'
entries.mainstream: The Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556-1605) built a new capital at Fatehpur Sikri from 1571, near the shrine of the Sufi Sheikh Salim Chishti who had predicted the birth of his son Jahangir; the city was largely abandoned after about 1585. In 1575 he built there the Ibadat Khana (House of Worship), where he held debates between Sunni and Shia Muslim scholars, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians, Jesuit missionaries from Goa and others. In 1582 he propounded the Din-i Ilahi ('Divine Faith' or 'Oneness of the Divine'), a syncretic set of beliefs and practices that drew on several of these traditions, with vegetarianism and non-violence among its ideals. Only around 19 followers are identified, and it lapsed after his death.

alternatives.label: A new religion
alternatives.text: Many Muslim scholars of the period denounced it as blasphemy and called Akbar an apostate, and some accounts describe him as leaving Islam to found a new faith.

alternatives.label: A discipleship and a policy
alternatives.text: Some modern scholars argue it was a spiritual discipleship of Akbar's own beliefs rather than a full religion, its followers being called chelah ('disciples'), and that its core was the policy of sulh-i kul ('universal peace') used to govern a diverse empire.

entries.title: The 'dumb house': Akbar and the forbidden experiment
entries.mainstream: Rulers in several cultures are said to have tried to find humanity's 'natural' language by raising infants without hearing speech, which the scholar Roger Shattuck called the 'forbidden experiment'. Herodotus wrote that the Egyptian pharaoh Psamtik I (664-610 BCE) had a child raised in this way, and that its first word sounded like bekos, which meant 'bread' in Phrygian, so he concluded the Phrygians were older than the Egyptians. The monk Salimbene di Adam wrote that Emperor Frederick II (13th century) had infants nursed in silence, and that they all died. James IV of Scotland (r. 1488-1513) was said to have sent two children with a mute woman to the island of Inchkeith, and they reportedly spoke good Hebrew. The Mughal emperor Akbar, who held that speech comes from hearing, is recorded as having had children raised by mute nurses in a building that became known as the 'dumb house'; when he visited in 1582, the children made no speech at all.

alternatives.label: Akbar's test probably real
alternatives.text: Historians consider Akbar's experiment the most likely to be authentic, and its outcome supported his view that language is learned rather than innate.

alternatives.label: Tales with a moral
alternatives.text: Some authors doubt that the experiments of Psamtik and James IV took place as told, and probably that of Frederick II too; Salimbene was hostile to Frederick and used the story to show his cruelty and curiosity.

alternatives.label: Modern echoes
alternatives.text: Real cases of children raised in severe isolation, and debates over a language instinct, mean the question behind the stories is still discussed in linguistics, while such an experiment is now considered unethical.

entries.title: The 'Tejo Mahalaya' theory: was the Taj Mahal a Hindu temple?
entries.dateNote: Theory from 1965; Taj Mahal built from c. 1632
entries.mainstream: The Taj Mahal in Agra was built from about 1632 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, on land given by Raja Jai Singh I in exchange for a palace in the centre of Agra. From 1965 the writer P. N. Oak argued in books such as 'The Taj Mahal was a Rajput Palace' and 'Taj Mahal: The True Story' (1989) that it was an older Hindu temple-palace dedicated to Shiva, 'Tejo Mahalaya', which Shah Jahan had taken over. Oak made similar claims about the Kaaba, Westminster Abbey and Vatican City.

alternatives.label: Hidden temple
alternatives.text: Supporters point to the Mughal chronicle Padshahnama's statement that a mansion of Jai Singh's family stood on the site as evidence of an earlier Hindu building; several court cases have been inspired by the theory.

alternatives.label: Pseudohistory
alternatives.text: Historians reject the theory. The the Padshahnama and other records describe the acquisition of the land and construction of the tomb; the art historian Giles Tillotson called Oak's work a 'startling piece of pseudo-scholarship'. India's Supreme Court dismissed Oak's petition in 2000, saying he had a 'bee in his bonnet', and in 2017 the Archaeological Survey of India stated there was no evidence that the monument had been a temple.

media.title: Is this the most beautiful building in the world? - Stephanie Honchell Smith

entries.title: The Koh-i-Noor: a diamond's journey and its 'curse'
entries.mainstream: The Koh-i-Noor ('Mountain of Light') is one of the world's largest cut diamonds, now 105.6 carats. It first appears in the record in the late 15th or early 16th century: in 1526, after the First Battle of Panipat, Babur's son Humayun received a great diamond from the family of the ruler of Gwalior, and Babur wrote that its value could feed the whole world for a day. It later adorned Shah Jahan's Peacock Throne, was carried off to Persia by Nader Shah in 1739, passed to the Durrani rulers of Afghanistan and then to Ranjit Singh of the Sikh Empire in 1813. After the Second Anglo-Sikh War it was surrendered to Queen Victoria in 1849 by the 11-year-old Maharaja Duleep Singh, recut in 1852, and set in the crowns of British queens. India, Pakistan, Iran and Afghanistan have each claimed it.

alternatives.label: The curse
alternatives.text: A rumour that the stone was cursed, bringing violent ends to the men who owned it, may have begun in the Delhi Gazette and was repeated in the Illustrated London News; Queen Victoria herself expressed concern. A counter-rumour held that the curse affected only male rulers, and the diamond has since been worn only by female members of the royal family.

alternatives.label: Ancient origins
alternatives.text: Some traditions identify it with diamonds in older Indian accounts, including a large diamond Alauddin Khalji acquired from the Kakatiya kingdom around 1310; historians note the link cannot be proven.

alternatives.label: A spoil of war
alternatives.text: The Governor-General Lord Dalhousie treated the stone as a spoil of war; Britain says it was acquired legally under the Last Treaty of Lahore, while claimant countries call it taken unjustly. Queen Victoria herself later became uneasy about the way the diamond had been acquired.

media.title: Crown Jewels: Why is the Koh-i-Noor diamond so controversial? – BBC News

entries.title: Óc Eo and Funan: a naga princess, a foreign prince and Roman gold in the Mekong Delta
entries.mainstream: Funan is generally considered the first known kingdom of Southeast Asia, a network of Indianised states in the Mekong Delta and neighbouring parts of Cambodia, Thailand and Vietnam from about the 1st to the 7th century CE. The name Funan does not appear in local texts, and what its people called their polity is unknown; most of what is written about it comes from Chinese histories, especially the reports of the 3rd-century Wu envoys Kang Tai and Zhu Ying. Its great port at Óc Eo in southern Vietnam, excavated by Louis Malleret from the 1940s, has yielded jewellery, religious statues, locally minted silver coins, and Roman gold medallions of the reign of Antoninus Pius (138-161 CE) and possibly Marcus Aurelius.

alternatives.label: Founding legend
alternatives.text: Chinese and later Cambodian traditions tell that a foreign Brahmin or prince, called Hùntián in Chinese and usually identified with Kaundinya, sailed in and shot an arrow from a divine bow through the ship of the local queen Liǔyè ('Willow Leaf', identified with Soma), after which the two married. In Khmer folklore she becomes Neang Neak, a naga (serpent) princess, and he Preah Thaong, and Soma and Kaundinya are held to be the first kings of Cambodia.

alternatives.label: Cattigara?
alternatives.text: Malleret and others identified Óc Eo with Cattigara, the easternmost port named in Ptolemy's Geography; the Roman medallions were found near the region where Chinese texts say Romans first landed before travelling on to China on a diplomatic mission in 166 CE. Others place Cattigara elsewhere.

alternatives.label: Whose kingdom?
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether Funan's people were mainly Khmer, as Michael Vickery argued, or Austronesian; the Vietnamese historian Hà Văn Tấn argued that a single 'Funan culture' stretching from the Mekong to Burma cannot yet be demonstrated.

entries.title: Bagan: 10,000 temples, a dragon princess's son, and the Mongol question
entries.mainstream: From 1044 to 1287 Bagan (Pagan), on the Irrawaddy in Myanmar, was the capital of the Pagan Kingdom, the first state to unify the lands that became Myanmar, expanded under King Anawrahta in the 1050s and 1060s. At its height more than 10,000 Buddhist temples, pagodas and monasteries were built on the Bagan plain, of which over 2,300 survive. It lies in an earthquake zone, and quakes in 1975 and 2016 damaged hundreds of temples; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

alternatives.label: Chronicle origins
alternatives.text: Burmese chronicles trace the city back to around 107 CE and say the dynasty was founded in 167 CE by Pyusawhti, who in versions before the 19th century was the descendant of a solar spirit and a dragon (naga) princess. The royal Glass Palace Chronicle of 1832 instead traced his line to Maha Sammata, the first king of the world in Buddhist mythology.

alternatives.label: Scholarly reconstruction
alternatives.text: Modern historians hold that the Pagan dynasty was founded by the Mranma (Burmans) of the Nanzhao kingdom in the mid-to-late 9th century, and that the early chronicle kings are adopted Pyu legends; a historical Pyusawhti may have lived in the mid-to-late 8th century, perhaps coming from Nanzhao during its raids on the Irrawaddy valley.

alternatives.label: Fall to the Mongols?
alternatives.text: The kingdom collapsed after Mongol invasions from 1277, but recent research suggests Mongol armies may never have reached Bagan itself; Michael Aung-Thwin argues that provincial governors who successfully resisted the Mongols became the new power elite, leaving Bagan a backwater.

entries.title: Aguada Fénix: the biggest and oldest Maya monument, found by lidar
entries.mainstream: Aguada Fénix in Tabasco, Mexico, was announced in June 2020 by a team led by Takeshi Inomata after lidar laser mapping from the air revealed it in an area that had been surveyed on the ground before. Its main platform of earth and clay is about 1,400 metres long, built from around 1000 to 800 BCE and abandoned around 750 BCE. It is the oldest and largest known Maya ceremonial structure, and its construction is estimated to have required 10-13 million person-days of labour. Its cruciform layout resembles Olmec centres such as San Lorenzo and La Venta and the Maya site of Seibal, but its pottery and obsidian (from Maya sources in Guatemala) link it more closely to the Maya lowlands.

alternatives.label: Builders without kings
alternatives.text: The excavators note that, unlike Olmec centres, no sculptures of high-status rulers have been found, and suggest the platform was raised by communal labour in a society with less pronounced inequality, challenging the idea that monumental building requires powerful rulers.

alternatives.label: Olmec or Maya?
alternatives.text: The site sits in the region the project was designed to study, where Maya lowland and Olmec cultures met; the excavators note that the pottery does not necessarily show the builders spoke a Mayan language, only that they had closer cultural ties to the Maya lowlands than to the Olmec area.

sources.title: Monumental architecture at Aguada Fénix and the rise of Maya civilization

entries.title: San Bartolo: the Maya creation murals and an early Maya script
entries.mainstream: San Bartolo is a small Maya site in Petén, northern Guatemala, famous for Late Preclassic mural paintings, still strongly influenced by Olmec tradition, and for some of the earliest examples of Maya writing. The murals, found in 2001 by William Saturno inside a pyramid known as Las Pinturas, have been carbon-dated to about 100 BCE. They depict scenes of Maya creation mythology, the life of the maize god, and the crowning of a king.

alternatives.label: Myths older than the books
alternatives.text: William Saturno, David Stuart and Karl Taube have argued that the north and west walls show creation mythology reminiscent of the Popol Vuh, the K'iche' Maya book written down in the colonial era, as well as of Yucatec traditions.

alternatives.label: Early kingship
alternatives.text: The coronation scene, showing the divine right to rule coming from the gods, is taken as evidence that the Maya had full-fledged monarchies centuries earlier than previously thought.

alternatives.label: Death of the maize god?
alternatives.text: One scene shows the maize god flying in the sky or perhaps falling into the water; it has been suggested to represent the death of the deity, but readings of individual scenes vary.

entries.title: The Uluburun shipwreck: a Bronze Age world in one cargo
entries.mainstream: Uluburun is a Late Bronze Age shipwreck off Kaş in southern Turkey, found in 1982 by the sponge diver Mehmed Çakır and excavated from 1984 to 1994 by the Institute of Nautical Archaeology under George Bass and Cemal Pulak. The ship, estimated at about 15 metres long with planks of Lebanese cedar, sank in the late 14th century BCE with a cargo of over 20 tonnes: 354 copper ingots (about 10 tonnes) and about a tonne of tin for making bronze, plus jars of terebinth resin, glass ingots, ebony, ivory, gold and silver jewellery, and a gold scarab bearing the name of Queen Nefertiti. A 2022 study traced about 30 percent of the tin to Central Asia (Mušiston in Tajikistan, or Uzbekistan) and about 65 percent to Kestel in Anatolia.

alternatives.label: Royal gift or trade?
alternatives.text: The cargo is generally thought to have been intended for a wealthy and powerful recipient, perhaps a Mycenaean king, on a ship sailing west from the Levant or Cyprus; it is impossible to tell whether it was a diplomatic gift like those in the Amarna letters, goods bought by Levantine (Canaanite) merchants for a sponsor, or both.

alternatives.label: Bronze Age globalisation
alternatives.text: With goods from at least seven areas (Eric Cline calls it a 'microcosm' of international trade), the wreck is cited as evidence of an 'age of internationalism' or ancient 'world-system' that later broke down in the Late Bronze Age collapse.

alternatives.label: Dating debate
alternatives.text: Tree rings in a branch on board ended in 1305 BCE, but with no bark the felling date is uncertain, and the scarab only shows the ship sank after Nefertiti's time; the exact date of the wreck is still discussed.

entries.title: The Tollense valley: Europe's oldest great battlefield
entries.mainstream: In 1996 a volunteer found an arm bone with a flint arrowhead embedded in it on the bank of the small Tollense river in north-eastern Germany. Excavations since 2007 have uncovered the remains of about 140 people (by 2017), over 40 skulls, many with battle wounds, horse bones, bronze and flint arrowheads, wooden clubs and other weapons, all radiocarbon-dated to around 1300-1200 BCE. Estimates suggest perhaps 4,000 warriors from Central and Northern Europe took part. A bundle of 31 bronze items, and the forms of many arrowheads, suggest that some fighters came from southern Central Europe, hundreds of kilometres away.

alternatives.label: Organised war
alternatives.text: The finds forced archaeologists to rethink Bronze Age Europe, previously imagined as largely peaceful, with weapons as status symbols; a quarter of the skeletons show healed earlier injuries, suggesting experienced fighters, some mounted, and one theory is that a better-armed group was trying to cross the valley on a centuries-old causeway.

alternatives.label: Part of a wider crisis
alternatives.text: Kristian Kristiansen and others link the battle to an era of upheaval stretching from the Mediterranean to the Baltic, the same period as the Late Bronze Age collapse in the eastern Mediterranean.

alternatives.label: How big was it?
alternatives.text: The size of the battle is an extrapolation: by 2017 only 460 square metres had been excavated of a battlefield thought to be at least ten times larger, and estimates of the dead range from about 750 to more than 1,000.

media.title: Europe's Earliest Battle? - The Mystery of the Tollense Valley // Ancient History Documentary

entries.title: Pedra Furada: humans in Brazil 30,000+ years ago, or monkeys and rockfalls?
entries.mainstream: Pedra Furada is a rock shelter in the Serra da Capivara of Piauí, north-eastern Brazil, part of a region with over 800 archaeological sites and hundreds of rock paintings, the oldest about 12,000 years old. Excavations from 1973 by a Brazilian-French team led by Niède Guidon found charcoal from hearths and broken quartz and quartzite stones dated to between about 48,000 and 32,000 years ago; Guidon first reported the dates in Nature in 1986. The region became a World Heritage Site in 1991.

alternatives.label: Very early Americans
alternatives.text: Guidon and her supporters argue that the hearths and tools show humans in South America tens of thousands of years before the Clovis culture; in 2014 Guidon suggested people might have arrived by boat from Africa, perhaps 100,000 years ago.

alternatives.label: Natural causes
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists, such as James Adovasio, argue the 'tools' are geofacts, stones broken by falling from the cliff, and the charcoal from natural fires; geneticists note there is no genetic trace of such an early population in living Native Americans.

alternatives.label: Monkey tools
alternatives.text: In 2016 researchers reported that wild bearded capuchin monkeys in Serra da Capivara break stones and unintentionally produce sharp flakes that look like human-made tools, which complicates the identification of the oldest stone artefacts in the region.

alternatives.label: Shifting consensus
alternatives.text: The 'Clovis first' model has been largely abandoned since Monte Verde in Chile, generally dated to about 14,500 years ago, was widely (though not universally) accepted; Pedra Furada's far older dates have not won the same acceptance.

sources.title: Carbon-14 dates point to man in the Americas 32,000 years ago

entries.title: The Ingá Stone: Brazil's undeciphered rock of signs
entries.dateNote: Age unknown; date shown is a placeholder for pre-colonial carving
entries.mainstream: The Ingá Stone (Pedra do Ingá or Itacoatiara do Ingá; ita means 'stone' in Tupi) is a gneiss rock formation in the Ingá River in Paraíba state, north-eastern Brazil. A vertical wall about 46 metres long and 3.8 metres high, and surrounding areas, are covered with deeply carved low-relief symbols, including what may be animals, fruits, humans and astronomical features. The meaning of the signs is unknown, and the site is threatened by scavengers and vandals.

alternatives.label: Indigenous art
alternatives.text: Scholars attribute the carvings to Indigenous peoples who lived in the area until the 18th century.

alternatives.label: Sky calendar
alternatives.text: From 1976 the Spanish engineer Francisco Pavía Alemany studied the site mathematically and argued that cup-marks and signs formed a solar calendar and representations of constellations such as Orion and the Milky Way.

entries.title: Hunga Tonga 2022: the biggest atmospheric explosion ever recorded
entries.mainstream: On 15 January 2022 the submarine volcano Hunga Tonga-Hunga Haʻapai, 65 km north of Tongatapu, erupted in a climax that produced the largest atmospheric explosion recorded by modern instruments. Its plume reached about 57-58 km, into the mesosphere; the pressure wave circled the Earth several times and was recorded by weather stations worldwide; tens of thousands of lightning flashes were detected; and tsunamis reached Japan, the Americas and beyond. In Tonga waves of up to 15 m struck, and at least four people died there, plus two in Peru. The eruption also blasted an estimated 146 million tonnes of water into the stratosphere, about 10 percent of its normal water vapour.

alternatives.label: Warming not cooling
alternatives.text: Big eruptions usually cool the climate with sulphate aerosols, but this one's huge injection of water vapour, a greenhouse gas, is thought by many researchers to have had a net warming effect.

alternatives.label: Tsunamis from the sky
alternatives.text: The atmospheric pressure wave coupled with the ocean to create tsunamis far from the volcano that arrived earlier than forecast; in Japan, the meteorological agency said the tsunami struck 2.5 hours earlier than predicted.

alternatives.label: How big?
alternatives.text: Its ranking on the Volcanic Explosivity Index is still debated; in recent centuries only Krakatoa in 1883 is thought to have produced a comparable disturbance of the atmosphere.

entries.title: 3I/ATLAS: the third interstellar visitor, a comet or alien technology?
entries.mainstream: 3I/ATLAS (C/2025 N1) was discovered on 1 July 2025 by the NASA-funded ATLAS survey telescope in Chile. Its hyperbolic orbit shows it came from outside the Solar System, making it the third known interstellar object after ʻOumuamua (2017) and 2I/Borisov (2019). It passed no closer than about 1.8 AU from Earth and reached perihelion at about 1.36 AU at the end of October 2025. Hubble, Webb, SPHEREx and spacecraft at Mars and elsewhere observed it as an active comet with a coma, unusually rich in carbon dioxide, with water, carbon monoxide, methane, cyanide and nickel vapour detected; images from Hubble and spacecraft suggest its nucleus is less than 1 km across. It came from the Milky Way's thin or thick disk; if from the thick disk, it could be at least 7 billion years old, older than the Solar System.

alternatives.label: Comet
alternatives.text: The overwhelming consensus among astronomers is that 3I/ATLAS is a natural comet; its chemistry, though unusual in some respects, resembles that of Solar System comets, and it offers a rare sample of material formed around another star.

alternatives.label: Alien technology?
alternatives.text: On 16 July 2025 Avi Loeb of Harvard and two colleagues from the Initiative for Interstellar Studies posted an arXiv paper, described by them as largely a pedagogical exercise, hypothesising that it could be technological and even hostile, citing its orbit close to the ecliptic and near approaches to Venus, Mars and Jupiter. They also wrote that the most likely outcome was that it is a natural comet.

alternatives.label: Criticism
alternatives.text: Astronomers including Chris Lintott, Samantha Lawler, Scott Manley and David Kipping criticised the paper's reasoning and statistics, and Snopes and others noted that viral claims of an alien ship heading for Earth misrepresented it. In 2017 Loeb had similarly raised the possibility that ʻOumuamua was artificial.

entries.title: Where did the Etruscans come from?
entries.mainstream: The Etruscans dominated central Italy from roughly the 9th century BCE until they were absorbed by Rome, speaking a non-Indo-European language that is readable (it uses a Greek-derived alphabet) but still only partly understood. Ancient writers disagreed about their origin: Herodotus said they came from Lydia in Anatolia, while Dionysius of Halicarnassus said they were native to Italy. Most archaeologists trace Etruscan culture to the local Villanovan culture, and a 2021 ancient-DNA study (Posth et al., Science Advances) found that Etruscans were genetically similar to their Latin neighbours, with steppe-related ancestry and no sign of a recent Anatolian migration.

alternatives.label: Lydian migration
alternatives.text: The Herodotus account of a migration from Lydia was long popular and some earlier modern DNA studies of cattle and present-day Tuscans were read as supporting an eastern link; the 2021 ancient-DNA results weigh against this.

alternatives.label: Language puzzle
alternatives.text: Because Etruscan is related only to the scarcely attested Raetic and Lemnian languages, some researchers propose an Aegean or Alpine connection for the language even if the population was largely local.

entries.changed: Debated since antiquity; archaeology from the 20th century favoured local origins, and ancient DNA in 2021 found no recent Anatolian ancestry.

sources.title: The origin and legacy of the Etruscans through a 2000-year archeogenomic time transect

entries.title: Liber Linteus: an Etruscan book wrapped around an Egyptian mummy
entries.mainstream: The Liber Linteus Zagrabiensis is the longest surviving Etruscan text and the only known surviving linen book from antiquity. It was cut into strips and used to wrap a female mummy in Ptolemaic Egypt; a Croatian official bought the mummy in Alexandria in 1848 and it is now in the Archaeological Museum in Zagreb. Only in 1891-92 was the writing identified as Etruscan. Its roughly 1,200 legible words appear to form a ritual calendar listing ceremonies and offerings to gods, dated to around the 3rd century BCE.

alternatives.label: Why in Egypt
alternatives.text: How an Etruscan religious book ended up as mummy wrappings is unknown; suggestions include an Etruscan community in Egypt or linen simply being reused, and none is proven.

entries.title: Pyrgi Tablets: an Etruscan-Phoenician bilingual
entries.mainstream: Three gold sheets found in 1964 at Pyrgi, the harbour sanctuary of the Etruscan city of Caere, record a dedication by the ruler Thefarie Velianas to the goddess Uni, identified with the Phoenician Astarte, around 500 BCE. Two are in Etruscan and one in Phoenician, making them a partial bilingual text that has helped scholars understand Etruscan vocabulary, though the two versions are not word-for-word translations. They also show close Etruscan-Carthaginian ties at the time.

alternatives.label: Interpretation
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether the dedication implies Phoenician/Carthaginian political influence over Caere or simply religious and trade links.

entries.title: Phaistos Disc
entries.mainstream: A fired clay disc about 16 cm across, found in 1908 by Luigi Pernier in the Minoan palace of Phaistos on Crete, is stamped on both sides with 241 impressions of 45 different signs arranged in a spiral, made with individual punches, an early form of movable-type printing. It is usually dated to the Middle or Late Minoan Bronze Age (roughly 1850-1600 BCE). The script matches no other known find, and with so short a text it has not been deciphered; most specialists think it cannot be without further examples.

alternatives.label: Proposed decipherments
alternatives.text: Many readings have been published, as Greek, Luwian, Minoan prayers, a calendar or a game board; none has gained scholarly acceptance.

alternatives.label: Forgery suggestion
alternatives.text: A minority view (e.g. Jerome Eisenberg, 2008) argues the disc is a modern forgery; this is not widely accepted and the museum has not permitted thermoluminescence testing.

entries.title: Linear A: the undeciphered Minoan script
entries.mainstream: Linear A was used by the Minoans of Crete from about 1800 to 1450 BCE, mostly on clay tablets recording goods. Its successor Linear B was deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952 as an early form of Greek, so many Linear A signs can be given approximate sound values, but the resulting words do not match Greek or any known language and the script remains undeciphered.

alternatives.label: Language family
alternatives.text: Proposals link the underlying Minoan language to Luwian/Anatolian, Semitic, Indo-Iranian or Tyrsenian (Etruscan-related) languages; none is generally accepted.

entries.title: Tutankhamun's tomb and the 'curse'
entries.mainstream: Howard Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, found the almost intact tomb KV62 of the boy king Tutankhamun (died c. 1323 BCE) in the Valley of the Kings in November 1922. It held over 5,000 objects, including the gold mask. Carnarvon's death in April 1923 from an infected mosquito bite fuelled press stories of a 'curse'; studies of the people present at the opening found no unusual death rates. CT scans and DNA work (2010) examined his health and family, suggesting he was a son of Akhenaten.

alternatives.label: Hidden chambers
alternatives.text: In 2015 Nicholas Reeves proposed hidden chambers behind the tomb walls, possibly the tomb of Nefertiti; radar surveys gave conflicting results and the idea remains unconfirmed.

alternatives.label: Curse
alternatives.text: The curse story is treated by historians as a media creation; some writers have suggested mould or bacteria in sealed tombs could cause illness, which is speculative for this case.

entries.changed: Found 1922; curse stories 1923; DNA and CT study 2010; hidden-chamber debate since 2015.

sources.title: Ancestry and Pathology in King Tutankhamun's Family

entries.title: The Sea Peoples
entries.mainstream: Egyptian records, above all the reliefs of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu (c. 1175 BCE), describe a confederation of seafaring invaders, including the Peleset, Sherden, Shekelesh and Denyen, who attacked Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean at the end of the Bronze Age. The modern term 'Sea Peoples' dates from the 19th century. The Peleset are widely identified with the Philistines, whose settlement in southern Canaan is supported by ancient DNA showing a European-related component (Feldman et al., 2019). Their role in the wider Bronze Age collapse is debated.

alternatives.label: Cause or symptom
alternatives.text: Some historians see the Sea Peoples as the main cause of the collapse; others see them as displaced people fleeing drought, famine, earthquakes and systems failure.

alternatives.label: Origins
alternatives.text: Homelands proposed include the Aegean, western Anatolia, Sardinia (Sherden) and Sicily (Shekelesh), based on name similarities that are not proven.

entries.title: Caligula's Nemi ships
entries.mainstream: Two huge ships, about 70 and 73 metres long, were built on the small volcanic Lake Nemi near Rome for the emperor Caligula (reigned 37-41 CE), apparently as floating palaces and temples. Legends of the sunken ships persisted for centuries and divers recovered pieces from the 15th century onwards. Mussolini's government drained the lake in 1928-32 to recover them, revealing advanced features such as bilge pumps and rotating platforms on bearings. They were displayed in a purpose-built museum but burned in 1944 during the Second World War; who set the fire is disputed.

alternatives.label: The 1944 fire
alternatives.text: An Italian commission blamed retreating German troops; others have suggested American shelling or local looters. It has never been settled.

entries.title: Talos, the bronze giant of Crete
entries.mainstream: In Greek myth Talos was a giant bronze man made by Hephaestus (or given to Minos by Zeus) who circled Crete three times a day, throwing rocks at ships. He had a single vein closed by a bronze nail; in Apollonius of Rhodes' Argonautica (3rd century BCE) Medea brings about his death and the ichor drains out. He is often cited as one of the earliest imagined robots or automata, and appears on a 5th-century BCE vase, the Talos Vase.

alternatives.label: Ancient technology readings
alternatives.text: Classicist Adrienne Mayor (Gods and Robots, 2018) explores Talos as evidence that ancient Greeks imagined artificial life and automata; claims that the myth preserves memories of real ancient robots are speculative and not supported.

media.title: The Greek myth of Talos, the first robot - Adrienne Mayor

entries.title: Herculaneum papyri and the Vesuvius Challenge
entries.mainstream: About 1,800 carbonised papyrus scrolls were found from 1752 in the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum, buried by Vesuvius in 79 CE; it is the only intact library known from the classical world. Many were damaged by early attempts to unroll them. Most of those read so far are Epicurean works, many by Philodemus. From 2015, X-ray tomography and later machine learning allowed unopened scrolls to be read virtually; in 2023-24 the Vesuvius Challenge prize was won by students who recovered passages from a sealed scroll, apparently by Philodemus on pleasure. In 2025 researchers reported reading the title of another scroll.

alternatives.label: Unexcavated library
alternatives.text: Parts of the villa remain unexcavated and some scholars hope more scrolls, perhaps including lost Latin or Greek works, are still buried; this is unproven.

entries.changed: Found 1752; destructive unrolling 18th-19th c.; virtual unrolling from 2015; Vesuvius Challenge readings 2023-25.

entries.title: Sungir: Ice Age burials with thousands of beads
entries.mainstream: Sungir, near Vladimir in Russia, is an Upper Palaeolithic site excavated from 1957 by Otto Bader. Its burials, dated to about 34,000-31,000 years ago, include an adult man and two children buried head to head, wearing clothing sewn with more than 13,000 mammoth-ivory beads in total, along with ivory spears, carved animals and fox-tooth belts. Making the beads would have taken thousands of hours. Ancient DNA (Sikora et al., 2017) showed the individuals were not close relatives, suggesting these hunter-gatherers avoided inbreeding through wider social networks.

alternatives.label: Social rank
alternatives.text: The rich child burials have been read as evidence of inherited status in Ice Age society; others suggest the children were special for other reasons, such as ritual roles, since one had a skeletal condition.

sources.title: Ancient genomes show social and reproductive behavior of early Upper Paleolithic foragers

entries.title: Rurik and the calling of the Varangians
entries.mainstream: The Russian Primary Chronicle, compiled in Kyiv around 1113, says that in 862 feuding Slavic and Finnic tribes invited a Varangian (Scandinavian) named Rurik and his brothers to rule them, founding the dynasty that ruled Rus' and later Muscovy until 1598. Archaeology at Staraya Ladoga, Gnezdovo and Novgorod confirms a strong Scandinavian presence in the 9th-10th centuries. Whether Rurik himself existed as described is uncertain, since the chronicle was written 250 years later.

alternatives.label: Normanist vs anti-Normanist
alternatives.text: From the 18th century a long, often politicised debate set the Normanist view (Scandinavian founders of the Rus' state) against anti-Normanists who stressed Slavic origins; most historians now accept a substantial Scandinavian role alongside Slavic, Finnic and Baltic peoples.

alternatives.label: Identity of Rurik
alternatives.text: Some historians have tentatively identified Rurik with Rorik of Dorestad, a Danish Viking known from Frankish sources; this is not proven.

entries.title: Tsar Bomba, the largest explosion ever made
entries.mainstream: On 30 October 1961 the Soviet Union detonated the AN602 hydrogen bomb, later nicknamed Tsar Bomba, over Novaya Zemlya in the Arctic. Its yield was about 50 megatons, roughly 1,500 times the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombs combined; it was designed for 100 megatons but scaled down to reduce fallout. The mushroom cloud rose about 60 km and windows broke hundreds of kilometres away. It was a demonstration and was never meant as a practical weapon.

alternatives.label: Propaganda value
alternatives.text: Historians generally see the test as a political display during the Berlin crisis rather than a military step; the full yield figures were confirmed after the Soviet era.

entries.title: Petrozavodsk phenomenon
entries.mainstream: Early on 20 September 1977 residents of Petrozavodsk in Soviet Karelia and observers across northern Europe saw a glowing 'jellyfish' shaped object with rays of light. Soviet press reports led to an official study (programme 'Setka'). Researchers, including Yuli Platov and others in the Soviet Academy of Sciences, attributed it to the launch of the secret Kosmos-955 satellite from the Plesetsk cosmodrome, whose rocket exhaust lit by the sun at high altitude produced the effect.

alternatives.label: Rocket explanation
alternatives.text: The rocket launch explanation is accepted by most researchers and matches the timing; similar lights were later seen after other Plesetsk launches.

alternatives.label: Unexplained
alternatives.text: Some UFO researchers argue that not all reports, such as claims of holes in windows, are explained by a launch; these claims are not verified.

entries.title: Lake Vostok: a lake sealed under Antarctic ice
entries.mainstream: Lake Vostok lies about 4 km beneath the ice near Russia's Vostok Station in Antarctica and is the largest known subglacial lake, about 250 km long. It was suggested by Russian geographer Andrey Kapitsa from seismic soundings in the 1950s-60s and confirmed by radar and satellite data in 1996. It may have been isolated for millions of years. Russian drilling reached the lake water in 2012. Analyses of refrozen water have reported possible DNA traces of microbes, but contamination from drilling fluid makes these results disputed.

alternatives.label: Life in the lake
alternatives.text: Some studies (e.g. 2013) reported thousands of gene sequences suggesting a diverse ecosystem; critics argue these mostly reflect contamination. It is also studied as an analogue for ice-covered moons such as Europa.

entries.title: Qalupalik, the Inuit sea creature
entries.dateNote: Traditional; date is a placeholder for Inuit oral tradition
entries.mainstream: In Inuit oral tradition the qalupalik is a human-like creature with green skin and long hair that lives in the sea and snatches children who wander too close to the water's edge or the ice, carrying them off in a pouch or amauti on its back. Its humming may be heard before it appears. Folklorists note that such stories also served to keep children away from dangerous sea ice. The tradition is old; the date shown is a placeholder.

alternatives.label: Function
alternatives.text: Scholars generally interpret the qalupalik as a cautionary tale, while for many Inuit it is also part of a living spiritual world of sea beings.

entries.title: Kushtaka, the land-otter people
entries.mainstream: In the traditions of the Tlingit and Tsimshian peoples of south-east Alaska and British Columbia, the kushtaka ('land otter man') is a shapeshifting being that can take human form, lure people (especially those lost or drowning at sea) by imitating the cries of babies or relatives, and turn them into kushtaka. Shamans were said to be able to rescue victims.

alternatives.label: Interpretations
alternatives.text: Anthropologists link the stories to the real dangers of drowning and exposure; some cryptid writers have connected them to Bigfoot-like creatures, which is speculative.

entries.title: Kostenki: early modern humans on the Don
entries.mainstream: The Kostenki-Borshchevo sites on the Don River in Russia contain over 20 Upper Palaeolithic sites, some layers dated to around 45,000-42,000 years ago, among the earliest evidence of modern humans on the East European plain. Later layers include mammoth-bone dwellings. The genome of 'Kostenki 14', a man who lived about 37,000 years ago, published in 2014, showed that the main ancestral lineages of later Europeans had already split by then.

alternatives.label: Early arrival
alternatives.text: The earliest dates, below a volcanic ash layer from the Campanian Ignimbrite eruption (about 40,000 years ago), are taken by many as evidence of a fast spread of modern humans; some researchers question the cultural attribution of the oldest layers.

sources.title: Genomic structure in Europeans dating back at least 36,200 years

entries.title: Raven steals the light
entries.mainstream: Across the North Pacific coast, among the Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian and others, the trickster and creator Raven is central to oral tradition. In a widespread story the world is dark because a chief keeps the sun, moon and stars in boxes; Raven becomes a hemlock needle, is swallowed by the chief's daughter, is reborn as her son, and as a spoiled child persuades his grandfather to let him play with the boxes, releasing the light. Related Raven stories are told in Siberia among the Chukchi and Koryak.

alternatives.label: Transpacific links
alternatives.text: Shared Raven stories in Siberia and North-West America have been read by some folklorists as evidence of very old connections across the Bering region; others see parallel development.
