entries.title: Ozette: a village buried by a mudslide
entries.dateNote: Radiocarbon c. 1560; some sources say c. 1750
entries.mainstream: Ozette, a Makah village on the Olympic Peninsula coast of Washington State, was partly engulfed by a mudslide, dated by radiocarbon to around 1560 (other accounts give around 1750). Waterlogged clay preserved collapsed houses and their contents, giving an unusually complete picture of a whaling and fishing community before abandonment or looting: tens of thousands of objects such as baskets, harpoons, weaving gear and a carved cedar whale fin inlaid with sea-otter teeth. After storm erosion exposed the site, it was excavated from 1970 to 1981 by the Makah together with Washington State University archaeologists. Finds are kept at the Makah Museum in Neah Bay.

alternatives.label: Dating
alternatives.text: The exact date of the slide differs between sources, and more than one slide may have affected the village over time.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ozette Indian Village Archeological Site

entries.title: Sannai-Maruyama: a large Jomon village
entries.mainstream: Sannai-Maruyama in Aomori, northern Japan, was a settlement of Jomon hunter-gatherers occupied from about 3900 to 2200 BCE. Excavations from 1992, when the site was due to become a baseball stadium, revealed hundreds of pit dwellings, large buildings, storehouses, burial areas, thousands of clay figurines (dogu) and the post holes of a structure built on six huge chestnut posts. Evidence suggests chestnut trees were managed. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage 'Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan' (2021).

alternatives.label: Complexity
alternatives.text: The size and long occupation challenge the old idea that complex settled communities require farming; how many people lived there at once is debated.

alternatives.label: Six-pillar structure
alternatives.text: Its purpose is unknown; proposals include a watchtower, a shrine or a platform aligned with the solstices, and the reconstruction on site is a hypothesis.

sources.title: Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan (UNESCO)

entries.title: The kamikaze: divine winds against the Mongol fleets
entries.mainstream: Kublai Khan's Mongol-led Yuan dynasty attempted to invade Japan in 1274 and 1281. Both times storms struck the fleet: the 1281 fleet, reportedly with over 4,000 ships, was destroyed by a typhoon off Takashima. The Japanese came to call these 'kamikaze' (divine winds), sent in answer to prayers at shrines such as Ise. Underwater archaeology at Takashima from the 1980s has found wrecks, anchors, weapons and early explosive bombs (tetsuhau); study suggested many ships were hastily built river boats unsuited to the open sea.

alternatives.label: Role of the storms
alternatives.text: Some historians stress the samurai defence and the coastal wall at Hakata as much as the storms; the 1274 storm is less certain in sources than that of 1281.

alternatives.label: Legacy
alternatives.text: The idea of divine protection was later used in nationalist ideology and gave its name to the suicide pilots of 1944-45.

entries.title: Kappa, the water imp
entries.mainstream: The kappa is a water spirit (yokai) of Japanese folklore, child-sized with a beak, a shell and a dish-like hollow on its head holding water that gives it strength. It was said to drown people and horses and pull out the shirikodama, a mythical ball in the anus, but also to be polite and to keep promises. Mummified 'kappa' relics kept in temples have been found to be composites or animal remains. Some scholars link kappa stories to drowning deaths and to the bodies of children in rivers.

alternatives.label: Origins
alternatives.text: Folklorists see the kappa as an Edo-period merging of earlier river deities and Chinese water creatures; some writers have speculated about aliens or unknown animals, which is unsupported.

entries.title: Bonampak murals
entries.mainstream: In 1946 Giles Healey and the Lacandon Maya brought to outside attention three painted rooms in a small temple at Bonampak, Chiapas, Mexico, painted around 790 CE. The murals show a royal court, a battle, captives being tortured and celebrations, overturning the 1940s view that the Classic Maya were a peaceful society of priest-astronomers.

alternatives.label: Interpretation
alternatives.text: The murals were long read as straightforward history; recent scholars note they also served royal propaganda shortly before the site was abandoned.

entries.changed: Before 1946 many scholars considered the Maya peaceful; Bonampak and the decipherment of Maya glyphs showed frequent warfare.

entries.title: The Mesoamerican ballgame
entries.mainstream: A ritual team game played with a heavy solid rubber ball was played across Mesoamerica for over 3,000 years. The oldest known court, at Paso de la Amada in Chiapas, dates to about 1650 BCE, and rubber balls from El Manati date to around 1600 BCE. In some contexts the game was linked to cosmology and human sacrifice; in the K'iche' Maya Popol Vuh the Hero Twins play ball against the lords of the underworld, Xibalba. A version called ulama is still played in Sinaloa.

alternatives.label: Who was sacrificed
alternatives.text: Popular accounts say the winners were sacrificed; most scholars think captives or losers were, and that practice varied greatly over time and place.

media.title: How This Mayan Legend Inspired a Deadly Ballgame

entries.title: The Huey Tzompantli: the Aztec skull rack
entries.mainstream: Spanish conquistadors described a great rack of skulls (tzompantli) in front of the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan. From 2015, archaeologists of Mexico's INAH excavated part of the Huey Tzompantli in Mexico City, finding a rack and towers of skulls set in mortar, with hundreds of skulls of men, women and children. The finds confirm the scale of Aztec sacrifice described in Spanish and Indigenous sources, though they also show that victims were not only adult male warriors.

alternatives.label: Numbers
alternatives.text: Older accounts claimed 130,000 skulls; archaeologists caution that the full count is unknown and the Spanish had reasons to exaggerate.

media.title: The dark discovery of Mexico's huge tower of human skulls - BBC REEL

entries.title: Codex Zouche-Nuttall and the Mixtec lord Eight Deer
entries.mainstream: The Codex Zouche-Nuttall is one of a few surviving pre-Hispanic Mixtec screenfold books, painted on deerskin and now in the British Museum. It records genealogies and the life of the 11th-century ruler Eight Deer Jaguar Claw (1063-1115), who expanded his power through conquest and alliance and was eventually sacrificed. Many Mixtec codices were destroyed after the Spanish conquest, making this one of the few Indigenous historical books from the Americas.

alternatives.label: History or myth
alternatives.text: Scholars debate how far the codices record real events and how far they blend royal history with sacred and mythic time.

entries.title: Hachiko, the loyal dog
entries.mainstream: Hachiko was an Akita dog who met his owner, Professor Hidesaburo Ueno, at Shibuya Station in Tokyo each day. After Ueno died suddenly in May 1925, Hachiko kept returning to the station for almost ten years until his death in 1935. His story became famous after a 1932 newspaper article and a statue was put up in 1934. Scientists studied his remains in 2011 and found terminal cancer and a filarial worm infection.

alternatives.label: Why he waited
alternatives.text: Some writers suggest that vendors at the station feeding him was one reason he kept coming; this does not alter the documented story of his long vigil.

entries.title: Taira no Masakado's head and the Tokyo curse
entries.mainstream: Taira no Masakado was a 10th-century warrior who rebelled against the court in Kyoto and declared himself 'new emperor'. He was killed in 940 and his head was displayed in Kyoto. Legend says the head flew back east to his home region and fell at Shibasaki village, now in central Tokyo, where the Masakado Kubizuka (head mound) still stands among office towers in Otemachi. Popular stories blame misfortunes on his vengeful spirit whenever the mound has been disturbed or threatened by redevelopment, and the site is still carefully maintained and visited.

alternatives.label: Historical Masakado
alternatives.text: His revolt is recorded in the Shomonki chronicle; he later became a folk hero and was enshrined at Kanda Myojin.

alternatives.label: The curse
alternatives.text: The curse stories are folklore; no evidence links disturbance of the mound to the misfortunes, though many people treat the site with respect.

entries.title: Tsuchinoko, the fat snake of Japan
entries.dateNote: Edo-period sources; modern sighting boom in the 1970s
entries.mainstream: The tsuchinoko is a cryptid of Japanese folklore described as a thick-bodied snake, sometimes able to jump or roll like a hoop, appearing in Edo-period sources. Sightings boomed in the 1970s and several municipalities and companies have offered rewards for a captured specimen. None has ever been confirmed. Sceptics suggest sightings may be of known snakes that have just eaten a large meal, or of other misidentified reptiles.

alternatives.label: Undiscovered snake
alternatives.text: Some enthusiasts argue an unknown species of viper may exist in rural Japan; no specimen supports this.

entries.title: Lubbock Lights
entries.mainstream: In August-September 1951 several professors at Texas Technological College in Lubbock, and many other residents, reported arcs of faint lights flying silently overhead in formation. Student Carl Hart Jr. took photographs of a V-shaped group of lights. The US Air Force's Project Blue Book investigated; its head Edward Ruppelt wrote that the professors' sightings were probably birds (plovers) reflecting street lights, while the photographs were never fully explained.

alternatives.label: Birds
alternatives.text: The bird explanation is widely accepted by sceptics; some witnesses rejected it.

alternatives.label: Unexplained
alternatives.text: UFO researchers regard the case as one of the classic unexplained sightings, particularly the Hart photographs.

entries.title: 1952 Washington, D.C. UFO incident
entries.mainstream: On the weekends of 19-20 and 26-27 July 1952 air traffic controllers at Washington National Airport and Andrews Air Force Base tracked unidentified radar targets near the capital, and pilots and ground observers reported lights. Jet interceptors were sent up. Headlines nationwide led to the largest Pentagon press conference since the Second World War, where General John Samford attributed the targets to temperature inversions causing false radar returns. The event contributed to the CIA's 1953 Robertson Panel.

alternatives.label: Weather explanation
alternatives.text: The Air Force and later the Condon Report favoured temperature inversion and misidentified stars.

alternatives.label: Disputed explanation
alternatives.text: Some controllers and later researchers argued the targets did not behave like inversion effects and that visual sightings matched them.

entries.title: The Condon Report
entries.mainstream: From 1966 to 1968 the University of Colorado, funded by the US Air Force, studied UFO reports under physicist Edward Condon. The final report, published in 1969, concluded that nothing had come from UFO studies in the past 21 years that had added to scientific knowledge and that further extensive study was probably not justified. A National Academy of Sciences panel endorsed its methods, and Project Blue Book was closed in December 1969. About 30% of the cases studied were left unexplained.

alternatives.label: Criticism
alternatives.text: Critics, including astronomer J. Allen Hynek and physicist James McDonald, argued that Condon had decided his conclusions in advance and pointed to the 'Low memo' suggesting the project would look objective while finding nothing; defenders argue the case studies speak for themselves.

entries.title: Majestic 12 documents
entries.mainstream: In 1984 TV producer Jaime Shandera received a roll of film showing a supposed 1952 briefing for President-elect Eisenhower about 'Operation Majestic Twelve', a secret group said to have recovered alien craft and bodies at Roswell. The FBI investigated and described the documents as 'completely bogus', and analysts found anachronistic date formats, a copied Truman signature and other problems. They are generally considered forgeries, though some UFO researchers still debate them.

alternatives.label: Defenders
alternatives.text: Researchers such as Stanton Friedman argued the documents could be genuine; the US Air Force and most investigators regard them as fakes.

alternatives.label: Disinformation
alternatives.text: Some have suggested the documents were planted by intelligence officers as disinformation; this is speculative.

entries.title: Clever Hans, the horse who could count
entries.mainstream: In early 1900s Berlin a horse called Hans, owned by Wilhelm von Osten, appeared to do arithmetic, tell time and spell by tapping his hoof. A 1904 commission found no trickery, but in 1907 psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed that Hans was responding to tiny unconscious cues in the posture and face of the questioner, and could not answer when the questioner did not know the answer. The 'Clever Hans effect' became a key reason for blind testing in psychology and animal cognition research.

alternatives.label: Animal intelligence
alternatives.text: The case is sometimes used to dismiss animal intelligence; researchers note that Hans was remarkably skilled at reading human cues, which is a form of intelligence in itself.

entries.title: The Sokal affair
entries.mainstream: In 1996 physicist Alan Sokal had a deliberately nonsensical article, arguing that quantum gravity is a social construct, published in the cultural studies journal Social Text, then revealed it as a hoax to show weak scrutiny of postmodernist work. The episode fed wider 'science wars' debates. A 2017-18 'grievance studies' affair by Peter Boghossian, James Lindsay and Helen Pluckrose repeated the approach with several journals.

alternatives.label: Interpretation
alternatives.text: Supporters see it as exposing lack of rigour in some humanities scholarship; critics see it as an ethically questionable stunt that proved little about whole fields.

entries.title: Archaeoraptor: the fake feathered dinosaur
entries.mainstream: In November 1999 National Geographic announced 'Archaeoraptor liaoningensis' from China as a missing link between dinosaurs and birds. It turned out to be a composite: a farmer had glued together a bird's body and the tail of a small dromaeosaur dinosaur to make it more valuable. CT scans in 2000-2001 confirmed the forgery. The parts were later identified as the bird Yanornis and the dinosaur Microraptor, which itself turned out to be a genuine feathered dinosaur.

alternatives.label: Lesson
alternatives.text: The episode is often cited in debates on the fossil trade and on peer review before publicity; it did not weaken the evidence for the dinosaur origin of birds, which rests on many genuine fossils.

entries.title: The Tully monster
entries.mainstream: Tullimonstrum gregarium is a soft-bodied animal about 30 cm long from the 307-million-year-old Mazon Creek fossil beds in Illinois, first collected by amateur Francis Tully in 1955. It had a long proboscis ending in a toothed claw and eyes on a bar. Its classification has been a long puzzle: a 2016 study proposed it was a vertebrate related to lampreys, while later studies (2017, 2023) argued it was not a vertebrate. It is the state fossil of Illinois.

alternatives.label: Cryptozoology
alternatives.text: Some cryptozoologists have linked the Tully monster to lake-monster sightings; it is known only from fossils over 300 million years old, and there is no evidence it survived.

media.title: The Bizarre Case of the Tully Monster

entries.title: The UMMO affair
entries.mainstream: From 1966, beginning in Madrid, Spanish and later French UFO enthusiasts and esoteric groups received long typewritten letters claiming to come from aliens from the planet Ummo, said to orbit a star in Virgo, covering physics, biology and philosophy. Photographs of a disc bearing the same symbol, supposedly taken at San José de Valderas near Madrid on 1 June 1967, were circulated. José Luis Jordán Peña, who had himself reported seeing a craft with the symbol in 1966, later claimed responsibility for writing the letters, and most investigators regard the affair as an elaborate hoax; who else was involved is unknown.

alternatives.label: Hoax
alternatives.text: Most researchers accept that the letters were written on Earth, probably by Jordán Peña and possibly others; Jacques Vallée compared the authors to Borges' fictional inventors of a world.

alternatives.label: Believers
alternatives.text: French physicist Jean-Pierre Petit has argued since 1991 that some letters show superior scientific ideas, and small groups of followers remain.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Planetary objects proposed in religion, astrology, ufology and pseudoscience

entries.title: The Betz mystery sphere
entries.mainstream: In 1974 the Betz family found a polished metal sphere about 20 cm across and weighing about 10 kg near Jacksonville, Florida. It appeared to roll by itself and the press speculated about alien or spy technology. In April 1974 the US Navy said it was simply a large stainless-steel ball bearing of the kind used as a check valve in industrial piping; the rolling was attributed to the uneven floors of the old house. Later, an artist reported having lost several such check-valve balls from his van's roof rack near Jacksonville in 1971.

alternatives.label: Unexplained
alternatives.text: The family disputed the Navy verdict at the time and some UFO literature still lists the sphere as an anomaly; investigators regard it as an ordinary industrial ball.

entries.title: Ranginui and Papatuanuku: the separation of sky and earth
entries.dateNote: Oral tradition; first written down in the 19th century
entries.mainstream: In Maori tradition the sky father Ranginui and earth mother Papatuanuku lay locked in an embrace, their children trapped in darkness between them. The forest god Tane pushed them apart, letting light into the world; Rangi's tears are the rain and mist. Versions of a sky-earth separation are found across Polynesia and in many other cultures worldwide, including Egyptian (Geb and Nut) and Chinese (Pangu) stories.

alternatives.label: Comparative mythology
alternatives.text: Some scholars treat the separation of sky and earth as one of the most widespread creation motifs, possibly very ancient; others see independent invention of an intuitive image.

entries.title: The Kumulipo: a Hawaiian creation chant
entries.mainstream: The Kumulipo is a Hawaiian genealogical chant of over 2,000 lines tracing the origin of the world from darkness (po), through the emergence of coral polyps, sea creatures, plants and animals, to gods and the chiefly line of Hawaii. It was composed for the chief Ka-I-imamao around the early 18th century and published by King Kalakaua in 1889; Queen Liliuokalani translated it into English in 1897. Its sequence from simple sea life to humans is often compared to evolution.

alternatives.label: Evolutionary reading
alternatives.text: Some modern readers see the chant as an indigenous anticipation of evolution; most scholars regard it as a genealogical cosmology whose order reflects Hawaiian ideas of kinship between all living things.

entries.title: Taniwha: Maori guardian water beings
entries.mainstream: Taniwha are powerful beings in Maori tradition living in rivers, lakes, caves and the sea. Some are protective guardians of a tribe, others dangerous. They remain culturally significant: in 2002 concerns about a taniwha named Karutahi were raised by Ngati Naho during the construction of a State Highway 1 section near Meremere, and the road was rerouted in consultation.

alternatives.label: Natural hazards
alternatives.text: Some researchers suggest taniwha stories encoded knowledge of dangerous waters, floods and unstable ground.

entries.title: Tupaia and his chart of the Pacific
entries.mainstream: Tupaia, a Raiatean priest and navigator, joined James Cook's Endeavour in 1769 at Tahiti. He produced a chart showing some 74 islands spread across a vast area of the Pacific, combining Polynesian navigational knowledge with European mapping. He guided the ship and acted as interpreter in New Zealand, where Maori addressed him rather than Cook. He died in Batavia in 1770. How to read his chart was long debated; scholars since the 2010s argue it uses a navigator-centred system of directions rather than a European north-up grid.

alternatives.label: Reinterpretation
alternatives.text: Earlier historians dismissed the chart as muddled; recent analyses argue it accurately encodes sailing directions from Tahiti.

entries.changed: Long considered inaccurate; re-read from the 2010s as a coherent Polynesian wayfinding map.

media.title: How did Polynesian wayfinders navigate the Pacific Ocean? - Alan Tamayose and Shantell De Silva

entries.title: Taputapuatea marae: centre of the Polynesian world
entries.mainstream: Taputapuatea on Raiatea in French Polynesia is a ceremonial complex of marae (sacred stone platforms) that was a political and religious centre of eastern Polynesia, associated with the god Oro. Voyagers from across the region reportedly gathered there, and stones from it were taken to found new marae elsewhere. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017.

alternatives.label: Hawaiki
alternatives.text: Raiatea (formerly Havai'i) is often linked with Hawaiki, the legendary Polynesian homeland, though Hawaiki may be a mythic as well as geographic place.

entries.title: The Moriori of the Chatham Islands
entries.mainstream: The Moriori are the Polynesian people of the Chatham Islands (Rekohu), east of New Zealand, who settled there from mainland New Zealand around the 16th century. They adopted Nunuku's law, a code forbidding war and killing. In 1835 Maori groups from Taranaki invaded; many Moriori were killed or enslaved. A myth arose in the 19th and 20th centuries that Moriori were a pre-Maori race in New Zealand displaced by Maori; this is rejected by historians.

alternatives.label: Pre-Maori race myth
alternatives.text: Once taught in New Zealand schools, the idea that Moriori were earlier, Melanesian inhabitants of mainland New Zealand was debunked by linguistic and archaeological work from the 1960s onwards.

entries.changed: Pre-Maori race theory popular c.1900-1960s; now discredited.

entries.title: Hatepe eruption of Lake Taupo
entries.mainstream: The Hatepe eruption of the Taupo volcano in New Zealand around 232 CE (plus or minus about 10 years) was one of the most violent eruptions of the last 5,000 years, with pyroclastic flows covering some 20,000 square km. New Zealand was uninhabited at the time. Claims that it produced red skies recorded in Rome and China have not been substantiated.

alternatives.label: Historical records
alternatives.text: Some writers link sky phenomena in ancient Roman and Chinese texts to the eruption; ice-core and dating studies do not support those links.

entries.title: Kon-Tiki expedition
entries.mainstream: In 1947 Thor Heyerdahl and five companions sailed the balsa raft Kon-Tiki from Peru to the Tuamotu Islands, about 6,900 km, to show South Americans could have reached Polynesia. The voyage succeeded, but his theory that Polynesia was settled from the Americas was rejected: linguistics, archaeology and genetics show Polynesians came from Island Southeast Asia. A 2020 genetic study did find evidence of some contact between Polynesians and Native Americans around 1200 CE.

alternatives.label: Heyerdahl theory
alternatives.text: Heyerdahl argued for American (and even bearded white) settlers of Polynesia; this is not supported, although limited trans-Pacific contact is now accepted.

entries.title: Mutiny on the Bounty and the Pitcairn settlement
entries.mainstream: In 1789 sailors led by Fletcher Christian mutinied against Lieutenant William Bligh on HMS Bounty. Bligh and 18 loyalists crossed some 6,700 km in an open boat to Timor. The mutineers, with Tahitian companions, settled the uninhabited Pitcairn Island in 1790 and burned the ship. They were not found until 1808, when only one mutineer, John Adams, survived. Their descendants still live on Pitcairn and Norfolk Island. Pitcairn had earlier been settled by Polynesians, who left before Europeans arrived.

alternatives.label: Christian's fate
alternatives.text: Rumours persisted that Fletcher Christian escaped back to England; there is no reliable evidence.

entries.title: Moa: the giant birds of New Zealand
entries.mainstream: Moa were nine species of flightless birds in New Zealand, the largest standing up to about 3.6 m with neck extended. They were hunted to extinction within about 100-200 years of Polynesian settlement around 1300 CE, one of the fastest human-caused megafauna extinctions known. Their only predator had been Haast's eagle, which died out with them. Occasional claims of moa surviving into the 20th century are unsupported.

alternatives.label: Surviving moa
alternatives.text: Reports such as a 1993 photo of a supposed moa in the Craigieburn Range are treated as hoaxes or misidentifications.

entries.title: The curse of Timur's tomb
entries.mainstream: On 19-22 June 1941 a Soviet team led by Mikhail Gerasimov opened the tomb of the conqueror Timur (Tamerlane) in the Gur-e-Amir mausoleum, Samarkand. Legend held that disturbing it would unleash war, and an inscription was reported to warn against it. Germany invaded the USSR on 22 June 1941. The remains were reburied with Islamic rites in November 1942, shortly before the Soviet victory at Stalingrad. The examination confirmed that Timur was tall and lame in the right leg, matching historical accounts.

alternatives.label: Curse
alternatives.text: Popular accounts treat the timing as proof of a curse; historians note the invasion had been planned for months (Operation Barbarossa) and the reburial timing is coincidental.

entries.title: Al-Khwarizmi and the birth of algebra
entries.mainstream: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a scholar from Khwarazm (in modern Uzbekistan/Turkmenistan) working at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, wrote around 820 CE a book on calculation by completion and balancing (al-jabr), which gave algebra its name. His work on Hindu-Arabic numerals, translated into Latin, spread the decimal system in Europe, and the word 'algorithm' derives from the Latin form of his name.

alternatives.label: Origins of algebra
alternatives.text: Historians debate how much he drew on earlier Babylonian, Greek (Diophantus) and Indian (Brahmagupta) work; his systematic treatment is generally credited as foundational.

media.title: Science in a Golden Age - Al-Khwarizmi: The Father of Algebra

entries.title: Ai-Khanoum: a Greek city in Afghanistan
entries.mainstream: Ai-Khanoum, on the Oxus (Amu Darya) in northern Afghanistan, was a Greco-Bactrian city founded around 280 BCE in the wake of Alexander's conquests, with a theatre, gymnasium and a copy of the Delphic maxims inscribed by Clearchus. It was abandoned around 145 BCE after nomadic invasion. Excavated by French archaeologists 1964-1978, it was heavily looted during the Afghan wars.

alternatives.label: Alexandria on the Oxus
alternatives.text: Some scholars identify it with Alexandria on the Oxus or Eucratidia known from ancient sources; its ancient name is uncertain.

entries.title: The Buddhas of Bamiyan
entries.mainstream: Two monumental Buddhas, about 55 m and 38 m tall, were carved into a cliff in the Bamiyan valley of Afghanistan in the 6th century CE (radiocarbon dated to about 570 and 618 CE). The Taliban destroyed them with explosives in March 2001. During conservation, researchers found cave paintings using oil binders from the 7th century, among the earliest known oil paintings.

alternatives.label: Reconstruction
alternatives.text: Whether to rebuild the statues (e.g. by anastylosis) or leave the empty niches as a memorial remains debated.

entries.title: Almas: the wild man of Mongolia
entries.mainstream: The almas (or almasty) is a reputed hairy wild human of the Caucasus and Mongolian folklore. Accounts date at least to the Bavarian traveller Johann Schiltberger in the 1420s. The most famous story concerns 'Zana', a 19th-century woman held captive in Abkhazia; a 2015 DNA study of a descendant's remains found she was of West African ancestry, not a relict hominin.

alternatives.label: Relict hominin
alternatives.text: Some cryptozoologists propose almas are surviving Neanderthals or Homo erectus; no physical evidence supports this.

entries.title: Tengri: the sky god of the steppe
entries.mainstream: Tengri was the supreme sky deity of the Xiongnu, Turkic and Mongol peoples; the term appears in Chinese records of the Xiongnu and in the 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions. Genghis Khan's rule was framed as mandated by the Eternal Blue Sky (Mongke Tengri). Tengrism has seen a revival in Central Asia since the 1990s.

alternatives.label: Monotheism debate
alternatives.text: Scholars disagree on whether historical Tengri worship was monotheistic, or part of a broader shamanic and polytheistic system.

entries.title: The Epic of Manas
entries.mainstream: The Epic of Manas is the traditional epic of the Kyrgyz people, telling of the hero Manas and his descendants who unite the Kyrgyz against enemies. Recited by bards (manaschi), some versions exceed 500,000 lines, among the longest epics in the world. It was first recorded in the 19th century and is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

alternatives.label: Historicity
alternatives.text: Some Kyrgyz scholars date its core to the 9th-10th century Kyrgyz Khaganate; others see it as shaped mainly by later conflicts with the Oirats.

entries.title: The shrinking of the Aral Sea
entries.mainstream: Once the world's fourth-largest lake, the Aral Sea between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan began shrinking in the 1960s after Soviet irrigation projects diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to grow cotton. By the 2010s it had largely split into remnant lakes and the exposed Aralkum desert. The receding water exposed medieval ruins on the former seabed, including a 14th-century mausoleum, showing the lake had also shrunk in the past. Kazakhstan's Kok-Aral dam (2005) has partly restored the North Aral.

alternatives.label: Natural cycles
alternatives.text: Archaeological finds on the seabed show earlier natural or human-induced regressions; the modern collapse is attributed primarily to irrigation.

entries.title: Tillya Tepe: the Bactrian gold
entries.mainstream: In 1978 Soviet-Afghan archaeologist Viktor Sarianidi excavated six burials at Tillya Tepe in northern Afghanistan dating to around the 1st century BCE-1st century CE, containing over 20,000 gold ornaments mixing Greek, Scythian, Indian and Chinese styles. The hoard was thought lost during the civil wars, but in 2003 it was revealed that museum staff had hidden it in a Central Bank vault in Kabul.

alternatives.label: Identity
alternatives.text: The buried nomads are variously linked with the Yuezhi/early Kushans or Saka; the attribution is debated.

entries.title: The Afrasiab "Ambassadors' Painting" of Samarkand
entries.mainstream: Wall paintings discovered in 1965 at Afrasiab, the old site of Samarkand, show the Sogdian king Varkhuman receiving envoys from China, Korea, and other lands around 648-660 CE. They are among the most important surviving Sogdian artworks and a rare visual record of diplomacy along the Silk Road.

alternatives.label: Korean envoys
alternatives.text: The identification of two figures with feathered caps as envoys from the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo is widely, though not universally, accepted.

entries.title: Soucouyant: the Caribbean fire-ball vampire
entries.mainstream: In folklore of Trinidad and Tobago, Dominica, Guadeloupe and other Caribbean islands, the soucouyant is an old woman who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire to suck the blood of sleepers. She can be stopped by scattering rice that she must count, or by salting her shed skin. The figure blends West African and European beliefs.

alternatives.label: Comparative
alternatives.text: Similar skin-shedding fire-ball witches appear in West African (e.g. Ashanti obayifo) folklore, suggesting origins brought by enslaved Africans.

entries.title: Olduvai Gorge
entries.mainstream: Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania preserves almost two million years of human prehistory in layered deposits. Louis and Mary Leakey worked there from the 1930s; Mary Leakey found 'Zinjanthropus' (Paranthropus boisei) in 1959 and the team described Homo habilis in 1964. Potassium-argon dating at Olduvai was among the first to show how old human evolution was. It gives its name to Oldowan stone tools.

alternatives.label: Earliest tools
alternatives.text: Older stone tools have since been found elsewhere (e.g. Lomekwi, 3.3 million years), so Olduvai no longer holds the earliest record.

entries.changed: 1959-1961 dating pushed human ancestry far further back than expected.

entries.title: Little Foot: the most complete Australopithecus skeleton
entries.mainstream: Little Foot (StW 573) is an Australopithecus skeleton from Sterkfontein Caves, South Africa. Ron Clarke identified foot bones in museum boxes in 1994, and in 1997 Stephen Motsumi and Nkwane Molefe found the matching bone in the cave. Excavating it from breccia took about 20 years. It is over 90% complete. Cosmogenic dating in 2015 gave about 3.67 million years, though the date remains debated.

alternatives.label: Species and date
alternatives.text: Clarke assigns it to Australopithecus prometheus, while others place it in A. africanus; some researchers argue for a younger age.

sources.title: New cosmogenic burial ages for Sterkfontein Member 2 Australopithecus and Member 5 Oldowan

entries.title: Wonderwerk Cave and the earliest controlled fire
entries.mainstream: In Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, researchers in 2012 reported burnt bone and plant ash about one million years old, deep inside the cave where natural wildfire is unlikely. It is one of the earliest proposed cases of hominins (probably Homo erectus) using fire. Other proposed earlier sites in Kenya (Koobi Fora, Chesowanja) are more contested.

alternatives.label: Control vs use
alternatives.text: Researchers debate whether this shows fire making and control or opportunistic use of natural fire.

sources.title: Microstratigraphic evidence of in situ fire in the Acheulean strata of Wonderwerk Cave, Northern Cape province, South Africa

entries.title: Pinnacle Point: the coastal refuge of early humans
entries.mainstream: Caves at Pinnacle Point near Mossel Bay, South Africa, contain evidence from about 164,000 years ago of shellfish eating, red ochre use and heat-treated stone blades. Curtis Marean has proposed that the southern Cape coast was a refuge where a small population of Homo sapiens survived a harsh glacial period.

alternatives.label: Bottleneck hypothesis
alternatives.text: The idea that all modern humans descend from a small coastal population is debated; genetic evidence favours a more widespread African origin.

sources.title: Early human use of marine resources and pigment in South Africa during the Middle Pleistocene

entries.title: Engaruka: the abandoned irrigation city of Tanzania
entries.mainstream: Engaruka, on the edge of the Great Rift Valley in northern Tanzania, is a ruined farming settlement with stone-terraced houses and an extensive irrigation and field system, occupied from about the 15th to 18th centuries. Its population may have been several thousand. It was abandoned perhaps because of declining water supply. Its builders are thought to be ancestors of local Iraqw or related peoples.

alternatives.label: Size
alternatives.text: Early estimates of tens of thousands of inhabitants have been revised downward by later surveys.

entries.title: Kintu and Nambi: the first man of Buganda
entries.mainstream: In Ganda tradition Kintu was the first man on Earth (and founding king of Buganda). He married Nambi, daughter of the sky god Ggulu, after passing tests; against warnings she returned for millet, so her brother Walumbe (death) followed them to Earth, bringing death to humanity. The Kabaka of Buganda trace descent from Kintu.

alternatives.label: Historical Kintu
alternatives.text: Some historians suggest a historical leader named Kintu founded a dynasty around the 13th-14th century; others treat him as wholly mythical.

entries.title: Columbus and the lunar eclipse of 1504
entries.mainstream: Stranded on Jamaica in 1503-04 and refused further food by the Taino, Christopher Columbus used Regiomontanus's astronomical almanac to predict the total lunar eclipse of 29 February 1504. According to his son Ferdinand, he told the caciques that God would show his anger by darkening the moon; when it happened, they resumed supplying the crew. The eclipse is confirmed by astronomical calculation; the details of the exchange come from Spanish accounts only.

alternatives.label: Taino perspective
alternatives.text: Historians note the story survives only from the Spanish side and may be embellished.

sources.title: NASA Five Millennium Catalog of Lunar Eclipses 1501-1600

entries.title: Mount Pelee eruption of 1902
entries.mainstream: On 8 May 1902 a pyroclastic flow (nuee ardente) from Mount Pelee on Martinique destroyed the city of Saint-Pierre in minutes, killing about 28,000 people. Famous survivors included Ludger Sylbaris, a prisoner protected by his thick-walled cell, who later toured with Barnum and Bailey's circus. The eruption led geologists to recognise pyroclastic flows as a distinct volcanic hazard.

alternatives.label: Elections
alternatives.text: Historians have argued that authorities discouraged evacuation partly because of an upcoming election; the extent of this is debated.

entries.title: Bois Caiman ceremony and the Haitian Revolution
entries.mainstream: According to tradition, in August 1791 enslaved people met at Bois Caiman in northern Saint-Domingue for a Vodou ceremony led by Dutty Boukman and the priestess Cecile Fatiman, shortly before the uprising that began the Haitian Revolution. The revolution produced the first independent Black republic in 1804. The ceremony is central to Haitian identity, but historians debate its details and date, since early accounts are scarce.

alternatives.label: Historicity
alternatives.text: Some historians argue the ceremony as usually told was elaborated in the 19th century; others accept a gathering occurred.

alternatives.label: Pact narratives
alternatives.text: Some evangelical preachers have claimed the ceremony was a pact with the devil; historians and Haitians widely reject this as a hostile myth.

entries.title: The Lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel
entries.mainstream: The Lion-man (Lowenmensch) is an ivory figurine about 31 cm tall of a human body with a cave lion's head, carved from mammoth ivory roughly 35,000-41,000 years ago. Fragments were found in a cave in southern Germany in 1939 and reassembled from 1969, with more pieces added in later decades. It is one of the oldest known figurative sculptures and one of the earliest depictions of an imagined being.

alternatives.label: Meaning
alternatives.text: Interpretations range from a deity or shamanic figure to a story character; there is no way to confirm its meaning.

media.title: Living with gods: the 40,000-year-old Lion Man

entries.title: Venus of Hohle Fels
entries.mainstream: A small mammoth-ivory figurine of a woman, found in 2008 in Hohle Fels cave in southern Germany, is at least 35,000 years old, the oldest undisputed depiction of a human. A bone flute was found nearby. The caves of the Swabian Jura were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017.

alternatives.label: Interpretation
alternatives.text: Readings include a fertility symbol, a self-portrait or erotic art; its purpose is unknown.

sources.title: A female figurine from the basal Aurignacian of Hohle Fels Cave in southwestern Germany

entries.title: The Schoningen spears
entries.mainstream: Ten wooden throwing spears found 1994-1999 in an open-cast coal mine at Schoningen, Germany, alongside butchered horse remains, date to roughly 300,000 years ago (a 2023 study suggested about 200,000). They are among the oldest complete hunting weapons, and showed that pre-Neanderthal hominins hunted large animals with planning and skill, overturning the view that they were mainly scavengers.

alternatives.label: Dating
alternatives.text: The age has been revised from around 400,000 to 300,000 and possibly about 200,000 years; debate continues.

entries.changed: 1997 publication challenged the 'scavenger' model of early hominins.

sources.title: Lower Palaeolithic hunting spears from Germany

entries.title: Kalambo Falls: the oldest wooden structure
entries.mainstream: At Kalambo Falls in Zambia, researchers reported in 2023 two logs joined by an intentionally cut notch, dated by luminescence to at least 476,000 years ago, before Homo sapiens existed. It is the earliest known evidence of deliberately constructed wooden structures, perhaps part of a platform or walkway, made by an unknown hominin.

alternatives.label: Function and maker
alternatives.text: The builder species and purpose remain unknown; Homo heidelbergensis is one candidate.

sources.title: Evidence for the earliest structural use of wood at least 476,000 years ago

entries.title: William Harvey and the circulation of the blood
entries.mainstream: In 1628 English physician William Harvey published De Motu Cordis, showing by experiment and calculation that the heart pumps blood around the body in a circuit, overturning Galen's 1,400-year-old idea that blood was continually made in the liver and consumed. He was widely ridiculed at first. Ibn al-Nafis had described pulmonary circulation in the 13th century, but his work was little known in Europe.

alternatives.label: Priority
alternatives.text: Historians debate whether Renaissance writers such as Servetus and Colombo knew Ibn al-Nafis's ideas.

entries.changed: Galenic model dominant until 1628; accepted within a few decades.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus

entries.title: Leeuwenhoek discovers the microbial world
entries.mainstream: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft draper using single-lens microscopes he made himself, reported to the Royal Society in 1676 tiny 'animalcules' in water, the first known observations of bacteria and protists. The Society was initially sceptical and sent witnesses to confirm his findings. He also described sperm cells and red blood cells, but kept his lens-making methods secret.

alternatives.label: Germ theory delay
alternatives.text: His observations did not lead to germ theory for nearly two centuries; historians discuss why.

media.title: The Gadget That Changed How We See The World | Cell | BBC Earth Science

entries.title: The transits of Venus 1761 and 1769
entries.mainstream: Following Edmond Halley's proposal, astronomers sent expeditions worldwide to time the transits of Venus in 1761 and 1769 in order to measure the distance from the Earth to the Sun. Cook's first voyage observed the 1769 transit from Tahiti before searching for the southern continent. Guillaume Le Gentil missed both transits (clouds and war), returning to France after 11 years to find himself declared dead. The results gave the Sun's distance to within a few percent.

alternatives.label: Black drop effect
alternatives.text: Timing was hampered by the black drop effect, an optical illusion that blurred contact times.

entries.title: Mary Toft, the woman who "gave birth" to rabbits
entries.mainstream: In 1726 Mary Toft of Godalming, England, appeared to give birth to rabbits, convincing several medical men including King George I's surgeon-anatomist Nathaniel St Andre. She confessed in December 1726 under threat of surgery that she had inserted rabbit parts. The scandal badly damaged the reputations of the doctors involved and was mocked by Hogarth.

alternatives.label: Maternal impression
alternatives.text: The case was taken seriously partly because of the then-common belief that a mother's experiences could shape her unborn child.

entries.title: The Vegetable Lamb of Tartary
entries.mainstream: Medieval and early modern European writers, including the travel book of 'Sir John Mandeville' (c.1350s), described a plant of Central Asia that grew sheep as its fruit. The legend probably grew from reports of cotton (wool growing on plants). Specimens shown in collections were made from the hairy rhizome of the tree fern Cibotium barometz. Naturalists debunked it by the 18th century.

alternatives.label: Origin
alternatives.text: Some scholars link the legend to the Jewish legend of the yeduah or to Scythian lamb-skins; cotton is the most widely accepted explanation.

entries.title: Beringer's lying stones
entries.mainstream: In 1725 Johann Beringer, a professor in Wurzburg, was given carved limestone 'fossils' showing lizards, stars, Hebrew letters and the name of God, and published a book on them in 1726. They had been made by colleagues J. Ignatz Roderick and Georg von Eckhart to discredit him. When Beringer found one with his own name, he realised the hoax and sued; the episode became a classic warning in palaeontology. Some stones survive in museums.

alternatives.label: Telling of the story
alternatives.text: Popular versions say Beringer ruined himself buying back copies of his book; historians consider this legend.

entries.title: The Bayon: smiling faces of Angkor Thom
entries.mainstream: The Bayon, at the centre of Angkor Thom in Cambodia, was built in the late 12th–early 13th century under the Khmer king Jayavarman VII. Its towers carry dozens of huge stone faces (commonly counted around 200), often identified with the bodhisattva Avalokitesvara and sometimes with the king himself. Bas-reliefs show markets, battles and daily life. The site is part of the Angkor UNESCO World Heritage property.

alternatives.label: Identity of the faces
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether the faces primarily represent Avalokitesvara, Jayavarman VII, Brahma, or a deliberate fusion of royal and divine imagery.

alternatives.label: Hidden technology claims
alternatives.text: Popular alternative books sometimes treat the precision of Khmer stonework as evidence of lost advanced technology; mainstream archaeology attributes it to large organised labour and skilled craft traditions.

media.title: From a live Smarthistory webinar: Dr. Melody Rod-Ari on Angkor Thom

entries.title: The fall of Ayutthaya, 1767
entries.mainstream: In April 1767 Burmese armies of the Konbaung dynasty sacked Ayutthaya, capital of Siam for over four centuries. Temples and libraries were burned, the royal family captured or killed, and the city largely abandoned. Siamese resistance regrouped under Taksin, who founded a new capital at Thonburi; the Chakri dynasty later established Bangkok. Ruined Ayutthaya is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Lost chronicles
alternatives.text: Much of Ayutthaya's archival record was destroyed; later Thai chronicles reconstruct the war from surviving and Burmese sources, so some details remain uncertain.

alternatives.label: Cyclical collapse readings
alternatives.text: Some popular histories frame the sack as cosmic or karmic punishment; historians treat it as a conventional early-modern siege war.

entries.title: Dong Son bronze drums
entries.mainstream: Dong Son drums are large, elaborately decorated bronze kettle drums produced from about the 6th century BCE by the Dong Son culture of the Red River valley (northern Vietnam) and traded widely across mainland and island Southeast Asia. Typical decoration includes frogs, birds, houses on piles, warriors and a central star or sun motif. They were status and ritual objects; related drums appear as far as Indonesia and southern China.

alternatives.label: Lost-civilisation diffusion
alternatives.text: 19th–20th century diffusionist writers sometimes treated the drums as proof of a single forgotten high culture spanning the Pacific; modern archaeology sees regional bronze-age networks.

alternatives.label: Rain magic
alternatives.text: Ethnographic analogies suggest some drums were used in rain or fertility rites; direct evidence for specific rituals is limited.

entries.title: The kingdom of Champa
entries.mainstream: Champa was a collection of Austronesian-speaking Hindu-Buddhist polities along the coast of what is now central and southern Vietnam, attested from the late 2nd century CE until its conquest by Dai Viet in 1832. Cham temples at My Son and elsewhere, Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions, and Chinese records document Indianised kingship, maritime trade and repeated wars with Angkor and Dai Viet. Cham communities remain in Vietnam and Cambodia.

alternatives.label: Origins
alternatives.text: Scholars debate how far Champa grew from local Sa Huynh culture versus migrant seafaring groups linked to Island Southeast Asia.

alternatives.label: Po Nagar and goddess cults
alternatives.text: Cham mythology centres goddesses such as Po Nagar; some colonial writers exoticised these as evidence of matriarchy beyond what the inscriptions support.

entries.title: The Hoabinhian: Southeast Asia's pebble-tool foragers
entries.mainstream: The Hoabinhian is an archaeological stone-tool tradition of mainland Southeast Asia, named after finds in Hoa Binh province, Vietnam, and roughly spanning the late Pleistocene to mid-Holocene (c. 10,000–2000 BCE, with earlier starts proposed). It is characterised by flaked pebble tools and associated with hunter-gatherer cave and rockshelter occupations. It was long a key reference for the region's pre-Neolithic past.

alternatives.label: Agricultural transition
alternatives.text: Debate continues over when and how rice farming replaced or absorbed Hoabinhian foraging ways of life.

alternatives.label: Deep antiquity claims
alternatives.text: Some popular accounts push continuous Hoabinhian occupation far earlier than the secure dated assemblages support.

entries.title: Phra Mae Thorani: the earth goddess who drowned Mara
entries.dateNote: Iconography widespread by the Angkorian and later Tai periods
entries.mainstream: In Theravada Buddhist art of Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Burma, Phra Mae Thorani (the earth goddess) is shown wringing water from her hair to drown the armies of Mara as the Buddha-to-be calls the earth to witness his right to enlightenment. The motif appears on temple murals, Buddha pedestals and amulets. It adapts older Indic ideas of the earth as witness into a distinctive mainland Southeast Asian image.

alternatives.label: Pre-Buddhist earth cult
alternatives.text: Some scholars see continuity with local earth and fertility goddesses folded into Buddhist narrative; others stress the Buddhist textual basis (the earth-touching gesture and Mara's defeat).

entries.title: My Son: holy land of the Cham kings
entries.mainstream: My Son in Quang Nam, Vietnam, is a cluster of Hindu temple towers dedicated mainly to Shiva, built by Cham kings from the 4th to 13th centuries. Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions record royal donations. Heavily bombed in the Vietnam War, the site was cleared of mines and inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. It is the foremost surviving Cham sanctuary.

alternatives.label: Indian architects
alternatives.text: Colonial-era writers sometimes attributed Cham temples to Indian colonists; inscriptions and archaeology support local Cham patronage within an Indianised cultural sphere.

entries.title: The Pyu ancient cities of Myanmar
entries.mainstream: The Pyu city-states (c. 2nd century BCE–9th century CE) in the Irrawaddy valley of Myanmar—especially Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra—were early urban Buddhist centres with brick walls, burial urns, silver coinage and Pyu-script inscriptions. UNESCO inscribed the three cities in 2014. Their decline coincided with the rise of Bagan.

alternatives.label: Indianisation vs local development
alternatives.text: Historians debate how much Pyu urbanism owed to Indian models versus indigenous trajectories.

alternatives.label: Lost chronicles
alternatives.text: Later Burmese chronicles project legendary origins onto the Pyu; archaeology is the primary evidence.

media.title: Myanmar hopes ancient cities make UNESCO list

entries.title: Sukhothai: first Thai kingdom
entries.mainstream: Sukhothai, in north-central Thailand, emerged in the 13th century as an early Tai polity often called the first Thai kingdom. King Ramkhamhaeng is traditionally credited with a 1292 inscription praising just rule, free trade and a Thai script; the inscription's authenticity has been debated. Sukhothai art developed a distinctive walking Buddha style. The kingdom was absorbed by Ayutthaya in the 15th century; its parks are a UNESCO site.

alternatives.label: Ramkhamhaeng inscription
alternatives.text: Some Thai and foreign scholars have questioned whether the famous inscription is a 19th-century fabrication; many epigraphers still accept it as 13th-century with possible later copies.

alternatives.label: National origin myth
alternatives.text: Modern Thai nationalism elevated Sukhothai as the cradle of the nation; historians describe a more gradual Tai political rise.

media.title: Historic Town of Sukhothai and Associated Historic Towns (UNESCO/NHK)

entries.title: The Trung sisters' rebellion
entries.mainstream: In 40 CE the sisters Trung Trac and Trung Nhi led a revolt against Han Chinese rule in the Red River Delta (Jiaozhi), briefly establishing independent rule before being defeated by the general Ma Yuan in 43 CE. They are national heroines in Vietnam, commemorated in temples and place names. The earliest accounts are Chinese; later Vietnamese histories and folklore elaborate their story, including the motif of riding war elephants.

alternatives.label: Historicity of details
alternatives.text: The broad revolt is accepted from Chinese sources; many colourful details (elephant cavalry, ritual suicide) come from later tradition.

alternatives.label: Feminist readings
alternatives.text: Modern writers cast the sisters as early feminist icons; that frame is anachronistic but reflects their lasting symbolic role.

entries.title: Capacocha: Inca child sacrifice on the high peaks
entries.mainstream: Capacocha (capac hucha) was an Inca state ritual in which children of high status were selected, ritually prepared and buried—often alive—on mountain summits with rich grave goods. Spanish chroniclers described the practice; archaeology has confirmed frozen mummies such as the Llullaillaco children (discovered 1999) and the Ice Maiden Juanita on Ampato (1995). Isotope and DNA studies show some children travelled long distances to the capitals before the final ascent.

alternatives.label: Scale
alternatives.text: Chroniclers imply large numbers of victims in major ceremonies; the archaeological sample is small and may over-represent high-altitude preserves.

alternatives.label: Volunteer vs coercion
alternatives.text: Some popular accounts stress willing sacrifice; ethnohistorians emphasise state power, status obligation and limited choice.

media.title: Virgins of the Sun and Incan Human Sacrifice

entries.title: Chan Chan: capital of the Chimú
entries.mainstream: Chan Chan, near Trujillo on Peru's north coast, was the adobe capital of the Chimú kingdom (Chimor) from about the 9th–15th centuries, until Inca conquest under Topa Inca Yupanqui around 1470. Its vast walled ciudadelas, friezes of fish and birds, and extensive irrigation supported one of the largest pre-Columbian cities in the Americas. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, threatened by erosion and El Niño rains.

alternatives.label: Labour organisation
alternatives.text: Debate continues over how rigidly Chimú society was stratified and whether the ciudadelas were royal compounds, administrative centres, or both.

alternatives.label: Outsider builders
alternatives.text: Fringe claims of non-Andean builders ignore clear continuity with earlier Moche and Sicán coastal cultures.

media.title: The Lost City of Chan Chan | Lost Cities with Albert Lin

entries.title: Quipu: knotted-string records of the Andes
entries.mainstream: Quipus (khipus) are assemblages of coloured, spun and knotted cords used by Andean societies—especially the Inca—to record numerical and possibly narrative information. Spanish officials described specialist quipucamayocs. Surviving quipus encode decimal place values in knot types and positions. Whether some quipus also encode phonetic or narrative data remains an active research question.

alternatives.label: Writing system
alternatives.text: Some researchers argue certain quipus are a writing system; others treat them primarily as accounting devices with limited non-numerical coding.

alternatives.label: Suppressed literacy myths
alternatives.text: Claims that the Spanish uniquely destroyed a full Andean alphabet go beyond the evidence; quipus were partly co-opted into colonial administration before declining.

entries.changed: Late 20th–21st century work revived interest in non-numerical quipu content.
