entries.title: Acre geoglyphs of the Amazon
entries.mainstream: Hundreds of geometric earthworks—circles, squares and enclosures—have been documented in Acre state and neighbouring parts of Brazil and Bolivia, many revealed by deforestation and remote sensing. Radiocarbon dates often fall between about 1000 BCE and 1400 CE. They show that parts of Amazonia supported large, organised societies that cleared and shaped landscapes long before modern ranching, overturning the idea of a pristine empty forest.

alternatives.label: Urban scale
alternatives.text: Researchers debate how densely populated the surrounding landscapes were and whether the enclosures were villages, ceremonial centres, or both.

alternatives.label: Lost continent myths
alternatives.text: Popular writers sometimes fold the geoglyphs into Atlantis or other pan-American lost-civilisation narratives not supported by the archaeology.

entries.changed: Mapped widely from the 2000s as forest clearance and lidar expanded coverage.

entries.title: Qhapaq Ñan: the Inca road system
entries.mainstream: Qhapaq Ñan ("the great road") was the Inca imperial road network spanning thousands of kilometres from Colombia to Chile, with paved stretches, suspension bridges, way stations (tambos) and storehouses. It moved armies, messengers (chasquis) and tribute. UNESCO inscribed a transnational serial property in 2014. Segments remain in use by Andean communities.

alternatives.label: Pre-Inca routes
alternatives.text: Many segments upgraded older Wari, Tiwanaku and local roads; calling the whole system purely Inca oversimplifies.

alternatives.label: Alien highway claims
alternatives.text: Internet myths sometimes attribute arrow-straight Andean roads to non-human engineers; they fit known imperial logistics.

entries.title: Paracas textiles of the south coast of Peru
entries.mainstream: The Paracas culture (c. 800–100 BCE) of Peru's south coast produced extraordinarily fine embroidered mantles and other textiles recovered from shaft tombs on the Paracas Peninsula, notably by Julio C. Tello in the 1920s. Motifs show flying figures, animals and supernatural beings in vivid colour. The textiles are among the finest surviving from the ancient Americas; many were looted into foreign collections.

alternatives.label: Elongated skulls link
alternatives.text: Paracas tombs also yielded intentionally elongated skulls (a separate entry); alternative writers sometimes claim the textiles depict "alien" biology—mainstream view treats the imagery as mythic and elite costume.

entries.title: The Wari: first empire of the Andes?
entries.mainstream: The Wari (Huari) polity, centred near Ayacucho in highland Peru (c. 600–1000 CE), expanded administrative centres, terracing and road segments across much of Peru before the Inca. Distinctive oversize pottery, D-shaped temples and planned compounds mark Wari presence. Its collapse left a politically fragmented Middle Horizon aftermath later unified by the Inca.

alternatives.label: Empire vs network
alternatives.text: Scholars disagree whether Wari was a territorial empire, a loose hegemonic network, or a mix varying by region.

alternatives.label: Tiwanaku rivalry
alternatives.text: Relations with Tiwanaku to the south are modelled as coexistence, competition or shared religious vocabulary.

entries.title: Machu Picchu
entries.mainstream: Machu Picchu, a 15th-century Inca estate in the cloud forest above the Urubamba River in Peru, was built for the emperor Pachacuti and later abandoned. Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention in 1911 with local guides; Indigenous farmers already knew the site. Carefully fitted stone architecture, terraces and astronomical alignments make it an icon of Andean engineering and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alternatives.label: Lost city myth
alternatives.text: Marketing as a "lost city" overlooks continuous local knowledge; Bingham was not its discoverer in an absolute sense.

alternatives.label: Aliens and vibes
alternatives.text: Fringe tourism sometimes credits extraterrestrials or mystical energy for the stonework; archaeology documents Inca quarrying, transport and fitting methods.

media.title: Machu Picchu - The secrets of the Inca builders | DW Documentary

entries.title: Coricancha: the Inca golden temple of the Sun
entries.mainstream: Coricancha (Qorikancha), in Cusco, was the Inca empire's principal temple of the sun (Inti), sheathed in gold plates according to Spanish accounts, with chapels for the moon, stars, thunder and other deities. After the conquest the Dominican monastery of Santo Domingo was built over and around it; earthquakes have repeatedly exposed Inca walls that outperform colonial masonry. Curved ashlar walls remain among the finest Inca stonework.

alternatives.label: Gold quantities
alternatives.text: Spanish reports of vast gold may be exaggerated; enough was looted to fuel legends of hidden Inca treasure.

alternatives.label: Temple of unknown technology
alternatives.text: Alternative guides sometimes claim impossible precision; the walls fit documented Inca ashlar techniques.

entries.title: Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna
entries.mainstream: Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna are massive adobe platform mounds of the Moche culture at Cerro Blanco near Trujillo, Peru (c. 100–800 CE). The Sun mound is among the largest adobe structures in the Americas; the Moon mound preserves polychrome reliefs of deities and sacrificed captives. Excavations show repeated ritual rebuilding and evidence of human sacrifice tied to Moche religion.

alternatives.label: Climate collapse
alternatives.text: One model links Moche political stress to severe El Niño floods; others stress internal conflict and religious change.

alternatives.label: Palace of giants
alternatives.text: Colonial and popular lore sometimes called the huacas works of giants; they are Moche monumental architecture.

entries.title: The obelisks (stelae) of Aksum
entries.mainstream: At Aksum in northern Ethiopia stand monumental granite stelae carved to imitate multi-storey buildings, marking elite burials of the Kingdom of Aksum (early first millennium CE). The tallest still standing is about 24 m; a larger fallen stele exceeded 30 m. One stele taken to Rome in 1937 was returned in 2005. They demonstrate Aksumite mastery of quarrying, transport and carving.

alternatives.label: Ark legends
alternatives.text: Local tradition links Aksum with the Ark of the Covenant; the stelae themselves are funerary monuments, not ark-related structures.

alternatives.label: Foreign architects
alternatives.text: Colonial writers sometimes denied African capacity to raise the stones; archaeology shows local Aksumite production.

entries.title: Kandake Amanitore of Kush
entries.mainstream: Amanitore was a queen (kandake) of the Kingdom of Kush in Nubia, ruling in the mid-1st century CE, often jointly with King Natakamani. Her name and image appear on temples at Naqa and Meroë. Kushite kandakes were powerful royal women; Roman sources remembered earlier kandakes who fought Rome. Amanitore's monuments show a flourishing Meroitic state building in Egyptianising and local styles.

alternatives.label: Warrior-queen stereotype
alternatives.text: Popular histories sometimes merge several kandakes into a single Amazon archetype; Amanitore is specifically attested as a builder-queen.

alternatives.label: Biblical Candace
alternatives.text: Acts 8 mentions a kandake of the Ethiopians; she is not Amanitore, though later tradition sometimes blurs Nubian queens.

media.title: What happened to the lost Kingdom of Kush? - Geoff Emberling

entries.title: The Nommo: Dogon ancestral water spirits
entries.dateNote: Oral tradition; ethnography recorded mainly in the 20th century
entries.mainstream: In Dogon religion of Mali, the Nommo are ancestral spirits associated with water, often described as amphibious or fish-like beings who brought knowledge and order. Marcel Griaule's mid-20th-century ethnography made them famous, intertwining them with creation narratives and—controversially—with astronomical lore about Sirius. Later anthropologists questioned how much of Griaule's systematic cosmology reflected prompting versus independent Dogon teaching.

alternatives.label: Sirius link
alternatives.text: Claims that Nommo lore encodes knowledge of Sirius B are highly disputed (see Dogon–Sirius entry); Nommo as water ancestors are better attested than the astronomy.

alternatives.label: Ancient astronaut reading
alternatives.text: Von Däniken-style authors treat Nommo as extraterrestrials; that is speculative and not required by Dogon tradition.

entries.title: Kanem–Bornu Empire
entries.mainstream: Kanem–Bornu was a long-lived Sahelian empire around Lake Chad, rising in Kanem by about the 8th–9th centuries, adopting Islam, then shifting its centre to Bornu (west of the lake) after the 14th century. It controlled trans-Saharan trade routes, maintained cavalry armies, and left king-lists and Arabic chronicles such as those used by Heinrich Barth. It persisted in various forms into the 19th century.

alternatives.label: Extent
alternatives.text: Chronicles and European travellers may inflate territorial control; effective power likely pulsed with trade and military success.

alternatives.label: Lost libraries
alternatives.text: Romantic accounts invent vast vanished archives; some Arabic manuscripts from the region survive, but not a single destroyed "Library of Chad".

entries.title: The Kebra Nagast: Glory of the Kings
entries.mainstream: The Kebra Nagast, compiled in Ge'ez in 14th-century Ethiopia, narrates how the Queen of Sheba (Makeda) bore Menelik I to King Solomon, and how Menelik brought the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum. It became a foundational national and Solomonic-dynasty charter. Scholars trace sources to earlier Jewish, Christian and Arabic traditions reshaped for Ethiopian royal ideology.

alternatives.label: Historical ark
alternatives.text: Whether any object called the Ark reached Ethiopia is unproven; the text is theological-political narrative rather than archive reportage.

alternatives.label: Ras Tafari readings
alternatives.text: Rastafari tradition draws on Solomonic Ethiopian identity popularised partly via this story-world; that is a modern religious reception.

entries.title: The Sao civilisation of Lake Chad
entries.mainstream: The Sao were Iron Age peoples south of Lake Chad (roughly early first millennium CE into the later Middle Ages) known archaeologically for distinctive pottery, terracotta figurines, metallurgy and settlement mounds in Cameroon, Chad and Nigeria. Oral traditions of later Kotoko and related groups claim Sao ancestry. They precede and partly overlap the rise of Kanem.

alternatives.label: Giant legends
alternatives.text: Regional folklore sometimes remembers the Sao as giants; this is mythic scale, not osteological fact.

alternatives.label: Single "civilisation" label
alternatives.text: "Sao civilisation" is an archaeological shorthand for related cultures rather than one centralised state.

entries.title: Djenné-Djenno: ancient city of the Inner Niger Delta
entries.mainstream: Djenné-Djenno (Old Djenné) in Mali's Inner Niger Delta was occupied from about the 3rd century BCE to the 14th century CE, with large-scale mud architecture, craft production and long-distance trade well before trans-Saharan Islamised empires peaked. Excavations by Roderick and Susan McIntosh demonstrated early urbanism in West Africa independent of Mediterranean models. Nearby modern Djenné inherited regional commercial importance.

alternatives.label: Pristine Africa myth
alternatives.text: The site helped overturn claims that complex cities in the Sahel required external founders.

alternatives.label: Atlantis of the Niger
alternatives.text: Fringe writers occasionally inflate it into a lost mega-civilisation beyond the archaeological footprint.

entries.title: The Great Mosque of Djenné
entries.mainstream: The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali is the world's largest mud-brick building, rebuilt in 1906–07 on earlier mosque sites going back centuries (traditionally to the 13th century). Annual community replastering maintains the Sudanese-style architecture. It is central to the UNESCO-listed Old Towns of Djenné. Non-Muslim tourists have been restricted from entering since the 1990s after disruptive fashion shoots.

alternatives.label: French reconstruction myth
alternatives.text: Some narratives claim the French invented the mosque; local building traditions and earlier mosques are well attested, though the present form dates to the early 20th-century rebuild.

alternatives.label: Forbidden ancient tech
alternatives.text: Online posts sometimes treat the mosque as prehistoric alien architecture; it is living Sahelian earthen architecture.

entries.title: Askia Muhammad I and the Songhai Empire's golden age
entries.mainstream: Askia Muhammad I (Askia the Great) seized power in the Songhai Empire in 1493, expanded territory across the western Sahel, reorganised administration and promoted Islamic scholarship in Timbuktu and Gao. The Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-fattash are major sources. He was deposed by his son in 1528 and died in 1538; Songhai fell to the Moroccan invasion of 1591.

alternatives.label: Extent of literacy
alternatives.text: Songhai's scholarly fame is real, but literacy was specialised; romantic portraits of universal schooling exaggerate.

alternatives.label: World's richest king comparisons
alternatives.text: Modern viral lists sometimes confuse Askia with Mansa Musa; both were wealthy Sahelian rulers of different empires.

entries.title: The Golden Stool of the Asante
entries.dateNote: Traditional origin late 17th century; historically attested thereafter
entries.mainstream: The Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi) is the sacred throne of the Asante (Ashanti) people of Ghana, said to have descended from the sky into the lap of the first Asantehene Osei Tutu with the help of the priest Anokye in the late 17th century. It embodies the soul of the nation and is never sat upon. British demands related to the stool helped spark the War of the Golden Stool in 1900, led by Yaa Asantewaa.

alternatives.label: Literal descent
alternatives.text: Tradition asserts miraculous origin; historians treat the stool's sanctity as foundational political theology of the Asante Union.

alternatives.label: Hidden stool legends
alternatives.text: Stories of the stool's secret hiding places during colonial conflict are partly confirmed by oral history; sensational treasure versions proliferate.

entries.title: The Amityville Horror
entries.mainstream: In December 1975 the Lutz family fled 112 Ocean Avenue in Amityville, New York, after 28 days, claiming intense hauntings. The house had been the scene of the 1974 DeFeo murders. Jay Anson's 1977 book and later films made the case world-famous. Investigators, including some initially sympathetic, found major contradictions; Ronald DeFeo's lawyer and others said the haunting story was concocted for money. It remains a landmark of modern haunted-house lore and media.

alternatives.label: Genuine haunting
alternatives.text: Believers cite alleged psychic corroboration and later residents' stories; mainstream investigators classify the Lutz account as a hoax or heavy embellishment.

alternatives.label: Demonic portal claims
alternatives.text: Paranormal literature sometimes treats the house as a gate; no verifiable evidence supports this.

entries.title: Area 51 (Groom Lake)
entries.mainstream: Area 51 is a highly classified US Air Force facility at Groom Lake, Nevada, established in the mid-1950s for flight testing of secret aircraft such as the U-2, A-12/Oxcart and later stealth prototypes. The US government publicly acknowledged the site's name and purpose in 2013. Secrecy, restricted airspace and desert sightings fuelled decades of UFO lore linking it to crashed saucers and alien technology—claims never substantiated by credible evidence.

alternatives.label: Alien reverse-engineering
alternatives.text: Bob Lazar's 1989 claims of Element 115 and saucer work at "S-4" near Area 51 remain unverified and widely disputed.

alternatives.label: Underground bases
alternatives.text: Popular maps of vast subterranean complexes go far beyond documented hangars and test infrastructure.

entries.changed: 2013 CIA history release confirmed the site's U-2 era role.

media.title: Experts Reveal What Really Happened (Full Episode) | Area 51: The CIA's Secret

entries.title: Cash–Landrum UFO incident (1980)
entries.mainstream: On the evening of 29 December 1980 Betty Cash, Vickie Landrum and Landrum's grandson reported a diamond-shaped fiery object above a road in Dayton, Texas, accompanied by presumed military helicopters. The women later reported severe health effects they attributed to radiation-like exposure and sued the US government; the case was dismissed. No official explanation has been confirmed; hypotheses include a military exercise, misidentified aircraft, or fabrication/exaggeration.

alternatives.label: Secret military craft
alternatives.text: UFO researchers often argue for a malfunctioning nuclear-powered test vehicle; no declassified proof has emerged.

alternatives.label: Hoax or psychogenesis
alternatives.text: Sceptics note inconsistencies and the financial incentive of litigation; medical causation remains contested.

entries.title: Operation Highjump in Antarctica
entries.mainstream: Operation Highjump (1946–47) was a large US Navy Antarctic expedition led by Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd, involving 13 ships and thousands of men, to train in polar conditions, map coastline and assert presence. It achieved aerial mapping before weather forced early wind-down. Decades later, fringe literature claimed Byrd fought UFO fleets or found Nazi/hollow-Earth bases—claims unsupported by the expedition's official records and logs.

alternatives.label: Hollow Earth / Nazi base myths
alternatives.text: Conspiracy books and a disputed "secret diary" allege polar openings and enemy fleets; historians treat these as postwar fiction layered onto a real military exercise.

alternatives.label: Byrd's warnings
alternatives.text: A frequently quoted interview about foes that could fly pole to pole is real Cold War commentary on aviation, later misread as a UFO confession.

entries.title: The Orontius Finaeus (Oronce Fine) map of 1531
entries.mainstream: French cartographer Oronce Fine (Orontius Finaeus) published a 1531 world map whose southern landmass some 20th-century writers, notably Charles Hapgood, compared to an ice-free Antarctica. Hapgood argued such maps preserved knowledge from an unknown Ice Age civilisation. Mainstream historians of cartography treat Fine's south land as a speculative Terra Australis of Renaissance geography, not a survey of Antarctica under ice.

alternatives.label: Hapgood / lost civilisation
alternatives.text: Alternative historians still cite Fine and the Piri Reis map as evidence of prehistoric Antarctic mapping; professional cartographic history rejects that reading.

alternatives.label: Authentic Antarctica
alternatives.text: No peer-reviewed geophysical match requires an ice-free surveyed Antarctica in Fine's sources.

entries.title: Archimedes of Syracuse
entries.mainstream: Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE) of Syracuse was a Greek mathematician and engineer who proved results on areas, volumes and the lever, approximated pi, and invented war machines used against Rome in the siege of Syracuse. Later sources credit a heat-ray of burning mirrors and a claw that lifted ships; modern reconstructions of the mirrors are generally unsuccessful at warship scale, while crane-like "claws" are more plausible. He was killed when Syracuse fell.

alternatives.label: Burning mirrors
alternatives.text: The heat-ray story is late and physically dubious at fleet scale; it remains a popular experimental challenge.

alternatives.label: Antikythera link
alternatives.text: Some popular accounts loosely credit Archimedes with the Antikythera mechanism's tradition; he worked in the right cultural sphere, but authorship is unproven.

entries.title: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) and the scientific method in optics
entries.mainstream: Hasan Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), working in Cairo, wrote the Book of Optics (Kitab al-Manazir), arguing that vision results from light entering the eye, analysing reflection and refraction, and stressing controlled testing of claims. Latin translations as Alhazen influenced medieval and early modern European optics. He also wrote on astronomy, mathematics and the camera obscura.

alternatives.label: Father of scientific method
alternatives.text: Popular histories sometimes call him the sole inventor of experimental science; historians place him among several medieval figures developing empirical argument.

alternatives.label: Suppressed genius myths
alternatives.text: Internet essays claim the Church uniquely suppressed him; his work was in fact transmitted into Latin Christendom.

media.author: Adolph Boÿ, engraved by Jeremias Falck. Used as the frontispiece to Johannes Hevelius, Selenographia, 1647
media.title: Ibn_al-Haytham_crop.jpg
The Brilliant Experiment That Changed The Way We See Light

entries.title: The Cairo Geniza
entries.mainstream: The Cairo Geniza is a vast cache of Jewish manuscript fragments (roughly 9th–19th centuries) recovered mainly from the Ben Ezra Synagogue in Fustat (Old Cairo), brought to scholarly attention especially by Solomon Schechter in the 1890s. Letters, contracts, liturgies and shopping lists illuminate Mediterranean social, economic and religious life. Most fragments are now in Cambridge and other libraries; digitisation continues.

alternatives.label: Hidden Atlantis of papers
alternatives.text: Romantic accounts exaggerate secret cabals; the geniza was a sacred storeroom for worn writings, not a sealed conspiracy archive.

alternatives.label: Lost gospel fantasies
alternatives.text: Occasional media claims of world-changing suppressed gospels from the geniza usually misfile ordinary liturgical or legal texts.

entries.changed: Mass scholarly exploitation from the 1890s; major digitisation in the 21st century.

media.title: A thousand year old seal from the Cairo Genizah

entries.title: Grauballe Man and the bog bodies of northern Europe
entries.mainstream: Grauballe Man is a bog body found in 1952 in Jutland, Denmark, dated to around the 3rd century BCE. His throat was cut, and the acidic peat preserved soft tissue to a rare degree. Together with Tollund Man and other finds he anchors debate over Iron Age ritual killing, execution and deposition in wetlands across northern Europe.

alternatives.label: Sacrifice vs execution
alternatives.text: Scholars disagree whether bog bodies were votive sacrifices, punished criminals, or both depending on case.

alternatives.label: Alien autopsy vibes
alternatives.text: Sensational media sometimes exoticises bog bodies as inexplicable anomalies; forensic archaeology explains preservation chemically.

media.title: The mystery of Europe's most famous bog bodies | BBC Global

entries.title: Denisova Cave and the discovery of Denisovans
entries.mainstream: Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of Siberia yielded a finger bone whose DNA, sequenced in 2010, revealed a previously unknown archaic human group—the Denisovans—distinct from Neanderthals and modern humans. Later finds include a jaw in Tibet and genetic traces in present-day Melanesians and others. The cave was also used by Neanderthals and modern humans, making it a key contact zone.

alternatives.label: Species status
alternatives.text: Whether Denisovans are a separate species or a subspecies remains taxonomically open; they are a clear genetic lineage.

alternatives.label: Hidden advanced race
alternatives.text: Fringe readings cast Denisovans as a lost technological civilisation; the archaeological footprint so far is sparse stone and bone, not cities.

entries.changed: 2010 DNA paper established a new archaic human group from minimal fossil remains.

sources.title: The complete mitochondrial DNA genome of an unknown hominin from southern Siberia

media.title: The Ancient Human Species With A Missing Body

entries.title: Anak Tomb No. 3: Goguryeo murals
entries.mainstream: Anak Tomb No. 3 in Anak County, North Korea, is a mid-4th-century Goguryeo chamber tomb famous for wall paintings of a noble couple, processions, kitchens and a hunting scene. An inscription is often read as dating the tomb to 357 CE and naming a figure associated with Dong Shou. The murals are key evidence for Goguryeo dress, architecture and elite life, and the site is part of the UNESCO Complex of Koguryo Tombs.

alternatives.label: Identity of the occupant
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether the tomb belongs to Dong Shou, a Goguryeo king, or another elite; the inscription's reading remains contested.

alternatives.label: Lost advanced colour tech
alternatives.text: Popular claims that the pigments prove forgotten high technology overstate ordinary mineral paint traditions well attested in East Asian tombs.

entries.title: Seokguram Grotto
entries.mainstream: Seokguram, on Mount Toham near Gyeongju, South Korea, is an 8th-century Silla granite grotto temple centred on a monumental seated Buddha, built under Prime Minister Kim Daeseong and completed around 774 CE. The artificial cave combines architecture, sculpture and planned light. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site paired with Bulguksa and a masterpiece of Buddhist art in East Asia.

alternatives.label: Exact consecration dates
alternatives.text: Chronicle dates for foundation and completion vary slightly; the mid-to-late 8th-century Silla context is secure.

alternatives.label: Impossible stonework myths
alternatives.text: Fringe tours sometimes treat the dome's precision as non-human; it fits documented Silla quarry and masonry skill.

entries.title: Hunminjeongeum: promulgation of Hangul
entries.mainstream: In 1446 (or 1443–44 by some reckonings of composition) King Sejong of Joseon promulgated Hunminjeongeum ("The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People"), introducing the Korean alphabet now called Hangul. The script was designed to match Korean speech more closely than Classical Chinese, with a famous scientific account of letter shapes. Elites long preferred hanja; Hangul later became central to Korean literacy and identity.

alternatives.label: Inventor myths
alternatives.text: Tradition credits Sejong personally; scholars also stress work by the Hall of Worthies (Jiphyeonjeon) scholars under his direction.

alternatives.label: Suppressed alphabet conspiracies
alternatives.text: Nationalist and popular narratives sometimes exaggerate elite conspiracy against Hangul beyond the documented social preference for Classical Chinese.

entries.title: Dokkaebi: Korean goblin spirits
entries.dateNote: Oral tradition; literary records mainly Joseon and later
entries.mainstream: Dokkaebi are supernatural beings in Korean folklore, often pictured with horns, magical clubs (bangmangi) and a taste for contests, tricks and punishing the greedy. They appear in folktales, shamanic contexts and modern media. Unlike Western demons they are frequently more mischievous than purely evil. Stories were collected and reshaped from the Joseon period into the present.

alternatives.label: Nature spirits vs ghosts
alternatives.text: Folklorists debate how far dokkaebi overlap with nature spirits, transformed objects, or restless dead; regional traditions differ.

alternatives.label: Ancient alien reading
alternatives.text: Internet lore sometimes recasts dokkaebi as extraterrestrials; that is a modern overlay on folk narrative.

entries.title: Korean shamanism (Muism)
entries.dateNote: Living tradition with deep historical roots; no single foundation year
entries.mainstream: Korean shamanism (musok/muism) centres on mudang (often women) who mediate with gods and ancestors through gut rituals involving song, dance and offerings. It absorbed and coexisted with Buddhism, Confucianism and later Christianity. State campaigns periodically suppressed shamans; the practice persists in South Korea and among diasporas, and is studied as living religion rather than mere superstition.

alternatives.label: Princess Bari as charter myth
alternatives.text: The abandoned princess Bari who becomes a shamanic psychopomp is a major narrative charter for mudang vocations; historicity is mythical, not biographical.

alternatives.label: Pure prehistoric survival
alternatives.text: Romantic claims that modern gut is an unchanged Ice Age religion ignore centuries of change and syncretism.

entries.title: Gold crowns of Silla
entries.mainstream: Elaborate gold crowns from Silla royal tombs at Gyeongju (notably the 5th–6th centuries) feature tree- or antler-like uprights, jade comma-shaped gogok pendants and dazzling sheet-gold work. They signal sacred kingship and links across the Eurasian steppe gold-working world. Many are National Treasures of South Korea and icons of the Gyeongju historic areas UNESCO property.

alternatives.label: Steppe connection
alternatives.text: Scholars debate how directly Silla crowns relate to Scythian–Siberian diadem traditions versus local invention within shared prestige styles.

alternatives.label: Alien royalty myths
alternatives.text: Fringe authors sometimes treat the otherworldly look of the crowns as proof of non-human elites; archaeology places them in East Asian burial practice.

entries.title: Balhae (Parhae): kingdom of the north
entries.mainstream: Balhae (Parhae; 698–926) was a kingdom in southern Manchuria and the northern Korean peninsula founded by Dae Joyeong after Goguryeo's fall. Chinese sources called it a regional power; it traded with Tang China and Japan and left capitals such as Sanggyeong. It fell to the Khitan Liao in 926. Modern Korean, Chinese and Russian scholarship contests how "Korean" versus multiethnic the state was.

alternatives.label: Ethnic identity
alternatives.text: National historiographies disagree over Balhae as Korean successor state, Mohe-led polity, or multiethnic kingdom; archaeology shows mixed material culture.

alternatives.label: Hidden northern empire myths
alternatives.text: Popular narratives sometimes inflate Balhae into a lost superpower erased by rivals beyond what the sources support.

entries.title: Goryeo celadon
entries.mainstream: Goryeo celadon (cheongja) of the 10th–14th centuries is celebrated for jade-green glazes and inlaid sanggam decoration of cranes, clouds and floral scrolls. Kilns in Jeolla and elsewhere supplied court and temples; pieces were prized in China and are now museum centrepieces. The ware declined with the dynasty's turmoil and the rise of Joseon white porcelain.

alternatives.label: Secret glaze formulas
alternatives.text: Romantic craft lore speaks of lost perfect recipes; technical studies show controllable iron glazes and reducing atmospheres, not vanished alchemy.

alternatives.label: Outsider master potters
alternatives.text: Some older colonial scholarship undervalued Korean agency; kiln archaeology confirms local Goryeo production.

media.title: Rediscovering Korea's Past
media.channel: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art

entries.title: Samseonghyeol: Jeju's three-clan origin myth
entries.dateNote: Mythic charter; Tamna polity historically attested later
entries.mainstream: Samseonghyeol ("Holes of the Three Clans") in Jeju City marks the legendary spot where three demigods—Go, Yang and Bu—emerged from the ground, married princesses from the sea, and founded Jeju's first clans. The shrine and myth anchor Jeju identity distinct from mainland Korean founding stories. Historical references and rituals surround the site into the modern tourism era.

alternatives.label: Literal emergence
alternatives.text: The story is origin mythology, not geology; lava tubes and volcanic landscape of Jeju invite symbolic readings.

alternatives.label: Lost civilisation of Tamna
alternatives.text: Some popular histories blend the myth with the historical Tamna polity into a single vanished high culture beyond the evidence.

entries.title: Hwandan Gogi: disputed Korean pseudo-history
entries.mainstream: Hwandan Gogi (Handan Gogi) is a text published in 1979 that purports to chronicle an ancient Northeast Asian empire far older and wider than mainstream Korean history allows. Professional historians in Korea and abroad treat it as a modern fabrication or unreliable compilation without credible manuscript pedigree. It remains influential in some nationalist and popular circles.

alternatives.label: Authentic ancient chronicle
alternatives.text: Supporters claim transmission from older sources; no verifiable premodern exemplar has convinced academic historians.

alternatives.label: Colonial suppression narrative
alternatives.text: Advocates argue Japanese colonial scholarship hid the text; mainstream historiography sees a late-20th-century pseudepigraph.

entries.changed: Published 1979; academic rejection followed soon after.

entries.title: Potala Palace
entries.mainstream: The Potala Palace in Lhasa, rebuilt under the 5th Dalai Lama from 1645 on an older sacred ridge associated with Songtsen Gampo, was the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas and a political-religious centre of Tibet. White and Red Palace sections hold stupas, murals and libraries. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (Historic Ensemble of the Potala Palace).

alternatives.label: Older fortress myths
alternatives.text: Tradition projects imperial foundations to the 7th century; the present monumental palace is essentially 17th-century and later.

alternatives.label: Forbidden alien archive
alternatives.text: Conspiracy tourism invents sealed ET halls; documented contents are Buddhist art, tombs and administration.

media.title: See Potala Palace, the Iconic Heart of Tibetan Buddhism | National Geographic

entries.title: Bön: Tibet's pre-Buddhist and parallel faith
entries.dateNote: Living tradition; "pre-Buddhist Bön" is partly retrospective construction
entries.mainstream: Bön denotes both the imagined pre-Buddhist religion of Tibet and a living organised tradition (Yungdrung Bön) that developed scriptures, monasteries and a nine-vehicle path parallel to Tibetan Buddhism. Scholars distinguish early court ritualists, later "eternal Bön" textual religion, and folk practices. Bönpo communities remain in Tibet, Nepal and exile.

alternatives.label: Pure pre-Buddhist survival
alternatives.text: Organised Bön scriptures and institutions largely took shape after Buddhism's arrival, partly in dialogue and rivalry with it.

alternatives.label: Alien sky-teachers
alternatives.text: Some New Age readings cast Bön founders as extraterrestrials; traditional narratives speak of teachers from Olmo Lungring / Tagzig, not spacecraft.

entries.title: Sky caves of Mustang
entries.mainstream: Hundreds of hand-carved cliff caves in Nepal's former Kingdom of Lo (Upper Mustang) were used as burials, meditation retreats and dwellings. Expeditions since the 2000s have documented human remains, texts and murals, some linked to early Buddhism and local polities along the Kali Gandaki corridor. Access is restricted; looting and tourism pressure are concerns.

alternatives.label: Age of the oldest caves
alternatives.text: Dates vary by cave; some burial use may be earlier than the medieval Buddhist fittings that attract most attention.

alternatives.label: Lost sky civilisation
alternatives.text: Popular media sometimes turns the caves into a single vanished aerial culture; archaeology shows long, varied reuse.

entries.changed: Major documentary and archaeological attention from the 2000s.

media.title: Sky Caves of Nepal, Part 2: The Scientist | Nat Geo Live

entries.title: Paro Taktsang (Tiger's Nest)
entries.mainstream: Paro Taktsang, the "Tiger's Nest" monastery, clings to a cliff above Paro Valley in Bhutan. Tradition holds that Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche) flew here on a tigress and meditated in a cave; the present temple complex was built in 1692 under Tenzin Rabgye and has been restored after fires. It is Bhutan's most famous sacred site and a major pilgrimage destination.

alternatives.label: Literal flight
alternatives.text: The tigress flight is hagiographic miracle narrative, not a historical aviation event.

alternatives.label: Pre-1692 temples
alternatives.text: Cave sanctity is older; the monumental monastery fabric dates mainly to the late 17th century and rebuilds.

entries.title: Kingdom of Guge
entries.mainstream: Guge was a Tibetan Buddhist kingdom in western Tibet (Ngari), rising after the fragmentation of the Tibetan Empire, with centres at Tholing and Tsaparang. It sponsored the second diffusion of Buddhism in Tibet, linked to figures such as Rinchen Zangpo and Atisha's invitation. The kingdom collapsed in the 17th century after war with Ladakh and upheaval; dramatic ruins remain.

alternatives.label: Cause of fall
alternatives.text: Accounts mix Ladakhi invasion, internal betrayal and religious conflict; details remain debated.

alternatives.label: Shangri-La identification
alternatives.text: Popular writers sometimes equate Guge with fictional Shangri-La; Shangri-La is a 20th-century novel construct.

entries.title: Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche)
entries.mainstream: Padmasambhava, the "Lotus-Born," is the tantric master credited in Tibetan tradition with establishing Buddhism in Tibet under King Trisong Detsen in the 8th century, subduing local spirits and concealing terma treasures for future discovery. Historians treat the richly miraculous biographies as religious literature layered on a likely historical missionary figure. He is central to Nyingma identity and Himalayan sacred geography.

alternatives.label: Historicity
alternatives.text: A core 8th-century Indian master at Samye is plausible; many episodes are later hagiography.

alternatives.label: Ancient astronaut guru
alternatives.text: Fringe authors reread his rainbow-body and flying motifs as spacecraft; that is not a traditional or scholarly reading.

entries.title: Thang Tong Gyalpo: iron-bridge builder saint
entries.mainstream: Thang Tong Gyalpo (c. 1385–1464 or later) was a Tibetan Buddhist yogi, treasure-revealer and engineer famed for forging iron-chain suspension bridges across Himalayan rivers and for founding opera-style performances to fund works. Several bridges and temples are attributed to him in Tibet and Bhutan. He became a model of practical compassion in Vajrayana lore.

alternatives.label: How many bridges
alternatives.text: Tradition credits dozens; surviving structures and later rebuilds make exact counts uncertain.

alternatives.label: Impossible metallurgy
alternatives.text: Popular claims of inexplicable ancient steel ignore known Himalayan iron-working and chain-link techniques.

entries.title: Druk: the Thunder Dragon of Bhutan
entries.dateNote: Symbol crystallised with Drukpa ascendancy in the later Middle Ages
entries.mainstream: The druk (thunder dragon) is a Himalayan dragon figure that became Bhutan's national symbol—Druk Yul, "Land of the Thunder Dragon"—and appears on the flag and in the title Druk Gyalpo (Dragon King). In Tibetan and Bhutanese lore, dragons relate to weather, treasure and protective power. The Drukpa Kagyu school's rise in Bhutan tied religious identity to the dragon name.

alternatives.label: Etymology of Bhutan's name
alternatives.text: "Druk Yul" reflects Drukpa political-religious dominance; older names for the region also existed.

alternatives.label: Living dinosaur theories
alternatives.text: Cryptozoological takes on druk as surviving pterosaurs are speculative entertainment, not ethnography.

media.author: See File history below for details.

Bhutan - A journey to the unknown south | DW Documentary

entries.title: Malla kingdoms of the Kathmandu Valley
entries.mainstream: From roughly the 13th to 18th centuries the Kathmandu Valley was ruled by Malla kings, whose rival city-states—Kathmandu, Patan (Lalitpur) and Bhaktapur—built the celebrated Durbar Squares, temples and artistic canons of Newar civilisation. Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha conquered the valley in 1768–69, founding modern Nepal's Shah dynasty. The squares are UNESCO-listed (with post-earthquake restoration after 2015).

alternatives.label: Golden age romanticism
alternatives.text: Art truly flourished, but politics were often fragmented and violent among the three cities.

alternatives.label: Lost pre-Malla megacity myths
alternatives.text: Fringe histories invent vast older valley empires; archaeology documents earlier Licchavi and other layers without those exaggerations.

media.title: Destruction of Nepal’s temples puts spiritual culture at risk

entries.title: Kumari: Nepal's living goddess
entries.dateNote: Living institution; royal Kathmandu form prominent by early modern era
entries.mainstream: A Kumari is a prepubescent girl worshipped in Nepal—most famously the Royal Kumari of Kathmandu—as a living embodiment of the goddess Taleju/Durga. Selected from Newar Shakya families by ritual criteria, she appears at festivals until menstruation or serious illness ends her term. The institution mixes Hindu and Buddhist Newar practice and has faced modern debates over schooling and children's rights.

alternatives.label: Ancient unbroken line
alternatives.text: The royal Kumari tradition in its present form is especially documented from the later Malla / early Shah period, not a proven Vedic survival.

alternatives.label: Exploitation vs vocation
alternatives.text: Activists stress child welfare; devotees emphasise sacred duty and family prestige—both frames shape current reforms.

media.title: Chosen to be a Kumari goddess - BBC World Service, Witness History

entries.title: Christianization of Kievan Rus' (988)
entries.mainstream: According to the Primary Chronicle, Prince Vladimir the Great of Kiev accepted baptism in 988 (often linked to Chersonesus) and ordered the Christianization of Kievan Rus', aligning the realm with Byzantine Orthodoxy. Churches and Slavic liturgy spread unevenly thereafter. The event is foundational in Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian historical memory.

alternatives.label: Exact circumstances
alternatives.text: Chronicle narrative blends politics, miracle tales and later monastic editing; Byzantine and other sources corroborate a late-10th-century conversion of the elite.

alternatives.label: Mass drowning myths
alternatives.text: Popular retellings exaggerate forced drownings of pagans; coercion occurred, but details are literary.

media.title: Russia, the Kievan Rus, and the Mongols: Crash Course World History #20

entries.title: The Firebird (Zhar-ptitsa)
entries.dateNote: Folk motif; literary fixation in early modern and 19th-century collections
entries.mainstream: In Slavic folklore the Firebird (Russian Zhar-ptitsa) is a radiant, prophetic bird whose feathers glow like fire. Heroes steal a feather and face quests set by tsars or sorcerers. The motif entered high culture through fairy-tale collections and Stravinsky's 1910 ballet The Firebird, which globalised the image without replacing the older folk figure.

alternatives.label: Solar myth reduction
alternatives.text: 19th-century scholars sometimes reduced the bird to a sun symbol; folklorists now stress narrative function over single allegory.

alternatives.label: Real cryptid bird
alternatives.text: Occasional paranormal blogs treat glowing birds as sightings; folklore study treats the Firebird as a tale type.

entries.title: Koschei the Deathless
entries.dateNote: Oral tradition; classic versions recorded in the 19th century
entries.mainstream: Koschei (Koshchei) the Deathless is a Slavic folklore antagonist who hides his soul or death in nested objects (needle in egg in duck in hare in chest) so he cannot be killed until the hiding place is found. He abducts princesses and battles heroes such as Ivan Tsarevich. The figure appears across East Slavic tale traditions and modern adaptations.

alternatives.label: Pre-Christian god survival
alternatives.text: Some writers cast Koschei as a degraded death god; evidence is speculative compared with his clear fairy-tale role.

alternatives.label: Immortality science myths
alternatives.text: Modern esoteric readings invent literal soul-technologies; they are creative rereadings of a folktale device.

entries.title: Vinča symbols
entries.mainstream: The Vinča culture of Southeastern Europe (c. 5700–4500 BCE) produced inscribed signs on pottery and figurines concentrated in Serbia and neighbouring regions. Whether these Vinča symbols constitute early writing, proto-writing, ownership marks or ritual signs is debated. Mainstream consensus does not treat them as a deciphered script comparable to later cuneiform or hieroglyphs.

alternatives.label: Old European literacy
alternatives.text: Marija Gimbutas and others argued for a sophisticated sign system; many archaeologists remain unconvinced they encode language.

alternatives.label: Suppressed oldest alphabet
alternatives.text: Fringe books claim a cover-up of Europe's first true writing; no decipherment has met epigraphic standards.

entries.title: Battle of Kosovo (1389)
entries.mainstream: On 15 June 1389 forces of Serbian Prince Lazar fought the Ottoman army of Sultan Murad I on Kosovo Field. Both leaders died; the Ottomans retained strategic momentum though immediate outcomes were complex. Later epic poetry transformed the battle into a central Serbian national and sacrificial myth (the Kosovo myth), shaping identity for centuries.

alternatives.label: Who "won"
alternatives.text: Contemporary and near-contemporary sources disagree on tactical outcome; long-term Ottoman advance is clearer than a simple victory label.

alternatives.label: Heavenly kingdom theology
alternatives.text: The epic choice of heavenly over earthly kingdom is literary-theological memory, not a battlefield transcript.

entries.title: The Bogomils
entries.mainstream: Bogomilism was a dualist Christian movement that arose in 10th-century Bulgaria under the priest Bogomil and spread through the Balkans, condemning church hierarchy and material creation as Satan's work. Hostile Orthodox and Catholic sources are the main evidence. It influenced or paralleled other dualist currents such as the Cathars. Persecution and assimilation erased organised Bogomil communities by the late Middle Ages.

alternatives.label: Direct Cathar pipeline
alternatives.text: Historians debate how directly Balkan Bogomils seeded Languedoc Catharism versus shared dualist ideas.

alternatives.label: Secret surviving churches
alternatives.text: Modern esoteric groups claiming unbroken Bogomil lineages lack strong documentary proof.

entries.title: Painted monasteries of Bucovina
entries.mainstream: The Churches of Moldavia in northern Romania (especially Bucovina) are late-15th and 16th-century Orthodox churches whose exterior frescoes narrate scripture and sacred history in vivid colour. Foundations under Stephen the Great and successors include Voroneț, Moldovița and Sucevița. UNESCO lists them as masterpieces of Byzantine-inspired mural art.

alternatives.label: Lost paint formulas
alternatives.text: Romantic craft lore speaks of vanished blue recipes; pigment studies identify known mineral and organic materials.

alternatives.label: Pre-Christian calendar codes
alternatives.text: Fringe readings find pagan star maps in the cycles; art historians read standard Orthodox programmes.

entries.title: Valley of the Thracian Kings
entries.mainstream: The Valley of the Thracian Kings near Kazanlak, Bulgaria, holds richly furnished tombs of Odrysian and other Thracian elites (roughly 5th–3rd centuries BCE), including the Kazanlak Tomb with its famous frescoes and the Golyama Kosmatka mound associated with Seuthes III. Gold wreathes, weapons and architecture show a powerful aristocratic culture often described by Greeks as both neighbouring and "other."

alternatives.label: Orphic afterlife maps
alternatives.text: Some interpret tomb art as Orphic initiation diagrams; others see elite banquet and hunt ideology.

alternatives.label: Atlantis of Thrace
alternatives.text: Popular books sometimes inflate Thracian tombs into a lost master civilisation beyond the archaeological polities.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Valley of the Thracian Rulers

entries.title: Cyril and Methodius and the Slavic liturgy
entries.mainstream: Brothers Constantine (Cyril) and Methodius of Thessalonica missionised among the Slavs in the 9th century, developing a Slavic script (Glagolitic) and translating scripture and liturgy. Their work in Great Moravia faced Frankish clerical opposition; their disciples later helped establish Slavic Christian culture in Bulgaria and beyond. They are patron saints of Europe and foundational for Orthodox Slavic literacy; Cyrillic script developed later from their tradition.

alternatives.label: Who invented Cyrillic
alternatives.text: Cyrillic is generally credited to disciples in Bulgaria/Preslav after Cyril's death, not to Cyril alone.

alternatives.label: Single overnight alphabet myth
alternatives.text: Popular timelines compress decades of script evolution into one miraculous event.

entries.title: The Amber Room
entries.mainstream: The Amber Room was a chamber panelled in amber, gold leaf and mirrors, first made in Prussia in the early 18th century and later installed at Catherine Palace near St Petersburg. Nazi forces looted it in 1941; the panels vanished in 1945 and remain missing despite searches. A full reconstruction opened at Catherine Palace in 2003. The loss is one of World War II's great art mysteries.

alternatives.label: Surviving cache theories
alternatives.text: Claims place the amber in mines, lagoons or private vaults; none has produced verified panels.

alternatives.label: Destroyed in bombing
alternatives.text: A leading hypothesis holds it burned in Königsberg Castle; absence of conclusive proof keeps alternate theories alive.

entries.changed: 2003 reconstructed room opened; original still missing.

media.title: Ellie Harrison discovers The Amber Room - The Treasure Hunters: Episode 2 Preview - BBC

entries.title: Falcon Lake incident (1967)
entries.mainstream: On 20 May 1967 industrialist Stefan Michalak reported encountering a landed craft near Falcon Lake, Manitoba; he claimed a grid-like exhaust burn on his chest and illness afterward. RCMP and UFOs investigators documented a burned site and medical visits; explanations range from a non-human craft to a hoax or accident with conventional materials. It remains Canada's best-known close-encounter injury case.

alternatives.label: Physical craft
alternatives.text: UFO researchers treat the burn pattern and soil samples as physical evidence; sceptics note possible fabrication and inconsistent details.

alternatives.label: Secret military test
alternatives.text: Another hypothesis posits an unacknowledged experimental vehicle; no declassified confirmation has appeared.

entries.title: Solway Firth Spaceman photograph (1964)
entries.mainstream: On 23 May 1964 Jim Templeton photographed his daughter near the Solway Firth, England; one frame shows a white figure in what looks like a spacesuit behind her. Templeton said no one was there. Kodak reportedly confirmed the photo was not manipulated. Explanations include an unnoticed person with their back turned (often Templeton's wife in a light dress), overexposure effects, or—popularly—an alien visitor. It became a classic anomalous photograph.

alternatives.label: Wife-in-overexposed-dress
alternatives.text: The leading sceptical reconstruction identifies the figure as a person facing away, washed out by the film; believers reject the match.

alternatives.label: Men in black visit
alternatives.text: Templeton reported odd interrogators; that episode is anecdotal and unverified.

entries.title: JWST and unexpectedly early galaxies
entries.mainstream: Since 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope has reported numerous high-redshift galaxy candidates that appear more massive or mature than many pre-launch models expected so soon after the Big Bang. Follow-up spectroscopy has confirmed some redshifts while revising others downward. The tension fuels productive debate over galaxy formation, initial mass functions and cosmological assumptions—not a collapse of the Big Bang framework.

alternatives.label: Cosmology crisis
alternatives.text: Popular headlines sometimes claim JWST disproved the Big Bang; researchers instead test and refine formation models within ΛCDM or mild extensions.

alternatives.label: Electric universe / alternative cosmologies
alternatives.text: Non-standard cosmologies cite JWST as vindication; mainstream papers treat the data as astrophysical puzzles under active measurement.

entries.changed: Deep-field galaxy candidates reported from 2022 onward; spectroscopic follow-up ongoing.

media.title: We Found Galaxies Too Old for the Universe

entries.title: Dinosaur soft tissue claims (Schweitzer)
entries.mainstream: In 2005 Mary Schweitzer and colleagues reported flexible soft-tissue-like structures and vessels from a Tyrannosaurus rex femur (Science). Later papers claimed proteins and other residues in Mesozoic bones. The work challenged assumptions about fossilisation speed. Critics argue for biofilms, contamination or chemical artifacts; supporters defend endogenous original material. The debate continues in the technical literature.

alternatives.label: Young-Earth reading
alternatives.text: Creationist authors cite soft tissue as proof dinosaurs lived recently; Schweitzer and most paleontologists reject that and argue for exceptional preservation chemistry over deep time.

alternatives.label: Full original tissue
alternatives.text: Media sometimes imply fresh flesh; the finds are degraded, mineral-associated structures and molecular signals, not butcher-ready meat.

entries.changed: 2005 Science paper ignited ongoing preservation debate.

entries.title: Kelly–Hopkinsville encounter (1955)
entries.mainstream: On the night of 21–22 August 1955 the Sutton family near Kelly and Hopkinsville, Kentucky, reported being besieged by small glowing beings after a sighting of a bright object. Police found shell casings and shaken witnesses but no creatures. The case entered UFO lore as a "goblin" encounter and later inspired fiction; explanations include meteors, owls, hoax or genuine unknown entities.

alternatives.label: Hobgoblin aliens
alternatives.text: UFO literature treats it as a close-encounter of the third kind; sceptical analyses favour misidentified animals and fear contagion.

alternatives.label: Military cover-up
alternatives.text: No solid evidence of a recovered craft has emerged despite decades of rumour.

entries.title: Karahan Tepe
entries.mainstream: Karahan Tepe, in Şanlıurfa Province, Turkey, is a Pre-Pottery Neolithic site related to the Taş Tepeler cluster that includes Göbekli Tepe. Excavations have revealed carved human faces, phallic pillars and communal structures dated to roughly the 10th–9th millennia BCE. It strengthens the picture of early ceremonial complexity in southeast Anatolia before agriculture fully dominated.

alternatives.label: Sister city of Göbekli
alternatives.text: Popular media pairs the sites as twin temples; each has distinct architecture and use-life despite regional links.

alternatives.label: Lost ice-age metropolis
alternatives.text: Fringe narratives scale Karahan Tepe into a continent-spanning civilisation; the excavated footprint is substantial but regional.

entries.changed: Excavations and public reporting accelerated in the 2010s–2020s.

media.title: Did Civilisation Begin At Karahan Tepe? - Humanity before Göbekli Tepe // Prehistory Documentary

entries.title: Wolfsegg Iron (Salzburg Cube)
entries.mainstream: The Wolfsegg Iron is a small iron object reportedly found in a Tertiary coal block at Wolfsegg am Hausruck, Austria, in the 19th century and once displayed as an out-of-place artifact. Analyses have generally identified it as cast iron consistent with mining equipment or a meteoritic/industrial miscellany rather than an ancient machined cube. It remains a staple of OOPArt lists.

alternatives.label: Machined ancient cube
alternatives.text: Alternative authors claim precision workmanship from before humans; metallurgical assessments favour modern cast iron.

alternatives.label: Meteorite core
alternatives.text: An older museum label tradition suggested meteoritic origin; composition studies have not established a famous exotic alloy.

entries.title: Burrows Cave
entries.mainstream: Burrows Cave refers to a claimed cave in Illinois from which Russell Burrows said he recovered hundreds of inscribed stones with apparent Near Eastern and other Old World motifs beginning in the 1980s. Professional archaeologists who have examined the claims treat the stones as modern fakes and note that no verified cave locus has been produced under controlled conditions. The affair is a well-known Midwestern archaeological hoax narrative.

alternatives.label: Hidden genuine cache
alternatives.text: Supporters allege suppression by mainstream archaeology; no peer-reviewed excavation has validated the site.

alternatives.label: Pre-Columbian contact proof
alternatives.text: Even if motifs look Mediterranean, fabrication better explains the assemblage than rewriting American prehistory.

entries.title: Kecksburg UFO incident (1965)
entries.mainstream: On 9 December 1965 a fireball was seen across the Great Lakes and northeastern US; residents of Kecksburg, Pennsylvania, reported an acorn-shaped object in the woods and a military recovery. The US Air Force listed it as a meteor; later FOIA-related attention and a NASA statement about a retrieved object that was not a spacecraft kept controversy alive. Unresolved claims include a Soviet Venus probe (Kosmos 96) re-entry—timeline problematic—or a secret US device.

alternatives.label: Alien craft
alternatives.text: Local lore and TV specials favour a non-human vehicle under military seal; hard public evidence is lacking.

alternatives.label: Meteor only
alternatives.text: Sceptics argue eyewitness embellishment layered onto a brilliant fireball; the acorn shape may be folkloric crystallisation.

entries.title: London Hammer (London Artifact)
entries.mainstream: The London Hammer is an iron-and-wood hammer said to have been found in Cretaceous limestone concretion near London, Texas, in 1936 (reported widely decades later). Young-Earth and OOPArt advocates call it a human tool sealed in ancient rock. Geologists note that mineral concretions can enclose recent objects, and the hammer's style matches 19th-century tools—so the find does not demonstrate humans in the Cretaceous.

alternatives.label: Cretaceous tool
alternatives.text: Creationist exhibits present it as proof of modern humans among dinosaurs; mainstream geology rejects the dating inference from the concretion alone.

alternatives.label: Planted hoax
alternatives.text: Some critics suggest deliberate planting; others accept a real find with misunderstood geology.

entries.title: Book of Kells
entries.mainstream: The Book of Kells is an illuminated Gospel book in Latin, produced by Columban monks around 800 CE, likely begun on Iona and completed or preserved at Kells in Ireland. Its carpet pages, Chi-Rho monogram and zoomorphic initials are masterpieces of Insular art. It is held at Trinity College Dublin and is among the most famous medieval manuscripts in the world.

alternatives.label: Exact place of production
alternatives.text: Scholars debate how much was made on Iona versus Kells or other Columban houses; Viking raids on Iona are often cited as context for moving the book.

alternatives.label: Encoded lost science
alternatives.text: Popular claims that the ornament hides advanced astronomy or alien contact go far beyond palaeographic and art-historical analysis.

entries.title: Hill of Tara
entries.dateNote: Neolithic activity from c. 3200 BCE; Iron Age floruit; literary high-kingship medieval
entries.mainstream: The Hill of Tara (Teamhair) in County Meath, Ireland, is a complex of monuments spanning Neolithic passage tombs (including the Mound of the Hostages) through Iron Age enclosures such as the Forrad and Tech Midchúarta earthworks. Early Irish literature casts Tara as the ceremonial seat of the High Kings. Archaeology shows long ritual and burial use rather than a single palace city.

alternatives.label: Capital of a high-kingship
alternatives.text: Medieval kingship tales project a unified high-kingship onto a landscape that was ceremonial and contested over millennia.

alternatives.label: Energy vortex / star-gate claims
alternatives.text: New Age tourism sometimes describes Tara as a planetary energy centre; that is modern spiritual geography, not an archaeological finding.

media.title: Who Were The First People In Ireland? - Ancient Irish Prehistory Documentary

entries.title: Cú Chulainn
entries.mainstream: Cú Chulainn ("the Hound of Culann") is the youthful hero of the Ulster Cycle in early Irish literature, famed for the ríastrad (warp-spasm) battle frenzy and for single-handedly defending Ulster in the Táin Bó Cúailnge. Stories were written down in monastic manuscripts from roughly the 8th–12th centuries from older oral tradition. He remains a major figure in Irish cultural memory and nationalist iconography.

alternatives.label: Historic warrior kernel
alternatives.text: Some folklorists seek a remembered Iron Age champion behind the tales; the surviving texts are literary myth, not biography.

alternatives.label: Demigod or alien hybrid readings
alternatives.text: Modern fringe retellings cast his frenzy and weapons as non-human technology; medieval sources frame him as a hero with divine ancestry (Lugh).

media.title: The myth of Ireland's two greatest warriors - Iseult Gillespie

entries.title: Mabinogion
entries.dateNote: Medieval Welsh prose; Guest title 19th century
entries.mainstream: The Mabinogion is the modern collective name for prose tales from medieval Welsh manuscripts (notably the White Book of Rhydderch and Red Book of Hergest), including the Four Branches of the Mabinogi—Pwyll, Branwen, Manawydan and Math—plus native romances and other stories. Lady Charlotte Guest popularised the English title in the 19th century. The tales mix Otherworld journeys, shape-shifting and early Arthurian material.

alternatives.label: Oral depth vs manuscript date
alternatives.text: Surviving books are 14th-century and later; linguistic and comparative study suggests earlier narrative strata of uncertain age.

alternatives.label: Lost pan-Celtic bible
alternatives.text: Romantic Celticism sometimes treats the collection as a single sacred canon; it is a modern grouping of distinct medieval texts.

entries.title: Fionn mac Cumhaill
entries.dateNote: Mythic cycle; medieval to modern transmission
entries.mainstream: Fionn mac Cumhaill (Finn McCool) leads the Fianna in the Fenian Cycle of Irish tradition. Tales credit him with tasting the Salmon of Knowledge, forming a roaming warrior band, and feats later tied in folklore to the Giant's Causeway and other landscapes. Stories range from early medieval poetry to modern oral legend across Ireland and Scotland.

alternatives.label: Historic Fianna
alternatives.text: Some scholars see memories of young warrior freelancers in early Irish society; the supernatural biography is literary and folk myth.

alternatives.label: Giant builder myths
alternatives.text: Folklore that Fionn built the Causeway as a path to Scotland is etiological legend, not geology (the Causeway is Paleogene basalt).

media.title: The Irish myth of the Giant's Causeway - Iseult Gillespie

entries.title: Táin Bó Cúailnge (Cattle Raid of Cooley)
entries.mainstream: Táin Bó Cúailnge is the central epic of the Ulster Cycle: Queen Medb of Connacht invades Ulster to seize the brown bull Donn Cúailnge, opposed by the boy-hero Cú Chulainn while Ulster's men lie under a debility curse. Recensions survive in the Book of the Dun Cow, Book of Leinster and later manuscripts. It is often called Ireland's nearest equivalent to a national epic.

alternatives.label: Iron Age snapshot
alternatives.text: Some readings treat the Táin as a window on pagan Irish society; others stress Christian-era literary composition and satire.

alternatives.label: Suppressed historical war
alternatives.text: Fringe historicisers turn the cattle raid into a datable Bronze/Iron Age campaign; no independent chronicle confirms it.

media.title: The myth of Ireland's two greatest warriors - Iseult Gillespie

entries.title: Lindisfarne Gospels
entries.mainstream: The Lindisfarne Gospels are an Insular illuminated Latin Gospel book produced at the monastery of Lindisfarne (Holy Island) in Northumbria, traditionally associated with Bishop Eadfrith (d. 721). Carpet pages and evangelist portraits fuse Mediterranean, Anglo-Saxon and Celtic styles. A later Old English gloss by Aldred is among the earliest substantial English gospel translations. The manuscript is in the British Library.

alternatives.label: Single artist tradition
alternatives.text: Medieval colophon tradition credits Eadfrith; modern analysis allows workshop collaboration while still centering Lindisfarne.

alternatives.label: Hidden map codes
alternatives.text: Internet theories that the carpet pages encode maps or ET messages are not supported by art history.

entries.title: Iona Abbey
entries.mainstream: Iona, a small island off Mull in the Scottish Hebrides, was founded as a monastery by the Irish monk Columba (Colum Cille) in 563 CE and became a major centre of Gaelic Christianity, learning and stone carving (high crosses, grave slabs). Viking raids devastated the community; the medieval Benedictine abbey ruins were later restored by the Iona Community. It remains a pilgrimage and ecumenical site.

alternatives.label: Extent of Columba's mission
alternatives.text: Adomnán's Life of Columba is hagiography; archaeology and sculpture confirm a powerful early medieval monastery even where miracle tales do not.

alternatives.label: Celtic church conspiracies
alternatives.text: Claims of a secret non-Roman mystical church uniquely surviving on Iona oversimplify Insular Christianity's links to wider Latin Christendom.

media.title: Pilgrimage to Iona | Island Crossings | BBC Scotland

entries.title: Pictish symbol stones
entries.mainstream: Across eastern and northern Scotland, Pictish symbol stones bear distinctive abstract and animal motifs (crescent and V-rod, double disc and Z-rod, Pictish beast) carved from roughly the 6th–9th centuries, later often combined with Christian crosses. The symbols' meaning—names, ranks, clans, theology—remains undeciphered despite many theories. They are primary evidence for Pictish visual culture before Gaelicisation.

alternatives.label: Readable script vs emblems
alternatives.text: Most scholars treat the classic symbols as a non-alphabetic emblem system; ogham and Latin inscriptions on some stones are separate.

alternatives.label: Lost advanced script of Atlantis
alternatives.text: Fringe decipherments claiming full historical chronicles or alien lexicons have not gained academic acceptance.

entries.title: Manannán mac Lir
entries.mainstream: Manannán mac Lir is a sea god and Otherworld figure in Irish (and Manx) tradition, associated with mist, magical boats, the Isle of Man, and gifts of hospitality and illusion. He appears in early Irish literature (e.g. Immram Brain, Echtra Cormaic) and later folklore. Place-names and modern sculpture (e.g. at Gortmore) keep his cultic memory visible.

alternatives.label: Euhemerised king
alternatives.text: Medieval texts sometimes treat him as an ancestral ruler of Man; that sits beside clearly divine portrayals.

alternatives.label: Ancient astronaut ferryman
alternatives.text: Modern UFO-tinged retellings of his mist-shrouded voyages are contemporary overlays on medieval myth.

entries.title: Persepolis
entries.mainstream: Persepolis (Parsa), in Fars, Iran, was a ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire founded under Darius I from about 518–515 BCE, with apadana, gateways and reliefs of subject peoples bringing tribute. Alexander burned parts of the complex in 330 BCE. Excavations and the UNESCO World Heritage listing make it a centrepiece of ancient Iranian archaeology.

alternatives.label: Administrative vs ritual capital
alternatives.text: Scholars debate how far Persepolis was seasonal court theatre versus year-round bureaucracy; both ritual and archive functions are attested.

alternatives.label: Pre-Achaemenid mega-builders
alternatives.text: Ancient-astronaut and lost-civ claims that the stonework exceeds Achaemenid skill ignore documented Persian and subject-labour organisation.

entries.title: Sasanian Empire
entries.mainstream: The Sasanian Empire (224–651 CE), founded by Ardashir I after defeating the Parthians, was the last pre-Islamic Iranian empire, rival to Rome/Byzantium, with Zoroastrianism as state religion, major cities such as Ctesiphon, and rich silverwork, rock reliefs and scholarly centres. It fell to the Arab-Muslim conquests in the mid-7th century. Sasanian political and artistic models deeply influenced Islamic and Central Asian cultures.

alternatives.label: Religious uniformity
alternatives.text: Although Zoroastrian orthodoxy was promoted, Christians, Jews, Manichaeans and others lived under varying constraints; policy shifted by reign.

alternatives.label: Secret technological empire
alternatives.text: Nationalist and fringe narratives sometimes invent suppressed Sasanian super-science beyond the impressive but historically attested engineering and scholarship.

entries.title: Parthian Empire
entries.mainstream: The Parthian (Arsacid) Empire dominated the Iranian plateau and Mesopotamia from the mid-3rd century BCE until Ardashir's victory in 224 CE, mediating Silk Road trade and repeatedly fighting Rome (e.g. Carrhae, 53 BCE). Power was often decentralised among noble houses. Parthian art mixes Hellenistic and Iranian styles; sources are thinner than for Achaemenids or Sasanians.

alternatives.label: Nomad vs sedentary character
alternatives.text: Debate continues over how "steppe" versus urban-Iranian the Arsacid state was across its long history.

alternatives.label: Erased civilisation myths
alternatives.text: Some popular histories claim Parthia was systematically erased; fragmentary sources reflect Roman bias and later Sasanian rewriting more than a conspiracy of silence.

entries.title: Armenian alphabet (Mesrop Mashtots)
entries.mainstream: Tradition and historical sources credit the cleric Mesrop Mashtots, working with Catholicos Sahak Partev and under King Vramshapuh, with inventing the Armenian alphabet around 405 CE so scripture and liturgy could be written in Armenian. The script enabled a rapid golden age of translation and original literature. It remains central to Armenian identity in the homeland and diaspora.

alternatives.label: Sole inventor vs team
alternatives.text: Hagiography centres Mashtots; scholars also stress ecclesiastical and royal collaboration and possible models in Greek, Syriac and Pahlavi scripts.

alternatives.label: Pre-Mashtots secret script
alternatives.text: Claims of a fully developed earlier Armenian alphabet lack convincing pre-5th-century exemplars accepted by mainstream epigraphy.
