entries.title: Etchmiadzin Cathedral
entries.mainstream: Etchmiadzin (Ejmiatsin) Cathedral in Vagharshapat, Armenia, is the mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church. Tradition dates a foundation to the early 4th century under Gregory the Illuminator after King Tiridates III's conversion; the building was rebuilt and enlarged across centuries. It is part of a UNESCO World Heritage ensemble and a focal point of Armenian Christianity.

alternatives.label: Fabric of the earliest church
alternatives.text: The standing fabric is multi-period; the exact 4th-century footprint is debated even while the site's early Christian importance is secure.

alternatives.label: Heavenly descent myths literalised
alternatives.text: The name "Descent of the Only-Begotten" encodes Gregory's vision; treating it as a physical sky-landing is a category mistake.

entries.title: Shahnameh (Book of Kings)
entries.mainstream: The Shahnameh, completed by the poet Ferdowsi around 1010 CE, is a vast Persian epic recounting mythical and historical kings of Iran from creation to the Arab conquest. Drawing on earlier prose and oral traditions, it preserved pre-Islamic lore in New Persian and became a cornerstone of Iranian cultural identity, endlessly illustrated in manuscript painting.

alternatives.label: Historical chronicle vs epic
alternatives.text: The later Sasanian sections mix memory and legend; the mythical Pishdadian and Kayanian ages are literary, not datable history.

alternatives.label: Prophetic encoded timeline
alternatives.text: Esoteric readings that treat the poem as a secret chronology of lost epochs go beyond literary and historical scholarship.

media.title: Shahnameh: The Epic Of The Persian Kings | The Persians: A History Of Iran | BBC Select

entries.title: Mithraism (Mithraic mysteries)
entries.mainstream: Mithraism was a mystery religion popular among Roman soldiers and officials in the 1st–4th centuries CE, centred on the god Mithras slaying a bull (tauroctony) in underground mithraea. It shares a name with Iranian Mitra/Mithra but developed distinct Roman forms. It declined with the rise of Christianity; no complete Mithraic "bible" survives.

alternatives.label: Iranian continuity
alternatives.text: Scholars disagree on how directly Roman Mithraism descends from Iranian cult versus reinvention using Eastern names and motifs.

alternatives.label: Secret world government cult
alternatives.text: Conspiracy literature casts Mithraism as an unbroken elite cabal ruling modernity; ancient evidence shows a voluntary mystery cult, not a global state.

entries.title: Manichaeism
entries.dateNote: Founded mid-3rd century CE; organised communities into medieval era
entries.mainstream: Manichaeism was a dualist world religion founded by the prophet Mani in 3rd-century Sasanian Mesopotamia, blending Christian, Zoroastrian, Buddhist and Gnostic elements into a cosmic struggle of Light and Darkness. It spread from the Roman Empire to China along the Silk Roads before successive persecutions extinguished it as an organised church. Substantial texts survive from Turfan, the Medinet Madi codices and other finds.

alternatives.label: Mani as synthesising apostle
alternatives.text: Manichaeans presented Mani as the final seal of prophets; opponents called the system a heresy or foreign corruption.

alternatives.label: Suppressed true Christianity
alternatives.text: Some modern esoteric writers treat Manichaeism as the authentic suppressed gospel; historians see a distinct late antique religion.

entries.title: Taq Kasra (Arch of Ctesiphon)
entries.dateNote: Likely 6th century CE; earlier palace phases possible
entries.mainstream: Taq Kasra is the monumental brick barrel vault of the Sasanian palace at Ctesiphon (near modern Baghdad), among the largest unreinforced brick arches ever built. Often linked to Khosrow I (6th century), it symbolises Sasanian imperial architecture. Partial collapses and modern restoration efforts have marked its recent history.

alternatives.label: Exact builder and date
alternatives.text: Attribution wavers among Sasanian kings; a 6th-century context is commonly favoured.

alternatives.label: Impossible ancient concrete myths
alternatives.text: Claims that the vault requires lost proprietary concrete ignore skilled Sasanian brick vaulting techniques documented across Iran and Iraq.

entries.title: Pasargadae
entries.mainstream: Pasargadae, in Fars, Iran, was the first dynastic capital of Cyrus the Great (r. c. 559–530 BCE), with gardens, gatehouses and the tomb traditionally ascribed to Cyrus. Greek authors and inscriptions anchor the site in early Achaemenid history. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a key complement to later Persepolis.

alternatives.label: Tomb identification
alternatives.text: The gabled stone tomb is conventionally Cyrus's; absolute proof is circumstantial but widely accepted.

alternatives.label: Older cyclopean civilisation
alternatives.text: Fringe tours sometimes redate the masonry to a pre-Cyrus mega-culture; mainstream chronology places the complex in the mid-6th century BCE.

entries.title: Orisha: Yoruba divine beings
entries.dateNote: Living tradition with deep precolonial roots
entries.mainstream: Orisha (òrìṣà) are divine beings and forces in Yoruba religion of West Africa, each linked to domains such as thunder (Ṣàngó), the sea (Yemoja), fate and wisdom (Ifá/Ọ̀rúnmìlà), and iron (Ogun). Worship involves shrines, possession dance, offerings and ethics of character (ìwà). The system travelled with the Atlantic diaspora into Candomblé, Santería/Lucumí and related traditions.

alternatives.label: Gods vs ancestors vs forces
alternatives.text: Theological descriptions vary: orisha may be described as divinities, elevated ancestors, or faces of a single ultimate reality (Olódùmarè).

alternatives.label: Ancient astronaut orisha
alternatives.text: Internet lore sometimes casts orisha as extraterrestrials; that is not a traditional Yoruba framing.

media.title: African Pantheons and the Orishas: Crash Course World Mythology #11

entries.title: Oduduwa: progenitor of the Yoruba
entries.dateNote: Mythic charter; Ifẹ̀ urban florescence roughly 1st–15th centuries CE
entries.mainstream: Oduduwa is the culture hero and ancestral figure credited in Yoruba tradition with founding Ilé-Ifẹ̀ and fathering lineages of Yoruba kings. Myths variously describe descent from the sky with a chain and sand to create land, or migration from elsewhere. Ifẹ̀ remains a sacred centre; Oduduwa's story anchors dynastic legitimacy across Yorubaland.

alternatives.label: Historical migrant founder
alternatives.text: Some historians seek a real early leader or migrant group behind the myth; archaeology of Ifẹ̀ shows urban complexity without confirming a single biography.

alternatives.label: Lost high technology at Ifẹ̀
alternatives.text: Bronze and terracotta heads of Ifẹ̀ inspire exaggerated claims of impossible tech; they fit sophisticated West African lost-wax and ceramic traditions.

entries.title: Ifá divination
entries.dateNote: Living system; classical corpora crystallised over centuries
entries.mainstream: Ifá is a Yoruba divination and wisdom system in which trained babaláwo cast palm nuts or a chain to produce one of 256 odù, each with extensive verse corpora (ese Ifá) guiding ethics and decision-making. UNESCO has recognised Ifá as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Related systems appear in Afro-Atlantic religions.

alternatives.label: Age and origin
alternatives.text: Verses encode centuries of accumulation; claims of a single antediluvian author are theological, not historical datings.

alternatives.label: Binary computer prophecy
alternatives.text: Popular essays liken Ifá's 256 odù to digital bits; the analogy is suggestive but Ifá is a ritual-hermeneutic practice, not a silicon algorithm.

entries.title: Lautaro and Mapuche resistance
entries.dateNote: Lautaro active 1550s; wider Arauco War centuries-long
entries.mainstream: Lautaro (Leftraru, d. 1557) was a Mapuche military leader who, after time as a captive of the Spanish, helped organise resistance in the Arauco War in Chile, notably contributing to the defeat and death of Pedro de Valdivia. Mapuche polities maintained independence in large areas south of the Bío-Bío for centuries. Lautaro became a national and indigenous symbol of resistance.

alternatives.label: Unity of "the Mapuche"
alternatives.text: Mapuche-speaking groups were politically diverse; colonial and modern labels simplify fluid alliances.

alternatives.label: Hidden undefeated empire
alternatives.text: Romantic accounts sometimes invent a single Mapuche empire ruling the Southern Cone; the historical picture is of resilient, decentralised resistance.

entries.title: Guaraní Land without Evil (Yvy Maraëy)
entries.dateNote: Living mythic-ritual theme; documented especially from colonial era onward
entries.mainstream: Among Guaraní peoples of the Atlantic forests and hinterlands of South America, Yvy Maraëy ("Land without Evil") is a longed-for perfect land free of suffering, sought through prophecy, migration and ritual. Colonial and Jesuit-period sources and modern ethnography record messianic journeys toward that horizon. The theme shaped responses to conquest and mission life.

alternatives.label: Geographic destination
alternatives.text: Some movements sought a literal earthly paradise to the east or across water; others treat the Land as a spiritual state.

alternatives.label: Pre-Columbian map of Atlantis
alternatives.text: Fringe writers sometimes equate Yvy Maraëy with Atlantis or ET refuges; ethnography places it in Guaraní cosmology and colonial-era prophecy.

entries.title: Tiwanaku
entries.dateNote: Major florescence c. 500–1000 CE; earlier occupations
entries.mainstream: Tiwanaku (Tiahuanaco), near Lake Titicaca in Bolivia, was a major Andean ceremonial and urban centre flourishing roughly 500–1000 CE (with earlier phases), famed for monumental gateways (Gateway of the Sun), precisely cut andesite blocks, and a wide cultural sphere. It collapsed before the Inca rise; the Inca and modern Aymara reclaim its memory. Distinct from the nearby Pumapunku complex sector often highlighted in alternative media.

alternatives.label: Absolute chronology
alternatives.text: Radiocarbon and ceramic sequences have revised older diffusionist dates; debate continues on exact peak and collapse causes (climate, politics).

alternatives.label: Alien precision stonework
alternatives.text: Ancient-astronaut claims that Tiwanaku's joints require non-human tools are rejected by Andean archaeology, which documents skilled quarrying and dressing.

media.title: Tiwanaku: Spiritual and Political Centre of the  ... (UNESCO/NHK)

entries.title: Kalevala
entries.mainstream: The Kalevala is Finland's national epic, compiled and shaped by Elias Lönnrot from Karelian and Finnish oral rune songs and published in 1835 (expanded 1849). It recounts heroes such as Väinämöinen, Lemminkäinen and the forging and theft of the Sampo. The work crystallised Finnish literary identity under Russian imperial rule and influenced art, music (Sibelius) and later fantasy literature.

alternatives.label: How much is "folk" vs Lönnrot
alternatives.text: Lönnrot edited, ordered and sometimes composed linking material; the poem is both folklore anthology and literary creation.

alternatives.label: Ice Age memory chronicle
alternatives.text: Speculative readings treat the Kalevala as a literal Ice Age history; mainstream folkloristics sees mythic and shamanic themes, not a dated chronicle.

entries.changed: First edition 1835; "new" Kalevala 1849.

media.title: The myth of the Sampo— an infinite source of fortune and greed - Hanna-Ilona Härmävaara

entries.title: Väinämöinen
entries.dateNote: Oral mythic figure; epic form 19th century
entries.mainstream: Väinämöinen is the eternal sage-singer and culture hero of Finnish–Karelian myth, central to the Kalevala: born of the Air Maiden Ilmatar, he shapes land, courts with song-magic, and vies for the Sampo. He embodies the power of the sung word (runo). Related figures appear across Baltic-Finnic tradition beyond Lönnrot's epic.

alternatives.label: Historic shaman
alternatives.text: Some interpreters see a remembered ritual specialist behind the figure; evidence is comparative folklore, not a biography.

alternatives.label: Alien sky-singer
alternatives.text: Modern fringe casts his heavenly origins as spacecraft myth; traditional songs speak of primordial waters and song-magic.

media.title: The myth of the Sampo— an infinite source of fortune and greed - Hanna-Ilona Härmävaara

entries.title: Kingdom of Kongo
entries.mainstream: The Kingdom of Kongo was a Central African state around the lower Congo River, prominent from the late 14th century, with its capital at M'banza-Kongo. It established early diplomatic and religious ties with Portugal after 1483, adopted Christianity at the elite level, and later suffered from the Atlantic slave trade and internal fragmentation. Its history is unusually well documented for sub-Saharan Africa in this period.

alternatives.label: Degree of conversion
alternatives.text: Christianity mixed with local religious practice; Portuguese sources often overstated or misunderstood Kongolese Christianity.

alternatives.label: Hidden Egyptian colony myths
alternatives.text: Afrocentrist fringe sometimes derives Kongo institutions straight from pharaonic Egypt without linguistic or archaeological support for direct colonisation.

media.title: Kongo and the Scramble for Africa - History Of Africa with Zeinab Badawi [Episode 19]

entries.title: Swahili coast city-states
entries.mainstream: From the later first millennium CE, Swahili-speaking Muslim city-states along East Africa's coast—such as Kilwa, Mombasa, Lamu and others—linked inland African trade to the Indian Ocean world of Arabia, Persia and India. Coral-stone mosques, Chinese porcelain and the Kilwa Chronicle attest to cosmopolitan wealth. Portuguese intervention from 1498 disrupted but did not erase Swahili urban culture.

alternatives.label: African vs "Arab colony" origins
alternatives.text: Older colonial scholarship overstated foreign founders; archaeology emphasises African coastal societies adopting Islam and overseas styles.

alternatives.label: Lost white civilisation myths
alternatives.text: Some 19th–20th century racist theories denied African agency at sites like Kilwa; they are discredited.

media.title: Coast and Conquest - History Of Africa with Zeinab Badawi [Episode 12]

entries.title: Phantom time hypothesis (Heribert Illig)
entries.mainstream: The phantom time hypothesis, promoted by Heribert Illig from the early 1990s, claims that roughly AD 614–911 were invented, compressing the early Middle Ages and making Charlemagne largely fictional. Mainstream historians reject it: it conflicts with dendrochronology, ice cores, Islamic, Byzantine and Chinese synchronisms, and abundant documentary and archaeological evidence for the 7th–9th centuries.

alternatives.label: Calendar conspiracy
alternatives.text: Illig argues papal and imperial calendar manipulation fabricated three centuries; specialists find no such coordinated fabrication mechanism.

alternatives.label: Partial revisionism
alternatives.text: A few writers soft-pedal full phantom time while still doubting Carolingian scale; professional medieval studies does not accept the core claim.

entries.changed: Hypothesis popularised from 1991; academic rejection followed.

entries.title: Fomenko's New Chronology
entries.dateNote: Developed late 20th century; books widely circulated from 1980s–2000s
entries.mainstream: Anatoly Fomenko and collaborators' "New Chronology" claims that conventional ancient and medieval history is a duplicated, wildly misdated construct and that most of "ancient" history happened after roughly 1000 CE. The theory uses statistical parallels among king-lists and radical redating rejected by historians, archaeologists and physicists. It remains popular in some Russian popular markets.

alternatives.label: Statistical proof of duplication
alternatives.text: Critics argue the methods find spurious parallels and ignore material culture, radiometric dating and independent chronologies.

alternatives.label: Western cover-up narrative
alternatives.text: Advocates claim academia hides the truth to protect ideology; consensus sees a fringe rewriting incompatible with global evidence.

entries.title: Tartarian Empire / mud-flood myth
entries.dateNote: Modern internet myth; "Tartary" as map label early modern
entries.mainstream: Internet conspiracy culture since the 2010s has imagined a technologically advanced "Tartarian Empire" erased by a world-wide "mud flood," reinterpreting Beaux-Arts and exposition architecture as stolen Tartarian ruins. Historians note that "Tartary" was a vague early-modern European label for Inner Asian lands, not a single lost super-civilisation, and that mud-flood claims ignore ordinary urban stratigraphy and building records.

alternatives.label: Misread maps
alternatives.text: Old maps marking "Tartaria" are treated as proof of a unified empire; cartography used the term for poorly known regions.

alternatives.label: Free-energy architecture
alternatives.text: Some strands claim Tartaria had free energy buried by elites; no engineering evidence supports the claim.

entries.title: Origins of Freemasonry
entries.dateNote: Grand Lodge 1717; roots in earlier lodge culture
entries.mainstream: Speculative Freemasonry emerged publicly with the Grand Lodge of England in 1717, drawing on earlier stonemasons' lodge customs, Enlightenment sociability and invented legendary histories tying the craft to Solomon's Temple and ancient mystery schools. Documented lodge minutes and constitutions (e.g. Anderson's, 1723) anchor the modern fraternity. How far operative medieval masonry continuously became speculative Masonry remains debated among historians.

alternatives.label: Ancient unbroken mystery school
alternatives.text: Masonic legend and some esoteric writers claim direct descent from Egypt, Templars or mystery cults; professional history finds 17th–18th century crystallisation with imaginative pedigrees.

alternatives.label: World-control cabal
alternatives.text: Conspiracy literature treats Masonry as a single occult government; membership was influential in some eras but not a monolithic secret state.

entries.title: Valensole UFO encounter (1965)
entries.mainstream: On 1 July 1965, farmer Maurice Masse reported seeing an egg-shaped craft and two small beings in a lavender field near Valensole in southern France; he described paralysis and later plant damage in the field. French UFO investigators (including GEPAN-era attention in later literature) catalogued the case. Explanations range from a close encounter of the third kind to a misperceived conventional event or hoax.

alternatives.label: Physical traces
alternatives.text: Supporters cite flattened plants and Masse's consistency; sceptics note the limits of anecdotal and agricultural evidence.

alternatives.label: Official disclosure withheld
alternatives.text: Some ufologists claim French authorities confirmed non-human craft privately; public scientific consensus remains unestablished.

entries.changed: Reported 1 July 1965.

entries.title: Trans-en-Provence UFO case (1981)
entries.mainstream: On 8 January 1981, farmer Renato Nicolai reported a saucer-like craft landing and taking off on his property at Trans-en-Provence, France. GEPAN (the French CNES UFO study unit) analysed soil and plant samples and published a report often cited by ufologists as among the best-documented physical-trace cases. Sceptics argue the traces could have mundane causes and that single-witness limits remain.

alternatives.label: GEPAN validation
alternatives.text: Ufologists treat the official sampling as strong anomalous evidence; critics say the agency never proved an extraterrestrial craft.

alternatives.label: Military test device
alternatives.text: Alternative mundane hypotheses include a terrestrial experimental craft or misidentified equipment.

entries.changed: Incident 8 January 1981; GEPAN report followed.

entries.title: Hudson Valley UFO sightings (1980s)
entries.mainstream: From about 1982–1986 (peak publicity 1983–84), thousands of people in New York's Hudson Valley reported large, silent, V- or boomerang-shaped lights moving slowly across the night sky. Investigators documented many witnesses; explanations include ultralight formations, small-plane hoaxes, and unidentified phenomena. It is one of the largest mass-sighting waves in modern US ufology.

alternatives.label: Coordinated ultralight pilots
alternatives.text: A leading sceptical explanation points to groups of pilots flying in formation with lights; not all witnesses accept that account.

alternatives.label: Craft of non-human origin
alternatives.text: Ufologists argue size, silence and manoeuvres exceed ultralights; no public physical craft was recovered.

entries.title: Belgian UFO wave (1989–90)
entries.mainstream: From November 1989 through 1990, Belgium experienced a wave of reports of large silent triangular craft, including a well-known 30 March 1990 night when Belgian Air Force F-16s were scrambled after radar locks. SOBEPS and official statements fuelled international attention; later analyses disputed radar interpretations and photograph authenticity (notably a famous triangular object photo). The wave remains contested.

alternatives.label: Radar-visual confirmation
alternatives.text: Supporters cite military radar and pilot reports; sceptics argue locks were spurious or conventional and photos were faked or misread.

alternatives.label: NATO black-project aircraft
alternatives.text: Another mundane hypothesis posits secret terrestrial aircraft tests during the late Cold War.

entries.title: Sayburç (Taş Tepeler)
entries.mainstream: Sayburç is a Pre-Pottery Neolithic site in Şanlıurfa Province, Turkey, part of the wider Taş Tepeler cluster related to Göbekli Tepe. Excavations have revealed a communal building with stone benches and a striking carved male figure holding its genitalia beside animals—key evidence for early monumental art and ritual. It helps show Göbekli Tepe was not unique but part of a regional florescence.

alternatives.label: Function of the buildings
alternatives.text: Debate continues over temple vs multi-use communal houses; feasting and ritual interpretations dominate.

alternatives.label: Oldest statue of a god
alternatives.text: Popular headlines sometimes declare a specific deity identity; archaeologists are cautious about naming gods from early Holocene iconography.

media.author: Natural Earth, Eylem Özdoğan, B. Köşker, K. Akdemir

entries.title: ʿAin Ghazal statues
entries.mainstream: ʿAin Ghazal, a major Neolithic settlement in modern Amman, Jordan, yielded caches of large plaster statues and busts (c. 8th–7th millennium BCE) with bitumen eyes and modelled bodies—among the earliest large-scale human statues. They were carefully buried and are now conserved in museums (including Jordan and the Louvre). The site illuminates Pre-Pottery Neolithic social and ritual life.

alternatives.label: Purpose of the figures
alternatives.text: Interpretations range from ancestor representations to deities or initiation figures; burial of the statues suggests formal decommissioning.

alternatives.label: Lost advanced civilisation portraits
alternatives.text: Fringe readings treat the stare of the statues as proof of a forgotten high culture or non-human teachers; archaeology places them in Levantine Neolithic communities.

media.title: Five Statues from Ain Ghazal, Jordan

entries.title: Great Temple of Yeha (Dʿmt)
entries.dateNote: Great Temple c. 7th century BCE (dates debated)
entries.mainstream: Yeha in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, preserves the Great Temple, a tall ashlar stone sanctuary usually dated to around the 7th century BCE, together with the nearby Grat Beal Gebri palace complex. Inscriptions and architecture show close links with the Sabaean culture of South Arabia, and Yeha is regarded as a centre of the pre-Aksumite kingdom of Dʿmt. It is often described as one of the oldest standing buildings in sub-Saharan Africa.

alternatives.label: Colony or local kingdom
alternatives.text: Older scholarship treated Dʿmt as a South Arabian colony; more recent work stresses a mixed Ethio-Sabaean elite drawing on strong local traditions.

alternatives.label: Lost Solomonic city
alternatives.text: Ethiopian tradition and popular writing sometimes link Yeha to the Queen of Sheba and Solomon; this is legend layered on a real pre-Aksumite site, not an archaeological finding.

entries.title: Fasil Ghebbi, Gondar
entries.mainstream: Fasil Ghebbi is the walled royal enclosure at Gondar, Ethiopia, begun by Emperor Fasilides (Fasil) after he made Gondar his capital around 1636. Successive emperors added castles, banqueting halls, churches and Fasilides' Bath, blending Ethiopian, Indian, Arab and Portuguese-influenced styles. Gondar remained the imperial capital until the mid-19th century, and the site was listed by UNESCO in 1979.

alternatives.label: Foreign builders
alternatives.text: Some accounts credit Portuguese or Indian masons for the castles; historians see foreign influence absorbed into a distinctly Ethiopian royal architecture.

alternatives.label: Folk legends of the founding
alternatives.text: Local stories say the site was chosen by prophecy or by following a buffalo to a lake; these are founding legends rather than documentary history.

entries.title: Tiya stelae
entries.mainstream: Tiya, in the Gurage zone of southern Ethiopia, is one of nine megalithic pillar sites in the Gurage Zone. Its stone pillars, 32 of them engraved with enigmatic symbols including swords, mark a burial complex and were listed by UNESCO in 1980. Excavations led by Roger Joussaume dated the site to roughly the 11th–13th centuries CE, with later estimates spanning the 10th–15th centuries; who built them is not recorded.

alternatives.label: Warrior tally markers
alternatives.text: The carved swords are often read as indicating warriors or the number of enemies killed; this remains an interpretation.

alternatives.label: "Gran's stones"
alternatives.text: Local people call such stelae Yegragn Dingay, "Gran's stone", crediting the 16th-century conqueror Ahmad Gragn; the monuments are centuries older than him, so this is a later folk attribution.

alternatives.label: Older lost culture
alternatives.text: Because the builders are unnamed in written records, some popular accounts assign the stelae to a vanished prehistoric people; excavations point to medieval burials, within a much older Ethiopian megalith tradition.

entries.title: Makuria and the Faras Cathedral frescoes
entries.dateNote: c. 6th century to c. 15th century CE
entries.mainstream: Makuria was a Christian Nubian kingdom on the middle Nile, with its capital at Old Dongola, from roughly the 6th century until about the 15th. After repelling Arab armies in 642 and 652 it concluded the Baqt treaty with Egypt, a trade-and-peace arrangement that lasted for centuries. When Lake Nasser was about to flood Lower Nubia, a Polish mission led by Kazimierz Michałowski (1961–64) uncovered over a hundred wall paintings in the cathedral at Faras, which are now in Warsaw and Khartoum.

alternatives.label: A forgotten African Christendom
alternatives.text: Historians emphasise how long Nubian Christianity endured and how little it features in general histories; the extent of its contacts with Byzantium and Ethiopia is still researched.

alternatives.label: Saved from the flood
alternatives.text: The Faras rescue is sometimes told as a near-miraculous recovery; it was part of the large UNESCO Nubia campaign, and much of the site itself now lies under the lake.

entries.title: Queen Gudit (Yodit)
entries.mainstream: Ethiopian tradition remembers Gudit (Yodit, 'Judith') as a queen who sacked Aksum and destroyed churches in the 10th century, bringing about the end of the Aksumite kingdom. The 10th-century geographer Ibn Hawqal mentions, without naming her, a queen who had seized power and devastated the country around that time. Her identity is unclear; one proposal identifies her with Masoba Warq, daughter of the last Aksumite king Dil Na'od. Her religion and even her existence as one person are debated, and the traditions about her appear to have taken centuries to reach their final form.

alternatives.label: Jewish or pagan queen
alternatives.text: Some traditions make her Jewish (linked with the Beta Israel); others identify her as a non-Christian ruler from the southern kingdom of Damot or from Agaw lands.

alternatives.label: Legend built on a real crisis
alternatives.text: Many historians accept a real 10th-century invasion led by a queen while treating the detailed legends about her motives and curses as later elaboration.

media.title: The Rise Of Aksum - History Of Africa With Zeinab Badawi [Episode 5]

entries.title: Famadihana (turning of the bones)
entries.dateNote: Present form perhaps since c. 17th century; origins debated
entries.mainstream: Famadihana is a funerary tradition of the Malagasy highlands, especially among the Merina and Betsileo, in which families open the ancestral tomb, rewrap the remains in fresh silk shrouds, and dance with them before returning them. It is usually held every five to seven years and is understood as honouring the ancestors (razana), whose spirits are believed to fully join the ancestral world only after the body's complete decomposition and proper ceremonies. Early missionaries discouraged it; the Catholic Church now regards it as cultural, while many Evangelical Christians have abandoned it. The Malagasy government forbids the rite for people who died of plague.

alternatives.label: Ancient or recent custom
alternatives.text: It may have taken its present form only around the 17th century, possibly adapting older double-funeral customs from Southeast Asia and Oceania brought by Madagascar's Austronesian settlers.

alternatives.label: Talking with the dead
alternatives.text: Participants describe the ritual as sustaining a living relationship with ancestors; this is a religious understanding, not an empirical claim.

media.title: Taking dead bodies for a dance in Madagascar - BBC News

entries.title: Royal Hill of Ambohimanga
entries.mainstream: Ambohimanga, a fortified hilltop village north of Antananarivo, was the spiritual and political seat of the Merina kings. From here Andrianampoinimerina (r. c. 1787–1810) began unifying the Imerina highlands, a process his son Radama I extended over much of Madagascar. The hill is still a pilgrimage site for ancestor veneration and was listed by UNESCO in 2001.

alternatives.label: Sacred city
alternatives.text: Merina tradition treats the hill as sacred and once forbade certain foods and outsiders; heritage bodies recognise it as a living religious landscape.

alternatives.label: Fixed founding date
alternatives.text: Oral royal genealogies give earlier origins for the settlement; the documented political rise belongs to the late 18th century.

media.title: Royal Hill of Ambohimanga, Madagascar | Africa’s Cultural Landmarks

entries.title: Hagia Sophia
entries.mainstream: Hagia Sophia in Istanbul was built for Emperor Justinian I between 532 and 537 by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, after the previous church burned in the Nika riots. Its vast dome partly collapsed in 558 and was rebuilt higher. It served as the cathedral of Constantinople for over 900 years, became a mosque after 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

alternatives.label: A priest inside the wall
alternatives.text: A Greek legend says a priest celebrating the liturgy as the Ottomans broke in vanished into a wall and will reappear when the city is Christian again; it is a folk legend of the conquest.

alternatives.label: Sacred geometry and acoustics
alternatives.text: Modern studies explore the acoustics and geometry of the dome; claims of encoded esoteric knowledge go beyond the architectural evidence.

entries.title: Fall of Constantinople (1453)
entries.mainstream: On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman army of Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople after a siege of about 53 days, ending the Byzantine Empire; the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, died in the fighting. The Ottomans used large bombards, including guns cast by the engineer Orban, and dragged ships overland into the Golden Horn to bypass its defensive chain. The city became the Ottoman capital.

alternatives.label: The Kerkoporta gate
alternatives.text: Doukas reports that a small postern gate left open let the attackers in; some historians doubt the story or think it was minor.

alternatives.label: The sleeping emperor
alternatives.text: Greek legend says Constantine XI was turned to marble by an angel and will awaken to retake the city, a sleeping-hero motif shared with many cultures.

media.title: The city of walls: Constantinople - Lars Brownworth

entries.title: Nika riots (532)
entries.mainstream: In January 532 the Blue and Green chariot-racing factions of Constantinople united against Emperor Justinian I, shouting 'Nika!' ('Conquer!'), burning much of the city including the church of Hagia Sophia, and proclaiming Hypatius emperor. According to Procopius, Empress Theodora persuaded Justinian not to flee. The generals Belisarius and Mundus trapped the crowd in the Hippodrome, and Procopius reports around 30,000 deaths.

alternatives.label: Theodora's speech
alternatives.text: Her famous line that "royalty is a good burial shroud" comes from Procopius, who may have shaped it rhetorically.

alternatives.label: Size of the massacre
alternatives.text: The figure of 30,000 comes from ancient authors and cannot be checked independently; it may be exaggerated.

entries.title: Karakorum, Mongol capital
entries.mainstream: Karakorum, in the Orkhon Valley of Mongolia, was founded as a base by Genghis Khan around 1220 and walled as the imperial capital under Ögedei in 1235. The Franciscan William of Rubruck, who visited in 1254, described a quarter for Muslims and Chinese, many temples and a silver tree fountain made by the captive Parisian goldsmith Guillaume Boucher, an automaton in which a trumpeting angel signalled serpents to pour out drinks. Kublai moved the capital to Dadu (Beijing); Ming armies damaged the city in 1372 and razed it in 1380, and in 1585 the Erdene Zuu monastery was built beside it, largely from Karakorum's stones and bricks.

alternatives.label: Silver tree fountain
alternatives.text: Rubruck's description is the only detailed account; its mechanics are reconstructed from his text.

alternatives.label: Cosmopolitan capital
alternatives.text: Excavations confirm workshops, a palace area and mixed communities, supporting Rubruck while correcting some of his details.

entries.title: Secret History of the Mongols
entries.mainstream: The Secret History of the Mongols is the oldest surviving literary work in Mongolian, written for the royal family after Genghis Khan's death (often dated to 1228 or 1240). It traces his ancestry to a blue-grey wolf and a fallow doe and tells how the widow Alan Gua conceived sons by a shining yellow man who came in through the smoke-hole of her tent. It then narrates Temüjin's rise to become Genghis Khan. It survives mainly in a Chinese-character transcription made in the Ming period.

alternatives.label: History or epic
alternatives.text: Historians use it as a key source on Genghis Khan's life while recognising its epic, partisan and legendary layers.

alternatives.label: Light-being ancestor
alternatives.text: Ancient-astronaut writers have read the shining visitor of Alan Gua as an extraterrestrial; scholars see a sky-born royal origin myth common to Inner Asian dynasties.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Secret History of the Mongols

media.title: Who was Genghis Khan? (Full Episode) | Secret History of the Mongols | National Geographic

entries.title: Mal'ta boy (MA-1)
entries.mainstream: The Mal'ta boy is the skeleton of a child buried about 24,000 years ago at Mal'ta near Lake Baikal in Siberia, a site also known for ivory figurines of women and birds. His genome, published in 2013, showed that he belonged to a population related to western Eurasians and that this population contributed an estimated 14–38% of the ancestry of Native Americans. The result reshaped models of how the Americas were peopled.

alternatives.label: Western Eurasians in the Americas
alternatives.text: Early fringe readings claimed the genome proved Europeans reached America first; the data show deep shared ancestry in Siberia, not a European migration.

alternatives.label: Ancient North Eurasians
alternatives.text: Geneticists now call this lineage "Ancient North Eurasian" and also find it in later Europeans, linking peoples on both sides of the world.

sources.title: Upper Palaeolithic Siberian genome reveals dual ancestry of Native Americans

entries.title: Orkhon inscriptions
entries.mainstream: The Orkhon inscriptions are memorial stelae erected in the Orkhon Valley of Mongolia in 732 and 735 for the Second Turkic Khaganate prince Kül Tigin and his brother Bilge Khagan. Written in the Old Turkic runiform script (with a Chinese text on one), they are the oldest known extended texts in a Turkic language. Found by Nikolai Yadrintsev's expedition in 1889, the script was deciphered by the Danish linguist Vilhelm Thomsen in 1893.

alternatives.label: Origins of the script
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether the Old Turkic letters derive from Sogdian/Aramaic models, tamga clan signs, or both.

alternatives.label: Runes of a lost world-empire
alternatives.text: Because the script resembles Germanic runes, some fringe writers have linked the two; linguists treat the resemblance as superficial.

entries.title: Patomskiy crater
entries.dateNote: Formation estimated at c. 300 years ago (dendrochronology)
entries.mainstream: The Patomskiy crater is a cone of broken limestone about 40 m high and 160 m across with a central mound, in the forest of Irkutsk Oblast, Siberia. It was reported in 1949 by the geologist Vadim Kolpakov, and tree-ring studies suggest it formed only about 300 years ago. Local Yakut people called it the 'fire eagle's nest'. Its origin is still debated.

alternatives.label: Deep-fluid eruption
alternatives.text: A study by V. S. Antipin and A. M. Fedorov argued from its shape, structure and chemistry that it is volcanic in origin, formed by a rapid outburst of deep fluids and gases (CO2, water, CO, hydrogen).

alternatives.label: Meteorite or Tunguska fragment
alternatives.text: Early theories proposed an impact, including a fragment linked to Tunguska; the lack of meteoritic material makes this unlikely.

alternatives.label: Alien or secret-weapon site
alternatives.text: Popular media have suggested alien activity or Soviet secrets; no evidence supports these ideas.

entries.title: Andrée's Arctic balloon expedition
entries.mainstream: On 11 July 1897 Salomon August Andrée, Nils Strindberg and Knut Frænkel launched the hydrogen balloon Örnen ('Eagle') from Svalbard to try to fly over the North Pole. The balloon came down on the pack ice after about two days, and the men trekked for months before dying on Kvitøya (White Island). Their camp, diaries and exposed film were found by chance by the Bratvaag expedition in 1930, and the photographs were developed, revealing images of the doomed journey.

alternatives.label: Cause of death
alternatives.text: Proposals include trichinosis from polar-bear meat, cold, vitamin A poisoning, carbon-monoxide poisoning and exhaustion; none is proven.

alternatives.label: Hero or reckless venture
alternatives.text: The men were mourned as national heroes in Sweden; later historians stress the known leakiness of the balloon and Andrée's optimism.

entries.title: Zhokhov Island Arctic hunters and sled dogs
entries.dateNote: c. 9,000–8,000 years ago (Wikipedia gives occupation from c. 6000 BCE)
entries.mainstream: On Zhokhov Island in the New Siberian Islands, far above the Arctic Circle, archaeologists led by Vladimir Pitulko excavated a Mesolithic camp, about 9,000–8,000 years old, where people hunted polar bears and reindeer. The site preserved remains of dogs, sledge runners and tools. A 2020 genomic study showed that a roughly 9,500-year-old dog from Zhokhov belongs to an Arctic-adapted lineage ancestral to modern sled dogs, suggesting dog sledding is at least 9,500 years old.

alternatives.label: Earliest sled dogs
alternatives.text: Most researchers accept the genetic and archaeological case; some caution that sledge use is inferred from parts and dog morphology.

alternatives.label: A vanished land bridge
alternatives.text: At the time sea levels were lower and Zhokhov was part of a larger landmass; the people are sometimes romanticised as a lost Arctic civilisation, but they were a mobile hunting group.

sources.title: Arctic-adapted dogs emerged at the Pleistocene–Holocene transition

media.author: USGS/NASA Landsat Program; cropped by Fenix down

entries.title: Royal Cemetery at Ur and Queen Puabi
entries.mainstream: Leonard Woolley's excavations at Ur in southern Iraq (1922–34) uncovered about 1,800 graves, including some 16 'royal tombs' of around 2600–2500 BCE. Queen Puabi's tomb held an elaborate gold headdress, and the 'Great Death Pit' contained 74 attendants. Treasures included the Standard of Ur and the 'Ram in a Thicket'. CT scans of skulls published by the Penn Museum in 2009 suggest some attendants were killed by blows to the head.

alternatives.label: Willing sacrifice or execution
alternatives.text: Woolley pictured attendants drinking poison calmly; newer forensic work points to violent killing, though how widespread it was is debated.

alternatives.label: Woolley's flood
alternatives.text: Woolley claimed a thick silt layer at Ur was evidence of Noah's Flood; geologists see a local river flood, not a universal one.

media.author: Nic McPhee from Morris, Minnesota, USA
media.title: Queen_Puabi_with_attendants.jpg
Great Lyre from the "King's Grave," c. 2650-2550 B.C.E.

entries.title: Code of Hammurabi
entries.mainstream: The Code of Hammurabi is a Babylonian legal text inscribed around 1755–1750 BCE on a basalt stele that shows King Hammurabi receiving authority from the sun-god Shamash. It contains about 282 rulings, including 'eye for an eye' penalties that varied by social class. The stele was taken to Susa as war booty by an Elamite king in the 12th century BCE and was found there by a French expedition in 1901; it is now in the Louvre.

alternatives.label: Law code or royal showcase
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether it was applied in courts or was a model of royal justice; few surviving court records cite it.

alternatives.label: The first laws
alternatives.text: It is often called the first law code, but earlier codes such as those of Ur-Nammu and Lipit-Ishtar are known.

media.title: The Law Code Stele of King Hammurabi

entries.title: Kanesh (Kültepe) merchant archives
entries.mainstream: At Kültepe (ancient Kanesh) in central Turkey, excavations have yielded over 23,000 cuneiform tablets from the houses of Old Assyrian merchants, dating to about 1950–1750 BCE. The letters, contracts and lawsuits record donkey caravans carrying tin and textiles from Assur to Anatolia in exchange for silver and gold, along with family affairs run by women in Assur. Personal names in the texts are the earliest evidence of the Hittite (Nesite) language.

alternatives.label: An early market economy
alternatives.text: Some economists see private firms, credit and partnerships; others stress the role of family and state institutions.

alternatives.label: Lost Anatolian homeland
alternatives.text: The tablets inform debates about the origin of the Hittites and Indo-European languages in Anatolia, which remain unresolved.

entries.title: Poverty Point earthworks
entries.mainstream: Poverty Point in northeastern Louisiana is a complex of six concentric C-shaped earthen ridges and several large mounds built by hunter-fisher-gatherers between about 1700 and 1100 BCE. Mound A, one of the largest earthworks in North America, may have been built in a matter of months. Exotic stone from hundreds of kilometres away shows a wide exchange network, and the site was listed by UNESCO in 2014.

alternatives.label: Monuments without farming
alternatives.text: Poverty Point challenges the old assumption that only farming societies build large monuments, similar to Göbekli Tepe.

alternatives.label: Astronomical alignments
alternatives.text: Some researchers have proposed solstice alignments; these are debated and not widely accepted.

sources.title: UNESCO: Monumental Earthworks of Poverty Point

entries.title: Walam Olum
entries.mainstream: The Walam Olum was published in 1836 by the naturalist Constantine Rafinesque as a pictographic migration chronicle of the Lenape (Delaware) people, supposedly copied from painted sticks. For over a century it was cited as a genuine Native American historical record. Research by David Oestreicher in the 1990s showed it was a fabrication, most likely by Rafinesque himself, and Lenape leaders have rejected it.

alternatives.label: Genuine tradition
alternatives.text: A few defenders argued it preserved real oral history; linguistic analysis found it was built from dictionaries and contained errors.

alternatives.label: Part of the Mound Builder myth
alternatives.text: It was used to support theories that a lost race built the mounds; those theories are rejected.

entries.title: Sky Woman and Turtle Island
entries.dateNote: Oral tradition; recorded from the 17th century
entries.mainstream: In the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) creation story, Sky Woman falls from the Sky World through a hole beneath a great tree. Birds catch her, and animals dive for mud, which is spread on the back of a great turtle to become the land — Turtle Island. Her grandsons, the twins Sapling and Flint, shape the world. Similar 'earth-diver' myths are found across North America and Siberia.

alternatives.label: Shared earth-diver motif
alternatives.text: Folklorists suggest the motif may be very old and spread with early populations across the Bering region; others see independent invention.

alternatives.label: Star people
alternatives.text: Some modern writers link Sky Woman to ancient visitors from the stars; Haudenosaunee storytellers present her as a sacred origin figure.

entries.title: Newark Earthworks
entries.mainstream: The Newark Earthworks in Ohio are among the largest geometric earthworks in the world, built by people of the Hopewell culture between about 100 BCE and 400 CE; they cover what was once about 1,200 hectares, less than a tenth of which survives. They include a huge circle and an octagon whose alignments track the 18.6-year cycle of moonrises, as studied by Ray Hively and Robert Horn. In 2023 they were listed by UNESCO as part of the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks; part of the Octagon long served as a golf course.

alternatives.label: Lunar observatory
alternatives.text: The lunar alignment interpretation is widely respected but still discussed.

alternatives.label: The Newark Holy Stones
alternatives.text: In 1860 stones inscribed with Hebrew were "found" nearby, claimed as proof of lost Israelites; most scholars regard them as a hoax.

entries.title: Nemrut Dağ
entries.mainstream: On top of Mount Nemrut in southeastern Turkey, King Antiochus I of Commagene (r. c. 70–38 BCE) built a tomb-sanctuary with colossal seated statues of himself among Greek and Persian gods. A relief known as the Lion Horoscope shows a lion with stars and the planets Jupiter, Mercury and Mars, interpreted as a date. The site was found by the engineer Karl Sester in 1881 and listed by UNESCO in 1987. Antiochus' burial chamber has never been found.

alternatives.label: Dating the Lion Horoscope
alternatives.text: Proposals include 62 BCE and 109 BCE, linked to events in Antiochus' reign.

alternatives.label: A hidden chamber
alternatives.text: The tomb may lie beneath the rubble mound; searches have not found it.

entries.title: Messinian salinity crisis and Zanclean flood
entries.mainstream: Around 5.97–5.33 million years ago, the Mediterranean was largely cut off from the Atlantic and parts dried out, leaving salt layers over a kilometre thick. In the Zanclean flood, about 5.33 million years ago, the Atlantic broke through the Strait of Gibraltar. A 2009 Nature study suggested the basin may have refilled in a few years. The scale and speed of the drying and refilling are still debated.

alternatives.label: Catastrophic vs gradual refilling
alternatives.text: Some researchers argue for a slower refilling over thousands of years.

alternatives.label: Memory of the flood
alternatives.text: Fringe writers sometimes connect it to Atlantis or flood myths; humans did not exist then.

sources.title: Catastrophic flood of the Mediterranean after the Messinian salinity crisis

media.title: That Time the Mediterranean Sea Disappeared

entries.title: Jack Hills zircons
entries.mainstream: Tiny zircon crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, up to about 4.4 billion years old, are the oldest known pieces of Earth. A 2001 Nature study showed that their oxygen isotopes suggest liquid water and continental crust existed within 150 million years of Earth's formation. This challenged the old picture of an early Earth that was hot and molten for a long time.

alternatives.label: Cool early Earth
alternatives.text: The 2001 findings support a "cool early Earth"; some researchers still debate how widespread oceans and continents were.

alternatives.label: Early life
alternatives.text: A 2015 study found possibly biological carbon in a 4.1-billion-year-old zircon; this is still debated.

sources.title: Evidence from detrital zircons for the existence of continental crust and oceans on the Earth 4.4 Gyr ago

entries.title: Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
entries.mainstream: About 56 million years ago, a huge release of carbon caused global temperatures to rise by around 5–8 °C over a few thousand years. Oceans acidified, many deep-sea foraminifera died out, and early primates, horses and other mammals spread across the northern continents. It is studied as an ancient example of fast climate change.

alternatives.label: Cause
alternatives.text: Proposed causes include volcanism in the North Atlantic and the release of methane hydrates; a 2016 study suggested a comet impact, which is disputed.

alternatives.label: A model for today
alternatives.text: It is often compared with modern warming, but the rate of carbon release today appears faster.

sources.title: The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum: A Perturbation of Carbon Cycle, Climate, and Biosphere with Implications for the Future

media.title: The Last Time the Globe Warmed

entries.title: Prambanan and the legend of Roro Jonggrang
entries.mainstream: Prambanan in Central Java is a 9th-century Hindu temple complex dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, with a central Shiva temple about 47 m high. The Shivagrha inscription of 856 CE is linked to its construction under the Mataram kingdom. In Javanese legend, Princess Roro Jonggrang demanded that her suitor Bandung Bondowoso build 1,000 temples in one night; she tricked him by making the cocks crow early, and he cursed her into a statue. The site was listed by UNESCO in 1991 and damaged in an earthquake in 2006.

alternatives.label: Hindu-Buddhist rivalry
alternatives.text: Prambanan's proximity to Buddhist Borobudur has prompted debates about dynastic and religious rivalry in Java.

alternatives.label: Built by spirits
alternatives.text: The legend that spirits built the temples is folklore that explains the many small shrines.

entries.title: Battle of Mactan
entries.mainstream: On the morning of 27 April 1521, on a beach of Mactan Island (now part of Cebu, Philippines), warriors of the chieftain Lapulapu defeated a small Spanish contingent and killed the expedition leader Ferdinand Magellan, who had sought to force Mactan to submit to Spain and to his new ally Rajah Humabon of Cebu. Almost everything known comes from the account of the survivor Antonio Pigafetta. The expedition went on under Juan Sebastián Elcano to complete the first circumnavigation in 1522, and Lapulapu is honoured as the first Filipino national hero.

alternatives.label: Who was Lapulapu
alternatives.text: Little is known beyond Pigafetta; in 2019 the Philippine National Quincentennial Committee settled on the spelling "Lapulapu", noting his name may have carried the honorific "Si" (from Sanskrit Sri).

alternatives.label: He never died
alternatives.text: Local legend says Lapulapu was turned to stone and still guards the seas of Mactan; fisherfolk once threw coins at a man-shaped rock to ask his permission to fish, and the grouper fish is named after him.

entries.title: Ebu gogo
entries.dateNote: Folklore; tale set in the 18th century
entries.mainstream: In the folklore of the Nage people of central Flores, Indonesia, the ebu gogo (roughly "grandparent who eats anything") were small, hairy, fast-running wild people about 1.5 m tall who murmured in their own language and could repeat human words. In one tale recorded in the 18th-century setting, villagers gave them palm fibre for clothing and then set their cave alight, killing almost all of them. After the small hominin Homo floresiensis was found on Flores in 2003–04, the stories drew global attention as a possible folk memory.

alternatives.label: Memory of a real hominin
alternatives.text: The ethnologist Gregory Forth and others suggested ebu gogo tales preserve encounters with Homo floresiensis; this has little mainstream support since the species' last known remains were redated to around 50,000 years ago.

alternatives.label: Folklore and animals
alternatives.text: Nature reported the legends were traditionally attributed to monkeys; folklorists compare them with little-people stories worldwide, such as the menehune.

media.title: Are These People the Descendants of Real Life Hobbits? | Mystery of the Human Hobbit | BBC Studios

entries.title: 'Pink': earliest human face in western Europe
entries.mainstream: In March 2025 a team led by Rosa Huguet described ATE7-1, a partial left midface of a human found at Sima del Elefante, Atapuerca (Spain), in layers dated to about 1.1–1.4 million years ago. Nicknamed 'Pink', it is the earliest human face known from western Europe. Its flatter, less projecting features differ from the later Homo antecessor found nearby, so the authors provisionally assigned it to Homo affinis erectus.

alternatives.label: Several early populations
alternatives.text: The authors argue Europe was entered by more than one human lineage in the Early Pleistocene; others await more fossils before accepting a separate population.

alternatives.label: Classification open
alternatives.text: The "aff. erectus" label signals affinity, not a firm species assignment; future finds may revise it.

entries.changed: Before 2025 the oldest western European face was Homo antecessor from Gran Dolina (c. 850,000 years ago).

sources.title: The earliest human face of Western Europe

entries.title: Mantell UFO incident (1948)
entries.mainstream: On 7 January 1948, Captain Thomas F. Mantell, 25, of the Kentucky Air National Guard was sent with other P-51 Mustangs to approach an unidentified object reported over Godman Field, Fort Knox. Climbing past 20,000 feet without adequate oxygen equipment, he lost consciousness and crashed near Franklin, Kentucky, making him the first widely publicised death linked to a UFO chase. Project Blue Book head Edward Ruppelt later concluded he had most probably been chasing a top-secret Skyhook research balloon.

alternatives.label: Skyhook balloon
alternatives.text: Tower descriptions of "a parachute" or "an ice cream cone tipped with red" and an astronomer's report of a balloon with a basket support the Skyhook explanation; an early Project Blue Book explanation blaming Venus was later retracted by J. Allen Hynek.

alternatives.label: Downed by a craft
alternatives.text: Early UFO writers claimed Mantell was destroyed by an alien ship; the wreck showed no evidence of attack, and hypoxia fully explains the crash.

entries.title: Pascagoula abduction (1973)
entries.mainstream: On the night of 11 October 1973, Charles Hickson (45) and Calvin Parker (17) reported to the sheriff in Pascagoula, Mississippi, that while fishing on the river they had been taken aboard an oval craft by three creatures with pincer-like hands and examined. Deputies left them alone in a room while secretly recording them, and the two men's private conversation stayed consistent with their story. The case came during a regional flap of UFO reports in the US South and became one of the best-known abduction claims.

alternatives.label: Sincere experience
alternatives.text: Investigators noted the men seemed genuinely terrified on the secret tape; a local polygraph examiner concluded Hickson told the truth as he believed it, and Parker published his own account in 2018.

alternatives.label: Hoax or misperception
alternatives.text: Philip Klass found discrepancies, noted Hickson declined a test by a more experienced examiner, and concluded it was a hoax; polygraphs are in any case unreliable, and others suggest hallucination.

entries.title: Travis Walton incident (1975)
entries.mainstream: On 5 November 1975, a logging crew in the Apache–Sitgreaves National Forests near Heber, Arizona, reported that their colleague Travis Walton had walked towards a glowing craft, been struck by a beam of light, and vanished. After a five-day search Walton reappeared, saying he had been taken aboard a flying saucer. His book The Walton Experience (1978) was adapted, with liberties, into the film Fire in the Sky (1993).

alternatives.label: Genuine abduction
alternatives.text: Supporters cite the crew's consistent statements and some passed polygraph tests.

alternatives.label: Hoax for a contract
alternatives.text: Philip Klass and Michael Shermer argued it was a hoax, possibly so the crew could escape penalties for missing a Forest Service contract deadline; in 2021 crew leader Mike Rogers posted that he renounced his status as a witness, without explanation.

entries.title: O'Hare Airport UFO sighting (2006)
entries.mainstream: At about 4:15 pm on 7 November 2006, a ramp worker pushing back United Airlines Flight 446 at Chicago O'Hare saw a dark grey, silent, disc-shaped object hovering over Gate C-17. About a dozen United employees, including pilots and supervisors, reported it, and some said it shot straight up leaving a clear hole in the clouds. It did not appear on radar, and the Federal Aviation Administration called it a weather phenomenon; the story became public through a Chicago Tribune Freedom of Information request.

alternatives.label: Unknown craft
alternatives.text: Witnesses insist it was a solid object, and the airline and FAA initially denied knowing about the reports.

alternatives.label: Weather or misperception
alternatives.text: Witness accounts disagree on shape, height and movement; sceptics suggest low cloud features such as a hole-punch cloud or a mistaken balloon.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2006 O'Hare International Airport UFO sighting

entries.title: Ogopogo and n'ha-a-itk
entries.dateNote: Indigenous tradition; settler sightings from 19th century, name from 1910s–20s
entries.mainstream: Ogopogo is a serpent-like lake monster said to live in Okanagan Lake, British Columbia, a 127 km glacial lake. The sceptic Benjamin Radford notes it is more closely tied to Indigenous tradition than any other lake monster: the Syilx and Secwepemc peoples spoke of n'ha-a-itk (variously translated 'water-demon' or 'sacred creature of the water'), to which small animals were offered for safe crossing of the lake. The name 'Ogopogo' comes from an English music-hall song and was applied in the 1910s–20s; sightings and films have continued ever since.

alternatives.label: Unknown animal
alternatives.text: Cryptozoologists propose a surviving primitive whale such as Basilosaurus or a giant eel; no specimen has ever been found.

alternatives.label: Waves, logs and otters
alternatives.text: Sceptics attribute sightings to boat wakes, floating logs, swimming animals and the expectation created by the legend.

media.author: Hamedog at English Wikipedia; cropped by Beyond My Ken (talk) 18:39, 26 September 2011 (UTC)
media.title: OgoPogo_crop.jpg

entries.title: Dover Demon
entries.mainstream: On 21–22 April 1977, three teenagers in Dover, Massachusetts, reported seeing a thin creature about 1.2 m tall with a large watermelon-shaped head and glowing eyes. Seventeen-year-old Bill Bartlett drew it and swore he had seen it. The sightings lay along a line over 3 km long, and the cryptozoologist Loren Coleman compared the case with the 1955 Kelly–Hopkinsville encounter.

alternatives.label: Animal misidentification
alternatives.text: Explanations include a foal or moose calf; Joe Nickell suggested a snowy owl, which others dispute.

alternatives.label: Prank
alternatives.text: Police called it "probably nothing more than a school vacation hoax", though the witnesses kept to their stories.

entries.title: Calaveras Skull
entries.mainstream: On 25 February 1866, miners in Calaveras County, California, said they had found a human skull 40 m down a shaft beneath a layer of lava. California's state geologist Josiah Whitney declared it proof of Pliocene humans in North America. Miners later said it had been planted as a joke, Bret Harte mocked it in the poem 'To the Pliocene Skull', and radiocarbon dating in 1992 showed it was probably less than 1,000 years old.

alternatives.label: Pliocene humans
alternatives.text: Whitney never abandoned his view, and some Theosophists continued to cite the skull as evidence of very ancient humans.

alternatives.label: A prank on an Easterner
alternatives.text: Several witnesses said miners had planted a skull from a local Native American burial to fool Whitney; this is now the accepted explanation.

entries.title: Kinderhook plates
entries.mainstream: In 1843 six small, bell-shaped brass plates engraved with strange characters were 'discovered' in a mound near Kinderhook, Illinois, and shown to Joseph Smith, founder of the Latter Day Saint movement, who said they were ancient and translated part of them. In 1879 Wilburn Fugate wrote that he and two other men had made the plates using acid and beeswax to test or mock Smith. Testing of the surviving plate in 1980 confirmed it was a 19th-century creation.

alternatives.label: Ancient record
alternatives.text: Some early Latter Day Saints regarded the plates as an ancient record; the LDS Church defended them until 1981.

alternatives.label: Hoax
alternatives.text: The 1980 tests support Fugate's confession.

entries.title: Narmer Palette
entries.mainstream: The Narmer Palette is a ceremonial siltstone palette about 64 cm tall, found in 1897–98 by James Quibell and Frederick Green in the temple deposit at Hierakonpolis, Upper Egypt, and now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo. It shows King Narmer wearing the White Crown of Upper Egypt on one face and the Red Crown of Lower Egypt on the other, smiting an enemy and inspecting rows of decapitated captives, with intertwined long-necked 'serpopards' at the centre. It dates to about 3100 BCE and is often presented as one of the earliest images of the unification of Egypt.

alternatives.label: Record of a real conquest
alternatives.text: Many Egyptologists read the scenes as commemorating an actual military unification of north and south under Narmer.

alternatives.label: Ritual and symbolic image
alternatives.text: Others argue the palette shows idealised royal ideology (the king as bringer of order over chaos) rather than a specific historical battle, and that unification was a longer process.

alternatives.label: Narmer, Menes or Aha
alternatives.text: Classical and later king lists name Menes as Egypt's first king; whether Menes was Narmer, his successor Hor-Aha, or a composite figure is still debated.

entries.title: Diary of Merer (Wadi al-Jarf papyri)
entries.mainstream: In 2013 a French–Egyptian mission led by Pierre Tallet found papyrus fragments at the ancient harbour of Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast. They date to about year 27 of King Khufu's reign and are the oldest inscribed papyri yet known. The best preserved, the logbook of an official named Merer, records his team of about 40 men moving limestone blocks by boat from the Tura quarries along the Nile and canals to Giza, under the oversight of Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother.

alternatives.label: Eyewitness to pyramid building
alternatives.text: Most Egyptologists see the diary as direct documentary evidence that Khufu's workforce supplied the Great Pyramid, consistent with the dynastic Egyptian construction of the monument.

alternatives.label: Only casing stone
alternatives.text: Some alternative writers argue the papyri cover only the transport of fine Tura limestone casing blocks late in the project, and so say nothing on who built or planned the core; mainstream scholars reply that the diary fits a wider body of evidence (workers' town, quarries, tombs of overseers).

alternatives.label: Older-structure theories
alternatives.text: Proponents of a much older or lost-civilisation origin for the Giza pyramids regard the diary as evidence of Egyptian work on, or renovation of, the site rather than original construction; this view is speculative and not supported by excavators.

entries.title: Amarna letters
entries.mainstream: The Amarna letters are an archive of about 380 clay tablets, mostly in Akkadian cuneiform, discovered in 1887 at Tell el-Amarna, the capital founded by Akhenaten. They contain diplomatic correspondence between the Egyptian court (Amenhotep III, Akhenaten and perhaps their successors) and the great kings of Babylonia, Assyria, Mitanni, Hatti and Alashiya (Cyprus), as well as many letters from vassal rulers in Canaan and Syria, dating to about 1360–1332 BCE. The tablets are now spread across museums including the British Museum, Berlin and Cairo.

alternatives.label: A Late Bronze Age "club of great powers"
alternatives.text: Historians use the letters to reconstruct an international system of royal 'brothers' exchanging gold, brides and gifts before the Late Bronze Age collapse.

alternatives.label: Habiru and the Hebrews
alternatives.text: Several letters complain about the Habiru (ʿApiru), unsettled groups raiding Canaanite cities. Since the 19th century some have linked the term to the biblical Hebrews; many scholars now treat Habiru as a social label for outsiders rather than an ethnic name, though the debate continues.

alternatives.label: Biblical-era identifications
alternatives.text: Some writers have attempted to match Amarna rulers such as Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem or Labaya of Shechem with biblical figures; these identifications are speculative and depend on contested chronologies.

media.title: Reading the Pharaoh's private mail with Irving Finkel | The Amarna Letters  | Curator's Corner Ep100

entries.title: Battle of Kadesh and the first peace treaty
entries.dateNote: battle c. 1274 BCE; treaty c. 1259 BCE
entries.mainstream: In about 1274 BCE Ramesses II of Egypt and Muwatalli II of the Hittite Empire fought near Kadesh on the Orontes River in Syria, in what is often called the largest chariot battle known. Ramesses had his near-defeat and personal heroism carved on temple walls at Abu Simbel, Karnak, Luxor and the Ramesseum (the 'Poem' and 'Bulletin'). Kadesh stayed in Hittite hands, and about 16 years later the two powers concluded a treaty, preserved in both an Egyptian hieroglyphic version and an Akkadian cuneiform version found at Hattusa, often described as the earliest surviving peace treaty.

alternatives.label: Egyptian victory
alternatives.text: Ramesses II's inscriptions present the battle as a great triumph won almost single-handedly by the king with divine help.

alternatives.label: Hittite strategic success
alternatives.text: Many historians conclude that the Hittites achieved their aims, since Egypt withdrew and Hittite control of Kadesh and Amurru continued; Hittite texts allude to Egyptian defeat.

alternatives.label: Draw and propaganda
alternatives.text: A common middle view is that the battle was tactically indecisive and that the monumental Egyptian accounts are a classic example of royal propaganda shaping the record.

media.title: The Battle of Kadesh: Ancient Egypt vs. The Hittites

entries.title: Osiris, Isis, Set and Horus
entries.dateNote: earliest allusions Pyramid Texts c. 24th century BCE; Plutarch c. 100 CE
entries.mainstream: The Osiris myth is the best-known story of ancient Egyptian religion. The god-king Osiris is murdered by his brother Set; his sister-wife Isis searches for and restores his body, conceives their son Horus, and Osiris becomes ruler of the dead, while Horus contends with Set for the throne. Allusions appear in the Pyramid Texts of the 24th century BCE, but the fullest continuous narrative is the Greek writer Plutarch's 'On Isis and Osiris' (c. 100 CE), which gives the familiar detail of the body cut into fourteen pieces. The myth underpinned Egyptian kingship (the living king as Horus, the dead king as Osiris) and funerary beliefs for millennia.

alternatives.label: Myth of kingship and agriculture
alternatives.text: Egyptologists read it as a charter for royal succession and as linked to the annual Nile flood and the renewal of grain.

alternatives.label: Dying-and-rising god
alternatives.text: J. G. Frazer grouped Osiris with Adonis, Attis and Tammuz as a 'dying-and-rising god'; later scholars such as Jonathan Z. Smith criticised the category as too broad, and the debate continues.

alternatives.label: Sky readings
alternatives.text: Ancient texts identify Osiris with the constellation Orion and Isis with Sirius; some alternative writers build on this (for example the Orion correlation idea for Giza), which most Egyptologists regard as speculative.

alternatives.label: A deified ancient ruler
alternatives.text: Euhemerist readings, from antiquity to some modern alternative authors, suggest Osiris was a real early civiliser king; there is no archaeological evidence for this.

media.title: The Egyptian myth of the death of Osiris - Alex Gendler

entries.title: Abu Simbel: the sun temple that was moved
entries.mainstream: The two rock-cut temples at Abu Simbel in Nubia were carved for Ramesses II and his queen Nefertari in the 13th century BCE (work is usually dated c. 1264–1244 BCE). Covered by sand, the Great Temple was seen by Johann Ludwig Burckhardt in 1813 and entered by Giovanni Belzoni in 1817. Threatened by Lake Nasser behind the Aswan High Dam, both temples were cut into large blocks and reassembled about 65 m higher and some 200 m back between 1964 and 1968, in a UNESCO-led international campaign. Twice a year, in late February and late October, the rising sun reaches the inner sanctuary and lights statues of Ra-Horakhty, Amun and the deified Ramesses, leaving the underworld-linked Ptah largely in shadow.

alternatives.label: Deliberate solar alignment
alternatives.text: Most researchers accept that the axis was oriented so sunlight reaches the sanctuary on particular dates, part of the temple's solar theology.

alternatives.label: Birthday and coronation dates
alternatives.text: A widely repeated claim says the two dates mark Ramesses II's birthday and coronation; this is a modern popular tradition without known ancient documentation.

alternatives.label: Did the move shift the effect?
alternatives.text: Reports state that after the relocation the illumination occurs about a day later than before; how precisely the original builders fixed the dates is debated.

sources.title: UNESCO: Nubian Monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae

media.title: Engineers to the Rescue! | National Geographic

entries.title: Tel Dan stele ("House of David")
entries.mainstream: Fragments of a basalt stele inscribed in Old Aramaic were found in 1993 and 1994 at Tel Dan in northern Israel by Avraham Biran's excavation team. The text, usually dated to the 9th century BCE and attributed to a king of Aram-Damascus (often identified as Hazael), boasts of killing the king of Israel and a king of the 'bytdwd'. Most scholars read this as 'House of David', which would make it the earliest widely accepted reference to David's dynasty outside the Bible. It is displayed at the Israel Museum.

alternatives.label: House of David
alternatives.text: The majority view takes bytdwd as the name of the Judahite royal dynasty, supporting the existence of a historical David as dynastic founder, though not the biblical details of his reign.

alternatives.label: Alternative readings
alternatives.text: A minority of scholars proposed other readings, such as a place name, a temple ('house of the beloved') or a divine epithet.

alternatives.label: Authenticity questions
alternatives.text: Shortly after discovery some critics suggested the fragments might be forged or planted; this was not widely accepted, as they were found in excavation contexts.

entries.title: Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone)
entries.mainstream: The Mesha Stele is a basalt inscription of about 34 lines set up around 840 BCE by Mesha, king of Moab, at Dhiban in present-day Jordan. Seen by the missionary F. A. Klein in 1868, it was broken by local people before it could be removed; the text was recovered thanks to a paper squeeze made for Charles Clermont-Ganneau, and the reassembled stone is in the Louvre. Mesha describes Moab's oppression by Omri, king of Israel, and his son, his successful revolt, and his dedication of Israelite spoils to the god Chemosh; it contains one of the earliest known extra-biblical references to Israel and to the god YHWH.

alternatives.label: Same war, other side
alternatives.text: Historians compare it with 2 Kings 3, which tells of Mesha's rebellion from the Israelite viewpoint; the accounts differ on outcome and details, illustrating how each side recorded events.

alternatives.label: A second "House of David"?
alternatives.text: In 1994 André Lemaire proposed that a damaged line reads 'House of David'; others have suggested different readings (including a name such as Balak), and the passage remains debated.

alternatives.label: Divine wrath theology
alternatives.text: The inscription explains defeat as the anger of Chemosh, closely paralleling biblical explanations of Israel's misfortunes, which scholars see as shared regional religious thinking.

entries.title: Natufians: the last hunter-gatherers before farming
entries.mainstream: The Natufian culture flourished in the Levant from roughly 15,000 to 11,500 years ago. Natufians lived in semi-permanent villages of round stone houses, harvested wild cereals with sickles, buried their dead beneath their homes (sometimes with dogs or puppies, as at Ain Mallaha) and produced early decorated art. Residues from Raqefet Cave in Israel have been interpreted as evidence of beer-like brewing about 13,000 years ago. Many archaeologists see the Natufians as the bridge between foraging and the first farming communities of the Neolithic.

alternatives.label: Climate push
alternatives.text: A long-standing view links the Younger Dryas cold spell (c. 12,900–11,700 years ago) to stresses that encouraged Natufians to cultivate cereals; others argue the transition was gradual and driven by social factors.

alternatives.label: Feasting and beer first
alternatives.text: Some researchers suggest feasting and brewing, rather than bread, helped motivate early cereal cultivation; this is debated.

alternatives.label: Abu Hureyra and a cosmic impact
alternatives.text: Proponents of the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis argue that melted glass and other markers at Abu Hureyra in Syria record an airburst affecting a late Natufian–early farming village (Moore et al. 2020); critics dispute both the evidence and its interpretation.

sources.title: Fermented beverage and food storage in 13,000 y-old stone mortars at Raqefet Cave, Israel: Investigating Natufian ritual feasting

entries.title: Proto-Sinaitic: the first alphabet
entries.mainstream: Short inscriptions found by Flinders Petrie in 1904–05 at the turquoise mines of Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai use signs adapted from Egyptian hieroglyphs to write a Semitic language, each sign standing for the first sound of the word it pictures (an ox head, ʾalp, for ʾ). In 1916 Alan Gardiner read the recurring sequence l-bʿlt, 'to Baʿalat'. Similar inscriptions found at Wadi el-Hol in Egypt in the 1990s by John and Deborah Darnell are dated to around 1900–1800 BCE. This script is regarded as the ancestor of Phoenician and through it of Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Greek and Latin letters.

alternatives.label: Invented by workers
alternatives.text: Orly Goldwasser has argued that the alphabet was invented by non-literate Canaanite miners or soldiers who borrowed hieroglyphic pictures without learning Egyptian scribal rules; others favour bilingual scribes or officials as the inventors.

alternatives.label: Dating disputes
alternatives.text: Dates for the Sinai inscriptions range from the 19th to the 15th century BCE depending on archaeological and palaeographic arguments.

alternatives.label: Hebrew and Exodus readings
alternatives.text: Some writers, such as Douglas Petrovich, have claimed the inscriptions are early Hebrew and connected to the Israelites in Egypt; most epigraphers reject these readings as unsupported.
