entries.title: Siege of Vienna 1683 (and the croissant legend)
entries.mainstream: In July 1683 an Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha besieged Vienna, the Habsburg capital. On 12 September a relief army of Polish, Imperial and German forces, led by King Jan III Sobieski of Poland, attacked from the Kahlenberg heights; a massed cavalry charge including the Polish winged hussars broke the besiegers. Kara Mustafa was executed in Belgrade that December on the Sultan's orders, and the defeat opened the long Habsburg counter-offensive in Hungary. The siege also gathered famous legends about the origins of Viennese food and coffee.

alternatives.label: Turning point
alternatives.text: Many historians treat 1683 as the moment Ottoman expansion into central Europe ended; others stress that Ottoman decline was gradual and that the empire remained a major power for long after.

alternatives.label: Croissant legend
alternatives.text: A popular story says bakers invented the crescent-shaped croissant to celebrate the victory; food historians note that crescent-shaped Kipferl breads are older and that the French croissant is a 19th-century development, so the tale is treated as legend.

alternatives.label: Coffee legend
alternatives.text: Another tradition credits the spy Jerzy Franciszek Kulczycki with opening Vienna's first coffee house using sacks of coffee left by the Ottomans; records show an Armenian, Johannes Diodato, received an early coffee licence in 1685, and the Kulczycki story is regarded as embellished.

entries.title: Devshirme and the Janissaries
entries.dateNote: Janissaries c. 1363–1826; devshirme c. late 14th–17th centuries
entries.mainstream: The Janissaries were the elite standing infantry of the Ottoman Empire, formed in the 14th century. From about the late 14th century they were recruited largely through the devshirme, a periodic levy of boys, mainly from Christian families in the Balkans, who were converted to Islam, trained and enrolled as the Sultan's servants; the most able rose to the highest offices of state, including grand vizier. The levy faded in the 17th century, and after the Janissaries became a powerful and rebellious political force, Sultan Mahmud II destroyed the corps in the 'Auspicious Incident' of 1826.

alternatives.label: Enslavement and forced conversion
alternatives.text: Many historians, and Balkan national traditions, describe the devshirme as a form of slavery that took children from their families and faiths.

alternatives.label: Route to power
alternatives.text: Other historians emphasise that devshirme recruits could reach great wealth and power, and note accounts of some families seeking to have sons taken; both aspects are documented.

alternatives.label: Secret brotherhood
alternatives.text: The Janissaries' close ties to the Bektashi Sufi order gave rise to stories of secret rites and heterodox beliefs; the extent of Bektashi influence on the corps is debated.

entries.title: Naqsh-e Jahan Square, Isfahan
entries.dateNote: laid out from 1598; main buildings c. 1602–1630s
entries.mainstream: After Shah Abbas I made Isfahan the Safavid capital in 1598, he laid out the vast Naqsh-e Jahan ('Image of the World') square, about 560 m long. It is framed by the Shah (Imam) Mosque, the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, the Ali Qapu palace and the gateway to the Qeysarieh bazaar, bringing royal, religious and commercial power together in one planned space. It was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1979 and is often cited as a high point of Safavid architecture.

alternatives.label: Statement of state and faith
alternatives.text: Historians read the square as a deliberate display of Safavid kingship and of Twelver Shiism as the state religion.

alternatives.label: Commerce first
alternatives.text: Others stress the economic role of the square and bazaar in Abbas's policy of drawing the silk trade and foreign merchants to Isfahan.

alternatives.label: Acoustic marvels
alternatives.text: Guides often describe multiple echoes under the Shah Mosque dome and the Ali Qapu music room's sound-absorbing niches; such acoustic effects are real but popular claims about their exact design intent are not well documented.

entries.title: Shah Ismail I: the boy king worshipped as divine
entries.mainstream: Ismail I (1487–1524), head of the Safavid Sufi order, was about 14 when his Qizilbash followers captured Tabriz in 1501 and proclaimed him Shah. He made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion of Iran, shaping the country's religious identity to the present. His Turkic-speaking Qizilbash followers venerated him as a divine or messianic figure, and in poems written under the pen name Khata'i he described himself in exalted, even divine terms. His defeat by the Ottoman Sultan Selim I at Chaldiran in 1514, where Ottoman artillery and firearms proved decisive, damaged the belief in his invincibility.

alternatives.label: Messianic leader
alternatives.text: Historians see Ismail's rise as an example of a millenarian movement: devotees believed he was an emanation of God or the forerunner of the Hidden Imam.

alternatives.label: Political strategy
alternatives.text: Other scholars emphasise his use of religious charisma and enforced conversion to build a state distinct from the Sunni Ottomans.

alternatives.label: After Chaldiran
alternatives.text: Contemporary sources say Ismail withdrew from active campaigning after 1514; how much his followers' faith in him declined is debated.

entries.title: Haitian Revolution
entries.mainstream: Beginning with an uprising of enslaved people in the northern plain of Saint-Domingue in August 1791, the Haitian Revolution became the only slave revolt to found an independent state. Leaders including Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines fought French, Spanish and British forces, and defeated Napoleon's expedition of 1802–03. Dessalines declared the independence of Haiti on 1 January 1804. In 1825 France demanded an indemnity of 150 million francs (later reduced to 90 million) in return for recognition, a debt Haiti paid off over many decades.

alternatives.label: Silenced revolution
alternatives.text: Historian Michel-Rolph Trouillot argued that the revolution was long 'silenced' in Western histories because it was unthinkable to contemporaries; it is now studied as central to the Age of Revolutions.

alternatives.label: Role of Vodou
alternatives.text: The Bois Caïman ceremony is remembered as the spiritual start of the uprising; historians debate how much is documented and how much is later tradition.

alternatives.label: A "pact with the devil"
alternatives.text: Some modern religious commentators have claimed Haiti's founders made a pact with the devil at Bois Caïman; historians and Haitian scholars regard this as a polemical reinterpretation without historical basis.

media.title: Haitian Revolutions: Crash Course World History #30

entries.title: Kalinago ("Island Caribs") and the cannibal label
entries.dateNote: first European accounts 1493; Kalinago Territory established 1903
entries.mainstream: The Kalinago are the Indigenous people of the Lesser Antilles whom Europeans called Caribs. Spanish accounts from Columbus's second voyage (1493) onwards described them as man-eaters; the word 'cannibal' itself derives from the Spanish name for the Caribs. In 1503 the Spanish Crown allowed people classified as cannibals to be enslaved, which gave colonists an incentive to apply the label. Kalinago resisted European settlement for centuries, and today a Kalinago Territory exists on Dominica.

alternatives.label: Ritual cannibalism happened
alternatives.text: Some historians and archaeologists accept that limited ritual consumption of enemies occurred, based on early accounts and finds of human remains.

alternatives.label: Colonial slander
alternatives.text: Others argue that cannibalism accusations were largely a colonial invention or exaggeration used to justify conquest and slavery, pointing to the lack of reliable eyewitness reports.

alternatives.label: Two languages, one people
alternatives.text: Chroniclers recorded that Kalinago men and women spoke differently and explained this by a legend that mainland Carib warriors had conquered Arawak-speaking islanders and taken their women; linguists note the language was Arawakan with a Carib-derived men's jargon, and the conquest story is debated.

entries.title: Joya de Cerén: the Maya village under the ash
entries.mainstream: Joya de Cerén in El Salvador is a farming village buried under several metres of ash by the eruption of the nearby Loma Caldera vent around 600 CE. Found in 1976 when a bulldozer cut into a building, and excavated by Payson Sheets and others, it preserves houses, storehouses, a sweat bath, a communal building, gardens and manioc fields, with pots, food remains and tools left where they were used. It was listed by UNESCO in 1993 and is often called the 'Pompeii of the Americas'.

alternatives.label: Everyday Maya life
alternatives.text: Archaeologists value it as a rare snapshot of ordinary commoner households rather than elite temples and kings.

alternatives.label: Where did the people go?
alternatives.text: No human remains have been found, suggesting the villagers had warning and fled; whether they survived the ash fall is unknown.

alternatives.label: Shaman's house
alternatives.text: One structure has been interpreted as a building used by a diviner or shaman, based on its contents; this identification is an interpretation.

sources.title: UNESCO: Joya de Cerén Archaeological Site

entries.title: Copán and the Hieroglyphic Stairway
entries.mainstream: Copán, in western Honduras, was a Classic Maya kingdom ruled by a dynasty founded in 426 CE by K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo'. Its Hieroglyphic Stairway, dedicated in 755 CE under the ruler K'ak' Yipyaj Chan K'awiil, carries about 2,200 glyphs, the longest known Maya inscription, recounting the dynasty's history. The stairway collapsed and when it was restored in the 1930s many blocks were reset out of order, so the text is only partly readable in sequence. Altar Q portrays all sixteen kings of the dynasty. Copán was listed by UNESCO in 1980.

alternatives.label: A foreign founder
alternatives.text: Isotope analysis of a skeleton thought to be Yax K'uk' Mo' suggests he grew up outside Copán, and his imagery shows links to Teotihuacan; scholars debate whether he was an outsider installed by central Mexican power or a local claimant using prestige symbols.

alternatives.label: Scrambled history
alternatives.text: Epigraphers have reconstructed parts of the stairway's order using old photographs and drawings, but large portions remain uncertain.

alternatives.label: Collapse of the kingdom
alternatives.text: Copán declined in the 9th century; explanations include soil erosion and deforestation, drought, warfare and loss of royal authority, with debate over their relative weight.

entries.title: La Ciudad Blanca (City of the Monkey God)
entries.dateNote: legend colonial era onward; ruins c. 1000–1500 CE; lidar 2012; expedition 2015
entries.mainstream: Legends of a 'White City' hidden in the rainforest of La Mosquitia, eastern Honduras, have circulated since the colonial era. In 1940 the adventurer Theodore Morde claimed to have found a 'Lost City of the Monkey God'; he never revealed its location. In 2012 an aerial lidar survey revealed extensive ruins in unexplored valleys, and a 2015 expedition, publicised by writer Douglas Preston and archaeologist Christopher Fisher, documented plazas, earthworks and a cache of stone sculptures from a pre-Columbian culture of about 1000–1500 CE.

alternatives.label: Legend found
alternatives.text: Media coverage presented the 2015 finds as the discovery of the legendary White City or a lost civilisation.

alternatives.label: Not one city, not lost
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists objected that the region was known to contain numerous sites of a recognised Mosquitia culture, that no single 'White City' has been identified, and that Indigenous groups were not credited; the legend and the archaeology are treated as separate.

alternatives.label: Morde's claims
alternatives.text: Morde's notebooks reportedly show little sign of a real city, and some researchers suspect his account was invented or embellished.

media.title: Lost City of the Monkey God // Ancient America Documentary

entries.title: El Cadejo: the spirit dogs of Central America
entries.dateNote: recorded colonial-era and modern folklore; origins uncertain
entries.mainstream: In the folklore of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and southern Mexico, the Cadejo is a supernatural dog that appears to people walking alone at night, often described with glowing red eyes and goat-like hooves. In many versions there are two: a white Cadejo that protects travellers and a black Cadejo that leads them to harm, especially drunkards and wrongdoers. The legend is widely told today and appears in art and literature.

alternatives.label: Christian moral tale
alternatives.text: Folklorists often read the paired white and black dogs as a colonial-era moral story of good and evil guardians.

alternatives.label: Older Mesoamerican roots
alternatives.text: Some writers suggest links to pre-Hispanic beliefs about dogs as guides of the dead or animal spirit companions (nahuales); such connections are proposed rather than demonstrated.

alternatives.label: Sightings
alternatives.text: People continue to report encounters, which researchers usually attribute to stray dogs, darkness and expectation; believers regard some experiences as genuine.

entries.title: Inuksuit: the stone messengers of the Arctic
entries.dateNote: Inuit tradition from c. 1000 CE in the eastern Arctic, possibly older; most structures undated
entries.mainstream: An inuksuk (plural inuksuit, 'that which acts in the capacity of a human') is a stone structure built by Inuit and other Arctic peoples across Alaska, Canada and Greenland. Inuksuit served many purposes: marking routes, travel directions and good fishing or hunting places, indicating food caches, and forming lines that helped steer caribou towards hunters. Figures built to resemble a person are distinguished by some Inuit as inunnguat. Enukso Point on Baffin Island, with more than 100 inuksuit, is a National Historic Site of Canada, and an inuksuk appears on the flag of Nunavut.

alternatives.label: Practical landmarks
alternatives.text: Most researchers and Inuit knowledge-holders stress their everyday functions as messages and tools in a landscape with few natural markers.

alternatives.label: Sacred stones
alternatives.text: Some inuksuit are described in Inuit tradition as objects of veneration or associated with spiritual power, and should not be disturbed.

alternatives.label: How old?
alternatives.text: Inuksuit are very hard to date; some may have been built by earlier Paleo-Inuit (Dorset) peoples, but most individual structures have no secure date.

entries.title: Sieidi: the sacred stones of the Sámi
entries.dateNote: offerings from c. Iron Age/medieval era; tradition continues
entries.mainstream: A sieidi (seite) is a natural feature, often an unusually shaped boulder, rock outcrop or carved wooden post, regarded in traditional Sámi religion as a sacred place or being. Offerings such as reindeer antlers, bones, fish and metal objects were left at sieidis to secure luck in hunting, fishing and herding. Archaeologists have studied hundreds of such sites across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, some with offerings dating back to the Iron Age and medieval period. During the 17th and 18th-century Christian missions many sieidis were desecrated along with Sámi drums.

alternatives.label: Animist landscape
alternatives.text: Scholars describe sieidis as part of a relational worldview in which features of the landscape are persons to be respected and bargained with.

alternatives.label: Living tradition
alternatives.text: Some Sámi continue to treat sieidis with respect today, and several are protected as cultural heritage sites.

alternatives.label: Stone-age roots
alternatives.text: Some researchers propose that the tradition continues very ancient northern rock cults; dating individual sites before the Iron Age is difficult and such claims remain hypotheses.

entries.title: The potlatch ban (1885–1951)
entries.mainstream: The potlatch is a gift-giving feast of the Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast, such as the Kwakwaka'wakw, Haida, Tlingit, Tsimshian and Coast Salish, used to mark births, marriages, deaths and the transfer of names and rights. Canada amended the Indian Act in 1884 to outlaw the potlatch from 1885, and the ban stayed until 1951. In 1921, after a large potlatch held by Dan Cranmer at Village Island, dozens of people were prosecuted and masks and regalia were confiscated; part of the collection was later returned and is displayed at the U'mista Cultural Centre, opened in 1980.

alternatives.label: Colonial view
alternatives.text: Missionaries and officials claimed the potlatch was wasteful and an obstacle to assimilation and Christianisation.

alternatives.label: Economy and law
alternatives.text: Anthropologists such as Franz Boas and Marcel Mauss presented the potlatch as a sophisticated system of exchange, status and law; Indigenous communities describe it as their governance system.

alternatives.label: Resistance
alternatives.text: Many communities continued potlatches in secret during the ban, and the confiscated objects became central to modern repatriation movements.

entries.title: SGang Gwaay: the village of standing poles
entries.mainstream: SGang Gwaay Llanagaay (Ninstints) is a Haida village site on Anthony Island at the southern end of Haida Gwaii, British Columbia. It preserves the remains of longhouses and a rare group of standing carved mortuary and memorial poles. The village was abandoned in the 1880s after epidemics, notably the smallpox epidemic that began in 1862, devastated the Haida. Some poles were removed to museums in 1957; the site was inscribed by UNESCO in 1981 and is cared for by Haida Watchmen.

alternatives.label: Let the poles return to the earth
alternatives.text: Haida tradition holds that poles should be allowed to decay naturally; conservation is limited to stabilisation in line with Haida wishes.

alternatives.label: Museum rescue
alternatives.text: Mid-20th-century museum teams argued that removing poles would preserve the art; the removals are now part of debates about consent and repatriation.

alternatives.label: Epidemic history
alternatives.text: Historians debate how far the 1862 smallpox outbreak was worsened by colonial authorities expelling Indigenous people from Victoria; the scale of mortality is not disputed.

entries.title: Tabon Caves and the Manunggul Jar
entries.dateNote: Tabon Man tibia c. 47,000 years; Manunggul Jar c. 890–710 BCE
entries.mainstream: The Tabon Caves on Lipuun Point, Palawan, in the Philippines, were excavated from 1962 by Robert Fox of the National Museum. Human remains known as Tabon Man include a tibia fragment dated by uranium-series methods to about 47,000 years ago, among the oldest modern human fossils in the Philippines. The nearby Manunggul Cave yielded the Manunggul Jar, a burial jar of about 890–710 BCE whose lid shows two figures in a boat, interpreted as a voyage of souls to the afterlife. The jar is a National Treasure and appears on the Philippine 1000-peso note.

alternatives.label: Early sea-crossers
alternatives.text: The age of Tabon Man is used as evidence that modern humans reached the Philippine islands early, crossing water gaps.

alternatives.label: Dating uncertainty
alternatives.text: Dates for the earliest layers have been revised several times; some fossils are younger than first thought, and the precise antiquity of occupation is still studied.

alternatives.label: Ship of the dead
alternatives.text: The boat on the Manunggul lid is linked to widespread Austronesian beliefs about the soul travelling by boat, a connection most scholars accept though details are interpretive.

sources.title: Upper Pleistocene Homo sapiens from the Tabon cave (Palawan, The Philippines): description and dating of new discoveries

entries.title: Code of Kalantiaw
entries.mainstream: The Code of Kalantiaw is a supposed legal code issued in 1433 by Datu Kalantiaw, a chieftain on the island of Panay, with harsh penalties for offences. It became a fixture of Philippine textbooks and national memory, with monuments, an award and a historical marker. The text first appeared in 1913 in a manuscript, 'Las antiguas leyendas de la isla de Negros', presented by José E. Marco and attributed to a Spanish friar. In 1968 historian William Henry Scott showed in his doctoral thesis that the documents were fabrications, and later the National Historical Institute recognised Kalantiaw as not historical.

alternatives.label: Forgery
alternatives.text: Most historians accept Scott's conclusion that the code was invented in the early 20th century, likely by Marco, who also supplied other doubtful documents.

alternatives.label: Lingering belief
alternatives.text: Some local traditions and older publications still treat Kalantiaw as real, and the debunking was resisted for years because the code had become a symbol of pre-colonial civilisation.

alternatives.label: What it hid
alternatives.text: Scholars note the hoax overshadowed real pre-colonial evidence of Philippine law and literacy, such as the Laguna Copperplate Inscription.

entries.title: Java Man and the Trinil engraved shell
entries.dateNote: fossils c. 0.5–1 million years old (debated); found 1891–92
entries.mainstream: In 1891–92 the Dutch surgeon Eugène Dubois, who had gone to the Dutch East Indies to search for a 'missing link', found a skullcap, a femur and teeth at Trinil on the Solo River in Java. He named the species Pithecanthropus erectus. The claim was hotly disputed for decades, but the fossils are now classified as Homo erectus. In 2014 a re-examination of freshwater mussel shells from Dubois' collection reported a deliberately engraved zigzag pattern on one shell, dated to about 430,000–540,000 years ago and attributed to Homo erectus (Joordens et al., Nature, 2015).

alternatives.label: Missing link
alternatives.text: Dubois presented the find as the link between apes and humans; later finds showed human evolution as a branching bush rather than a single chain.

alternatives.label: Earliest abstract mark?
alternatives.text: The engraved shell is seen by its authors as the oldest known geometric engraving; some researchers are cautious about what the marks meant to their maker.

alternatives.label: Age of the fossils
alternatives.text: The age of the Trinil fossils is usually given as roughly 0.5–1 million years, but dating of the Trinil layers remains debated.

sources.title: Homo erectus at Trinil on Java used shells for tool production and engraving

media.title: Indonesia welcomes return of ‘Java Man’, first fossil evidence of Homo erectus

entries.title: Degei, the serpent god of Fiji
entries.mainstream: In Fijian tradition Degei is the great serpent god, a creator and ancestral deity said to live in a cave in the Nakauvadra mountains of northern Viti Levu. In one widely told story Degei found two eggs, kept them warm, and from them hatched the first man and woman. Fijian ancestral traditions also tell of the first chiefs, led by Lutunasobasoba, landing near Vuda. In some traditions the spirits of the dead go to Degei for judgement, and when he turns over in his cave the earth shakes.

alternatives.label: Creation and order
alternatives.text: Ethnographers read Degei as a creator and judge who explains the origin of people, crops and the moral order.

alternatives.label: Earthquake lore
alternatives.text: The idea that Degei's movements cause tremors parallels other myths of a great creature beneath the earth, such as Japan's Namazu; whether these reflect memory of real events is speculative.

alternatives.label: Migration memory
alternatives.text: Some writers link the Nakauvadra traditions to the arrival of Fiji's first settlers; how far such oral histories preserve real migration detail is debated.

entries.title: Marshall Islands stick charts
entries.dateNote: documented from the late 19th century; tradition older
entries.mainstream: Navigators of the Marshall Islands made charts from the midribs of coconut fronds tied together, with shells or coral marking islands. The curved and straight sticks represent ocean swell patterns and the places where swells bend and interfere around islands, which a navigator could feel through the motion of a canoe. There were different types, from teaching charts (mattang) to charts of particular island groups (meddo and rebbelib). The charts were memorised and generally not carried on voyages. Western observers documented them in the late 19th century, after colonial contact.

alternatives.label: Unique ocean science
alternatives.text: Scholars regard the charts as a sophisticated model of wave refraction developed without instruments or writing.

alternatives.label: Secret knowledge
alternatives.text: Navigation knowledge was closely guarded by chiefly families, so much was lost; modern projects work with remaining knowledge-holders to revive it.

alternatives.label: How old?
alternatives.text: No ancient charts survive, and the age of the practice is unknown; it is generally assumed to be much older than the first Western descriptions.

entries.title: Toraja funerals and Ma'nene
entries.dateNote: tradition of uncertain age; documented since the colonial era
entries.mainstream: Among the Toraja of the highlands of South Sulawesi, Indonesia, funerals (rambu solo') are the most important ceremonies of life. A dead person may be kept at home for months or years, treated as 'sick' rather than dead, while the family gathers resources for a funeral involving the sacrifice of water buffalo and pigs. The dead are placed in rock-cut tombs, cliff niches, caves or hanging graves, often watched over by wooden effigies called tau tau. In some areas a ritual called ma'nene is held every few years, in which remains are cleaned and re-dressed.

alternatives.label: Cosmology
alternatives.text: Anthropologists link the rites to the traditional religion Aluk To Dolo, in which buffalo help carry the soul to the afterlife, Puya.

alternatives.label: Tourism and change
alternatives.text: Since the 1970s mass tourism has reshaped how funerals are staged and seen, and many Toraja are now Christian while maintaining the rites.

alternatives.label: Shared island pattern
alternatives.text: Scholars compare Toraja practices with secondary-burial and ancestor-handling customs elsewhere in island Southeast Asia and Madagascar, such as famadihana, reflecting shared Austronesian roots; the depth of the link is debated.

entries.title: The Flannan Isles lighthouse keepers (1900)
entries.dateNote: keepers vanished c. 15 December 1900; discovered 26 December
entries.mainstream: On 26 December 1900 the relief vessel Hesperus reached the lighthouse on Eilean Mòr in the remote Flannan Isles, west of the Outer Hebrides, and found it deserted. The three keepers, James Ducat, Thomas Marshall and Donald MacArthur, had vanished; the light had not been seen since mid-December. Investigator Robert Muirhead of the Northern Lighthouse Board found storm damage at the west landing and concluded the men had probably been swept away by an exceptionally large wave while securing equipment. No bodies were found.

alternatives.label: Freak wave
alternatives.text: The official explanation, still favoured by most researchers, is that a large wave or surge struck the men at the west landing during or after a storm.

alternatives.label: Murder or madness
alternatives.text: Some writers have suggested one keeper killed the others or that a dispute ended in tragedy; there is no direct evidence for this.

alternatives.label: Embellished legend
alternatives.text: Wilfrid Wilson Gibson's 1912 poem 'Flannan Isle' and later retellings added details such as an untouched meal and an overturned chair, and dramatic logbook entries that historians consider fictitious; stories of sea serpents, ghosts or abduction belong to this later legend.

entries.title: The Mad Gasser of Mattoon (1944)
entries.mainstream: In late August and September 1944, residents of Mattoon, Illinois, reported that a prowler was spraying a sweet-smelling gas into their homes at night, causing nausea, dizziness and temporary paralysis. Dozens of incidents were reported and local newspapers gave them sensational coverage. Police found no culprit and no trace of a gas, and officials concluded the episode was largely a case of mass hysteria; the reports stopped within a few weeks. A similar 'gasser' scare had occurred in Botetourt County, Virginia, in 1933–34.

alternatives.label: Mass hysteria
alternatives.text: Psychologist Donald M. Johnson's 1945 study argued that newspaper coverage spread anxiety and that symptoms followed the reports, a classic case study of collective behaviour.

alternatives.label: A real attacker
alternatives.text: Some later researchers, including author Scott Maruna, have proposed a real perpetrator, such as a local man with chemistry training; these identifications are speculative.

alternatives.label: Industrial fumes
alternatives.text: Others suggest that pollution from local chemical plants could have triggered some genuine symptoms, which fear then multiplied.

sources.title: The "phantom anesthetist" of Mattoon: a field study of mass hysteria.

entries.title: The ghost rockets of Scandinavia (1946)
entries.mainstream: In 1946 people in Sweden, Finland and other Nordic countries reported rocket- or missile-like objects in the sky; about 2,000 sightings were logged between May and December, peaking on 9 and 11 August. On 19 July 1946 witnesses saw an object fall into Lake Kölmjärv in northern Sweden; a military search of the lake found nothing. The Swedish defence staff investigated, fearing Soviet tests of captured German V-weapon technology. Their report concluded that most sightings were explainable as meteors, aircraft and other ordinary phenomena, while a minority remained unexplained.

alternatives.label: Soviet missiles
alternatives.text: Early official and press suspicion focused on Soviet tests launched from the former German base at Peenemünde; no evidence of such flights was found.

alternatives.label: Meteors and misperception
alternatives.text: Investigators found that many reports coincided with meteor showers and that heightened attention after the war generated many misidentifications.

alternatives.label: UFO precursor
alternatives.text: UFO researchers see the ghost rockets as a forerunner of the 1947 'flying saucer' wave and argue that some radar-tracked cases remain unexplained.

entries.title: Discovery of the Higgs boson (2012)
entries.mainstream: On 4 July 2012 the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider announced the discovery of a new particle with a mass of about 125 GeV, consistent with the Higgs boson predicted in 1964 by Peter Higgs, François Englert and Robert Brout, and by Gerald Guralnik, Carl Hagen and Tom Kibble. The boson is the visible sign of the Higgs field, which in the Standard Model gives elementary particles their mass. Englert and Higgs received the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics.

alternatives.label: Completing the Standard Model
alternatives.text: Physicists see the discovery as confirming the last missing piece of the Standard Model, while leaving questions such as dark matter unanswered.

alternatives.label: "God particle"
alternatives.text: The nickname comes from the title of Leon Lederman's 1993 book; most physicists, including Higgs, disliked it, and it carries no religious meaning.

alternatives.label: Doomsday fears
alternatives.text: Before the LHC started, some critics claimed it could create dangerous black holes; safety reviews concluded there was no risk. Separate theoretical work on the possible metastability of the vacuum is speculative and concerns timescales far beyond the age of the universe.

entries.title: Helicobacter pylori: the doctor who drank the bacteria
entries.mainstream: For most of the 20th century peptic ulcers were blamed on stress, diet and excess stomach acid. In 1979 pathologist Robin Warren in Perth, Australia, observed curved bacteria in stomach biopsies, and with gastroenterologist Barry Marshall he cultured the organism, now called Helicobacter pylori, in 1982. Their 1984 Lancet letter linked it to gastritis and ulcers. To demonstrate the link Marshall drank a culture in 1984 and developed gastritis. Antibiotic treatment of ulcers became standard in the 1990s, and Marshall and Warren won the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

alternatives.label: Lone rebels
alternatives.text: The story is often told as two outsiders defeating a sceptical medical establishment.

alternatives.label: Normal science at work
alternatives.text: Some historians argue acceptance was fairly rapid by medical standards, with a US NIH consensus in 1994, and that scepticism was a reasonable demand for evidence.

alternatives.label: Forgotten forerunners
alternatives.text: Spiral bacteria in the stomach had been reported by earlier researchers since the late 19th century, but their significance was not pursued.

entries.title: Champ, the Lake Champlain monster
entries.dateNote: newspaper reports from the 19th century; Mansi photograph 1977
entries.mainstream: Champ is the name for a large, long-necked creature reported in Lake Champlain, between New York, Vermont and Quebec. Reports in local newspapers go back to the 19th century, and the best-known image is a photograph taken by Sandra Mansi in 1977 and published in 1981. The states of Vermont and New York passed resolutions in the 1980s protecting the creature, and Champ is a local mascot. It is often claimed that Samuel de Champlain himself saw the monster in 1609; his writings instead describe a large fish, the 'chaousarou', usually identified as a gar.

alternatives.label: Misidentification
alternatives.text: Sceptics attribute sightings to large fish such as sturgeon, swimming deer or moose, floating logs and unusual waves (seiches) in the long, deep lake.

alternatives.label: Unknown animal
alternatives.text: Some cryptozoologists suggest a surviving plesiosaur or an unknown species; biologists note the lake formed after the last Ice Age and could not have harboured a plesiosaur lineage.

alternatives.label: The Mansi photo
alternatives.text: Analyses of the 1977 photograph have proposed a log or other floating object; Mansi maintained she saw a living animal, and the location was never precisely identified.

entries.title: The Vinland Map
entries.mainstream: The Vinland Map is a world map on parchment that surfaced in 1957, was bought and later donated to Yale University, and was announced in 1965 as a mid-15th-century map showing 'Vinlanda Insula', the Norse Vinland, west of Greenland, decades before Columbus. In 1973 chemist Walter McCrone's team reported anatase, a form of titanium dioxide first produced commercially in the 1920s, in the ink. In 2021 a full analysis by Yale conservators and scientists found titanium compounds throughout the lines and text, and an altered inscription on the back, and Yale declared the map a forgery. The parchment itself appears to be genuine 15th-century material, probably taken from blank leaves of a real medieval manuscript.

alternatives.label: Modern forgery
alternatives.text: The 2021 Yale study concluded 'there is no reasonable doubt' that the map is a 20th-century fake; who made it is unknown.

alternatives.label: Earlier defenders
alternatives.text: From the 1980s some researchers argued, partly from PIXE analyses, that titanium levels were too low to prove forgery; later work found errors in those measurements.

alternatives.label: Real Vinland regardless
alternatives.text: The forgery does not affect the archaeological evidence for Norse presence in North America, confirmed at L'Anse aux Meadows from 1960.

sources.title: Yale News: Analysis unlocks secret of the Vinland Map — it's a fake (2021)

media.title: The Puzzling Mystery Behind the Vinland Map

entries.title: Glozel: the field of impossible tablets
entries.mainstream: In 1924 a young farmer, Émile Fradin, and his grandfather found a pit in a field at Glozel, near Vichy in central France. Over the following years thousands of objects emerged: fired clay tablets bearing alphabet-like signs, carved bones and stones, pottery and figurines. Physician Antonin Morlet promoted them as a Neolithic writing system far older than the Phoenician alphabet. An international commission of archaeologists declared the finds inauthentic in 1927, and the affair became one of France's great scientific scandals. Later thermoluminescence dates on some ceramics fell largely in the Iron Age to Roman era, while some bones gave medieval dates.

alternatives.label: Hoax
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists regard Glozel as a modern fabrication, perhaps with genuine older objects mixed in; the signs resemble no known script and the stratigraphy was poorly recorded.

alternatives.label: Genuine but misdated
alternatives.text: Some researchers argue the site may be a genuine Iron Age, Gallo-Roman or medieval deposit, and that the tablets reflect a local use of writing; this remains unproven.

alternatives.label: Lost prehistoric script
alternatives.text: Supporters in Morlet's tradition and some alternative writers still claim Glozel preserves a forgotten Neolithic alphabet; this is not supported by the dating evidence.

entries.title: Chernobyl disaster (1986)
entries.mainstream: In the early hours of 26 April 1986, during a safety test, reactor No. 4 of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Soviet Ukraine suffered a power surge, explosions and a graphite fire that released large amounts of radioactive material over Europe. Two workers died on the night and 28 more emergency workers and staff died of acute radiation syndrome within months. The nearby city of Pripyat was evacuated on 27 April, and Sweden's detection of radiation at the Forsmark plant on 28 April helped force Soviet acknowledgement. An exclusion zone around the plant remains. Estimates of eventual cancer deaths vary widely, from about 4,000 among the most exposed groups (WHO-led Chernobyl Forum, 2005) to much higher figures in other studies.

alternatives.label: Operator error
alternatives.text: Early Soviet reports in 1986 placed the main blame on operators violating procedures.

alternatives.label: Design flaws
alternatives.text: The 1992 INSAG-7 review gave greater weight to design features of the RBMK reactor, including its positive void coefficient and the design of the control rods, alongside a weak safety culture.

alternatives.label: Prophecy and fringe theories
alternatives.text: Because 'chornobyl' is a Ukrainian word for a kind of mugwort, some linked the disaster to the star 'Wormwood' in the Book of Revelation; others proposed that a small earthquake triggered it. Both are speculative and rejected by mainstream investigations.

entries.title: The 1918 influenza pandemic ("Spanish flu")
entries.mainstream: The influenza pandemic of 1918–1920, caused by an H1N1 influenza A virus, infected perhaps a third of the world's population and killed an estimated 17 to 50 million people, with some estimates as high as 100 million. It came in several waves, and unusually killed many healthy young adults. It was called 'Spanish' because wartime censorship elsewhere meant neutral Spain's press reported it openly. In 2005 scientists reconstructed the virus from preserved tissue samples, including from a victim buried in Alaskan permafrost.

alternatives.label: Kansas origin
alternatives.text: Historian John M. Barry and others have argued the pandemic began in Haskell County, Kansas, and spread through army camps such as Camp Funston in early 1918.

alternatives.label: European or Asian origin
alternatives.text: Other researchers point to earlier outbreaks in the British army camp at Étaples in France (1916–17) or to northern China, with spread via the Chinese Labour Corps; the origin remains unresolved.

alternatives.label: Treatment as a factor
alternatives.text: A minority hypothesis (Karen Starko, 2009) proposes that very high doses of aspirin contributed to some deaths; this is debated and not the mainstream explanation of the high mortality.

entries.title: Alexander the Great: conqueror, son of a god, and a tomb nobody can find
entries.mainstream: Alexander III of Macedon (356–323 BCE) became king in 336 BCE and within about a decade defeated the Persian Achaemenid Empire, took Egypt (where the oracle of Ammon at Siwa reportedly greeted him as son of the god), and marched as far as the Punjab, where his army refused to go further after the battle of the Hydaspes (326 BCE). He died in Babylon in June 323 BCE aged 32. His empire split among his generals, but the Greek-speaking kingdoms that followed spread Hellenistic culture from Egypt to Afghanistan. His body was taken to Egypt and displayed in Alexandria for centuries; the location of the tomb has been lost since late antiquity.

alternatives.label: How did he die?
alternatives.text: Ancient sources disagree. Modern suggestions include malaria, typhoid fever, alcohol-related illness, poisoning (an ancient rumour blamed Antipater's sons) and, in a 2018 proposal by physician Katherine Hall, Guillain–Barré syndrome; none can be confirmed without remains.

alternatives.label: Legend: the Alexander Romance
alternatives.text: From late antiquity onward the Alexander Romance turned him into a hero who descended under the sea in a glass bell, flew in a basket drawn by griffins and searched for the water of life. Versions spread in dozens of languages from Iceland to Ethiopia and Malaysia.

alternatives.label: Dhul-Qarnayn and Iskandar
alternatives.text: Many traditional and modern commentators identify the Qur'anic Dhul-Qarnayn ("the two-horned"), who builds a wall against Gog and Magog, with Alexander; others reject this identification. In Persian tradition (Shahnameh) he appears as Iskandar, sometimes as a half-Persian prince, while Zoroastrian texts remember him as "the accursed" destroyer.

alternatives.label: The lost tomb
alternatives.text: Excavators have searched Alexandria and the Siwa oasis for the tomb; claims to have found it (e.g. at Siwa in 1995) have not been accepted. Some writers have speculated that his remains were moved or misidentified as those of another figure; this is unproven.

entries.title: Eratosthenes measures the Earth (c. 240 BCE)
entries.mainstream: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, head of the Library of Alexandria, estimated the circumference of the Earth around 240 BCE. According to the later account of Cleomedes, he noted that at Syene (Aswan) the noon sun at the summer solstice stood almost directly overhead, while at Alexandria it cast a shadow corresponding to about one-fiftieth of a circle (7.2°). Taking the distance between the two cities as 5,000 stadia, he obtained 250,000 stadia (later given as 252,000). Depending on which length of stadion he used, his result was within roughly 2% to 16% of the modern value of about 40,000 km. He also produced a map of the inhabited world, a system of latitude and longitude lines and the 'sieve' method for finding prime numbers.

alternatives.label: Exact accuracy is uncertain
alternatives.text: Because the stadion varied (about 157 to 185 m), and Syene is not exactly on the Tropic of Cancer or due south of Alexandria, historians debate whether his good result reflects skill, luck or both.

alternatives.label: The "flat-Earth Middle Ages" myth
alternatives.text: Educated Europeans throughout the Middle Ages knew the Earth was round. The popular idea that Columbus's contemporaries believed in a flat Earth was largely spread in the 19th century, notably by Washington Irving's 1828 biography of Columbus; the real dispute with Columbus was about the Earth's size, where Eratosthenes-type estimates were closer to correct.

alternatives.label: Modern flat-Earth belief
alternatives.text: Small modern flat-Earth movements reject the measurement; repeated experiments, including school replications of Eratosthenes' method, satellite imagery and navigation, all support a spherical Earth.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Myth of the flat Earth

entries.title: Thermopylae (480 BCE): the 300 Spartans and the numbers game
entries.mainstream: In August or September 480 BCE a Greek force of several thousand men under the Spartan king Leonidas, including his 300 Spartans, held the narrow coastal pass of Thermopylae against the invading army of the Persian king Xerxes for three days. According to Herodotus, a local man named Ephialtes showed the Persians a mountain path that let them outflank the Greeks; Leonidas sent most allies away and died with the Spartans, Thespians and Thebans who remained. The Greek navy fought simultaneously at Artemisium, and the Persians were defeated at Salamis later that year and at Plataea in 479 BCE.

alternatives.label: How big was Xerxes' army?
alternatives.text: Herodotus gives over 2.6 million fighting men (more than 5 million with support). Modern historians consider this impossible and usually estimate somewhere between about 70,000 and 300,000.

alternatives.label: Only 300?
alternatives.text: The famous "300" counts only Spartan citizens; ancient sources indicate roughly 5,000–7,000 Greeks at the start, and helots and other allies also died there. The film 300 (2006) is based on a graphic novel and is not intended as history.

alternatives.label: Heroic sacrifice or tactical retreat?
alternatives.text: Some historians read the last stand as a deliberate rearguard to cover the Greek withdrawal; others see it as rooted in Spartan law and religion (an oracle reportedly said Sparta or its king must fall).

media.title: This is Sparta: Fierce warriors of the ancient world - Craig Zimmer

entries.title: The "Mask of Agamemnon": the wrong king, and a debated authenticity
entries.mainstream: In 1876 Heinrich Schliemann excavated Grave Circle A at Mycenae and found gold funerary masks in the shaft graves. On finding one in Shaft Grave V, he is often reported (from later accounts) to have declared he had 'gazed on the face of Agamemnon'. The graves date to about 1600–1500 BCE, some 300 years before the time traditionally assigned to the Trojan War, so the mask cannot belong to the Agamemnon of Homer, if he existed. It is now displayed in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

alternatives.label: Genuine Mycenaean mask
alternatives.text: Most archaeologists accept the mask as an authentic Late Helladic object, stylistically different from the other masks but within Mycenaean variation.

alternatives.label: Partly or wholly faked?
alternatives.text: In the 1970s William M. Calder III and David Traill argued that Schliemann, who had a record of embellishing his finds, may have had the mask made or altered (for example its upturned moustache). Specialists have mostly rejected this, but the mask has never been scientifically tested to settle the question.

alternatives.label: Homer's heroes as history
alternatives.text: The find fed a long-running debate on whether Homer's epics preserve memories of real Bronze Age kings; Linear B tablets and Hittite texts (Ahhiyawa, Wilusa) show a real Mycenaean world, but no named Homeric king has been confirmed.

entries.changed: 1876: hailed as the face of Agamemnon. 20th c.: redated to c. 1550–1500 BCE, centuries before any Trojan War. 1972 onward: authenticity questioned by Calder and Traill; still debated but mostly accepted as genuine.

media.title: Mask of Agamemnon, Mycenae, c. 1550-1500 B.C.E.

entries.title: The Sibylline Books: Rome's secret oracles, burned twice
entries.dateNote: traditionally acquired 6th c. BCE; burned 83 BCE; destroyed early 5th c. CE
entries.mainstream: The Sibylline Books were a collection of Greek oracular verses kept in the temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline Hill in Rome and consulted only on the Senate's order by a priestly college (later the quindecimviri sacris faciundis) in times of crisis, such as plagues, prodigies and military disasters. Their advice typically prescribed new rites or the import of foreign cults, such as that of Cybele in 204 BCE. The original collection burned with the temple in 83 BCE; a new one was gathered from across the Mediterranean, moved by Augustus to the temple of Apollo on the Palatine, and, according to the poet Rutilius Namatianus, was burned by the general Stilicho in the early 5th century CE.

alternatives.label: The legend of the purchase
alternatives.text: Roman tradition says a mysterious old woman, the Sibyl of Cumae, offered nine books to king Tarquinius; when he refused her price she burned three, then three more, and he finally bought the last three for the original price. Historians regard this as a foundation legend.

alternatives.label: Political tool or genuine prophecy?
alternatives.text: Ancient writers such as Cicero already suspected the books could be interpreted to suit those in power; believers saw them as divinely inspired. Their contents were kept secret and almost nothing of the original text survives.

alternatives.label: Not the Sibylline Oracles
alternatives.text: A separate surviving collection called the Sibylline Oracles was written largely by Jewish and Christian authors from about the 2nd century BCE onward; it is sometimes confused with the lost Roman books.

media.author: Francesco Salviati

entries.title: Caesar's Comet (44 BCE): a murdered dictator becomes a star
entries.mainstream: In July 44 BCE, a few months after Julius Caesar was assassinated, a bright comet was seen in Rome for seven days during the games held in his honour by his adopted heir Octavian. Romans widely interpreted it as Caesar's soul ascending to join the gods. Octavian (later Augustus) promoted it as the sidus Iulium ('Julian star'), placed a star on statues of Caesar and minted coins showing it, supporting Caesar's official deification in 42 BCE. Chinese records also describe a comet in 44 BCE, which some astronomers consider the same object.

alternatives.label: A real comet
alternatives.text: Astronomers generally accept that a genuine, unusually bright (possibly sungrazing) comet appeared; it is only known from historical records and has no modern identification.

alternatives.label: Political propaganda
alternatives.text: Historians emphasise how Octavian exploited the omen to legitimise his position; some have questioned how widely it was seen in Rome, as the Roman reports are mostly from writers favourable to him.

alternatives.label: Comets as omens worldwide
alternatives.text: The episode fits a much wider pattern in which comets and new stars were read as signs of the death or rise of rulers, from Chinese court astrology to the 1066 comet on the Bayeux Tapestry.

entries.title: Teutoburg Forest (9 CE): three legions lost, and a battlefield found by a metal detectorist
entries.mainstream: In September 9 CE an alliance of Germanic tribes led by Arminius, a Cheruscan noble who had served as an officer with the Roman army, ambushed and destroyed three Roman legions (XVII, XVIII and XIX) and auxiliaries under the governor Publius Quinctilius Varus in northern Germany. Augustus is said to have cried 'Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!' The legion numbers were never reused, and Rome never permanently held Germania east of the Rhine. From 1987, after finds of Roman coins and sling-shot by British officer Tony Clunn, excavations at Kalkriese near Osnabrück uncovered a battlefield with Roman equipment, bones and a turf rampart used by the attackers.

alternatives.label: Is Kalkriese the site?
alternatives.text: Most archaeologists identify Kalkriese with the Varus battle; a minority argue it may instead record fighting during Germanicus' campaigns in 15–16 CE, since the finds are hard to date to a single year.

alternatives.label: Turning point or overstatement?
alternatives.text: It is often said to have kept Germany outside the Roman (and later Romance-language) world; some historians argue Roman expansion was already slowing for financial and strategic reasons.

alternatives.label: A national myth
alternatives.text: In the 19th century "Hermann" (Arminius) became a German national hero; the Hermannsdenkmal monument was completed in 1875, and the battle was later used in nationalist propaganda.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Battle of the Teutoburg Forest

entries.title: The vanishing Ninth Legion
entries.dateNote: last dated inscription at York 108 CE; disappears by c. 165 CE
entries.mainstream: Legio IX Hispana served in Britain from the invasion of 43 CE and built the fortress at York, where an inscription of 108 CE is the last firmly dated evidence for it in Britain. By the later 2nd century it no longer appears in lists of legions. For much of the 19th and 20th centuries scholars, following Theodor Mommsen, assumed it was destroyed in northern Britain around 117 CE, an idea popularised by Rosemary Sutcliff's novel The Eagle of the Ninth (1954). Later finds of stamped tiles and other material at Nijmegen in the Netherlands suggest that at least part of the legion was transferred to the Rhine.

alternatives.label: Lost in Britain
alternatives.text: Some historians still argue for a disaster in northern Britain in the 110s–120s, possibly connected with unrest before Hadrian's Wall was built.

alternatives.label: Lost in the East
alternatives.text: Others propose the legion was destroyed later elsewhere, for example in the Bar Kokhba revolt in Judaea (132–136 CE) or at the start of the Parthian war (c. 161 CE); no direct evidence names it in either.

alternatives.label: Disbanded rather than destroyed
alternatives.text: A further view is that the legion was disbanded or merged; there is no surviving record of its end, which is why the mystery persists.

entries.changed: 19th c.: Mommsen proposes destruction in Britain c. 117 CE. 1954: Sutcliff's novel fixes the image of a legion lost in Scotland. Late 20th c.: Nijmegen finds suggest transfer to the Continent; fate still unknown.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Eagle of the Ninth

entries.title: Liqian: did lost Roman soldiers settle in China?
entries.dateNote: Battle of Zhizhi 36 BCE; Dubs's hypothesis 1955–57
entries.mainstream: In 1955–57 the American sinologist Homer Dubs proposed that Roman soldiers captured by the Parthians after Crassus's defeat at Carrhae (53 BCE) later served as mercenaries for the Xiongnu leader Zhizhi and were captured by Han Chinese forces at the battle of Zhizhi (36 BCE), where Chinese sources describe a 'fish-scale formation' and a double palisade. He suggested they were then settled in a Han county called Liqian (Li-jien), a name similar to a Han term for the Roman or Hellenistic West. Villagers in Zhelaizhai, Gansu province, some with light hair or eyes, have since been linked to the story by media and local tourism.

alternatives.label: Mainstream scepticism
alternatives.text: Most historians regard Dubs's chain of identifications as unproven: the Chinese texts do not say the soldiers were Roman, the formation and palisade are not uniquely Roman, and no Roman artefacts have been found at Liqian.

alternatives.label: Genetic tests
alternatives.text: A 2007 Y-chromosome study of men from the Liqian area found mostly East Asian paternal lineages and concluded the data did not support a Roman-soldier origin; varied appearance in north-west China is generally attributed to long-standing Silk Road and Central Asian ancestry.

alternatives.label: Still possible
alternatives.text: Supporters argue that a small group of foreign captives could have been absorbed without leaving clear genetic or archaeological traces; the hypothesis therefore remains open but speculative.

sources.title: Testing the hypothesis of an ancient Roman soldier origin of the Liqian people in northwest China: a Y-chromosome perspective

entries.title: Hypatia of Alexandria (killed 415 CE)
entries.dateNote: born c. 350–370 CE; killed March 415 CE
entries.mainstream: Hypatia was a Neoplatonist philosopher, astronomer and mathematician in Alexandria, daughter of the mathematician Theon. She taught pupils including Synesius of Cyrene (later a Christian bishop, whose letters to her survive) and edited or commented on mathematical works. In March 415 CE she was murdered by a Christian mob during a bitter political conflict between the Roman prefect Orestes, whom she advised, and the bishop Cyril of Alexandria. The main sources are the church historian Socrates Scholasticus, who condemned the killing, and later writers such as John of Nikiu, who justified it.

alternatives.label: Martyr of reason
alternatives.text: From the Enlightenment onwards writers such as Voltaire and Edward Gibbon, and later the film Agora (2009), presented her as a symbol of science destroyed by religious fanaticism, sometimes wrongly linking her death to the destruction of the Library of Alexandria.

alternatives.label: Victim of local politics
alternatives.text: Many modern historians stress that she was killed as part of a power struggle in the city rather than for her philosophy or sex, and that pagan and Christian students studied with her.

alternatives.label: Cyril's responsibility
alternatives.text: How far Bishop Cyril (later a saint) was responsible is disputed: some ancient and modern writers blame him directly, others see the mob as acting without his explicit order.

media.title: The murder of ancient Alexandria's greatest scholar - Soraya Field Fiorio

entries.title: The Rök runestone: heroic legend, or fear of a climate catastrophe?
entries.mainstream: The Rök runestone in Östergötland, Sweden, was carved in the early 9th century and carries the longest known runic inscription, about 760 characters, on all its faces, partly written in cipher runes and different runic alphabets. It was raised by a man named Varin in memory of his dead son Vämod. The text poses a series of riddling questions and mentions a ruler of the Goths, usually identified with the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, riding his horse.

alternatives.label: Heroic legends
alternatives.text: The traditional interpretation, developed from the 19th century, reads the text as a collection of allusions to heroic legends and battles, perhaps meant to show the dead son's connection to a great tradition.

alternatives.label: Fear of Fimbulwinter
alternatives.text: A 2020 interdisciplinary study by Per Holmberg and colleagues argued that the riddles refer to the sun, darkness and winter, and that the stone expresses fear of a climate catastrophe like the cooling after the eruptions of 536–540 CE, linked to Norse ideas of Ragnarök. Critics consider this one possible reading among several.

alternatives.label: Cipher and magic
alternatives.text: Some researchers see the cipher runes as playful scholarly display; others suggest ritual or magical intentions. The inscription remains one of the most debated texts of the Viking Age.

sources.title: The Rök Runestone and the End of the World

entries.title: The Lambton Worm: a dragon, a crusader and a nine-generation curse
entries.dateNote: legend set in the 14th–15th c.; recorded in the 19th c.
entries.mainstream: The Lambton Worm is a legend from County Durham in north-east England. Young John Lambton skipped church to fish in the River Wear and caught a small eel-like 'worm', which he threw into a well before leaving for the Crusades. The creature grew huge, coiled around a hill (identified with Worm Hill near Fatfield), and devoured livestock and children. Returning years later, Lambton killed it wearing armour studded with spearheads, on the advice of a wise woman, but broke his vow to kill the first living thing he met afterwards, which was his father, and so his family was cursed for nine generations not to die in their beds. The story was recorded in the 19th century, including in Robert Surtees's History of Durham and a popular 1867 song.

alternatives.label: Folk memory of real deaths?
alternatives.text: Supporters of a historical core note that some Lambton family members did die violently or unusually; folklorists consider the curse a later explanation attached to these deaths.

alternatives.label: A dragon-slaying pattern
alternatives.text: Folklorists place the tale among British "worm" legends (such as the Laidly Worm of Spindleston Heugh and the Sockburn Worm) and the wider dragon-slayer tradition, often tied to local landowning families and landmarks.

alternatives.label: Real animals or fossils?
alternatives.text: Some writers have suggested the legend was inspired by large eels, escaped exotic animals or fossil finds; there is no evidence for these specific origins, which remain speculative.

entries.title: The Golem of Prague
entries.dateNote: attributed to the late 16th c.; Prague legend printed in the 19th c.
entries.mainstream: In Jewish folklore a golem is a human-like figure made of clay or earth and brought to life by sacred words or divine names; the idea draws on the Talmud (which tells of a rabbi who created a man) and on mystical speculation about the Sefer Yetzirah. The most famous version credits Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel (the Maharal of Prague, died 1609) with creating a golem to defend Prague's Jewish community against blood-libel accusations; it was deactivated by removing the letter or name that animated it. The story linking the golem to Rabbi Loew appears in print only in the 19th century; earlier golem stories were attached to Rabbi Elijah of Chełm.

alternatives.label: Legend versus the historical Maharal
alternatives.text: Historians note that Rabbi Loew was a real and influential scholar, but none of his writings or contemporary sources mention a golem.

alternatives.label: The golem in the attic
alternatives.text: A popular tradition holds that the golem's remains lie in the attic of Prague's Old New Synagogue; the attic has been visited (for example by journalist Egon Erwin Kisch in the 1920s) without finding any remains.

alternatives.label: Ancestor of robots and AI
alternatives.text: The golem is often cited, together with Frankenstein and Karel Čapek's R.U.R. (1920, which coined "robot"), as a cultural ancestor of fears and hopes about artificial beings that escape their makers' control.

entries.title: Malleus Maleficarum (1486) and the European witch hunts
entries.mainstream: The Malleus Maleficarum ('Hammer of Witches') was written by the German Dominican inquisitor Heinrich Kramer (Institoris) and printed in 1486; the theologian Jacob Sprenger was named as co-author, though his role is disputed. It argued that witchcraft was real, heretical and mostly practised by women, and gave procedures for prosecuting witches. It reprinted Pope Innocent VIII's bull Summis desiderantes affectibus (1484). It went through many editions, although the Church never officially adopted it. Across Europe, witch trials between about 1450 and 1750 led to an estimated 40,000 to 60,000 executions, concentrated in the Holy Roman Empire.

alternatives.label: How influential was it?
alternatives.text: Some historians see the book as a major engine of the witch hunts; others argue it was one text among many and that most prosecutions were driven by local secular courts, community tensions, wars and climate stresses such as the Little Ice Age.

alternatives.label: "Nine million witches"
alternatives.text: A figure of nine million victims, traceable to an 18th-century extrapolation and repeated by some 20th-century writers, is rejected by modern historians, whose archival studies support tens of thousands.

alternatives.label: Suppression of folk healers?
alternatives.text: Some writers argue the trials targeted midwives, healers or surviving pagan practices; historians have found limited evidence that midwives were especially targeted, and the "surviving pagan witch-cult" theory of Margaret Murray (1921) has been largely rejected.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Witch trials in the early modern period

media.title: The book that fuelled 150 years of witch hunting frenzy | Deja Vu

entries.title: Halley's Comet on the Bayeux Tapestry (1066)
entries.mainstream: In April 1066 Halley's Comet was visible across Europe and Asia. The Bayeux Tapestry, an embroidered cloth about 70 m long probably made in England in the 1070s, shows people pointing at it with the caption 'ISTI MIRANT STELLA' ('these men wonder at the star'), next to the newly crowned King Harold II, months before his defeat and death at the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066. The chronicler William of Malmesbury later reported that the monk Eilmer of Malmesbury, who had once tried to fly with wings, greeted the comet as a sign of disaster for England.

alternatives.label: Omen in hindsight
alternatives.text: Historians note that the tapestry was made after the Norman victory and frames the comet as a portent of Harold's fall, consistent with its role as Norman-commissioned (probably by Bishop Odo) account of the conquest.

alternatives.label: A propaganda document?
alternatives.text: Some scholars find subtle English sympathies in the embroidery, which was probably sewn by Anglo-Saxon needleworkers; the balance between Norman propaganda and English perspective is debated.

alternatives.label: Comets as messages
alternatives.text: Across cultures comets were taken as signs of the death of kings or coming wars; the same comet's periodic return was only predicted by Edmond Halley in 1705 and confirmed in 1758–59.

media.title: What's the story in the Bayeux Tapestry?

entries.title: Ibn Battuta's travels (1325–1354)
entries.mainstream: Ibn Battuta (1304–c. 1368/69), a Muslim legal scholar from Tangier, left home in 1325 to make the pilgrimage to Mecca and kept travelling for nearly 30 years. His journeys took him across North Africa, the Middle East, East Africa (Mogadishu, Kilwa), Anatolia, the Golden Horde, Central Asia, India (where he served as a judge for the Sultan of Delhi), the Maldives, Sri Lanka, possibly China, Al-Andalus and across the Sahara to the Mali Empire. On his return to Morocco he dictated his account, known as the Rihla, to the writer Ibn Juzayy, completed in 1355.

alternatives.label: Trustworthy eyewitness
alternatives.text: Historians rely on the Rihla as a unique source on the 14th-century Islamic world, including the Maldives, the Swahili coast and the court of Mansa Sulayman of Mali.

alternatives.label: Borrowed passages and doubtful trips
alternatives.text: Scholars have shown that some passages were copied from the earlier traveller Ibn Jubayr, and many doubt that Ibn Battuta made all the journeys he describes, especially to the Volga Bulgars and to China, which may be based on others' accounts.

alternatives.label: Distance record
alternatives.text: He is often said to have covered around 117,000 km, more than Marco Polo; the figure is an approximate modern reconstruction.

media.title: Great Voyages: Traveler's Tips from the 14th Century: The Detours of Ibn Battuta

entries.title: Hildegard of Bingen's visions
entries.mainstream: Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179) was a German Benedictine abbess, composer, writer on medicine and natural history, and visionary. In 1141 she began recording the visions she said she had experienced since childhood, which she described as a 'living light', in the book Scivias ('Know the Ways'), completed around 1151 and illustrated with striking images. She also invented an alphabet and a partly constructed language (Lingua ignota), corresponded with popes and emperors, and composed some of the earliest liturgical music whose composer is known by name. She was declared a saint and a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

alternatives.label: Divine revelation
alternatives.text: Within her lifetime Pope Eugenius III approved her visions, and Catholic tradition considers them genuine religious experiences.

alternatives.label: Migraine aura
alternatives.text: In 1917 historian Charles Singer, and later neurologist Oliver Sacks, suggested that the shimmering lights, fortifications and falling stars in her descriptions and illustrations resemble migraine aura; others caution against retrospective diagnosis and note that such an explanation does not address the content or meaning of her visions.

alternatives.label: A woman's authority
alternatives.text: Historians emphasise that presenting her knowledge as visionary gave a 12th-century woman the authority to teach and write on theology at a time when women were generally barred from doing so.

entries.title: Melusine: the serpent-woman ancestor of noble houses
entries.mainstream: Melusine is a female spirit of fresh waters in European folklore, usually depicted as a woman who becomes a serpent or fish from the waist down. The best-known version is the Roman de Mélusine written by Jean d'Arras in 1393 for the Duke of Berry: Melusine marries Raymondin on condition that he never sees her on a Saturday; when he spies on her bathing and discovers her serpent tail, she flies away in the form of a dragon. She was claimed as an ancestor by the House of Lusignan, rulers of Cyprus and Jerusalem, and by other noble families including the counts of Luxembourg.

alternatives.label: Political genealogy
alternatives.text: Historians see the romance partly as dynastic propaganda: a supernatural ancestress gave prestige to the Lusignans and helped legitimise claims, including the Duke of Berry's to the castle of Lusignan.

alternatives.label: A widespread pattern
alternatives.text: Folklorists classify Melusine among "fairy bride" or supernatural-wife tales with a broken taboo, a pattern also found in Japanese, Celtic and other traditions (for example selkie stories).

alternatives.label: Older roots
alternatives.text: Some scholars connect her with earlier water deities or serpent-goddess traditions; these links are possible but hard to demonstrate.

media.title: The Folktale of Melusine, the Medieval Face of the Starbucks Logo

entries.title: The Travels of Sir John Mandeville: a bestseller from an armchair
entries.mainstream: The Book of Sir John Mandeville appeared in French around 1357–1371, claiming to be the account of an English knight who travelled to the Holy Land, Egypt, India, China and beyond between 1322 and 1356. It describes real places alongside wonders such as dog-headed men, headless people with faces in their chests, the land of Prester John and the vegetable lamb of Tartary. It was translated into many languages and was among the most popular books of the late Middle Ages; it argued that the Earth was round and could be circumnavigated.

alternatives.label: Compiled from other books
alternatives.text: Scholars have shown that most of the text was compiled from earlier sources, including the travels of Odoric of Pordenone and William of Boldensel and the encyclopedia of Vincent of Beauvais; the author probably travelled little, if at all.

alternatives.label: Who was "Mandeville"?
alternatives.text: The author's identity is unknown. Proposals include the Liège physician Jean de Bourgogne and the chronicler Jean d'Outremeuse; many scholars think "Sir John Mandeville" is a pen name.

alternatives.label: Influence on explorers
alternatives.text: Columbus and other explorers are reported to have known the book, and its round-Earth arguments and accounts of wealthy eastern lands shaped late medieval expectations of the wider world.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Travels of Sir John Mandeville

entries.title: Codex Gigas, the "Devil's Bible"
entries.mainstream: The Codex Gigas is the largest surviving medieval European manuscript, about 92 cm tall and weighing around 75 kg. It was produced in the early 13th century, probably at the Benedictine monastery of Podlažice in Bohemia, and contains the Vulgate Bible, Josephus's Jewish Antiquities, Isidore's Etymologies, medical texts, a chronicle of Bohemia, magical formulas and a calendar. One full page shows a large horned devil, opposite a page depicting the Heavenly City. Swedish troops took it from Prague in 1648 at the end of the Thirty Years' War; it is now in the National Library of Sweden in Stockholm.

alternatives.label: Legend: a pact with the Devil
alternatives.text: A later legend says a monk who had broken his vows was to be walled up alive, promised to write a book containing all human knowledge in a single night, and called on the Devil to finish it, adding the portrait in gratitude.

alternatives.label: One scribe, many years
alternatives.text: Palaeographic studies indicate the whole book was written in a remarkably uniform hand by a single scribe, which modern researchers estimate would have taken roughly 20 to 30 years of work; a note in the manuscript names Herman the Recluse (Hermannus inclusus), traditionally taken to be the scribe.

alternatives.label: Why the devil?
alternatives.text: Scholars generally read the devil opposite the Heavenly City as a didactic contrast between damnation and salvation, perhaps linked to the confession texts nearby, rather than evidence of diabolical authorship.

entries.title: Hanno the Navigator: a Carthaginian voyage to West Africa and the "gorillas"
entries.dateNote: c. 500 BCE (5th c. BCE; date uncertain)
entries.mainstream: The Periplus of Hanno is a short Greek text that claims to translate a Punic inscription set up in the temple of Baal Hammon at Carthage. It describes how Hanno sailed through the Strait of Gibraltar with 60 ships, reportedly carrying 30,000 settlers, founding colonies along the Atlantic coast of Morocco and then exploring further south. The account mentions crocodiles and hippopotamuses in a river, a land where fires burned at night, a tall burning mountain called the 'Chariot of the Gods' (Theon Ochema), and hairy 'wild people' whom interpreters called Gorillai; three females were captured, killed and their skins taken back to Carthage. The voyage is usually dated to around 500 BCE.

alternatives.label: As far as Cameroon or Gabon
alternatives.text: Many scholars identify the burning mountain with Mount Cameroon, an active volcano, which would mean Hanno reached the Gulf of Guinea; the "gorillas" may have been chimpanzees, gorillas or people.

alternatives.label: A much shorter voyage
alternatives.text: Others argue the realistic part of the voyage ended in southern Morocco, Senegal or Sierra Leone, and that winds and currents along the Saharan coast made a longer return trip very difficult for ancient ships; the text may be shortened, exaggerated or partly literary.

alternatives.label: The name "gorilla"
alternatives.text: In 1847 the American missionary Thomas Savage and naturalist Jeffries Wyman borrowed Hanno's word to name the newly described great ape, Gorilla, giving the ancient text a modern afterlife.

entries.title: The Mutapa kingdom and the European search for King Solomon's Ophir
entries.mainstream: The Mutapa (Mwenemutapa or Monomotapa) state was a Shona kingdom founded in the 15th century, by tradition by Nyatsimba Mutota, in the region between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers in present-day Zimbabwe and Mozambique. It grew rich from gold and ivory trade with Swahili merchants on the Indian Ocean coast, and from the 16th century the Portuguese tried to control its gold, eventually making the kingdom a vassal in 1629. It declined in the 17th and 18th centuries. Portuguese writers from the 16th century onward speculated that its gold-producing lands, and the stone ruins of the interior, were the biblical Ophir, from where King Solomon's ships brought gold.

alternatives.label: Ophir in Africa?
alternatives.text: The location of the biblical Ophir is unknown; proposals include southern Arabia, the Horn of Africa, India and southern Africa. There is no archaeological evidence connecting Solomon or the Queen of Sheba to Mutapa or Great Zimbabwe.

alternatives.label: Colonial myth-making
alternatives.text: The German geologist Karl Mauch (1871) and later Rhodesian colonial writers attributed Great Zimbabwe to Phoenicians or Sheba; archaeologists from David Randall-MacIver (1905) and Gertrude Caton-Thompson (1929) onward showed that the stone towns were built by ancestors of the Shona, and the colonial denial is now studied as politically motivated.

alternatives.label: Literature
alternatives.text: The Ophir legend inspired H. Rider Haggard's novel King Solomon's Mines (1885), which helped spread the idea of lost white or foreign builders in Africa.

entries.title: Battle of Adwa (1896): an African army defeats a European invasion
entries.mainstream: On 1 March 1896 the Ethiopian army of Emperor Menelik II, with Empress Taytu Betul and regional commanders, decisively defeated an invading Italian army under General Oreste Baratieri near Adwa in northern Ethiopia. The war had grown out of a dispute over the 1889 Treaty of Wuchale, whose Italian text made Ethiopia a protectorate while the Amharic text did not. Italy lost several thousand men killed, and the Treaty of Addis Ababa (October 1896) recognised Ethiopian independence. Ethiopia remained independent while the rest of Africa was colonised, until the Italian invasion of 1935–36.

alternatives.label: Symbol of African independence
alternatives.text: Adwa became a major symbol for Pan-African and anti-colonial movements; the colours and history of Ethiopia influenced movements in the Caribbean and the Americas, including Rastafari.

alternatives.label: Divine help
alternatives.text: Ethiopian Orthodox tradition holds that the tabot (consecrated altar tablet) of St George was carried to the battle and that the saint aided the Ethiopian army; the victory is commemorated on St George's feast and in Addis Ababa's St George's Cathedral.

alternatives.label: Why Ethiopia won
alternatives.text: Historians point to Menelik's large, well-armed army (with modern rifles bought partly from Europe), Ethiopian unity, poor Italian intelligence and maps, and Baratieri's decision to attack; Italian nationalist accounts long blamed individual generals.
