entries.title: Heike crabs: samurai faces on crab shells
entries.dateNote: legend linked to the battle of 1185
entries.mainstream: Heikea japonica is a small crab of Japanese waters whose shell bears ridges and grooves resembling an angry human face. Japanese legend says the crabs carry the spirits of the Taira (Heike) samurai who drowned at the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185, when the Taira clan was destroyed by the Minamoto and the child emperor Antoku died in the sea.

alternatives.label: Artificial selection by fishermen
alternatives.text: In 1952 biologist Julian Huxley proposed that fishermen had for centuries thrown back crabs with the most face-like shells out of respect, unintentionally selecting for human-like faces. Carl Sagan popularised the idea in Cosmos (1980) as an example of selection.

alternatives.label: Ordinary anatomy and pareidolia
alternatives.text: Critics, including crab biologist Joel W. Martin (1993), note that these crabs are generally not eaten (so there is little reason for fishermen to select them), that the ridges mark muscle attachments, and that related species and fossils show similar patterns; the face is seen as an example of human pattern-seeking (pareidolia).

alternatives.label: Living memory
alternatives.text: Whatever the biology, the legend keeps the memory of the Genpei War alive, alongside the ghost stories of Hōichi the Earless set at the same strait.

entries.title: The Ainu: Japan's Indigenous people and the debate over their origins
entries.dateNote: Ainu culture from c. 13th c.; recognised as Indigenous 2008/2019
entries.mainstream: The Ainu are the Indigenous people of Hokkaido, and historically also of Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands and northern Honshu. Ainu culture, with its own language (an isolate), bear ceremony (iomante), oral epics (yukar) and trade networks reaching Manchuria, is usually traced from around the 13th century, developing out of the Satsumon and Okhotsk cultures. The Japanese Matsumae domain increasingly controlled trade with them; Shakushain's revolt (1669) was suppressed. After 1869 Hokkaido was colonised, and the Hokkaido Former Aborigines Protection Act of 1899 promoted assimilation. Japan's parliament recognised the Ainu as an Indigenous people in 2008, and a 2019 law gave them legal recognition.

alternatives.label: Jōmon descendants
alternatives.text: Genetic and skeletal studies indicate that the Ainu descend largely from Jōmon-period populations of the Japanese archipelago, with later contributions from the Okhotsk culture of the Sea of Okhotsk region.

alternatives.label: Discarded "Caucasoid" theories
alternatives.text: Nineteenth- and early 20th-century anthropologists, impressed by facial features and body hair, claimed the Ainu were a lost European or "Caucasian" people; modern genetics has rejected this.

alternatives.label: The original Japanese?
alternatives.text: Some writers argue that Ainu or Jōmon peoples were the original inhabitants of all Japan and that their role has been downplayed in national history; placenames of possible Ainu origin in northern Honshu support a former presence there, but the wider picture remains debated.

entries.title: The Peach Blossom Spring: a hidden valley outside time
entries.mainstream: The Peach Blossom Spring is a short prose fable written by the Chinese poet Tao Yuanming (Tao Qian) in 421 CE. A fisherman from Wuling follows a stream lined with blossoming peach trees to a cave, and passes through into a peaceful farming valley whose people say their ancestors fled the chaos of the Qin dynasty centuries earlier; they know nothing of the Han or later dynasties. They feed him and ask him not to tell anyone. He marks his route, but when he returns with officials the place can never be found again. The phrase 'peach blossom spring' (taohuayuan) became the standard Chinese expression for a hidden utopia.

alternatives.label: Pure fiction and philosophy
alternatives.text: Most literary scholars read it as a Daoist-influenced allegory of escape from war and politics, written by a poet who had himself withdrawn from office.

alternatives.label: Real refugee communities
alternatives.text: The historian Chen Yinke (1936) argued that the story reflects real fortified refugee settlements (wubao) that existed in northern China during the wars of the 4th century; others think the parallels are general rather than specific.

alternatives.label: Shangri-La and other hidden valleys
alternatives.text: The tale belongs to a worldwide pattern of hidden valleys outside time, from Tibetan beyul and Shambhala to James Hilton's Shangri-La (1933); whether such stories reflect isolated real communities, religious ideals or simple storytelling varies by case.

entries.title: The Pueblo Revolt of 1680
entries.mainstream: On 10 August 1680 the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico rose in a coordinated revolt against Spanish colonial rule, which had suppressed their religion and imposed forced labour and tribute. The leader most associated with it, Po'pay of Ohkay Owingeh, had been flogged in 1675 for 'sorcery'. Runners carried knotted cords to the pueblos to count down the days to the uprising. About 400 Spanish colonists and 21 Franciscan friars were killed, Santa Fe was besieged, and the surviving Spanish withdrew to El Paso. The Pueblos remained independent for 12 years until Diego de Vargas reconquered the region from 1692.

alternatives.label: Spirit guidance
alternatives.text: Spanish testimony records that Po'pay claimed to receive instructions in a kiva at Taos from spirit beings; some Pueblo traditions remember the revolt as a restoration of religious and cosmic order.

alternatives.label: First American revolution?
alternatives.text: Some historians and Pueblo people call it the first successful revolution in what is now the United States; others note it was a coalition of many independent communities with varied aims, which later divided.

alternatives.label: Lasting effects
alternatives.text: Although the Spanish returned, many historians argue that the revolt led to greater tolerance of Pueblo religion and land rights, helping Pueblo cultures survive. A statue of Po'pay was placed in the US Capitol in 2005.

entries.title: Ponce de León and the Fountain of Youth: a legend added later
entries.mainstream: The Spanish conquistador Juan Ponce de León led the first recorded European expedition to Florida in 1513. He is widely said to have been searching for a Fountain of Youth. However, his royal contract and contemporary records say nothing about such a fountain; the link first appears in the writings of the royal chronicler Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo (1535), who appears to have mocked him with it, and was repeated by later writers such as Hernando de Escalante Fontaneda and Antonio de Herrera. Stories of waters that restore youth are far older, found in Herodotus (the long-lived Ethiopians' spring), the Alexander Romance and medieval European legends.

alternatives.label: Myth about history
alternatives.text: Most historians conclude that Ponce de León was seeking land, gold and a governorship, and that the fountain story was attached to him after his death, partly to ridicule him.

alternatives.label: Indigenous rumours
alternatives.text: Some sources say Taíno or other Indigenous people told Spaniards of a restorative spring or river (sometimes called Bimini); scholars debate whether such reports reflect real Indigenous traditions or European expectations.

alternatives.label: Tourist site
alternatives.text: In St. Augustine, Florida, a "Fountain of Youth Archaeological Park", promoted since the early 20th century, has real colonial and Timucua archaeology but no evidence of a magical spring or of Ponce de León's landing there.

entries.title: Hampi, the city of victory, and Hanuman's birthplace
entries.mainstream: Hampi in Karnataka, India, was the core of Vijayanagara, capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, founded around 1336 by the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty. By the 15th–16th centuries it was among the largest cities in the world, described with wonder by visitors such as the Persian envoy Abdur Razzaq and the Portuguese Domingo Paes. After the empire's defeat by an alliance of Deccan sultanates at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, the city was sacked and abandoned. Its temples, bazaars and royal enclosures among granite boulders are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986).

alternatives.label: Founded with a sage's guidance
alternatives.text: Tradition credits the sage Vidyaranya with inspiring the founding of the city; historians debate the extent of his role, which is mainly documented in later sources.

alternatives.label: Kishkindha of the Ramayana
alternatives.text: Local tradition identifies the area with Kishkindha, the monkey kingdom of the Ramayana, and Anjanadri hill near Hampi as the birthplace of Hanuman; other places in India (for example in Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand) also claim the birthplace. This is a matter of faith and tradition, not archaeology.

alternatives.label: Why did it fall so completely?
alternatives.text: Some historians emphasise the battle and the following sack, others longer-term political divisions, the betrayal of Muslim commanders in Vijayanagara service, or shifts in trade.

entries.title: Monte Albán and the Danzantes: dancers, captives or something else?
entries.mainstream: Monte Albán, on a flattened mountain ridge above the Valley of Oaxaca, Mexico, was founded around 500 BCE and became the capital of the Zapotec state for over a thousand years, declining by about 750–850 CE. Among its earliest monuments are more than 300 carved stone slabs called the Danzantes ('dancers'), showing naked men in contorted poses, some with closed eyes and mutilated bodies, along with some of the earliest writing in Mesoamerica. Building J, shaped like an arrowhead, is set at an unusual angle to the rest of the plaza. In 1932 Alfonso Caso found Tomb 7, reused by Mixtec people and filled with gold, jade and carved bone. Monte Albán and Oaxaca's historic centre are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1987).

alternatives.label: Captives, not dancers
alternatives.text: Most archaeologists now interpret the Danzantes as slain or sacrificed war captives, displayed to show Monte Albán's military power; the name reflects 19th-century impressions.

alternatives.label: Other readings
alternatives.text: Earlier interpretations saw them as dancers, swimmers, people with medical conditions, or shamans in trance; some fringe writers have also claimed they show foreign peoples, a view not supported by archaeologists.

alternatives.label: Building J and the sky
alternatives.text: Building J's orientation has been linked by archaeoastronomers to the rising of the star Capella and to the zenith passage of the sun; others see the shape as a conquest monument listing subject towns. The two ideas are not exclusive.

sources.title: Historic Centre of Oaxaca and Archaeological Site of Monte Albán (UNESCO)

entries.title: The Oak Island Money Pit
entries.mainstream: According to the most widely told story, in 1795 a young man named Daniel McGinnis found a circular depression on Oak Island, Nova Scotia, and with friends dug down through layers of logs. Later treasure companies (from about 1803 onward) reported platforms of logs at regular intervals, a stone with strange symbols at around 90 feet (now lost, with no surviving photograph), and flooding by seawater, which some interpreted as deliberately engineered booby-trap tunnels. Excavations over two centuries have produced few datable finds; six people have died in accidents, including four in 1965 overcome by gas in a shaft. Since 2014 the TV series The Curse of Oak Island has followed a new search.

alternatives.label: Hidden treasure
alternatives.text: Proposed treasures include pirate gold (Captain Kidd, Blackbeard), Spanish or British military payrolls, French crown jewels, Knights Templar relics or the Holy Grail, and manuscripts proving Francis Bacon wrote Shakespeare. None has been found, and these remain speculative.

alternatives.label: Natural sinkhole
alternatives.text: Geologists note that the area contains soluble anhydrite and gypsum layers that form natural sinkholes and caverns, and that seawater infiltration through porous rock can explain the flooding; many early "platform" reports could be fallen trees or debris.

alternatives.label: Embellished early accounts
alternatives.text: Historians have found that the earliest detailed written accounts date from the 1860s, decades after the claimed discovery, and that details such as the inscribed stone grew in retelling.

entries.title: The Beale ciphers: buried treasure or 1885 hoax?
entries.mainstream: The Beale Papers, a pamphlet published in Lynchburg, Virginia, in 1885 by James B. Ward, tells how a man named Thomas J. Beale buried a large treasure of gold, silver and jewels in Bedford County, Virginia, around 1819–1821, and left three encrypted messages with an innkeeper, Robert Morriss. The pamphlet says an unnamed friend decoded the second cipher using the United States Declaration of Independence as a key, revealing a description of the treasure; the first (location) and third (names of owners) have never been solved.

alternatives.label: Real treasure, unsolved code
alternatives.text: Treasure hunters and amateur cryptographers have searched and dug in Bedford County for over a century, believing the first and third ciphers conceal a genuine location.

alternatives.label: Hoax
alternatives.text: Statistical analyses of the unsolved ciphers suggest patterns unlikely in real encrypted text, and writer Joe Nickell (1982) pointed to anachronistic words such as "stampeding" in Beale's supposed letters; no record of Thomas J. Beale matching the story has been firmly established. Many researchers conclude the pamphlet was a fiction, possibly a money-making scheme or a Masonic-style allegory.

alternatives.label: Still open
alternatives.text: Supporters argue that the absence of a solution does not prove a hoax, and the ciphers remain a popular challenge in cryptography courses.

entries.title: Symmes's hole: the Hollow Earth with openings at the poles
entries.mainstream: In 1818 John Cleves Symmes Jr., a former US Army officer, sent a circular to scientists and governments declaring 'I declare the earth is hollow, and habitable within', containing concentric spheres open at the poles. He lectured widely and petitioned Congress to fund an expedition to the polar opening. Hollow-Earth ideas had a scientific pedigree: in 1692 the astronomer Edmond Halley proposed concentric shells inside the Earth to explain shifts in the magnetic field. Symmes's follower Jeremiah Reynolds helped build support for polar exploration that fed into the United States Exploring Expedition (1838–42).

alternatives.label: Disproved by geophysics
alternatives.text: Seismology from the early 20th century (Richard Oldham's detection of the core in 1906, Inge Lehmann's inner core in 1936) and gravity measurements show a dense solid inner core and liquid outer core, incompatible with a hollow Earth; polar regions have been mapped and crossed without openings.

alternatives.label: Modern versions
alternatives.text: Hollow-Earth beliefs survive in some esoteric and conspiracy traditions, often combined with Agartha, Shambhala, Nazi-escape stories or Admiral Byrd's polar flights; these are not supported by evidence.

alternatives.label: Literary legacy
alternatives.text: The idea inspired fiction such as Symzonia (1820), Edgar Allan Poe's work and Jules Verne's Journey to the Centre of the Earth (1864).

entries.changed: 1692: Halley proposes concentric shells. 1818: Symmes adds polar openings. 1906–1936: seismology reveals solid inner and liquid outer core, ruling out a hollow Earth.

media.title: Why Scientists Briefly Thought the Earth Was Hollow

entries.title: The Shaver Mystery: "I Remember Lemuria!" and the deros underground
entries.mainstream: In March 1945 the pulp magazine Amazing Stories, edited by Ray Palmer, published 'I Remember Lemuria!' by Richard Sharpe Shaver, a Pennsylvania welder. Presented as fiction but promoted as true, it claimed that cave systems beneath the Earth were inhabited by 'deros', degenerate descendants of an ancient super-race, who used advanced machines to torment surface people with voices, accidents and evil thoughts. The magazine received thousands of letters from readers claiming similar experiences, and sales rose sharply. Shaver had earlier spent time in a psychiatric hospital, a fact not widely known to readers at the time.

alternatives.label: Psychological explanation
alternatives.text: Many writers interpret Shaver's "voices" as symptoms of mental illness, and the reader response as a mix of play, belief and shared anxieties of the war years.

alternatives.label: A bridge to flying saucers
alternatives.text: Historians of the UFO phenomenon note that Palmer, after the Kenneth Arnold sighting of 1947, shifted from the Shaver Mystery to flying saucers, co-founding Fate magazine in 1948, and that Shaver material helped prepare an audience for UFO narratives.

alternatives.label: Believers
alternatives.text: A small group of supporters continued to believe in Shaver's caves; Shaver himself later claimed that patterns in cut rocks were "rock books" left by the ancient race. These claims are not supported by evidence.

entries.title: Ley lines: from old straight tracks to earth energies
entries.mainstream: In 1921 the English businessman and antiquarian Alfred Watkins noticed that ancient sites in Herefordshire, such as standing stones, hillforts, churches and crossroads, seemed to fall on straight lines. In The Old Straight Track (1925) he proposed that these 'leys' marked prehistoric trackways laid out by surveyors. Archaeologists did not accept the idea. In the 1960s ley lines were revived in a new form, especially through John Michell's The View Over Atlantis (1969), as lines of earth energy, sometimes linked to UFO flight paths, dowsing and ancient wisdom; a 'ley hunter' movement grew up around them.

alternatives.label: Chance alignments
alternatives.text: Statisticians and archaeologists have shown that in a landscape dense with ancient and medieval sites, many straight alignments of three or more points are expected by chance; the sites on a given ley are also often of widely different dates. Archaeologists generally classify ley lines as pseudoarchaeology.

alternatives.label: Real ancient alignments
alternatives.text: Some genuine prehistoric alignments do exist, for example monuments oriented to solstice sunrise or sunset (as Norman Lockyer argued) or Roman roads, but these are specific and testable rather than a network.

alternatives.label: Earth energies
alternatives.text: Many practitioners of dowsing, earth mysteries and New Age spirituality regard ley lines as real channels of subtle energy; no instrument has detected such energy, so the claim remains a matter of belief.

entries.title: Velikovsky's Worlds in Collision (1950)
entries.mainstream: In 1950 the psychiatrist Immanuel Velikovsky published Worlds in Collision, arguing that around 1500 BCE a comet ejected from Jupiter passed close to Earth, causing the plagues of Egypt, the parting of the sea and manna, before settling as the planet Venus; later close passes of Mars caused catastrophes in the 8th–7th centuries BCE. He drew mainly on myths and ancient texts from many cultures. The book became a bestseller, but astronomers, led by Harlow Shapley, reacted fiercely; after threats of a textbook boycott, the publisher Macmillan transferred it to Doubleday within two months. Velikovsky also proposed a radically revised chronology of ancient Egypt in Ages in Chaos (1952).

alternatives.label: Physically impossible
alternatives.text: Astronomers argue that the orbital mechanics, the composition of Venus and Earth's geological and ice-core records rule out the proposed events; Carl Sagan presented a detailed critique at the 1974 AAAS symposium.

alternatives.label: Successful predictions?
alternatives.text: Supporters point to his statements that Venus would be hot and that Jupiter would emit radio noise, which were later confirmed; critics reply that these were not uniquely derived from his theory, and that many of his other predictions failed.

alternatives.label: Suppression or quality control
alternatives.text: The campaign against the book is often cited as an example of scientific establishment suppression; others see it as a heavy-handed but legitimate rejection of unsupported ideas. The episode influenced later debates on catastrophism, cosmic impacts and the sociology of science.

entries.title: The Versailles "time slip" (1901)
entries.mainstream: On 10 August 1901 two English academics, Charlotte Anne Moberly, principal of St Hugh's Hall, Oxford, and Eleanor Jourdain, visited the gardens of the Petit Trianon at Versailles. They later reported feeling oppressed and seeing people in 18th-century dress, including a woman sketching whom Moberly came to believe was Marie Antoinette. After research they concluded they had somehow entered the queen's memories or the year 1789. In 1911 they published their account, An Adventure, under the pseudonyms Elizabeth Morison and Frances Lamont; it became one of the most famous ghost or time-slip stories.

alternatives.label: Costume party
alternatives.text: In 1965 Philippe Jullian suggested that the women had stumbled on a costume rehearsal or party organised by the poet Robert de Montesquiou, who lived nearby and reportedly staged such events in period dress.

alternatives.label: Memory and suggestion
alternatives.text: Psychical researchers and sceptics noted that the account was written down months later, revised over years and shaped by shared discussion and historical reading, making it unreliable as evidence.

alternatives.label: Genuine paranormal experience
alternatives.text: Believers in time slips regard it as a classic case of retrocognition, pointing to the authors' respectability and apparent sincerity; the claim cannot be tested.

entries.title: Princess Caraboo of Javasu (1817)
entries.mainstream: In April 1817 a young woman in exotic dress appeared in Almondsbury, near Bristol, England, speaking an unknown language. With the help of a Portuguese sailor who claimed to understand her, she was presented as Princess Caraboo from the island of Javasu in the Indian Ocean, kidnapped by pirates before escaping by jumping overboard. She was taken in by a local magistrate's family, fenced, swam, prayed to a god she called 'Allah-Talla' and became a sensation. A boarding-house keeper, Mrs Neale, recognised her from a newspaper portrait as Mary Baker (née Willcocks), a cobbler's daughter from Devon. She left for Philadelphia in 1817 and in later life sold leeches to Bristol Infirmary.

alternatives.label: Skilled impostor
alternatives.text: Most accounts present her as a talented performer who exploited Regency fascination with the exotic East; how she sustained an invented language and customs for weeks remains impressive.

alternatives.label: Experts fooled
alternatives.text: The case is often cited as an example of how "experts" can project their expectations onto a mystery: visitors identified her language and writing with various Asian scripts.

alternatives.label: Poverty and survival
alternatives.text: Social historians emphasise that she had endured poverty, illness and servitude, and that the imposture offered shelter and attention.

entries.title: Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859)
entries.mainstream: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species on 24 November 1859, arguing that species change over time and descend from common ancestors through natural selection: individuals with heritable variations better suited to their environment leave more offspring. The idea had been presented jointly with Alfred Russel Wallace, who reached it independently, at the Linnean Society in 1858. The book provoked intense debate, including the 1860 Oxford exchange between Thomas Huxley and Bishop Samuel Wilberforce. Combined with genetics in the 'modern synthesis' of the 1930s–40s and supported by fossils, comparative anatomy and DNA, evolution by natural selection became the foundation of modern biology.

alternatives.label: Mainstream science
alternatives.text: Biologists regard common descent as overwhelmingly confirmed; debates continue on the relative roles of selection, genetic drift, development and other mechanisms.

alternatives.label: Religious views
alternatives.text: Many religious traditions and believers accept evolution as compatible with faith (theistic evolution); others hold to special creation or young-Earth creationism, and the intelligent-design movement argues some features require a designer. Courts in the USA (e.g. Kitzmiller v. Dover, 2005) ruled intelligent design to be religious rather than science.

alternatives.label: Earlier evolutionary ideas
alternatives.text: Ideas of transformation of species existed before Darwin, from ancient Greek and medieval Islamic thinkers to Lamarck and Darwin's grandfather Erasmus; Darwin's contribution was a mechanism backed by extensive evidence.

entries.title: The Miller–Urey experiment (1952–53): making life's building blocks in a flask
entries.mainstream: In 1952 Stanley Miller, a graduate student working with Harold Urey at the University of Chicago, passed electric sparks through a mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour meant to imitate the early Earth's atmosphere. Within days the water turned brown and contained amino acids such as glycine and alanine, the building blocks of proteins. The results, published in Science in May 1953, launched the experimental study of the origin of life (abiogenesis). In 2008 a re-analysis of Miller's archived samples with modern instruments found more than 20 amino acids, especially in a variant simulating a volcanic eruption.

alternatives.label: What was the early atmosphere?
alternatives.text: Many geochemists later concluded that the early atmosphere was less reducing (more carbon dioxide and nitrogen) than Miller assumed, which yields fewer amino acids; volcanic plumes or local environments may still have been suitable.

alternatives.label: Other origin-of-life scenarios
alternatives.text: Researchers also study deep-sea hydrothermal vents, hot springs on land, an "RNA world" in which self-copying RNA came first, mineral surfaces and delivery of organics by meteorites (amino acids have been found in meteorites such as Murchison).

alternatives.label: Panspermia and creation
alternatives.text: Some scientists propose that life or its precursors arrived from space (panspermia); religious traditions attribute life to divine creation. How life first arose remains unresolved in science.

entries.title: Atrahasis: the Babylonian flood story where noisy humans anger the gods
entries.mainstream: The Atrahasis epic is an Akkadian poem known from Old Babylonian tablets of roughly the 17th century BCE, with later Assyrian and Babylonian copies. In it the lesser gods rebel against digging canals, so the gods create humans from clay mixed with the flesh and blood of a slain god to do the work. Humanity multiplies and its noise keeps the god Enlil awake; he sends plague, drought and famine, and finally a great flood. The wise god Enki warns the man Atrahasis to build a boat, and he survives with his family and animals. Afterwards the gods set limits on human numbers, such as infertility and infant death. The flood section closely parallels Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh and has many similarities with the Genesis flood narrative.

alternatives.label: Which story came first?
alternatives.text: Most scholars see Atrahasis (and the Sumerian Ziusudra story) as older than the written Genesis account and as one source of a shared Mesopotamian flood tradition. Some religious commentators instead see the stories as independent memories of a real worldwide event.

alternatives.label: A real flood behind it?
alternatives.text: Researchers have linked Mesopotamian flood stories to destructive local river floods, such as flood layers excavated at Ur, Shuruppak and Kish, or to wider events such as post-glacial sea-level rise. None of these is proven to be the specific source.

alternatives.label: Ancient astronaut reading
alternatives.text: Ancient-astronaut writers such as Zecharia Sitchin read the story of gods creating workers as genetic engineering by the Anunnaki; Assyriologists reject these translations. This view is speculative.

entries.title: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon and its dragons (c. 575 BCE)
entries.mainstream: The Ishtar Gate was the eighth gate of the inner city of Babylon, built around 575 BCE on the orders of King Nebuchadnezzar II. Its walls were faced with glazed blue bricks showing rows of aurochs and mušḫuššu (a scaly dragon with a snake's head, lion forelegs and bird hind legs, sacred to the god Marduk), while lions lined the Processional Way leading to it. German archaeologist Robert Koldewey excavated it between 1902 and 1914, and a reconstruction using the original bricks was opened in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin in the 1930s. Other panels are in museums around the world, and a smaller replica stands at the site in Iraq.

alternatives.label: Mainstream: a composite beast
alternatives.text: Historians of Mesopotamian art see the mušḫuššu as a mythical composite creature, a symbol of Marduk, comparable to griffins and sphinxes.

alternatives.label: A dinosaur memory?
alternatives.text: Some cryptozoologists and young-Earth creationists have suggested the mušḫuššu depicts a living animal such as a sauropod, sometimes linking it to African reports of Mokele-mbembe. No zoological or palaeontological evidence supports this; it is speculative.

alternatives.label: Who owns the gate?
alternatives.text: Iraq has called for the return of the gate material held in Berlin, while the museum states it was legally divided and exported under the agreements of the time.

entries.title: The Rosetta Stone: the key that unlocked hieroglyphs (196 BCE / 1822)
entries.mainstream: The Rosetta Stone is a granodiorite slab carrying a decree issued at Memphis in 196 BCE on behalf of King Ptolemy V, written three times: in Egyptian hieroglyphs, in Demotic script and in ancient Greek. French soldiers found it in July 1799 near the town of Rashid (Rosetta) during Napoleon's campaign in Egypt. After the French defeat it passed to Britain under the Capitulation of Alexandria in 1801 and has been in the British Museum since 1802. Because the Greek text could be read, scholars could compare the scripts. Thomas Young made important early progress with the Demotic and the royal names in cartouches, and Jean-François Champollion announced in 1822 that hieroglyphs combined sound signs with idea signs, which opened up Egyptian texts.

alternatives.label: Who deserves the credit?
alternatives.text: Champollion is usually credited with the decipherment, but Young's supporters argued he identified key sound values first. Most historians now see Young's work as a real but partial contribution and Champollion's system as the breakthrough.

alternatives.label: Should it go back to Egypt?
alternatives.text: Egyptian archaeologists, including former antiquities minister Zahi Hawass, and petitions have called for its return; the British Museum maintains it was legally acquired under the 1801 treaty.

alternatives.label: Older ideas about hieroglyphs
alternatives.text: Before decipherment, Renaissance and early modern scholars such as Athanasius Kircher believed hieroglyphs were purely symbolic, mystical writing hiding secret wisdom. The stone showed they also wrote ordinary language, including tax and priestly matters.

entries.changed: Before 1822 hieroglyphs were widely seen as mystical symbols; after Champollion they could be read as a language, transforming knowledge of ancient Egypt.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Decipherment of ancient Egyptian scripts

entries.title: The Galilee Boat ("Jesus boat"), found in a drought (1986)
entries.dateNote: built c. 1st century BCE–1st century CE; found 1986
entries.mainstream: In January 1986, during a severe drought that lowered the Sea of Galilee, brothers Moshe and Yuval Lufan noticed the outline of an ancient boat in the mud near Kibbutz Ginosar in Israel. Archaeologists excavated it in a rapid 12-day operation and preserved it in polyethylene glycol. The 8.2 m wooden fishing boat was built from several kinds of timber and repaired many times. Radiocarbon dating and the pottery and nails found with it place it between about the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE. It is displayed at the Yigal Allon Centre at Ginosar.

alternatives.label: Connection to Jesus?
alternatives.text: Because it dates to roughly the time of Jesus and comes from the lake where the Gospels set many events, it was nicknamed the Jesus boat. Archaeologists stress there is no evidence linking it to Jesus or his disciples; it shows the kind of boat used on the lake then.

alternatives.label: A window on everyday life
alternatives.text: For historians its value is in what it shows about ordinary fishing boats and shortages of good timber, as it reused wood from older vessels.

entries.title: The Colossus of Rhodes: a wonder that stood for only 54 years
entries.mainstream: The Colossus of Rhodes was a bronze statue of the sun god Helios, about 33 m tall, built by the sculptor Chares of Lindos to celebrate the city's survival of a siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes in 305–304 BCE. It was completed around 280 BCE and stood near the harbour of Rhodes until an earthquake toppled it around 226 BCE. Pliny the Elder wrote that even lying on the ground it was a marvel, as few people could wrap their arms around its thumb. The ruins reportedly lay for about 800 years until Arab forces sold the bronze in the 7th century CE. It is listed among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

alternatives.label: Did it straddle the harbour?
alternatives.text: The famous image of the statue standing with legs astride the harbour entrance comes from medieval and later artists. Modern engineers and historians consider this impossible for a bronze statue of that era, and the harbour would have had to be closed for years during construction; most think it stood on a pedestal on land.

alternatives.label: The 900 camels
alternatives.text: The story that a merchant needed 900 camels to carry away the scrap comes from the Byzantine chronicler Theophanes, writing long after the event; some historians doubt the details.

alternatives.label: Where exactly?
alternatives.text: Its exact site is unknown. Proposals include the harbour mole and the acropolis of Rhodes near the temple of Helios; no foundation has been firmly identified.

entries.title: The Pharos of Alexandria: the lighthouse of the ancient world
entries.mainstream: The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood on the island of Pharos at the entrance to Alexandria's harbour. It was begun under Ptolemy I and completed around 280 BCE under Ptolemy II, with its dedication attributed to Sostratus of Cnidus. Estimates of its height range around 100 m or more, making it one of the tallest human-made structures of its time; coins and descriptions show a three-tiered tower with a statue on top. It was damaged by a series of earthquakes between the 10th and 14th centuries and was ruined by about 1323. In 1477 the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built a fort on its site, partly from its stones. Divers led by Jean-Yves Empereur documented large blocks and statues in the harbour from 1994.

alternatives.label: The burning mirror
alternatives.text: Medieval Arab writers told of a huge mirror at the top that could spot ships far out at sea or even set them on fire. Historians treat the burning mirror as legend, though a polished reflector to project the fire's light is plausible.

alternatives.label: Rebuilding plans
alternatives.text: Egyptian authorities and others have periodically proposed rebuilding the lighthouse or creating an underwater museum at the site; these remain proposals.

alternatives.label: Word legacy
alternatives.text: The name Pharos became the word for lighthouse in several languages, such as French phare, Italian and Spanish faro.

entries.title: The Nimrud lens: an Assyrian telescope?
entries.mainstream: The Nimrud lens is a piece of polished rock crystal, about 4 cm across, found in 1850 by Austen Henry Layard in the palace of Nimrud in present-day Iraq. It dates from about the 8th or 7th century BCE and is now in the British Museum. It is slightly oval and ground to a convex shape, and it magnifies somewhat, though unevenly. Similar polished crystals have been found at other ancient sites.

alternatives.label: Mainstream: inlay or burning glass
alternatives.text: Many archaeologists think it was a decorative inlay, perhaps for furniture, though it could also have served as a magnifying glass or to focus sunlight to start fires.

alternatives.label: A telescope?
alternatives.text: In 1999 Assyriologist Giovanni Pettinato proposed that it was used by Assyrian astronomers, which might explain their knowledge of the heavens. Optical studies found it too irregular to work as a useful telescope lens, and no other part of a telescope has been found; most scholars do not accept this idea.

alternatives.label: Ancient optics more broadly
alternatives.text: The lens is often cited in discussions of ancient technology alongside Roman magnifying glass references (Seneca, Pliny) and Viking-age Visby lenses.

entries.title: Cyclops and the skulls of dwarf elephants
entries.mainstream: During the Pleistocene, elephants that reached Mediterranean islands such as Sicily, Malta, Crete and Cyprus evolved into dwarf species, some only about 1 m tall. Their skulls have a single large central opening for the trunk, which can look like one huge eye socket to someone unfamiliar with elephants. In 1914 the palaeontologist Othenio Abel suggested that ancient Greeks who found such skulls may have taken them for the remains of one-eyed giants, the Cyclopes known from Homer's Odyssey (around the 8th century BCE), which places the Cyclops Polyphemus on an island often identified with Sicily.

alternatives.label: Fossil folklore
alternatives.text: Historian of science Adrienne Mayor's The First Fossil Hunters (2000) argues that ancient Greeks and Romans did collect and interpret large fossil bones as remains of giants and heroes, which makes this idea plausible.

alternatives.label: Unproven link
alternatives.text: No ancient text describes a skull of this kind as a Cyclops, so the connection remains a hypothesis. The Cyclops may also come from storytelling motifs found widely around the world.

alternatives.label: Other sources of giants
alternatives.text: Other suggestions link Greek giant legends to mammoth and mastodon bones found on the mainland, and the griffin to Protoceratops fossils in Central Asia, also proposed by Mayor and debated by palaeontologists.

entries.title: The Minoan snake goddesses: ancient figurines and modern forgeries
entries.mainstream: In 1903 Arthur Evans found faience figurines of women holding snakes in the Temple Repositories at the palace of Knossos on Crete, dated to about 1600 BCE. They became famous as the Minoan snake goddess, though one was found headless and was restored with a head and a cat-like animal on top, and the other is missing parts. Evans saw them as evidence of a Minoan mother goddess religion. In the following decades, several ivory and gold snake goddess figurines without secure find spots appeared on the antiquities market, including one bought by the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston in 1914.

alternatives.label: Goddess, priestess or votary?
alternatives.text: Scholars debate whether the Knossos figures show a goddess, priestesses or worshippers; the label goddess comes from Evans and his interest in a supreme female deity.

alternatives.label: Forgeries
alternatives.text: Archaeologist Kenneth Lapatin's 2002 study argued that the Boston ivory figurine and several similar pieces are modern forgeries, possibly made by craftsmen who worked on Evans's restorations. The Boston museum itself now presents its figure with doubts about authenticity.

alternatives.label: How much is restoration?
alternatives.text: Critics point out that much of the popular image of Minoan Crete, from frescoes to these figurines, was shaped by Evans's reconstructions, which reflected early 20th-century ideas.

entries.title: Tall el-Hammam: Sodom and a cosmic airburst?
entries.dateNote: destroyed c. 1650 BCE; airburst paper 2021, retracted 2025
entries.mainstream: Tall el-Hammam is a large Bronze Age settlement in the Jordan Valley, north-east of the Dead Sea in Jordan. Excavations led by Steven Collins since 2005 found that it was destroyed around 1650 BCE. In 2021 a team led by Ted Bunch published a paper in Scientific Reports arguing that a cosmic airburst, an exploding meteor like the one at Tunguska, destroyed the city, citing melted pottery, shocked quartz and scattered human bones. The paper was retracted by the journal in April 2025 (see below). The authors had suggested that memories of the event might lie behind the biblical story of Sodom and Gomorrah destroyed by fire from heaven.

alternatives.label: The airburst paper was retracted
alternatives.text: Other researchers, including Jaret and Harris (2022) and Boslough and Bruno (2025), reported errors in the mineral and geochemical analysis and argued that the comparison with Tunguska overestimated that blast. After author corrections in 2022 and 2023, the journal's editors retracted the paper in April 2025, saying they no longer had confidence in its conclusions. Eleven of the co-authors stated that they disagree with the retraction.

alternatives.label: Is it Sodom?
alternatives.text: Collins identifies Tall el-Hammam with biblical Sodom. Most archaeologists and biblical scholars do not accept this identification, noting differences in dates and geography and the difficulty of matching legends to specific sites.

alternatives.label: Part of a wider debate
alternatives.text: The study comes from researchers associated with the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis, which is also contested; both remain under debate.

entries.title: The Ramayana: Rama, Sita, Hanuman and a bridge to Lanka
entries.dateNote: composed c. 5th century BCE–early centuries CE
entries.mainstream: The Ramayana is a Sanskrit epic traditionally attributed to the sage Valmiki. Scholars think it was composed in stages, with core books perhaps from around the 5th to 4th century BCE and later additions into the early centuries CE. It tells how Prince Rama of Ayodhya is exiled, how his wife Sita is abducted by Ravana, the king of Lanka, and how Rama rescues her with the help of his brother Lakshmana and an army of monkeys and bears led by Hanuman, after building a bridge across the sea. It became one of the most influential stories in Asia, retold in hundreds of versions such as Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, the Thai Ramakien, the Khmer Reamker and the Javanese Kakawin Ramayana, and in dance, puppetry and temple carvings from India to Indonesia.

alternatives.label: Myth or history?
alternatives.text: Many Hindus regard Rama as a historical figure and an avatar of Vishnu who lived in the Treta Yuga, an earlier world age. Historians treat the epic as literature built over centuries, though it may preserve memories of real places and kingdoms in ancient India.

alternatives.label: Rama's Bridge
alternatives.text: The chain of shoals between India and Sri Lanka, called Ram Setu or Adam's Bridge, is identified by many believers with the bridge in the epic. Geologists describe it as a natural formation of sand and coral shoals.

alternatives.label: Flying chariots
alternatives.text: Ravana's flying chariot, the Pushpaka vimana, is cited by some modern writers as evidence of ancient aircraft. Scholars read it as a mythological vehicle of the gods; the aircraft claim is speculative.

entries.title: Shennong, the Divine Farmer who tasted every herb
entries.mainstream: Shennong (the Divine Farmer) is a legendary ruler of ancient China, counted among the Three Sovereigns, who is said to have taught people to farm with the plough and to have tested hundreds of plants on himself to find which were medicines and which were poisons, sometimes being poisoned dozens of times in a day. The classic herbal Shennong Bencao Jing, which lists 365 medicinal substances, bears his name but was compiled around the Han dynasty (roughly the 1st–2nd century CE). A popular later legend says he discovered tea in 2737 BCE when leaves blew into his boiling water; this date is traditional, not historical.

alternatives.label: Historical person?
alternatives.text: Historians see Shennong as a mythological culture hero, possibly a personification of the beginnings of agriculture in China, rather than a real king.

alternatives.label: Real early farming
alternatives.text: Archaeology shows millet farming in northern China and rice farming in the Yangtze region from roughly 9,000–7,000 years ago, much earlier than the traditional date for Shennong.

alternatives.label: Civilising teachers
alternatives.text: Shennong belongs to a worldwide group of figures who teach farming or crafts, such as Osiris, Quetzalcoatl and Oannes; some alternative writers read this pattern as memory of real visiting teachers, which is speculative.

entries.title: Yamato Takeru: the prince who became a white bird
entries.dateNote: recorded 712 and 720; set in the legendary early Yamato period
entries.mainstream: Yamato Takeru is a legendary prince of Japan, son of Emperor Keikō, whose adventures are told in the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720). He defeats the Kumaso chiefs in the west disguised as a woman and campaigns against the Emishi in the east. His aunt, the priestess of Ise, gives him the sword Kusanagi, with which he cuts the grass to escape a fire set by enemies. After offending the god of Mount Ibuki he falls ill and dies, and his soul flies away as a great white bird. The sword Kusanagi became one of the Three Sacred Treasures of the Japanese imperial regalia.

alternatives.label: Real person or composite?
alternatives.text: Historians generally see him as a legendary figure who may combine the deeds of several generals of the early Yamato state, used to explain its expansion; his historicity cannot be confirmed.

alternatives.label: The sacred sword today
alternatives.text: Kusanagi is said to be kept at Atsuta Shrine in Nagoya, but it is never shown, so whether an ancient sword exists there is unknown.

entries.title: The Ajanta Caves, rediscovered by a tiger hunter (1819)
entries.dateNote: c. 2nd century BCE and c. 460–480 CE; rediscovered 1819
entries.mainstream: The Ajanta Caves are about 30 Buddhist monuments cut into a horseshoe-shaped cliff above the Waghur river in Maharashtra, India. The earliest were made around the 2nd century BCE; most of the rest were carved and painted in a burst of activity in the 5th century CE under the Vakataka dynasty. Their wall paintings of the Buddha's lives and Jataka tales are among the finest surviving examples of ancient Indian painting. The caves were abandoned and overgrown until April 1819, when a British cavalry officer, John Smith, came upon them while hunting a tiger and scratched his name on a painting in Cave 10. They became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.

alternatives.label: How long did the second phase take?
alternatives.text: Art historian Walter Spink argued that most of the later caves were made in an intense period of under 20 years, roughly 460–480 CE; other scholars favour a longer timescale.

alternatives.label: Lost to whom?
alternatives.text: The caves were lost to outsiders, but local people likely knew of them; the word rediscovery reflects the colonial record.

entries.title: The Priest-King of Mohenjo-daro: a famous label for a mystery
entries.mainstream: The so-called Priest-King is a small steatite sculpture of a bearded man, about 17.5 cm high, found in 1927 at Mohenjo-daro, one of the largest cities of the Indus (Harappan) civilisation, now in Pakistan. It dates from roughly 2400–1900 BCE. The man wears a headband and an armband and a robe decorated with trefoil (three-lobed) patterns that were once filled with red pigment. It is in the National Museum of Pakistan in Karachi and is one of the best-known images of the Indus civilisation.

alternatives.label: Priest, king or neither?
alternatives.text: The name was given by early excavators by analogy with Mesopotamia and Egypt. Archaeologists note that the Indus cities show no obvious palaces, royal tombs or large temples, so it is unknown whether there were priest-kings at all; the figure might be an ancestor, an elite person or a deity.

alternatives.label: Undeciphered script
alternatives.text: Because the Indus script remains undeciphered, the identities and titles of people like this remain uncertain.

entries.title: The Chola navy raids Srivijaya (1025)
entries.mainstream: In 1025 the south Indian Chola emperor Rajendra I sent a naval expedition across the Bay of Bengal against the maritime empire of Srivijaya, which controlled the Strait of Malacca. Chola inscriptions, including the Tanjore (Thanjavur) inscription, list ports raided in Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, such as Kadaram (Kedah), and record the capture of the Srivijayan king Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman. The raid weakened Srivijaya and is one of the few overseas military expeditions by an Indian state before modern times.

alternatives.label: Why attack?
alternatives.text: Historians suggest the aim was to protect Chola and Tamil merchants and open the sea routes to China, rather than to conquer land; the Cholas did not keep lasting control.

alternatives.label: How big?
alternatives.text: The inscriptions list places but give no numbers; the scale of the fleet is unknown.

entries.title: Chang'e: the woman who flew to the Moon
entries.mainstream: In Chinese mythology Chang'e is the wife of the archer Hou Yi, who shot down nine of the ten suns. In the best-known versions, Hou Yi receives an elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West; Chang'e drinks it, alone or to keep it from a thief, and floats up to the Moon, where she lives in the Moon Palace with a jade rabbit pounding medicine. Early references appear in the Huainanzi (2nd century BCE) and in the Guizang divination text known from bamboo slips excavated at Wangjiatai. The story is closely tied to the Mid-Autumn Festival. China's lunar exploration programme is named after her: Chang'e 4 made the first soft landing on the Moon's far side in January 2019, carrying the Yutu-2 (Jade Rabbit 2) rover, and Chang'e 6 returned the first samples from the far side in 2024.

alternatives.label: Different versions
alternatives.text: In some early versions Chang'e is punished by being turned into a toad on the Moon, reflecting the old Chinese image of a toad in the Moon; later versions make her a graceful, lonely immortal.

alternatives.label: Moon patterns
alternatives.text: The rabbit and toad in the Moon are interpretations of the dark lunar maria. A rabbit in the Moon also appears in Indian, Japanese, Korean and Mesoamerican traditions, a case of similar pareidolia in different cultures.

entries.title: Penglai: the island of the immortals that emperors tried to reach
entries.mainstream: Penglai is a mythical mountain-island in the eastern sea where, in Chinese legend, immortals live in palaces of gold and jade and the herb of immortality grows. It is one of the three holy islands, with Fangzhang and Yingzhou, described in texts such as the Shiji of Sima Qian. According to the Shiji, the First Emperor of Qin sent the alchemist Xu Fu with ships and young men and women to find it in 219 BCE, and Emperor Wu of Han later sponsored more searches. The coastal city of Penglai in Shandong province takes its name from the legend.

alternatives.label: Mirages as inspiration?
alternatives.text: The coast near Penglai is known for sea mirages (superior mirages of distant islands and coasts). Several writers have suggested such mirages helped inspire the idea of floating islands of immortals; this is plausible but not provable.

alternatives.label: Did Xu Fu reach Japan?
alternatives.text: A later tradition, strong in Japan, holds that Xu Fu reached Japan and stayed; historians consider this legend rather than history.

alternatives.label: Paradise patterns
alternatives.text: Penglai fits a worldwide pattern of distant paradise islands, like the Celtic Isles of the Blessed, Avalon and Hy-Brasil.

entries.title: The Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji, Nara (752)
entries.mainstream: Tōdai-ji in Nara was founded by Emperor Shōmu, who in 743 ordered a giant bronze statue of the Vairocana Buddha after years of epidemic, famine and rebellion. Casting took place from about 745 to 749 and consumed a large share of Japan's copper, tin and gold. The eye-opening ceremony in 752 was performed by the Indian monk Bodhisena, with guests from across Asia. The statue, about 15 m tall, has been damaged by earthquakes and fires and repaired many times; its present head dates from the 17th century, and the current hall (Daibutsuden) was rebuilt in 1709. The temple's treasure house, the Shōsōin, preserves thousands of 8th-century objects, some brought along the Silk Road.

alternatives.label: A building with a toxic cost?
alternatives.text: Gilding the statue used gold dissolved in mercury, which was then evaporated by heating. Some researchers have suggested that mercury vapour may have caused illness in Nara; this remains a hypothesis.

alternatives.label: State and religion
alternatives.text: Historians see the project as both an act of devotion and a statement of imperial power, linking a network of provincial temples to Nara.

entries.title: The "stegosaurus" carving of Ta Prohm, Cambodia
entries.mainstream: Ta Prohm is a Khmer temple near Angkor, built from 1186 by King Jayavarman VII as a Buddhist monastery and famous for the trees growing over its ruins. Among the many small carved roundels on its doorframes is one showing a four-legged animal with a row of rounded shapes along its back. Since the late 1990s some writers, especially young-Earth creationists, have claimed it depicts a stegosaurus and shows that people saw living dinosaurs about 800 years ago.

alternatives.label: Mainstream view
alternatives.text: Archaeologists and scholars of Khmer art note that the shapes along the back match the leafy background decoration found around other roundels on the temple, and that the animal could be a rhinoceros, boar, chameleon or a mythological creature, since the temple is full of religious and imaginary beings. They see no evidence of a living dinosaur.

alternatives.label: Is it modern?
alternatives.text: Some sceptics have suggested the carving might be a modern addition; others reply that there is no evidence of this. Most commentators accept it as original but read it as an ordinary animal.

alternatives.label: Dinosaur claims elsewhere
alternatives.text: Similar claims of dinosaurs in ancient art include the Ica stones and Acámbaro figures; these are generally considered hoaxes or misinterpretations.

sources.title: Skeptical Inquirer: A Stegosaur Carving on the Ruins of Ta Prohm? Think Again (2019)

entries.title: The impundulu: the lightning bird of southern Africa
entries.dateNote: recorded from the 19th century; older oral tradition
entries.mainstream: In the folklore of the Zulu and neighbouring peoples of southern Africa, the impundulu or lightning bird is a black-and-white bird the size of a person that summons thunder and lightning with its wings and talons. It is said to be the servant or familiar of a witch, sent to attack the witch's enemies, and to have a vampire-like hunger for blood; sometimes it appears as a handsome young man who seduces women. Where lightning strikes, people have traditionally believed the bird laid an egg or left a trace, and traditional healers have been called on to dig it out or protect homes. The dateNote marks when such beliefs were first written down by outsiders; the tradition itself is older.

alternatives.label: Real birds behind it?
alternatives.text: Some writers link the lightning bird to real birds such as the hamerkop, which is surrounded by many beliefs about storms and bad luck in southern Africa; this connection is suggested rather than established.

alternatives.label: Lightning and witchcraft today
alternatives.text: South Africa's highveld has some of the highest lightning densities in the world, and in parts of the region lightning deaths are still sometimes blamed on witchcraft, which has led to violence against accused people.

alternatives.label: A global pattern
alternatives.text: Thunderbirds appear in many traditions, including Indigenous North America; the parallel is often noted as a widespread way of explaining storms.

entries.title: The Mfecane: southern Africa's time of upheaval and a history war
entries.mainstream: The Mfecane (Zulu, roughly 'the crushing') or Difaqane (Sotho) refers to a period of wars, migrations and new state formation in southern Africa, most intensely from about the 1810s to the 1840s. In this period the Zulu kingdom grew under Shaka, and groups such as the Ndebele under Mzilikazi, the Kololo and the Ngoni moved hundreds or thousands of kilometres, some as far as Zambia, Malawi and Tanzania. New kingdoms, such as Lesotho under Moshoeshoe I and Swaziland (Eswatini), took shape. Traditional estimates of deaths ran from one to two million, but these figures are controversial.

alternatives.label: The traditional view
alternatives.text: Older histories, many written by colonial-era authors, described the Mfecane as a chain reaction of destruction started by Shaka's Zulu expansion, which left land empty for European settlers.

alternatives.label: The Cobbing challenge
alternatives.text: In 1988 historian Julian Cobbing argued that the Mfecane as usually told was an alibi: that slave and labour raiding linked to the Portuguese at Delagoa Bay and to settlers and missionaries on the Cape frontier drove much of the violence, and that the Zulu-centred story served colonial interests.

alternatives.label: A middle position
alternatives.text: Most historians now see a mix of causes, including drought, competition over trade, internal political change and colonial pressure, and they reject the idea of empty land, while not accepting every point of Cobbing's thesis.

entries.changed: From the 1980s the Mfecane changed from a story of Zulu-caused devastation to a debated, multi-cause period, as historians questioned colonial sources.

entries.title: Thulamela: a gold-working hilltop kingdom in the Kruger Park
entries.mainstream: Thulamela is a stone-walled hilltop site south of the Luvuvhu (Levubu) River in the far north of South Africa's Kruger National Park, one of about 300 archaeological sites in the park. Excavations led by Sidney Miller from 1993 to 1995 found that a community lived there from about the 13th century to the 17th century, working gold, copper and iron into jewellery, hoes and blades. It was linked to the same cultural world and trade networks as Mapungubwe, Great Zimbabwe and Khami, which reached the Indian Ocean coast. Two elite burials with gold ornaments were found and given the names King Ingwe and Queen Losha, and the walls were partly rebuilt for visitors.

alternatives.label: Who were they?
alternatives.text: Local Venda and other communities claim connections with Thulamela, and descendants were involved in the reburial of the remains. Archaeologists link it to the wider Zimbabwe tradition but the exact identity of its people is debated.

alternatives.label: Older myths of foreign builders
alternatives.text: Colonial-era writers often claimed that stone-walled sites in southern Africa were built by outsiders such as Phoenicians. Archaeology at sites like Thulamela and Great Zimbabwe shows they were built by African societies, and the foreign-builder idea is rejected.

entries.title: The Sacred Cenote of Chichén Itzá and who was really sacrificed
entries.mainstream: The Sacred Cenote is a large natural sinkhole at the Maya city of Chichén Itzá in Yucatán, Mexico. Maya and Spanish colonial sources, including the bishop Diego de Landa, say people threw offerings and human beings into it, especially to the rain god Chaac in times of drought. Between 1904 and 1910 the American consul Edward H. Thompson dredged it and sent gold, jade, copal and human bones to Harvard's Peabody Museum; some objects were later returned to Mexico. Later excavations recovered more remains, including many of children and men.

alternatives.label: The virgin myth
alternatives.text: The popular idea that beautiful young women were thrown into the well comes largely from early 20th-century romantic writing. Studies of the bones found a wide range of victims, with many children.

alternatives.label: What DNA showed
alternatives.text: A 2024 genetic study in Nature of 64 children buried in an underground chamber near the cenote found all were boys, many closely related, including two pairs of identical twins, which the authors linked to Maya stories of the Hero Twins. The authors note this was a separate burial site from the cenote itself.

alternatives.label: Looting or rescue?
alternatives.text: Thompson's removal of artefacts is now widely viewed as looting, though some at the time saw it as salvage archaeology.

sources.title: Ancient genomes reveal insights into ritual life at Chichén Itzá

entries.title: Vlad the Impaler: the real prince behind Dracula
entries.mainstream: Vlad III, Prince of Wallachia (in present-day Romania), ruled three times: briefly in 1448, from 1456 to 1462, and in 1476, when he was killed. His father was a member of the Order of the Dragon, which gave him the name Dracul, so Vlad was called Dracula, 'son of the Dragon'. He fought the Ottoman Empire and rival boyars and became infamous for impaling enemies and captives; pamphlets printed in German lands in the 1460s–1490s spread horror stories about him. In Romania he is often remembered as a defender of the country and a stern enforcer of justice.

alternatives.label: Did he inspire Stoker's Dracula?
alternatives.text: Bram Stoker's 1897 novel took the name Dracula and some historical notes about a Wallachian voivode. Scholars such as Elizabeth Miller argue Stoker knew little about Vlad, and that the popular link between Vlad and the vampire was largely built up by later writers from the 1970s.

alternatives.label: How cruel was he?
alternatives.text: The worst stories come from his enemies, especially German pamphlets and Ottoman chroniclers, so historians debate how much is propaganda, while agreeing he used mass impalement.

alternatives.label: His tomb
alternatives.text: Snagov Monastery has traditionally been named as his burial place, but excavations there did not confirm it, and other proposals, including Comana monastery and a 2014 claim of a tomb in Naples, are not accepted.

entries.title: Mercy Brown and the New England vampire panic (1892)
entries.mainstream: In Exeter, Rhode Island, the family of George Brown was struck by tuberculosis (then called consumption): his wife and daughter Mary Olive died in the 1880s, and in January 1892 his daughter Mercy died aged 19 while his son Edwin was gravely ill. Neighbours persuaded George that one of the dead was draining the life of the living. In March 1892 the bodies were exhumed; Mercy's, kept in a cold above-ground crypt, appeared little decayed and had blood in the heart. Her heart was burned and the ashes mixed with medicine for Edwin, who died two months later. Newspapers reported the case widely.

alternatives.label: The wider panic
alternatives.text: Folklorist Michael Bell and others documented dozens of similar exhumations across New England from the late 18th to the late 19th century, all linked to tuberculosis outbreaks, which spread within families and slowly wasted people away.

alternatives.label: Why did the body look fresh?
alternatives.text: Medical explanations point to the winter cold, which slowed decay; such normal changes in corpses were often taken as signs of vampirism, as in European cases like that of Arnold Paole.

alternatives.label: Did it inspire Dracula?
alternatives.text: Some scholars have suggested that Bram Stoker knew of the case from newspaper reports and drew on it for the character Lucy Westenra in Dracula (1897); this link is plausible but unproven.

entries.title: Hannibal crosses the Alps with elephants (218 BCE)
entries.mainstream: In 218 BCE, at the start of the Second Punic War, the Carthaginian general Hannibal led an army of tens of thousands of soldiers, cavalry and about 37 war elephants from Spain over the Pyrenees and the Alps into Italy, to attack Rome from the north. The crossing in late autumn cost him many men and animals to cold, landslides and attacks by mountain tribes, but he went on to win great victories at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae (216 BCE). He stayed in Italy for about 15 years but never took Rome, and Carthage was defeated at Zama in 202 BCE. The main ancient accounts are by Polybius and Livy.

alternatives.label: Which pass?
alternatives.text: The route has been argued over since antiquity, with candidates including the Col du Mont Cenis, Col du Clapier, Col du Montgenèvre, Little St Bernard and Col de la Traversette.

alternatives.label: Evidence in the mud
alternatives.text: In 2016–2017 a team led by William Mahaney reported a disturbed layer of soil near the Col de la Traversette containing large amounts of microbes typical of horse dung, radiocarbon dated to around 200 BCE, and proposed it marks Hannibal's army. Other researchers consider this suggestive but not conclusive.

alternatives.label: How many elephants survived?
alternatives.text: Polybius says nearly all the elephants died after the battle of the Trebia that winter, leaving only one. A Roman tradition preserved by Pliny names a brave Carthaginian elephant Surus, and some writers identify it with that survivor; this is uncertain.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hannibal's crossing of the Alps
Biostratigraphic Evidence Relating to the Age-Old Question of Hannibal's Invasion of Italy, I: History and Geological Reconstruction

entries.title: Tikal: Maya super-city and the strangers from Teotihuacan (378 CE)
entries.mainstream: Tikal, in the rainforest of northern Guatemala, was one of the most powerful cities of the Classic Maya, with tall temple-pyramids, palaces and a royal dynasty recorded in carved inscriptions. It was settled by about the 1st millennium BCE and flourished roughly 200–900 CE, before being abandoned during the Classic Maya collapse. Inscriptions record that in 378 CE a warlord named Sihyaj K'ahk' arrived, on the same day the local king died, and a new king linked to the distant city of Teotihuacan in central Mexico was installed. In 2018 a lidar survey of the Maya lowlands revealed many previously unknown structures and defences around Tikal. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, and in 1977 it was filmed as the rebel base in Star Wars.

alternatives.label: Conquest or alliance?
alternatives.text: Epigraphers debate whether the 378 entrada was a military takeover by Teotihuacan, an alliance, or the work of a local faction using Teotihuacan symbols for prestige.

alternatives.label: How many people?
alternatives.text: Population estimates for Tikal and its surroundings have risen sharply with lidar, but range widely, from tens of thousands to more than 100,000.

entries.title: The Lost Dutchman's Gold Mine, Superstition Mountains
entries.mainstream: According to legend, a German immigrant named Jacob Waltz (c. 1810–1891), known as 'the Dutchman', found a fabulously rich gold mine in the Superstition Mountains east of Phoenix, Arizona, and took its location to the grave, leaving only vague clues told on his deathbed. Since then thousands of people have searched for it, and some have died or vanished in the rugged terrain, which added to stories of a curse. The tale grew through newspaper articles, books and later films and television. It is perhaps the most famous lost mine legend in the United States.

alternatives.label: Geology says unlikely
alternatives.text: Geologists have long noted that the Superstition Mountains are mainly volcanic rock considered unlikely to contain rich gold veins, though gold was mined elsewhere in the region.

alternatives.label: Waltz may have had gold
alternatives.text: Some researchers think Waltz really did have gold, perhaps from elsewhere or from high-grading at local mines, and that the legend grew around him.

alternatives.label: Apache traditions
alternatives.text: Some versions say the mountains were sacred to the Apache and guarded against outsiders; others tell of earlier Peralta family miners. Historians consider many of these details later inventions.

entries.title: The Man in the Iron Mask (died 1703)
entries.mainstream: The Man in the Iron Mask was a prisoner held in French state prisons from 1669 until his death in the Bastille in 1703, always in the custody of the same jailer, Bénigne Dauvergne de Saint-Mars. Records show he was arrested under the name Eustache Dauger and that his face was hidden from others; contemporary accounts say the mask was black velvet, not iron. His burial was registered under the name Marchioly. The mystery was made famous by Voltaire, and later by Alexandre Dumas's novel The Vicomte of Bragelonne, which made him Louis XIV's twin brother.

alternatives.label: Who was he?
alternatives.text: Many historians think he was indeed Eustache Dauger, possibly a valet who knew secrets linked to the imprisoned finance minister Nicolas Fouquet or to political dealings. Other candidates include the Italian diplomat Ercole Antonio Mattioli, whose name resembles the burial record.

alternatives.label: Royal twin or brother?
alternatives.text: Voltaire hinted, and Dumas dramatised, that he was a brother of Louis XIV; there is no evidence for this, though it remains the best-known version.

alternatives.label: Why so secret?
alternatives.text: The extreme secrecy may have been designed to make him seem more important than he was, or to stop him revealing what he knew; the reason remains unknown.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Man in the Iron Mask

entries.title: The Princes in the Tower (1483): murder or escape?
entries.mainstream: In 1483, after the death of King Edward IV of England, his sons Edward V (aged 12) and Richard, Duke of York (aged 9), were lodged in the Tower of London by their uncle Richard, Duke of Gloucester, ostensibly to prepare for Edward's coronation. Parliament instead declared the boys illegitimate, and their uncle took the throne as Richard III. The princes were seen less and less and then not at all after the summer of 1483. Richard III was killed at Bosworth in 1485 and Henry VII took the throne. In 1674 workmen at the Tower found a box with the bones of two children, which were placed in an urn in Westminster Abbey and examined in 1933; they have not been tested with modern methods.

alternatives.label: Richard III did it
alternatives.text: The traditional view, shaped by Thomas More and Shakespeare, is that Richard III ordered their murder, perhaps by Sir James Tyrell; many historians still think this most likely.

alternatives.label: Other suspects
alternatives.text: Other proposed culprits include Henry Stafford, Duke of Buckingham, and Henry VII, who also had reasons to want them dead; supporters of Richard III (Ricardians) argue the case against him rests on hostile Tudor sources.

alternatives.label: Did they survive?
alternatives.text: Pretenders such as Perkin Warbeck claimed to be Prince Richard. In 2023 Philippa Langley's Missing Princes Project published documents it says suggest both boys survived; many historians are not persuaded and consider the documents open to other readings.

entries.title: The death of Rasputin (1916): poisoned, shot and drowned?
entries.mainstream: Grigori Rasputin, a Siberian peasant and self-proclaimed holy man, gained great influence at the court of the last Russian tsar, Nicholas II, largely because the empress Alexandra believed he could ease the haemophilia of her son Alexei. Seen as a scandal and a danger during the First World War, he was killed in Petrograd on the night of 29–30 December 1916 (16–17 December in the old Russian calendar) by a group of nobles led by Prince Felix Yusupov. His body was found in the frozen Malaya Nevka river. Less than three months later the monarchy fell.

alternatives.label: The legend of the unkillable monk
alternatives.text: Yusupov's own memoirs describe Rasputin surviving cyanide-laced cakes and wine and several gunshots before being thrown into the river, and some accounts say he was still alive when he went under water. Historians note that the autopsy reportedly found no poison and attributed death to gunshot wounds, including one to the forehead, so the drowning story is doubtful.

alternatives.label: British involvement?
alternatives.text: Some writers and a 2004 BBC documentary argued that a British intelligence officer, Oswald Rayner, fired the fatal shot because Rasputin was thought to favour peace with Germany. This is debated and the evidence is circumstantial.

alternatives.label: Healer or charlatan?
alternatives.text: Whether Rasputin really eased Alexei's bleeding, perhaps by calming the family or by advising against aspirin, remains debated.

entries.title: The Coso artifact: a "500,000-year-old" spark plug
entries.mainstream: On 13 February 1961, Wallace Lane, Virginia Maxey and Mike Mikesell were collecting geodes near Olancha, California, when they cut open a stone and found what looked like a metal and porcelain mechanism inside. It was promoted, including in Fortean and creationist literature, as an out-of-place artefact encased in a 500,000-year-old geode, which would imply advanced technology long before humans could make it.

alternatives.label: Identified as a 1920s spark plug
alternatives.text: In 1999 investigators Pierre Stromberg and Paul Heinrich, consulting spark plug collectors, identified the object from X-rays as a Champion spark plug of the 1920s. The stone was not a geode but an iron-rich concretion, which can form around objects within decades.

alternatives.label: Proponents
alternatives.text: A few writers still cite the object as an anomaly, noting that it has not been publicly re-examined since its owner withheld it; its current whereabouts are unknown.

entries.title: SS Ourang Medan: the ghost ship whose crew died staring at the sun
entries.dateNote: first published 1940; best-known version set in 1947–1948
entries.mainstream: The Ourang Medan is a ghost ship story first published in Italy and England in 1940 and retold with new details in 1948 and 1952. In the best-known version, set in the Strait of Malacca in 1947 or early 1948, ships pick up a Morse distress call: all officers including the captain are dead, probably the whole crew, and finally 'I die'. The crew of the American ship Silver Star board the vessel and find every crew member, and a dog, dead with their faces frozen in terror, but a fire breaks out and the ship explodes and sinks before it can be towed. In the 1940 version the ship sank south of the Solomon Islands.

alternatives.label: Did the ship exist?
alternatives.text: Searches of shipping registers and accident records have found no vessel called Ourang Medan, and the location, date and details change between versions. Many researchers consider it an urban legend; some think it may embellish a real incident.

alternatives.label: Explanations offered
alternatives.text: Writers who think something happened have suggested a cargo of toxic chemicals, carbon monoxide from a faulty boiler, or smuggled nerve agents after the Second World War. Others have proposed paranormal or alien causes. None can be tested without a ship.

alternatives.label: Sea-mystery patterns
alternatives.text: The story shares features with the Mary Celeste and Flying Dutchman: a ship found with its crew gone or dead and no clear cause.
