entries.title: Radiocarbon dating rewrites prehistory (1949)
entries.mainstream: In the late 1940s the American chemist Willard Libby and colleagues showed that the age of once-living material can be measured from its content of carbon-14, a radioactive form of carbon created in the atmosphere that decays with a half-life of about 5,700 years. In 1949 James Arnold and Libby published dates for samples of known age, such as wood from Egyptian tombs, which matched the historical dates. Libby received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960. Researchers later found that the amount of carbon-14 in the air had varied over time, so radiocarbon dates are now calibrated using tree rings, corals and other records; accelerator mass spectrometry from the late 1970s allowed tiny samples to be dated.

alternatives.label: The radiocarbon revolution
alternatives.text: Calibrated dates showed that megalithic tombs in western Europe were older than the Egyptian pyramids. Archaeologist Colin Renfrew argued in Before Civilization (1973) that this overturned the idea that European monuments copied civilisations of the Near East.

alternatives.label: Limits and controversies
alternatives.text: Contamination and reservoir effects can give misleading dates, and results have sparked disputes, such as the 1988 dating of the Shroud of Turin to the Middle Ages, which some still contest.

alternatives.label: Young-Earth objections
alternatives.text: Some young-Earth creationists argue that measurable carbon-14 in coal and diamonds shows these are young. Physicists attribute such traces to contamination and instrument background; the method works only for the last roughly 50,000 years.

entries.changed: Before radiocarbon, prehistoric dates depended on guesswork and links to Egyptian chronology; after calibration many sites proved far older than assumed.

sources.title: Age Determinations by Radiocarbon Content: Checks with Samples of Known Age

entries.title: Nostradamus and the prophecies that fit anything (1555)
entries.mainstream: Michel de Nostredame (1503–1566), a French apothecary and astrologer known as Nostradamus, published Les Prophéties in 1555, a collection of four-line verses (quatrains) grouped in 'centuries' of 100. Written in obscure, mixed French with Latin, Greek and anagrams, and almost without dates, they won him fame at the court of Catherine de' Medici. Since then readers have claimed the quatrains foretold events such as the Great Fire of London, the French Revolution, Napoleon, Hitler and the 11 September 2001 attacks. His books have rarely been out of print.

alternatives.label: Believers
alternatives.text: Supporters see some quatrains as strikingly precise predictions, for example a verse mentioning Hister, which they read as Hitler.

alternatives.label: Sceptics and historians
alternatives.text: Scholars note that Hister was a classical name for the Danube, that interpretations are almost always made after events, and that the vague language can fit many outcomes; several famous quatrains circulated online are fabricated.

alternatives.label: Sources
alternatives.text: Researchers such as Peter Lemesurier have shown that many verses reworked earlier writings and historical events, using them as patterns for the future.

entries.title: Ball lightning: glowing spheres science still cannot fully explain
entries.mainstream: Ball lightning is a rarely observed phenomenon in which a glowing sphere, usually from a few centimetres to about a metre across, appears during thunderstorms, floats or drifts for seconds, and then fades or explodes. Accounts go back centuries; one of the earliest detailed reports is the Great Thunderstorm at Widecombe-in-the-Moor, England, in 1638, when a ball of fire reportedly entered a church during a service. In July 2012 Chinese scientists studying ordinary lightning on the Tibetan Plateau happened to record a ball lightning event with cameras and spectrometers, and published its spectrum in 2014, which showed elements from the soil such as silicon, iron and calcium.

alternatives.label: Vaporised soil
alternatives.text: One leading hypothesis, proposed by John Abrahamson and James Dinniss in 2000, is that lightning striking the ground vaporises silicon and other elements, which then slowly burn in air as a glowing ball; the 2012 observation is consistent with this.

alternatives.label: Other hypotheses
alternatives.text: Other proposals include microwave radiation trapped in a plasma bubble and electrical discharges. Some physicists have suggested that some reports may be hallucinations caused by the magnetic fields of nearby lightning acting on the brain.

alternatives.label: UFO confusion
alternatives.text: Ball lightning and similar luminous phenomena are sometimes suggested as explanations for UFO and ghost light reports, such as the Hessdalen lights; whether they explain specific cases is debated.

sources.title: Observation of the Optical and Spectral Characteristics of Ball Lightning

entries.title: Gef, the talking mongoose of the Isle of Man (1931)
entries.mainstream: From about 1931 the Irving family, living in a remote farmhouse at Cashen's Gap near Dalby on the Isle of Man, claimed that a creature living in the walls, which called itself Gef and said it was a mongoose born in New Delhi, India, in 1852, spoke to them, sang, swore, told jokes and brought back gossip from the island. The case attracted wide coverage in the British press and visits from psychical researchers, including Harry Price, Hereward Carrington and Nandor Fodor. Price and the journalist R. S. Lambert published The Haunting of Cashen's Gap in 1936. Few outsiders ever claimed to hear or see Gef, and photographs show only a blurry animal.

alternatives.label: Ventriloquism and a lonely teenager
alternatives.text: Some investigators at the time and later critics concluded the family, and especially the Irvings' teenage daughter Voirrey, produced the voice by ventriloquism and other tricks.

alternatives.label: An imaginary companion?
alternatives.text: Media scholar Jeffrey Sconce suggests Gef was most likely an imaginary companion created by the clever teenage daughter; sceptic Joe Nickell says its effects were hyped by family members, reporters and credulous investigators.

alternatives.label: Belief
alternatives.text: Fodor and some later writers took the case seriously as a poltergeist or unexplained phenomenon; it remains a favourite of the paranormal literature.

entries.title: The Enfield poltergeist (1977–1979)
entries.mainstream: Between 1977 and 1979, the Hodgson family in a council house at 284 Green Street, Enfield, north London, reported furniture moving, knocking sounds and objects thrown about, centred on sisters Janet (11) and Margaret (13). Janet appeared to speak in a gruff male voice claiming to be a former occupant who had died in the house. Investigators from the Society for Psychical Research, notably Maurice Grosse and writer Guy Lyon Playfair, spent months there and believed the events were genuine; press photographers and the BBC recorded some incidents.

alternatives.label: Faking
alternatives.text: Other SPR investigators, such as Anita Gregory and John Beloff, were unconvinced and found evidence the girls faked some incidents. A video camera caught Janet bending spoons, and Grosse himself saw her banging a broom handle on the ceiling. The sisters admitted some pranks to journalists, while Grosse and Playfair held that other incidents were genuine.

alternatives.label: Sceptics
alternatives.text: Sceptics including stage magician Milbourne Christopher and Joe Nickell argued the investigators were credulous and that the phenomena matched a children's hoax; critics say a famous photograph of Janet apparently levitating shows her bouncing off the bed.

alternatives.label: Cultural impact
alternatives.text: The case inspired documentaries and the film The Conjuring 2 (2016), which centres on American paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren; according to sceptic Brian Dunning their real visit was short.

entries.title: The Aurora, Texas airship crash (1897): an alien buried in a Texas cemetery?
entries.mainstream: On 19 April 1897, during a wave of mystery airship sightings across the United States, the Dallas Morning News printed a report by local correspondent S. E. Haydon that an airship had crashed into Judge J. S. Proctor's windmill in Aurora, Texas, on 17 April. The article said the pilot was 'not an inhabitant of this world', perhaps a Martian, and had been given a Christian burial in the town cemetery. The story was largely forgotten until it was revived in the 1960s and 1970s.

alternatives.label: A newspaper hoax?
alternatives.text: The hoax theory rests largely on Aurora resident Etta Pegues, who told Time magazine around 1979–1980 that Haydon wrote the story as a joke to bring interest to the town, which was dying after the railroad bypassed it. She also said Judge Proctor never had a windmill. Many historians regard the story as a tall tale of the 1897 airship craze.

alternatives.label: Investigations
alternatives.text: In 1973 a MUFON team led by Bill Case reported new witnesses and a grave marker that seemed to show a flying object; the cemetery association refused permission to exhume, and the marker later disappeared. MUFON called the evidence inconclusive without ruling out a hoax. Later investigators reported finding the remains of a windmill base near the well and, with ground-penetrating radar, an unmarked grave among 1890s burials; none of this confirms a crash.

alternatives.label: Part of a pattern
alternatives.text: The story is one of many 1896–1897 airship reports, which included both sightings of unexplained lights and many invented newspaper stories.
